animals.name: Lion
animals.summary: Lions are large social cats native to sub-Saharan Africa, with a small population in India's Gir Forest. They live in groups called prides, can weigh up to 250 kg (550 lb), and often hunt cooperatively. Wild lions typically live 10 to 14 years.

sections.heading: Behavior and social structure
sections.body: Lions are the most social of all big cats, living in prides of related females, their cubs, and a small coalition of males. Females do most of the hunting and stay with the pride for life, while males defend the territory and the pride's borders. Lions can rest for up to 20 hours a day, conserving energy for short, explosive hunts at dawn and dusk.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: As apex predators, lions hunt large herbivores such as zebra, wildebeest, buffalo, and antelope. They may hunt together to surround and ambush prey, although individuals also hunt alone. A single lion can eat up to 40 kg (88 lb) of meat in one sitting.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Most wild lions live in sub-Saharan Africa across savannas, grasslands, and open woodlands. Asiatic lions live in and around Gir and across parts of the wider Saurashtra landscape in Gujarat, India. Lions avoid dense rainforest and true desert.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Lions face habitat loss, conflict with livestock farmers, and declining prey. The species is assessed as Vulnerable globally; local populations face different pressures, so a global category should not be treated as a regional assessment. Protected reserves and community conservation programs are central to their survival.

sections.heading: Communication and roaring
sections.body: Lions have one of the most far-reaching calls of any land animal. A full roar can be heard up to 8 km (5 miles) away and is used to advertise territory and locate pride members. They also communicate through scent-marking, head-rubbing, and a range of grunts and growls that reinforce the social bonds of the pride.

sections.heading: Reproduction and cubs
sections.body: Lionesses in a pride often give birth around the same time and raise cubs communally, even nursing one another's young. Cubs arrive after a gestation of about 110 days, weigh roughly 1.5 kg at birth, and are hidden away for the first weeks before joining the pride. When new males take over a pride, they may kill existing cubs to bring the females back into breeding condition.

sections.heading: How to understand a lion pride
sections.body: A pride is a social group, not a promise that every hunt involves the whole family. Related females form its core; males may associate in coalitions. Lions also hunt alone, and males can catch their own prey. When reading about a lion sighting, distinguish the pride’s territory from the location of one animal. Where prey, cover and people overlap can matter as much as the number of lions present.

faqs.question: How much does a lion weigh?
faqs.answer: Adult males typically weigh 150 to 250 kg (330 to 550 lb) and females 120 to 180 kg (260 to 400 lb), making the lion the second-largest cat after the tiger.

faqs.question: What is a group of lions called?
faqs.answer: A group of lions is called a pride. A typical pride contains several related females, their cubs, and a coalition of one to four adult males.

faqs.question: How long do lions live?
faqs.answer: Wild lions live about 10 to 14 years. Females tend to live longer than males, who often die earlier due to injuries from territorial fights. In captivity, lions can reach 20 years or more.

faqs.question: What do lions eat?
faqs.answer: Lions are carnivores that eat large hoofed mammals such as zebra, wildebeest, antelope, and buffalo. They hunt cooperatively in prides and can consume up to 40 kg of meat in a single meal.

faqs.question: How fast can a lion run?
faqs.answer: A lion can sprint up to 80 km/h (50 mph), but only over short distances. They rely on stealth and ambush rather than sustained chases because they tire quickly.

faqs.question: Are lions endangered?
faqs.answer: Lions are classified as Vulnerable by the IUCN, meaning they face a high risk of extinction in the wild. The Asiatic population is concentrated in Gujarat, India; consult dated regional assessments rather than treating it as the entire species.

faqs.question: Why do male lions have manes?
faqs.answer: A male lion's mane signals age, health, and dominance to rivals and potential mates. Darker, fuller manes are linked to higher testosterone and tend to attract more females and intimidate competing males.

faqs.question: Do lions live in groups?
faqs.answer: Yes. Lions are the only big cats that live in social groups called prides, which typically include several related females, their cubs, and a coalition of one to four adult males.

faqs.question: Are lions the only cats that cooperate?
faqs.answer: Lions are unusual for their enduring prides, but cooperation is not exclusive to lions. Male cheetahs can form coalitions. “Social” describes several behaviours, including living together, defending space and hunting; it does not mean every individual participates in every hunt.

Where prey, cover and people overlap can matter as much as the number of lions present.

animals.name: Tiger
animals.summary: Tigers are the largest living cat species, reaching up to 300 kg (660 lb). They are solitary, primarily nocturnal hunters native to Asia, from Siberian forests to tropical mangroves. Every tiger's stripe pattern is unique, like a human fingerprint. Wild tigers live around 10 to 15 years.

sections.heading: Behavior
sections.body: Unlike lions, tigers are solitary and territorial, coming together only to mate. They are powerful swimmers and, unusually for cats, enjoy water, often cooling off in rivers and lakes. Tigers communicate through scent marks, scratch marks, and vocalizations that can carry for kilometers.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: Tigers are ambush predators that hunt deer, wild boar, and other large mammals. They stalk silently and use their immense strength to overpower prey, often dragging carcasses far heavier than themselves to cover. A tiger may eat up to 35 kg (77 lb) of meat in one night.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Tigers once roamed across much of Asia. Today they survive in scattered populations from the snowy forests of the Russian Far East to the mangroves of the Sundarbans and the tropical forests of India and Southeast Asia.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Wild tiger numbers crashed in the 20th century due to poaching and habitat loss, with as few as 3,200 remaining around 2010. Intensive conservation has since helped numbers begin to recover in some countries, but tigers remain Endangered.

sections.heading: Subspecies and size
sections.body: The tiger is the largest living cat. Surviving subspecies include the Bengal, Siberian (Amur), Sumatran, Indochinese, Malayan, and South China tiger. The Siberian tiger is the biggest, with large males exceeding 300 kg (660 lb), while island-dwelling Sumatran tigers are the smallest.

sections.heading: Hunting and territory
sections.body: Unlike lions, tigers are solitary and ambush prey alone, relying on their stripes for camouflage in tall grass and forest. Each tiger defends a large territory marked with scent and scratch marks, and a single adult may range over dozens of square kilometers in search of deer, wild boar, and other large prey.

sections.heading: Why tiger habitat needs more than trees
sections.body: A tiger landscape needs prey, space and connections between areas where animals breed. A patch of forest can appear intact while supporting too few prey animals. Roads and other barriers can isolate populations; conflict can increase where tigers encounter livestock. Conservation therefore combines habitat protection, prey recovery, action against illegal trade and work with people who share the landscape. A population estimate describes a place, method and time, not an exact real-time count.

faqs.question: Are tigers endangered?
faqs.answer: Yes. Tigers are listed as Endangered by the IUCN, with only a few thousand left in the wild, and the South China tiger may already be extinct in the wild.

faqs.question: Can tigers swim?
faqs.answer: Yes. Unlike most cats, tigers are strong swimmers that readily enter water to cool off or cross rivers, and they will even pursue prey into the water.

faqs.question: Are tigers the biggest cats in the world?
faqs.answer: Yes. Tigers are the largest of all living cat species. The Siberian (Amur) tiger is the biggest subspecies, with males weighing up to about 300 kg (660 lb).

faqs.question: What do tigers eat?
faqs.answer: Tigers are carnivores that mainly hunt large prey such as deer and wild boar. They are ambush hunters and can eat up to 35 kg of meat in a single feeding.

faqs.question: Why do tigers have stripes?
faqs.answer: A tiger's stripes provide camouflage in tall grass and dappled forest light, helping it stalk prey unseen. Each tiger's stripe pattern is unique, and the markings are also present on its skin.

faqs.question: How many tigers are left in the wild?
faqs.answer: Recent estimates put the wild tiger population at roughly 4,500 individuals. Numbers have begun to recover in some countries thanks to anti-poaching efforts and habitat protection, but tigers remain Endangered.

faqs.question: How long do tigers live?
faqs.answer: Wild tigers typically live 10 to 15 years, while tigers in captivity can live up to 20 to 25 years with veterinary care and a steady food supply.

faqs.question: Does a rise in tiger numbers mean tigers are safe?
faqs.answer: No. Recovery in one country does not remove threats across the species’ range. Read the date, geographic coverage and method behind a population estimate. Global status and local success measure different things.

animals.name: African Elephant
animals.summary: The African elephant is the largest living land animal, weighing up to 6,000 kg (13,200 lb) and standing up to 4 m (13 ft) at the shoulder. They are highly intelligent, deeply social, and use their trunks for breathing, drinking, grasping, and communication. Wild elephants can live 60 to 70 years.

sections.heading: Intelligence and social life
sections.body: Elephants live in tight matriarchal herds led by the oldest, most experienced female. They show empathy, cooperation, problem-solving, and apparent grief, returning to and touching the bones of dead relatives. Their large brains support remarkable long-term memory.

sections.heading: Diet
sections.body: Elephants are herbivores that eat grasses, leaves, bark, roots, and fruit. An adult can consume up to 150 kg (330 lb) of vegetation and drink up to 190 liters (50 gallons) of water in a single day, spending up to 16 hours feeding.

sections.heading: The trunk and tusks
sections.body: An elephant's trunk contains around 40,000 muscles and is used for breathing, smelling, drinking, grasping food, and social touch. Tusks are elongated incisor teeth used for digging, stripping bark, and defense, but they also make elephants a target for the ivory trade.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: African savanna elephants are Endangered and forest elephants are Critically Endangered, largely because of poaching for ivory and habitat fragmentation. As a keystone species, elephants shape entire ecosystems by clearing trees, spreading seeds, and digging waterholes.

sections.heading: Intelligence and memory
sections.body: Elephants have the largest brain of any land animal and show remarkable intelligence, including problem-solving, tool use, and self-recognition in mirrors. They display apparent grief, returning to and touching the bones of dead herd members, and can remember distant water sources and individual animals over many years.

sections.heading: Herd structure
sections.body: Elephant herds are matriarchal, led by the oldest and most experienced female, who guides the group to food and water. Adult males usually leave the herd as they mature and live alone or in loose bachelor groups, rejoining females mainly to breed.

sections.heading: African savanna, forest and Asian elephants
sections.body: Three living elephant species are generally recognised: African savanna, African forest and Asian elephants. This profile focuses on the African savanna elephant, Loxodonta africana. Large ears and two finger-like projections at the trunk tip help distinguish African elephants from Asian elephants, which have smaller ears and one projection. A photograph, however, is not enough to assign age, sex or health reliably. Always attach a size or conservation claim to the species being discussed.

faqs.question: How much does an elephant eat?
faqs.answer: Elephants are herbivores that can eat up to 150 kg (330 lb) of vegetation and drink up to 190 liters of water in a single day.

faqs.question: What is the difference between African and Asian elephants?
faqs.answer: African elephants are larger, with bigger ears, and both sexes usually have tusks. Asian elephants are smaller with smaller ears, and many individuals lack visible tusks.

faqs.question: What is the largest land animal?
faqs.answer: The African elephant is the largest land animal on Earth. Large males can weigh up to 6,000 kg (13,200 lb) and stand up to 4 m (13 ft) tall at the shoulder.

faqs.question: What do elephants eat?
faqs.answer: Elephants are herbivores that eat grasses, leaves, bark, roots, and fruit. An adult may eat up to 150 kg of plant matter and drink up to 190 liters of water each day.

faqs.question: How long do elephants live?
faqs.answer: Wild elephants typically live 60 to 70 years, making them one of the longest-lived land mammals. Lifespan in captivity is often shorter.

faqs.question: Why are elephants endangered?
faqs.answer: Elephants are endangered mainly because of poaching for ivory and the loss and fragmentation of their habitat. African forest elephants are now classified as Critically Endangered.

faqs.question: How many muscles are in an elephant's trunk?
faqs.answer: An elephant's trunk contains an estimated 40,000 muscles, giving it the dexterity to pick up a single blade of grass or carry hundreds of kilograms.

faqs.question: Do elephants really have good memories?
faqs.answer: Yes. Elephants have excellent long-term memory, which helps matriarchs remember distant water sources during droughts and recognize individuals after years apart.

faqs.question: Do elephants drink through their trunks?
faqs.answer: They draw water into the trunk and then deliver it to the mouth. The trunk is a nose and an extraordinarily versatile grasping structure, not a drinking straw connected directly to the stomach. It also helps elephants smell, communicate and manipulate food.

animals.name: Shortfin Mako Shark
animals.summary: The shortfin mako is the fastest shark in the world, reaching short bursts of about 74 km/h (46 mph). A warm-bodied, open-ocean predator found in temperate and tropical seas worldwide, it has a sleek, torpedo-shaped body built for speed. Shortfin makos are now listed as Endangered.

sections.heading: Built for speed
sections.body: The shortfin mako has a slender, torpedo-shaped body, a pointed snout, and a crescent-shaped tail that together make it the fastest shark in the sea. Like the great white, it is partially warm-blooded, keeping its muscles warmer than the surrounding water so it can swim in powerful, sustained bursts.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: Makos are open-ocean hunters that chase down fast prey such as tuna, mackerel, and swordfish, and will also take squid and smaller sharks. Their speed lets them ambush schooling fish from below, and they are known to leap clear of the water when hunting or when hooked.

sections.heading: Life cycle
sections.body: Shortfin makos grow slowly and mature late, and females give birth to live young after a long pregnancy. This slow reproduction means populations recover very slowly once their numbers fall — a key reason the species is now at risk.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: The shortfin mako is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. It is heavily affected by overfishing, both as a target for its meat and fins and as accidental bycatch in fisheries aimed at tuna and swordfish. International catch limits and stronger protections are now being introduced to help the species recover.

faqs.question: How fast can a shortfin mako shark swim?
faqs.answer: Shortfin makos are the fastest sharks on Earth, reaching short bursts of around 74 km/h (46 mph). Their speed helps them catch fast prey such as tuna and swordfish.

faqs.question: Are shortfin mako sharks endangered?
faqs.answer: Yes. The shortfin mako is classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List, mainly because of overfishing for its meat and fins and accidental capture in other fisheries.

faqs.question: How big do shortfin mako sharks get?
faqs.answer: Shortfin makos can grow up to about 4 m (13 ft) long and weigh over 500 kg (1,100 lb), though most are smaller.

faqs.question: Do shortfin mako sharks attack humans?
faqs.answer: Bites on people are very rare. Makos live mostly in the open ocean away from swimmers, and humans are not part of their natural diet.

faqs.question: What do shortfin mako sharks eat?
faqs.answer: They feed mainly on fast-swimming fish such as tuna, mackerel, and swordfish, along with squid and smaller sharks.

faqs.question: How long do shortfin mako sharks live?
faqs.answer: Shortfin makos can live around 30 years. They grow slowly and reproduce late, which makes their populations slow to recover.

range.nativeRange: Open temperate and tropical waters of every major ocean worldwide.

animals.name: Gray Wolf
animals.summary: The gray wolf is the largest wild member of the dog family and the ancestor of the domestic dog. Wolves live and hunt in family groups called packs, communicate through howls, and range across forests, tundra, and mountains of the Northern Hemisphere. Wild wolves live around 6 to 8 years.

sections.heading: Pack life
sections.body: Wolves live in packs that are essentially family units, usually a breeding pair and their offspring. The pack cooperates to hunt, raise pups, and defend territory. Far from the rigid 'alpha' myth, wild packs are led naturally by the breeding parents.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body: Wolves communicate through howls, body language, scent marking, and facial expressions. Howling helps reunite separated pack members, advertise territory, and reinforce social bonds, and can be heard several kilometers away.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: Gray wolves are carnivores that hunt large hoofed animals such as deer, elk, moose, and bison, along with smaller prey. By hunting in coordinated groups, they can take down animals far larger than a single wolf.

sections.heading: Ecological role
sections.body: Wolves are a keystone species. Their return to ecosystems such as Yellowstone National Park changed the behavior of prey animals and helped restore vegetation and river systems in a chain reaction known as a trophic cascade.

sections.heading: Pack structure
sections.body: Gray wolves live in family packs usually led by a breeding pair and their offspring of different ages. The pack cooperates to hunt large prey such as deer, elk, and moose, and defends a territory that can span hundreds of square kilometers.

faqs.question: Are wolves dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Wild wolves generally avoid people, and attacks on humans are very rare. A wolf is far more likely to flee than to approach.

faqs.question: How far can a wolf travel?
faqs.answer: Wolves are tireless travelers that can cover 50 km or more in a day, trotting for hours at around 8 km/h while hunting or patrolling their territory.

faqs.question: Are wolves the ancestors of dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes. Domestic dogs descend from gray wolves, which were domesticated by humans tens of thousands of years ago. Dogs and wolves remain closely related and can interbreed.

faqs.question: What do wolves eat?
faqs.answer: Gray wolves are carnivores that primarily hunt large hoofed mammals such as deer, elk, and moose. Hunting in packs lets them take down prey much larger than themselves.

faqs.question: Why do wolves howl?
faqs.answer: Wolves howl to locate pack members, mark and defend territory, and strengthen social bonds. A howl can travel several kilometers across open terrain.

faqs.question: How long do wolves live?
faqs.answer: Wild gray wolves usually live 6 to 8 years, though some reach their teens. Wolves in captivity can live up to 16 years.

faqs.question: Are gray wolves dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Wolves generally avoid people, and verified attacks on humans are very rare. They are far more likely to flee from human contact than to approach it.

faqs.question: Is the alpha wolf theory true?
faqs.answer: The rigid 'alpha' hierarchy is largely a myth based on captive wolves. Wild packs are family groups led naturally by the breeding parents, not by dominance fights.

range.nativeRange: Forests, tundra, and mountains across the Northern Hemisphere.

animals.name: Bottlenose Dolphin
animals.summary: Bottlenose dolphins are highly intelligent marine mammals found in warm and temperate seas worldwide. They live in social groups called pods, use echolocation to navigate and hunt, and communicate with clicks and whistles, including signature whistles that work like names. They typically live 40 to 60 years.

sections.heading: Intelligence
sections.body: Bottlenose dolphins are among the most intelligent animals on Earth. They use tools, recognize themselves in mirrors, solve complex problems, and teach skills to their young, such as covering their snouts with sponges to protect them while foraging.

sections.heading: Echolocation and communication
sections.body: Dolphins navigate and hunt using echolocation, emitting clicks and interpreting the echoes to build a sound picture of their surroundings. Each dolphin develops a unique signature whistle that functions much like a name within its pod.

sections.heading: Social life
sections.body: Dolphins live in fluid social groups called pods, cooperating to hunt, raise calves, and defend against predators such as sharks. They form strong, sometimes lifelong bonds and have been observed helping injured companions reach the surface to breathe.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Bottlenose dolphins are listed as Least Concern overall, but local populations face threats from accidental capture in fishing gear, pollution, habitat loss, and disturbance. As air-breathing marine mammals, they are sensitive indicators of ocean health.

faqs.question: How intelligent are dolphins?
faqs.answer: Bottlenose dolphins are among the most intelligent animals known. They use tools, pass the mirror self-recognition test, solve problems, and teach learned behaviors to their offspring.

faqs.question: How do dolphins use echolocation?
faqs.answer: Dolphins produce rapid clicks and listen to the returning echoes to locate objects, prey, and obstacles. This biological sonar lets them hunt and navigate even in murky water.

faqs.question: Do dolphins have names?
faqs.answer: In a sense, yes. Each bottlenose dolphin develops a unique signature whistle that other dolphins use to identify and call it, functioning much like a name.

faqs.question: What do bottlenose dolphins eat?
faqs.answer: Bottlenose dolphins are carnivores that eat fish, squid, and crustaceans. They often hunt cooperatively, herding fish into tight groups to feed.

faqs.question: How long do bottlenose dolphins live?
faqs.answer: Bottlenose dolphins typically live 40 to 60 years. Females generally live longer than males, and some individuals have been documented living into their sixties.

faqs.question: Are dolphins fish or mammals?
faqs.answer: Dolphins are mammals, not fish. They breathe air through a blowhole, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young, and nurse their calves with milk.

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Warm and temperate coastal and open seas

animals.name: Giant Panda
animals.summary: The giant panda is a bear native to the mountain forests of central China that eats almost nothing but bamboo. Despite being a carnivore by classification, it spends up to 14 hours a day eating bamboo. Thanks to major conservation efforts, it was downgraded from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2016. Wild pandas live around 20 years.

sections.heading: A bear that eats bamboo
sections.body: Although classified as a carnivore, the giant panda's diet is about 99% bamboo. Because bamboo is low in nutrients, pandas must eat enormous quantities, between 12 and 38 kg per day, and spend much of their waking life feeding.

sections.heading: The pseudo-thumb
sections.body: Pandas have an enlarged wrist bone that works like an opposable thumb, letting them grip bamboo stalks with precision. This adaptation makes them remarkably efficient at stripping and eating bamboo.

sections.heading: Behavior
sections.body: Giant pandas are mostly solitary and use scent marking to communicate and avoid one another outside the breeding season. Cubs are born tiny and pink, about the size of a stick of butter, and develop slowly over their first year.

sections.heading: Conservation success
sections.body: The giant panda is a global symbol of wildlife conservation. Decades of habitat protection and reserve creation in China helped its numbers recover enough for the IUCN to reclassify it from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2016, though habitat fragmentation remains a threat.

sections.heading: Diet and digestion
sections.body: Although it belongs to the order Carnivora, the giant panda eats almost entirely bamboo, consuming 12 to 38 kg a day. Its digestive system is poorly suited to plants, so it must feed for many hours daily, and it grips stalks using a pseudo-thumb, an enlarged wrist bone that works like an extra digit.

sections.heading: A bear with a specialised feeding strategy
sections.body: Giant pandas belong to the bear family, although their diet is dominated by bamboo. A modified wrist bone helps them grip stems; strong jaws and teeth process tough plant material. Their ancestry and digestive anatomy do not change simply because they eat mostly plants. Bamboo forests also need connections between them, so animals can move rather than remain confined in isolated patches.

faqs.question: What do giant pandas eat?
faqs.answer: Giant pandas eat almost exclusively bamboo, though they occasionally consume small animals or eggs. An adult may spend 10 to 16 hours a day feeding.

faqs.question: How many giant pandas are left?
faqs.answer: There are roughly 1,800 giant pandas in the wild, plus several hundred in breeding centers and zoos, mostly in the mountains of central China.

faqs.question: Are giant pandas still endangered?
faqs.answer: No. Thanks to conservation efforts, the giant panda was reclassified from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2016. It still faces risks from habitat fragmentation, so protection continues.

faqs.question: Why do pandas eat so much bamboo?
faqs.answer: Bamboo is low in nutrients and difficult to digest, so pandas must eat huge amounts to meet their energy needs, often feeding for up to 14 hours a day.

faqs.question: Do pandas have thumbs?
faqs.answer: Pandas have a 'pseudo-thumb,' an enlarged wrist bone that acts like an opposable thumb. It lets them grip and strip bamboo stalks efficiently.

faqs.question: How long do giant pandas live?
faqs.answer: Wild giant pandas live around 20 years, while pandas in captivity can live to 30 years or more with consistent food and veterinary care.

faqs.question: Where do giant pandas live?
faqs.answer: Giant pandas live only in the temperate mountain forests of central China, where dense bamboo provides their primary food source.

faqs.question: Are giant pandas and red pandas closely related?
faqs.answer: They share a common name and both eat bamboo, but giant pandas are bears and red pandas belong to a separate family. Similar foods can favour similar adaptations in different lineages. Compare their size, body form and climbing behaviour rather than assuming “panda” is a single animal group.

sourceUpdate.heading: A bear with a specialised feeding strategy
sourceUpdate.body: Giant pandas belong to the bear family, although their diet is dominated by bamboo. A modified wrist bone helps them grip stems; strong jaws and teeth process tough plant material. Their ancestry and digestive anatomy do not change simply because they eat mostly plants. Bamboo forests also need connections between them, so animals can move rather than remain confined in isolated patches.

animals.name: Emperor Penguin
animals.summary: The emperor penguin is the tallest and heaviest penguin species, standing up to 1.2 m (4 ft). It is the only animal that breeds during the brutal Antarctic winter, where males incubate a single egg on their feet through months of darkness and temperatures below -40°C. Emperor penguins live around 20 years.

sections.heading: Breeding in the cold
sections.body: Emperor penguins are the only species that breeds during the Antarctic winter. After the female lays a single egg, she returns to the sea to feed while the male balances the egg on his feet under a flap of skin for about two months, fasting the entire time.

sections.heading: Surviving the freeze
sections.body: To endure temperatures below -40°C and fierce winds, emperor penguins huddle together in dense groups, constantly rotating so each bird gets time in the warm center. This cooperative behavior is essential for survival and warmth.

sections.heading: Diving and feeding
sections.body: Emperor penguins are exceptional divers, reaching depths of up to 500 m and staying underwater for more than 20 minutes while hunting fish, krill, and squid. Their solid bones and streamlined bodies make them powerful swimmers.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Emperor penguins depend on stable sea ice to breed. Because climate change is reducing and destabilizing Antarctic ice, the species is increasingly threatened, and scientists warn that continued ice loss could sharply reduce their populations this century.

faqs.question: How do emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter?
faqs.answer: Emperor penguins survive by huddling together in large groups and rotating positions so every bird shares time in the warm center. Their dense feathers and fat reserves also insulate them against extreme cold.

faqs.question: Do male or female penguins incubate the egg?
faqs.answer: In emperor penguins, the male incubates the single egg. He balances it on his feet under a flap of skin for about two months while fasting, as the female feeds at sea.

faqs.question: What do emperor penguins eat?
faqs.answer: Emperor penguins are carnivores that eat fish, krill, and squid. They dive deep into the ocean to hunt, sometimes reaching depths of 500 m.

faqs.question: How deep can emperor penguins dive?
faqs.answer: Emperor penguins can dive up to 500 m (1,640 ft) deep and stay underwater for more than 20 minutes, making them the deepest-diving birds.

faqs.question: Are emperor penguins endangered?
faqs.answer: Emperor penguins are listed as Near Threatened. Their reliance on stable sea ice makes them especially vulnerable to climate change and shrinking Antarctic ice.

faqs.question: How tall are emperor penguins?
faqs.answer: Emperor penguins are the largest penguin species, standing up to about 1.2 m (4 ft) tall and weighing up to 45 kg (99 lb).

animals.name: Cheetah
animals.summary: The cheetah is the fastest land animal, capable of reaching 112 km/h (70 mph) in short bursts. Built for speed with a slender body, long legs, and a flexible spine, it relies on quick daytime chases rather than ambush. Cheetahs are found mainly in Africa and live around 10 to 12 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Built for speed
sections.body: Everything about the cheetah is designed for acceleration. A lightweight frame, long legs, enlarged heart and lungs, and a flexible spine let it reach 112 km/h and go from 0 to 100 km/h in just a few seconds. Its semi-retractable claws act like running spikes for grip.

sections.heading: Hunting strategy
sections.body: Unlike most big cats, cheetahs hunt during the day to avoid competition from lions and hyenas. They rely on a short, explosive chase, and because sprinting overheats their bodies, they can only run for around 20 to 30 seconds before needing to rest.

sections.heading: Behavior
sections.body: Cheetahs are more lightly built and less aggressive than other big cats. Females are usually solitary, raising cubs alone, while males sometimes form small coalitions, often brothers, to hold territory together.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Cheetahs are Vulnerable, with fewer than an estimated 7,000 left in the wild. They face habitat loss, conflict with farmers, low genetic diversity, and high cub mortality, making them one of Africa's most threatened big cats.

sections.heading: Hunting and challenges
sections.body: Cheetahs hunt by day, using sharp eyesight to spot prey and acceleration to run it down, then must rest to recover from the effort. Because they are relatively light, they often lose kills to lions and hyenas, and high cub mortality makes the species especially vulnerable.

sections.heading: Speed is only one part of a cheetah hunt
sections.body: A cheetah’s flexible spine, long limbs and tail support rapid acceleration and turning. A sprint is brief, so approaching prey and choosing the moment to run matter. Speed records should not be treated as the pace an animal maintains all day. Leopards and jaguars rely on different combinations of stealth and strength; comparing their markings, build and habitat is more useful for identification than a hypothetical fight.

faqs.question: How fast is a cheetah?
faqs.answer: A cheetah can reach about 110 km/h (68 mph) in short bursts, accelerating from a standstill to 100 km/h in around three seconds.

faqs.question: Are cheetahs endangered?
faqs.answer: Yes. Cheetahs are listed as Vulnerable, with fewer than about 7,000 left in the wild due to habitat loss, conflict with farmers, and loss of prey.

faqs.question: How fast can a cheetah run?
faqs.answer: Cheetahs are the fastest land animals, reaching speeds of up to 112 km/h (70 mph) in short bursts and accelerating from 0 to 100 km/h in just a few seconds.

faqs.question: Why can't cheetahs run for long?
faqs.answer: Sprinting at top speed rapidly overheats a cheetah's body, so it can only chase prey for about 20 to 30 seconds before it must stop and recover.

faqs.question: What do cheetahs eat?
faqs.answer: Cheetahs are carnivores that hunt small to medium antelope such as gazelles, as well as hares and young wildebeest. They hunt mostly during the day.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a cheetah and a leopard?
faqs.answer: Cheetahs have solid round spots and distinctive black 'tear marks' running from the eyes to the mouth, while leopards have rosette-shaped spots. Cheetahs are also slimmer and faster, while leopards are stockier and climb trees.

faqs.question: How long do cheetahs live?
faqs.answer: Wild cheetahs typically live 10 to 12 years. Cub mortality is high, but cheetahs in captivity can live to around 17 years.

faqs.question: How can I tell a cheetah from a leopard?
faqs.answer: Cheetahs have a slender build, mainly solid black spots and dark tear markings running down the face. Leopards are more robust and have rosette-shaped markings. Use several features together: lighting, age and camera angle can make one visual clue misleading.

animals.name: Polar Bear
animals.summary: The polar bear is the largest land carnivore, perfectly adapted to life on Arctic sea ice. It hunts seals from the ice, has black skin under white-looking translucent fur, and is classified as a marine mammal because it depends on the ocean. Polar bears live around 25 years and are threatened by melting sea ice.

sections.heading: Built for the Arctic
sections.body: Polar bears are superbly adapted to extreme cold, with a thick layer of fat, dense insulating fur, and large paws that spread their weight on thin ice and act as paddles when swimming. Their fur appears white but is actually translucent, and their skin underneath is black.

sections.heading: Hunting on the ice
sections.body: Polar bears mainly hunt ringed and bearded seals, waiting patiently beside breathing holes in the sea ice. The fat-rich seal blubber provides the energy they need to survive, which is why access to sea ice is essential to their survival.

sections.heading: Marine mammals
sections.body: Although they live and travel on land and ice, polar bears are classified as marine mammals because they depend on the ocean for food. They are powerful long-distance swimmers, capable of crossing many kilometers of open water.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Polar bears are Vulnerable and have become a global symbol of climate change. As the Arctic warms and sea ice forms later and melts earlier, bears have less time to hunt seals, leading to poorer body condition and lower cub survival.

sections.heading: Sea ice is a hunting platform
sections.body: Polar bears use Arctic sea ice to reach seals, their principal high-energy prey. Losing access to that platform can lengthen time spent ashore or swimming and change the energy balance of an animal already adapted to extreme conditions. A bear on land is not, by itself, proof of starvation; season, location and body condition provide essential context. One photograph cannot establish a population trend.

faqs.question: Are polar bears endangered?
faqs.answer: Polar bears are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, mainly because climate change is reducing the sea ice they need in order to hunt.

faqs.question: How big are polar bears?
faqs.answer: Polar bears are the largest land carnivore. Adult males typically weigh 350 to 700 kg (770 to 1,540 lb) and can stand over 3 m tall on their hind legs.

faqs.question: What do polar bears eat?
faqs.answer: Polar bears are carnivores that primarily eat seals, especially ringed and bearded seals. The fat-rich blubber provides the energy they need to survive in the Arctic.

faqs.question: Is polar bear skin really black?
faqs.answer: Yes. Beneath their translucent fur, polar bears have black skin, which helps absorb and retain heat from sunlight in the cold Arctic environment.

faqs.question: Are polar bears marine mammals?
faqs.answer: Polar bears are classified as marine mammals because they rely on the ocean and sea ice for hunting. They are also strong swimmers capable of covering long distances in open water.

faqs.question: Why are polar bears endangered?
faqs.answer: Polar bears are threatened mainly by climate change. Melting sea ice shortens their hunting season for seals, reducing their body condition and the survival of their cubs.

faqs.question: How long do polar bears live?
faqs.answer: Polar bears typically live around 25 years in the wild, though many do not survive their first few years. In captivity they can live into their thirties.

faqs.question: Do all polar bears hibernate?
faqs.answer: No. Pregnant females use maternity dens and live on stored energy while giving birth and nursing. Other polar bears generally remain active, although they may shelter during severe conditions. This is different from describing the entire species as sleeping through winter.

animals.name: Red Fox
animals.summary: The red fox is the largest and most widespread true fox, found across the Northern Hemisphere and adaptable to forests, mountains, farmland, and cities. It is an opportunistic omnivore famous for its intelligence and its distinctive pounce when hunting. Wild red foxes typically live 3 to 5 years.

sections.heading: Adaptability
sections.body: The red fox is one of the most adaptable mammals on Earth, thriving everywhere from Arctic tundra to busy cities. Its success comes from a flexible diet, sharp senses, and a willingness to live close to people, making it a common sight even in urban areas.

sections.heading: Diet and the pounce
sections.body: Red foxes are omnivores that eat rodents, rabbits, birds, insects, fruit, and scraps. They use a famous high-arcing pounce to catch prey hidden under grass or snow, and may even use the Earth's magnetic field to help judge the distance.

sections.heading: Behavior
sections.body: Foxes are mostly solitary or live in small family groups. They communicate with a wide range of vocalizations, scent marks, and body language, and they cache surplus food by burying it for later, remembering the locations with impressive accuracy.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: The red fox is listed as Least Concern and is not threatened. Its range is actually expanding in many regions, and it has been introduced to areas such as Australia, where it can become a damaging invasive predator.

faqs.question: What do red foxes eat?
faqs.answer: Red foxes are omnivores that eat rodents, rabbits, birds, insects, fruit, and human food scraps. Their flexible diet helps them survive in many different environments.

faqs.question: Where do red foxes live?
faqs.answer: Red foxes are the most widespread wild carnivore, living across the Northern Hemisphere in forests, mountains, grasslands, farmland, and even cities.

faqs.question: How long do red foxes live?
faqs.answer: Wild red foxes usually live just 3 to 5 years due to disease, predators, and traffic. In captivity, they can live up to 14 years.

faqs.question: Are red foxes dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Red foxes are generally shy and pose little threat to people. They rarely approach humans and usually flee when encountered, though they may take small pets or poultry.

faqs.question: Why do foxes pounce when hunting?
faqs.answer: Foxes use a high, arcing pounce to drop down on prey hidden beneath grass or snow. This 'mousing' technique lets them strike accurately even when they cannot see the animal.

faqs.question: Are red foxes related to dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes. Red foxes belong to the dog family, Canidae, which also includes wolves, coyotes, and domestic dogs, though foxes are not closely related enough to interbreed with them.

range.nativeRange: The most widespread wild carnivore on Earth, across the entire Northern Hemisphere.

animals.name: Blue Whale
animals.summary: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever existed, reaching up to 30 m (98 ft) long and 180 tonnes. It feeds almost entirely on tiny krill, eating up to 4 tonnes a day, and its heart alone can weigh as much as a small car. Blue whales can live 80 to 90 years.

sections.heading: The largest animal ever
sections.body: Blue whales are bigger than any dinosaur known to science. Their tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant, and their heart can be the size of a small car. A newborn calf is already around 7 m long and gains roughly 90 kg every day in its first months.

sections.heading: Feeding on the tiny
sections.body: Despite their size, blue whales eat some of the smallest animals in the ocean: shrimp-like krill. They feed by gulping huge volumes of water and filtering out krill through baleen plates, consuming up to 4 tonnes of krill on a single feeding day.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body: Blue whales produce some of the loudest and lowest-frequency sounds of any animal. These powerful calls can travel hundreds of kilometers through the ocean, helping whales communicate across vast distances.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Blue whales were hunted to the brink of extinction during 20th-century commercial whaling. Although they have been protected since the 1960s, recovery is slow, and they remain Endangered, facing threats from ship strikes, entanglement, and ocean change.

sections.heading: Feeding on krill
sections.body: Blue whales are filter feeders that strain tiny shrimp-like krill through baleen plates. During the feeding season an adult can eat up to 4 tonnes of krill a day, lunging through dense swarms and gulping enormous volumes of water before pushing it back out through the baleen.

sections.heading: A giant dependent on very small prey
sections.body: Blue whales use baleen to filter food rather than teeth to seize large prey. Their diet is dominated by krill. Seasonal feeding areas and travel between habitats expose them to pressures including vessel strikes and entanglement in fishing gear. Being enormous does not make an animal immune to human activity. Whale-watching should follow local approach rules, and a vessel should never chase or surround an animal for a closer view.

faqs.question: How big is a blue whale?
faqs.answer: Blue whales can reach about 30 m (98 ft) long and weigh up to 180 tonnes, making them the largest animals ever to have existed.

faqs.question: Are blue whales endangered?
faqs.answer: Yes. After being hunted nearly to extinction in the 20th century, blue whales are listed as Endangered, though some populations are slowly recovering under international protection.

faqs.question: What is the largest animal in the world?
faqs.answer: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, reaching up to 30 m (98 ft) in length and weighing as much as 180 tonnes, larger than any dinosaur.

faqs.question: What do blue whales eat?
faqs.answer: Blue whales eat almost exclusively krill, tiny shrimp-like crustaceans. They can consume up to 4 tonnes of krill in a single day during feeding season.

faqs.question: How big is a blue whale's heart?
faqs.answer: A blue whale's heart can weigh around 180 kg, roughly the size of a small car, making it the largest heart of any animal.

faqs.question: How long do blue whales live?
faqs.answer: Blue whales are believed to live 80 to 90 years on average, and some individuals may live even longer.

faqs.question: How loud are blue whales?
faqs.answer: Blue whales are among the loudest animals on Earth. Their low-frequency calls can exceed 180 decibels and travel hundreds of kilometers across the ocean.

faqs.question: Is the blue whale the largest fish?
faqs.answer: No. Blue whales are mammals: they breathe air and nurse their calves. Whale sharks are fish. For a meaningful size comparison, distinguish length from mass and typical adults from exceptional records. The longest individual is not automatically the heaviest.

Whale-watching should follow local approach rules, and a vessel should never chase or surround an animal for a closer view.

sourceUpdate.answer: No. Blue whales are mammals: they breathe air and nurse their calves. Whale sharks are fish. For a meaningful size comparison, distinguish length from mass and typical adults from exceptional records. The longest individual is not automatically the heaviest.

animals.name: Bald Eagle
animals.summary: The bald eagle is a large bird of prey native to North America, recognizable by its white head and tail against a dark brown body. It is not actually bald; "bald" comes from an old word meaning white-headed. Bald eagles mainly eat fish, build the largest tree nests of any North American bird, and can live 20 to 30 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Behavior and nesting
sections.body: Bald eagles mate for life and return to the same nest each year, adding material until it becomes the largest tree nest of any North American bird, sometimes weighing over a tonne. They are powerful fliers that can soar for hours on rising air, and they are known to steal fish from ospreys and other birds rather than always catching their own.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: Fish make up most of a bald eagle's diet. It hunts by swooping low over water and snatching prey from the surface with its talons. Eagles also eat waterbirds, small mammals, and carrion, and will gather in large numbers at salmon runs and other seasonal food sources.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Bald eagles live only in North America, from Alaska and Canada down to northern Mexico, almost always near open water with abundant fish and tall trees for nesting. Populations are densest along coasts, large rivers, and lakes.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Bald eagles were once endangered in the contiguous United States, devastated by the pesticide DDT, which thinned their eggshells. After DDT was banned and strong protections were put in place, the species recovered dramatically and was removed from the U.S. endangered species list in 2007. It is now listed as Least Concern.

faqs.question: Are bald eagles actually bald?
faqs.answer: No. Bald eagles have a full covering of white feathers on their heads. The name comes from an older meaning of "bald" that meant white-headed or marked with white, not hairless.

faqs.question: What do bald eagles eat?
faqs.answer: Bald eagles eat mainly fish, which they snatch from the water with their talons. They also take waterbirds, small mammals, and carrion, and will steal prey from other birds.

faqs.question: How fast can a bald eagle fly?
faqs.answer: Bald eagles cruise at around 50 km/h (30 mph) but can reach about 120 km/h (75 mph) when diving toward prey.

faqs.question: How long do bald eagles live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, bald eagles typically live 20 to 30 years. In captivity, protected from hazards, they can live even longer.

faqs.question: Are bald eagles endangered?
faqs.answer: Not anymore. After near collapse from DDT poisoning, bald eagle populations recovered and the species is now listed as Least Concern, though it remains protected by law in the United States.

faqs.question: How big is a bald eagle's nest?
faqs.answer: Bald eagles build the largest tree nests of any North American bird. Reused and expanded over years, a nest can reach 2.5 m (8 ft) across and weigh more than a tonne.

animals.name: Saltwater Crocodile
animals.summary: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile, with big males reaching up to 6 m (20 ft) and over 1,000 kg (2,200 lb). Found across the Indo-Pacific from India to northern Australia, it has the strongest bite force ever measured in a living animal and is an ambush predator that can survive in both fresh and salt water. Saltwater crocodiles can live 70 years or more.

sections.heading: Behavior and hunting
sections.body: Saltwater crocodiles are patient ambush predators. They lie almost motionless at the water's edge, then explode forward to seize prey and drag it under in a "death roll." They are highly territorial, and large males defend stretches of river and coast aggressively.

sections.heading: Diet and bite
sections.body: Salties eat almost anything they can overpower, from fish, crabs, and turtles to large mammals that come to drink. Their bite force is the strongest ever measured in a living animal, but the muscles that open the jaws are weak, which is why a crocodile's mouth can be held shut by hand.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The saltwater crocodile ranges across the Indo-Pacific, from eastern India and Southeast Asia to northern Australia and the western Pacific. Unusually for a reptile, it tolerates salt water well and can travel long distances along coastlines between river systems.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Hunted heavily for their skins in the 20th century, saltwater crocodiles were pushed to low numbers in many areas. Protection and managed populations, especially in Australia, allowed a strong recovery, and the species is now listed as Least Concern overall, though some regional populations remain at risk.

faqs.question: How big do saltwater crocodiles get?
faqs.answer: Saltwater crocodiles are the largest living reptiles. Large males commonly reach 4.5 to 5 m, and exceptional individuals exceed 6 m (20 ft) and weigh over 1,000 kg.

faqs.question: How strong is a saltwater crocodile's bite?
faqs.answer: The saltwater crocodile has the strongest bite force ever measured in a living animal, around 3,700 psi. However, the muscles that open its jaws are weak enough to be held shut by hand.

faqs.question: Can saltwater crocodiles live in the ocean?
faqs.answer: Yes. Unlike most crocodilians, saltwater crocodiles tolerate salt water and can swim long distances along coastlines, which is how they spread across so many islands.

faqs.question: What do saltwater crocodiles eat?
faqs.answer: They are opportunistic carnivores that eat fish, crustaceans, turtles, birds, and mammals. Large adults can take prey as big as water buffalo by ambushing animals at the water's edge.

faqs.question: How fast can a saltwater crocodile move?
faqs.answer: In water they can burst to around 29 km/h (18 mph) over short distances. On land they are much slower and rely on surprise rather than chasing prey.

faqs.question: How long do saltwater crocodiles live?
faqs.answer: Saltwater crocodiles are long-lived, commonly reaching 70 years and sometimes more in the wild and in captivity.

range.nativeRange: Coasts, rivers, and estuaries from eastern India through Southeast Asia to northern Australia.

animals.name: King Cobra
animals.summary: The king cobra is the longest venomous snake in the world, reaching up to 5.5 m (18 ft). Native to forests across South and Southeast Asia, it feeds almost entirely on other snakes. Its venom is potent enough to kill an elephant in large doses, yet it is shy and avoids people. King cobras are also the only snakes that build a nest for their eggs. They live around 20 years.

sections.heading: Behavior
sections.body: The king cobra is intelligent and alert for a snake. When threatened it can raise up to a third of its body off the ground, spread its narrow hood, and emit a low growl-like hiss. Despite its fearsome reputation, it is generally shy and prefers to flee rather than confront people.

sections.heading: Diet and venom
sections.body: Its scientific name, Ophiophagus, means "snake-eater," and the king cobra feeds mainly on other snakes, including venomous species. Its venom is a powerful neurotoxin delivered in large quantities; a single bite can deliver enough to be fatal to a human within hours if untreated.

sections.heading: Nesting
sections.body: King cobras are the only snakes known to build a nest for their eggs. The female gathers leaves into a mound, lays 20 to 40 eggs inside, and guards the nest until the young are ready to hatch, an unusual level of parental care for a reptile.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: King cobras are listed as Vulnerable, threatened by deforestation, collection for skins and traditional medicine, and persecution out of fear. Protecting the forests of South and Southeast Asia is key to their survival.

faqs.question: How long is a king cobra?
faqs.answer: The king cobra is the longest venomous snake, averaging 3 to 4 m and reaching up to 5.5 m (18 ft) in exceptional individuals.

faqs.question: How dangerous is a king cobra's venom?
faqs.answer: King cobra venom is a potent neurotoxin delivered in large amounts. An untreated bite can be fatal to a human within hours, though the snake is shy and bites on people are rare.

faqs.question: What do king cobras eat?
faqs.answer: King cobras eat mainly other snakes, including venomous ones, along with the occasional lizard. Their name Ophiophagus literally means "snake-eater."

faqs.question: Do king cobras build nests?
faqs.answer: Yes. King cobras are the only snakes that build a nest for their eggs. The female heaps up leaves, lays her eggs inside, and guards the nest until they are ready to hatch.

faqs.question: Are king cobras aggressive?
faqs.answer: Not usually. King cobras are alert and will display a raised hood when cornered, but they are generally shy and prefer to escape rather than attack.

faqs.question: Are king cobras endangered?
faqs.answer: King cobras are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, mainly due to habitat loss and collection. Their forest homes across Asia are shrinking.

range.nativeRange: The forests and jungles of India, southern China, and Southeast Asia.

animals.name: Komodo Dragon
animals.summary: The Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard, growing up to 3 m (10 ft) long and 90 kg (200 lb). Found only on a handful of Indonesian islands, it is a powerful ambush predator with serrated teeth and venom that lowers a victim's blood pressure. It can take prey as large as deer and water buffalo. Komodo dragons can live around 30 years.

sections.heading: Behavior and hunting
sections.body: Komodo dragons are ambush hunters that lie in wait and rush prey with a sudden burst of speed. They use serrated teeth to deliver deep wounds, and venom glands that release toxins which prevent clotting and lower blood pressure, weakening prey that escapes the initial attack. They have an excellent sense of smell, using their forked tongue to detect carrion from kilometers away.

sections.heading: Diet
sections.body: Komodo dragons eat almost any meat, from carrion and birds to deer, pigs, and even water buffalo. They can consume a large portion of their body weight in a single meal and may go weeks between large kills.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The species is found only on a few Indonesian islands, including Komodo, Rinca, Flores, and a couple of smaller ones, in tropical savanna and dry forest. This tiny range makes the entire species vulnerable to local threats.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Komodo dragons are listed as Endangered. Their limited island range, small total population, habitat loss, and the effects of climate change and rising seas all threaten their future. Most live within Komodo National Park, a World Heritage Site.

faqs.question: How big do Komodo dragons get?
faqs.answer: Komodo dragons are the largest lizards on Earth, reaching up to 3 m (10 ft) in length and around 90 kg (200 lb) in weight.

faqs.question: Are Komodo dragons venomous?
faqs.answer: Yes. Komodo dragons have venom glands that release toxins which prevent blood clotting and lower blood pressure, helping to weaken prey after a bite.

faqs.question: What do Komodo dragons eat?
faqs.answer: They are carnivores that eat carrion, birds, deer, pigs, and even water buffalo. A Komodo dragon can eat a huge amount in one meal and then go weeks without eating.

faqs.question: Where do Komodo dragons live?
faqs.answer: Komodo dragons live only on a few Indonesian islands, including Komodo, Rinca, and Flores, in tropical savanna and dry forest.

faqs.question: How fast can a Komodo dragon run?
faqs.answer: Komodo dragons can sprint up to about 20 km/h (12 mph) in short bursts, relying on ambush rather than long chases.

faqs.question: Are Komodo dragons endangered?
faqs.answer: Yes. Komodo dragons are listed as Endangered, threatened by their tiny range, habitat loss, and climate change. Most are protected within Komodo National Park.

facts.value: Tropical savanna and forest on Indonesian islands

animals.name: Green Sea Turtle
animals.summary: The green sea turtle is a large marine reptile found in warm oceans worldwide, named for the greenish color of its body fat rather than its shell. Adults are unusual among sea turtles in being mostly herbivorous, grazing on seagrass and algae. They migrate long distances between feeding grounds and the beaches where they hatched, and can live 70 to 80 years or more.

sections.heading: Behavior and migration
sections.body: Green sea turtles undertake some of the longest migrations of any reptile, traveling hundreds or thousands of kilometers between feeding areas and nesting beaches. Remarkably, females return to the very beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs, navigating using the Earth's magnetic field.

sections.heading: Diet
sections.body: Hatchlings and juveniles eat a mix of animals and plants, but adults switch to a largely herbivorous diet of seagrass and algae. This grazing keeps seagrass meadows healthy, making green turtles important to coastal ecosystems.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Green sea turtles live in tropical and subtropical waters around the world, favoring shallow coastal areas with seagrass beds and coral reefs. They come ashore only to nest, with females digging nests on sandy beaches at night.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Green sea turtles are assessed as Least Concern globally in the 2025 IUCN assessment, following decades of conservation. Some regional populations remain threatened. They face threats from hunting, egg collection, accidental capture in fishing gear, plastic pollution, and the loss of nesting beaches to coastal development and rising seas. Protected nesting sites and fishing regulations are helping some populations recover.

sections.heading: One turtle, several habitats and life stages
sections.body: Green turtles use different habitats as they grow and may travel long distances between feeding and nesting areas. Protecting a nesting beach alone cannot address every threat encountered at sea. Entanglement, vessel strikes and loss of suitable habitat can affect survival. Conservation labels also need context: a national legal listing, a regional population and a global Red List assessment are not interchangeable.

faqs.question: Why is it called a green sea turtle?
faqs.answer: The green sea turtle is named for the greenish color of the fat under its shell, not the color of the shell itself, which is usually brown or olive.

faqs.question: What do green sea turtles eat?
faqs.answer: Adult green sea turtles are mostly herbivores, grazing on seagrass and algae. Younger turtles also eat small animals such as jellyfish and crustaceans.

faqs.question: How long do green sea turtles live?
faqs.answer: Green sea turtles are long-lived, commonly reaching 70 to 80 years and sometimes more. They take decades to reach breeding age.

faqs.question: Do sea turtles return to where they were born?
faqs.answer: Yes. Female green sea turtles return to the same beach where they hatched to lay their eggs, navigating across open ocean using the Earth's magnetic field.

faqs.question: Are green sea turtles endangered?
faqs.answer: Green sea turtles are globally Least Concern in the 2025 IUCN assessment. Some regional populations remain threatened, and national legal protections can differ from the global Red List category. Bycatch, harvest and habitat loss still require conservation action.

faqs.question: How fast can a sea turtle swim?
faqs.answer: Green sea turtles usually cruise slowly but can burst to around 35 km/h (22 mph) when escaping danger.

faqs.question: Are all green turtles strictly herbivorous?
faqs.answer: No. Diet changes with life stage and location. Many adults feed predominantly on seagrasses and algae, while younger turtles can have a more mixed diet. A simple “herbivore” label is useful as an introduction but does not describe every individual throughout its life.

sourceUpdate.heading: One turtle, several habitats and life stages
sourceUpdate.body: Green turtles use different habitats as they grow and may travel long distances between feeding and nesting areas. Protecting a nesting beach alone cannot address every threat encountered at sea. Entanglement, vessel strikes and loss of suitable habitat can affect survival. Conservation labels also need context: a national legal listing, a regional population and a global Red List assessment are not interchangeable.

sourceUpdate.answer: No. Diet changes with life stage and location. Many adults feed predominantly on seagrasses and algae, while younger turtles can have a more mixed diet. A simple “herbivore” label is useful as an introduction but does not describe every individual throughout its life.

animals.name: Poison Dart Frog
animals.summary: Poison dart frogs are small, brightly colored amphibians from the rainforests of Central and South America. Their vivid colors warn predators that they are toxic. The most poisonous species, the golden poison frog, carries enough toxin to be dangerous to humans. They get their toxins from their diet of ants and mites, and frogs raised without those prey are not poisonous. Many live around 10 years.

sections.heading: Colors and toxicity
sections.body: Poison dart frogs are a classic example of warning coloration: their bright blues, yellows, oranges, and reds tell predators they are dangerous to eat. Toxicity varies widely by species. The golden poison frog of Colombia is one of the most toxic animals on Earth, with skin toxins potent enough to threaten a human.

sections.heading: Diet and the source of their poison
sections.body: These frogs do not make their poison from scratch. They acquire toxic compounds from the small invertebrates they eat, especially certain ants and mites. Poison dart frogs raised in captivity on a different diet lose their toxicity, which shows how closely their defense is tied to their food.

sections.heading: Behavior and parental care
sections.body: Despite their toxins, poison dart frogs are attentive parents. Many species carry their tadpoles on their backs to small pools of water in plants, and some females return to feed the tadpoles with unfertilized eggs until they develop.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Toxicity and status vary by species. Many poison dart frogs are listed as Least Concern, but several are threatened by deforestation, the pet trade, and the spread of amphibian diseases. Protecting intact rainforest is essential for the most restricted species.

faqs.question: Why are poison dart frogs so colorful?
faqs.answer: Their bright colors are a warning signal, called aposematism, telling predators that the frogs are toxic and not worth eating.

faqs.question: How poisonous are poison dart frogs?
faqs.answer: It varies by species. The golden poison frog is among the most toxic animals on Earth, with enough skin toxin to endanger a human, while many other species are only mildly toxic.

faqs.question: Where do poison dart frogs get their poison?
faqs.answer: They get it from their diet of certain ants, mites, and other small invertebrates. Frogs raised in captivity without those prey are not poisonous.

faqs.question: How were they used for darts?
faqs.answer: Some Indigenous peoples of Central and South America rubbed blowgun darts on the skin of the most toxic species to make them more effective for hunting, which is how the frogs got their name.

faqs.question: What do poison dart frogs eat?
faqs.answer: They eat tiny invertebrates such as ants, termites, and mites. This diet is also the source of the toxins many species store in their skin.

faqs.question: How long do poison dart frogs live?
faqs.answer: Many poison dart frogs live around 10 years, and some can live longer in captivity under good conditions.

animals.name: Axolotl
animals.summary: The axolotl is a salamander from Mexico that keeps its larval features for life, including feathery external gills, and lives permanently in water instead of moving onto land. It is famous for its extraordinary ability to regrow limbs, parts of organs, and even portions of its brain. Critically endangered in the wild, it survives mainly in captivity and labs. Axolotls can live 10 to 15 years.

sections.heading: Neoteny: the salamander that stays young
sections.body: Most salamanders transform from water-living larvae into land-living adults, but the axolotl keeps its juvenile form for life, a phenomenon called neoteny. It retains its feathery external gills and stays fully aquatic, breeding while still in what looks like a larval body.

sections.heading: Regeneration
sections.body: The axolotl is one of the most studied animals in regenerative biology. It can regrow lost limbs, tail, parts of the heart and other organs, and even sections of its brain and spinal cord, often with little or no scarring. Scientists study it to understand how regeneration works and whether similar processes might help in human medicine.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: In the wild, axolotls live only in the remnants of the lake and canal system around Mexico City, especially Lake Xochimilco. This habitat has been drained, polluted, and invaded by non-native fish, leaving very few wild axolotls.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: The axolotl is Critically Endangered in the wild, with wild numbers reduced to a tiny fraction of their former range. Paradoxically, it is abundant in captivity as a pet and a lab animal. Restoring the canals of Xochimilco and reducing pollution are central to saving the wild population.

sections.heading: A familiar aquarium animal with a very different wild story
sections.body: The axolotl is a salamander that usually retains juvenile features, including external gills, while becoming capable of reproduction. This life-history pattern is called neoteny. Its wild home is the Xochimilco wetland system in Mexico; abundant captive animals do not mean the wild population is secure. Habitat degradation and introduced fish are part of that conservation problem. The distinction matters whenever a pet-trade photograph is used to illustrate the species’ status.

faqs.question: Is the axolotl a fish?
faqs.answer: No. The axolotl is an amphibian, specifically a salamander. It looks fish-like because it keeps its larval form and external gills for life and lives permanently in water.

faqs.question: Can axolotls really regrow body parts?
faqs.answer: Yes. Axolotls can regenerate lost limbs, tail, parts of organs, and even portions of the brain and spinal cord, often without scarring. This makes them important in scientific research.

faqs.question: Why do axolotls stay in their larval form?
faqs.answer: Axolotls undergo neoteny, meaning they keep juvenile features such as external gills and remain aquatic for life rather than transforming into a land-dwelling adult.

faqs.question: Are axolotls endangered?
faqs.answer: Yes. Axolotls are Critically Endangered in the wild, surviving in just a few canals near Mexico City, even though they are common as pets and lab animals.

faqs.question: What do axolotls eat?
faqs.answer: Axolotls are carnivores that eat worms, insects, small crustaceans, and small fish, sucking prey into their mouths with a quick gulp.

faqs.question: How long do axolotls live?
faqs.answer: Axolotls typically live 10 to 15 years in captivity with good care. Wild lifespans are harder to measure given how few remain.

faqs.question: Is an axolotl a fish or a reptile?
faqs.answer: Neither: an axolotl is an amphibian. It belongs to the salamander group despite spending its normal adult life underwater. External gills and an aquatic lifestyle do not make an animal a fish. Compare axolotls with other amphibians to understand the diversity of their life cycles.

animals.name: Honey Bee
animals.summary: The honey bee is a social insect that lives in colonies of tens of thousands, built around a single egg-laying queen. Honey bees pollinate a large share of the crops people rely on, make honey from flower nectar, and communicate the location of food through a "waggle dance." Worker bees live only a few weeks in summer, while a queen can live several years.

sections.heading: Life in the colony
sections.body: A honey bee colony is a single tightly organized society. One queen lays all the eggs, thousands of female workers forage, build comb, feed young, and defend the hive, and male drones exist mainly to mate. Tasks shift as a worker ages, from cleaning and nursing inside the hive to foraging outside.

sections.heading: Pollination and honey
sections.body: As bees move between flowers collecting nectar and pollen, they transfer pollen and fertilize plants. This pollination underpins a large portion of global food crops. Back at the hive, bees convert nectar into honey, a stored food that sustains the colony through times when flowers are scarce.

sections.heading: The waggle dance
sections.body: Honey bees share the location of good food sources through a remarkable behavior called the waggle dance. A returning forager moves in a figure-eight pattern, and the angle and duration of the central "waggle" run encode the direction and distance of the flowers relative to the sun.

sections.heading: Threats and importance
sections.body: Honey bees face pressure from habitat loss, pesticides, parasites such as the varroa mite, and disease. Because they pollinate so many crops, their health is closely tied to food security, and beekeepers and researchers work to keep colonies strong.

faqs.question: How many bees live in a hive?
faqs.answer: A healthy honey bee colony usually contains 20,000 to 80,000 bees in summer, made up of one queen, many thousands of female workers, and some male drones.

faqs.question: Why are honey bees important?
faqs.answer: Honey bees pollinate a large share of the crops people eat, helping plants produce fruits, vegetables, nuts, and seeds. They also produce honey and beeswax.

faqs.question: What is the waggle dance?
faqs.answer: The waggle dance is how a honey bee tells hive mates where to find food. The direction and length of its waggling run encode the direction and distance to the flowers.

faqs.question: How long do honey bees live?
faqs.answer: Summer worker bees live only about six weeks, while the queen can live two to five years. Workers raised in autumn can survive through the winter.

faqs.question: Do honey bees die when they sting?
faqs.answer: Worker honey bees usually die after stinging a mammal, because their barbed stinger and part of their body are torn away. They sting mainly to defend the colony.

faqs.question: How fast can a honey bee fly?
faqs.answer: Honey bees fly at around 28 km/h (17 mph) when traveling to flowers, and a bit slower when returning loaded with nectar and pollen.

range.nativeRange: Native to Europe, Africa, and western Asia; now kept by beekeepers worldwide.

animals.name: Gorilla
animals.summary: Gorillas are the largest living primates, with dominant males (silverbacks) weighing up to 200 kg (440 lb). They are gentle, highly intelligent herbivores native to the forests of central Africa, living in close-knit family groups. Wild gorillas typically live 35 to 40 years.

sections.heading: Intelligence and social life
sections.body: Gorillas live in stable family groups led by a single dominant male called a silverback, named for the silver hair across his back. They are remarkably intelligent: they use tools, recognize themselves in mirrors, and some captive gorillas have learned hundreds of sign-language gestures. Group members communicate through more than 20 distinct vocalizations.

sections.heading: Diet and strength
sections.body: Gorillas are mostly herbivores, eating leaves, stems, shoots, fruit, and occasionally insects. An adult can eat up to 18 kg (40 lb) of vegetation a day. Despite their plant-based diet, silverbacks are extraordinarily strong, capable of lifting many times their own body weight, though they rarely use that strength aggressively.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Gorillas live only in the tropical and montane forests of central Africa, split into western and eastern species. They build a fresh nest of branches and leaves to sleep in each night, on the ground or in trees, and travel through their home range feeding as they go.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Both gorilla species are endangered, and the western lowland gorilla is Critically Endangered, threatened by poaching, disease such as Ebola, and habitat loss from logging and mining. Conservation programs, protected parks, and carefully managed gorilla tourism are central to their survival.

sections.heading: Social groups
sections.body: Gorillas live in stable family groups led by a dominant adult male known as a silverback, named for the silver hair across his back. The silverback makes decisions, mediates conflicts, and protects the group, which usually includes several females and their young.

sections.heading: Diet and intelligence
sections.body: Gorillas are mainly herbivores, eating leaves, stems, shoots, and fruit, and they are highly intelligent. Some have learned sign language in captivity, and wild gorillas have been seen using simple tools such as sticks to test the depth of water before crossing.

faqs.question: Are gorillas dangerous?
faqs.answer: Gorillas are generally shy and peaceful. A silverback may charge to defend his group, but this is usually a bluff display rather than a genuine attack.

faqs.question: Are gorillas endangered?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both gorilla species are Endangered or Critically Endangered, threatened by poaching, habitat loss, and disease such as Ebola.

faqs.question: How strong is a gorilla?
faqs.answer: Gorillas are among the strongest primates on Earth. A silverback can lift several times its own body weight, with estimates often cited around 800 to 900 kg, far beyond what a trained human can manage.

faqs.question: What do gorillas eat?
faqs.answer: Gorillas are mainly herbivores, eating leaves, shoots, stems, bark, and fruit, plus the occasional insect. An adult can consume up to 18 kg (40 lb) of vegetation in a single day.

faqs.question: Are gorillas dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Gorillas are generally shy and peaceful and avoid conflict. A silverback may charge to defend its family, but this is usually a bluff. Attacks on humans are rare and almost always defensive.

faqs.question: How long do gorillas live?
faqs.answer: Wild gorillas typically live 35 to 40 years. In captivity, with veterinary care and a steady food supply, some gorillas have lived into their 50s.

faqs.question: Why are gorillas endangered?
faqs.answer: Gorillas are endangered mainly because of poaching, disease such as Ebola, and habitat loss from logging, mining, and farming. The western lowland gorilla is listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN.

range.nativeRange: The tropical and montane rainforests of central Africa.
