animals.name: Northern Cardinal
animals.summary: The northern cardinal is a popular North American songbird, the male instantly recognizable by his brilliant red plumage, black face mask, and pointed crest. Females are warm tan with red highlights. A frequent visitor to backyard feeders, the cardinal sings rich, whistling songs year-round and does not migrate. Cardinals usually live about 3 years in the wild, sometimes much longer.

sections.heading: Color and appearance
sections.body: The male northern cardinal is unmistakable, with vivid red feathers, a black mask around the bill, and a tall crest. Females are a soft tan or olive with red tinges in the wings, crest, and tail, and both sexes have a stout, cone-shaped orange-red bill suited to cracking seeds. The male's bright color comes from pigments in the foods he eats.

sections.heading: Song and behavior
sections.body: Cardinals are accomplished singers, and unusually both males and females sing. Their clear, whistling phrases ring out through much of the year as they defend territory and stay in contact with a mate. Cardinals do not migrate, so their red against winter snow and their songs on cold mornings make them favorites in northern gardens.

sections.heading: Diet and feeders
sections.body: Northern cardinals eat mainly seeds, grains, and fruit, along with insects, especially when feeding their young. Their strong bills handle tough seeds with ease, and they are among the most common and welcome visitors to backyard feeders, where sunflower seeds are a particular favorite.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Cardinals live across the eastern and central United States, parts of the Southwest, Mexico, and Central America, and their range has expanded northward over the past century. They favor woodland edges, thickets, gardens, and shrubby areas, and have adapted well to suburbs and towns where feeders and plantings provide food and cover.

faqs.question: Why are male cardinals so red?
faqs.answer: Male northern cardinals get their bright red color from pigments called carotenoids in the seeds and fruit they eat. A healthy, well-fed male tends to show the most vivid red plumage.

faqs.question: Do female cardinals look different from males?
faqs.answer: Yes. Females are warm tan or pale olive with reddish tints in the wings, tail, and crest, while males are brilliant red. Both sexes share the crest, black face, and orange-red bill.

faqs.question: What do northern cardinals eat?
faqs.answer: Cardinals are omnivores that eat mainly seeds, grains, and fruit, plus insects, especially when raising chicks. They readily visit feeders, where sunflower seeds are a favorite.

faqs.question: Do cardinals migrate?
faqs.answer: No. Northern cardinals stay in their territory year-round, which is why their red plumage and songs are a familiar sight even in the middle of a snowy northern winter.

faqs.question: How long do cardinals live?
faqs.answer: Many cardinals live only about 3 years in the wild because of predators and harsh weather, but some individuals survive much longer, with banded birds recorded at over 15 years.

faqs.question: Do female cardinals sing?
faqs.answer: Yes. Unlike many songbirds, female cardinals sing too, often from the nest, and pairs may use song to communicate with each other while raising their young.

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: About 3 years in the wild, longer possible

range.nativeRange: Woodland edges, gardens, and shrubland across the eastern and central United States, the Southwest, Mexico, and Central America.

animals.name: Blue Jay
animals.summary: The blue jay is a striking, intelligent songbird of eastern and central North America, known for its blue crest, black necklace markings, and loud, varied calls. A member of the crow family, it is bold, social, and clever, famous for caching acorns and for mimicking the screams of hawks. Blue jays commonly live about 7 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Color and the trick of blue
sections.body: The blue jay's blue is not made by pigment but by the microscopic structure of its feathers, which scatters light to appear blue, an effect called structural color. A crushed blue feather looks dull brown because the structure is destroyed. The bird's blue crest, white face, and black collar make it one of North America's most recognizable songbirds.

sections.heading: Intelligence and acorns
sections.body: As members of the crow family, blue jays are highly intelligent and curious. They gather and bury thousands of acorns each autumn, and the ones they never retrieve grow into oak trees, so blue jays help spread and plant forests. They are also known to use tools and to remember rich food sources over long periods.

sections.heading: Calls and mimicry
sections.body: Blue jays are loud and have a wide range of calls. They are skilled mimics and often imitate the screams of hawks, which may warn other jays of danger or may scare other birds away from a feeder. They also make soft, musical notes among themselves that are very different from their familiar harsh "jay-jay" call.

sections.heading: Habitat and behavior
sections.body: Blue jays live across eastern and central North America in forests, woodlands, parks, and gardens, and are common at backyard feeders. They are social and often travel in family groups, and they can be bold and assertive, sometimes driving smaller birds away from food while keeping a sharp lookout for predators.

faqs.question: Why are blue jays blue?
faqs.answer: Blue jays are not blue because of pigment. Tiny structures in their feathers scatter light to create a blue appearance, so a crushed feather actually looks brown once that structure is broken.

faqs.question: What do blue jays eat?
faqs.answer: Blue jays are omnivores that eat acorns, nuts, seeds, fruit, and insects, and sometimes eggs or nestlings. Acorns are a favorite, and the jays bury many for winter.

faqs.question: Do blue jays really help plant trees?
faqs.answer: Yes. Blue jays bury thousands of acorns each autumn and never recover them all. Many of the forgotten acorns sprout, so blue jays play a real role in spreading and planting oak forests.

faqs.question: Why do blue jays imitate hawks?
faqs.answer: Blue jays often mimic hawk screams. This may warn other jays that a predator is near, or it may startle other birds away from a feeder so the jay can eat undisturbed.

faqs.question: Are blue jays aggressive?
faqs.answer: Blue jays can be bold and assertive, sometimes chasing smaller birds from feeders and mobbing predators near their nests, but they are also social and cooperative within their own family groups.

faqs.question: How long do blue jays live?
faqs.answer: Blue jays commonly live about 7 years in the wild, and some banded individuals have survived well over 15 years.

range.nativeRange: Forests, woodlands, parks, and gardens across eastern and central North America.

animals.name: American Robin
animals.summary: The American robin is a common North American thrush known for its orange-red breast, cheerful song, and habit of hopping across lawns to pull up earthworms. Often seen as a sign of spring, it is widespread from Canada to Mexico and adapts well to gardens and parks. Robins usually live about 2 years in the wild, though some live much longer.

sections.heading: A familiar garden bird
sections.body: The American robin is one of the most familiar birds in North America, often seen running and pausing across lawns as it hunts. It has a gray-brown back, a warm orange-red breast, and a cheery, caroling song that is among the first heard at dawn. Its return to northern areas in late winter has long been treated as a sign that spring is near.

sections.heading: Finding worms
sections.body: Robins are famous for hunting earthworms, tilting their heads as if listening but actually using sharp eyesight to spot a worm's movement in the grass. They also eat many insects, especially in spring and summer, switching to fruit and berries in autumn and winter, which lets them stay in many areas year-round rather than always migrating.

sections.heading: Nesting and eggs
sections.body: Female robins build cup-shaped nests of grass and mud in trees, shrubs, and on building ledges, and lay clutches of distinctive sky-blue eggs. A pair may raise two or three broods in a single season. The young leave the nest before they can fly well and continue to be fed by their parents while they find their feet.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: American robins range across nearly all of North America, from Alaska and Canada to Mexico. Many northern birds migrate south for winter, while others remain wherever fruit is available. Highly adaptable, robins thrive in suburbs, city parks, farmland, and forests alike, making them one of the continent's most abundant birds.

faqs.question: What do American robins eat?
faqs.answer: Robins are omnivores that eat earthworms and insects, especially in spring and summer, and switch to fruit and berries in autumn and winter, which helps them survive in many areas year-round.

faqs.question: How do robins find worms?
faqs.answer: Robins tilt their heads toward the ground as they hunt, but they rely mainly on sharp eyesight to detect the slight movement of a worm near the surface before pulling it out.

faqs.question: Are American robins a sign of spring?
faqs.answer: Their return and song in late winter are traditionally seen as a sign of spring, though many robins actually stay through winter wherever they can find fruit and berries.

faqs.question: What color are robin eggs?
faqs.answer: American robin eggs are a distinctive sky-blue, sometimes called robin's-egg blue. A female typically lays three to five eggs per clutch and may raise several broods each year.

faqs.question: How long do American robins live?
faqs.answer: Most American robins live only about 2 years in the wild because of predators and harsh conditions, but some individuals survive much longer, with records of over 13 years.

faqs.question: Is the American robin related to the European robin?
faqs.answer: No, not closely. The American robin is a thrush, while the smaller European robin is a different family. Early settlers named the American bird after the European robin because of its orange-red breast.

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: About 2 years in the wild, longer possible

range.nativeRange: Lawns, gardens, woodlands, and parks across nearly all of North America, from Alaska and Canada to Mexico.

animals.name: Mallard
animals.summary: The mallard is the most common and widespread wild duck in the world and the ancestor of nearly all domestic ducks. The male has a glossy green head, yellow bill, and chestnut chest, while the female is mottled brown for camouflage. A dabbling duck of lakes, rivers, and city ponds, the mallard adapts to almost any wetland and usually lives 5 to 10 years.

sections.heading: Appearance and the eclipse
sections.body: The drake mallard is striking, with an iridescent green head, white neck ring, chestnut breast, and bright yellow bill, while the hen is mottled brown to stay hidden on the nest. Both show a blue-purple wing patch called a speculum. For a few weeks in summer the male molts into a dull, female-like "eclipse" plumage while he is briefly unable to fly.

sections.heading: Dabbling and diet
sections.body: Mallards are dabbling ducks, tipping forward in the water with their tails in the air to reach plants and small animals below the surface rather than diving. They are omnivores, eating seeds, aquatic plants, insects, worms, and small invertebrates, and in parks they readily accept food from people, though bread is poor nutrition for them.

sections.heading: Breeding and ducklings
sections.body: The familiar "quack" most people know is actually the call of the female. Hens build hidden nests near water and lay around a dozen eggs. Ducklings hatch covered in down and able to swim and feed themselves within a day, following their mother to water while she guards them closely from predators.

sections.heading: Habitat and global success
sections.body: Mallards live across North America, Europe, Asia, and North Africa and have been introduced elsewhere, making them one of the most widespread ducks on Earth. They thrive in almost any wetland, from wild marshes to urban park ponds, and their adaptability and willingness to live near people have helped them flourish worldwide.

faqs.question: What do mallards eat?
faqs.answer: Mallards are omnivores that eat seeds, aquatic plants, insects, worms, and small invertebrates. They dabble at the surface and tip upside down to reach food rather than diving for it.

faqs.question: What is the difference between male and female mallards?
faqs.answer: The male has a glossy green head, yellow bill, and chestnut breast, while the female is mottled brown for camouflage. Both have a blue wing patch, and the classic loud quack comes from the female.

faqs.question: Are mallards the ancestors of domestic ducks?
faqs.answer: Yes. Almost all domestic duck breeds, except the Muscovy, descend from the wild mallard, which is why farmyard ducks vary so much in size and color.

faqs.question: Why should you not feed bread to mallards?
faqs.answer: Bread fills ducks up without giving them the nutrients they need and can harm their health and water quality. Cracked corn, oats, peas, or duck feed are far better if you want to feed them.

faqs.question: How fast can a mallard fly?
faqs.answer: Mallards are strong fliers and can reach speeds of around 88 km/h (55 mph), especially with a tailwind, and they migrate long distances between breeding and wintering grounds.

faqs.question: Where do mallards live?
faqs.answer: Mallards live across North America, Europe, Asia, and North Africa and have been introduced to other regions. They thrive in nearly any wetland, including lakes, rivers, marshes, and city ponds.

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Lakes, rivers, marshes, and city ponds

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 88 km/h (55 mph) in flight

range.nativeRange: Wetlands across North America, Europe, Asia, and North Africa, and introduced to other regions worldwide.

animals.name: Ibis
animals.summary: An ibis is a long-legged wading bird with a distinctive long, down-curved bill used to probe mud and shallow water for food. The sacred ibis was revered in ancient Egypt. Ibises feed on insects, frogs, and small aquatic animals, nest in colonies, and often live around 20 years.

sections.heading: The probing bill
sections.body: An ibis is built for wetlands. Its long, slender, down-curved bill works like forceps, probing soft mud, shallow water, and grass for insects, worms, frogs, and small fish that it locates largely by touch. This lets ibises feed in murky water where sight-hunting birds struggle.

sections.heading: Colonies and flight
sections.body: Ibises are social birds that feed, roost, and nest in groups, often alongside herons, egrets, and storks. In flight they alternate flapping with gliding and often travel in long lines or V-formations between feeding and roosting sites.

sections.heading: Sacred history
sections.body: The sacred ibis was closely linked to the ancient Egyptian god Thoth, and vast numbers were mummified as offerings. Although it no longer breeds along the Nile, it remains widespread across sub-Saharan Africa and has formed feral populations in parts of Europe.

sections.heading: Habitat and status
sections.body: Ibises live around wetlands, floodplains, farmland, and even city parks, adapting well to landscapes shaped by people. Most species are common, and the sacred ibis is listed as Least Concern, though wetland drainage threatens some of their rarer relatives.

faqs.question: What does an ibis eat?
faqs.answer: Ibises eat insects, worms, frogs, small fish, and other small animals, using their long curved bills to probe mud and shallow water by touch.

faqs.question: Why was the ibis sacred in Egypt?
faqs.answer: The sacred ibis was associated with Thoth, the ancient Egyptian god of wisdom and writing, and millions were mummified as religious offerings.

faqs.question: Where do ibises live?
faqs.answer: Ibises live around wetlands, marshes, rivers, and floodplains. The sacred ibis is widespread across sub-Saharan Africa, with feral populations in Europe.

faqs.question: Are ibises endangered?
faqs.answer: The sacred ibis is listed as Least Concern and is common, although some other ibis species are threatened by the loss of wetlands.

faqs.question: How long do ibises live?
faqs.answer: Ibises can live around 20 years, with survival depending on the health of the wetlands they rely on for food.

range.nativeRange: Wetlands, marshes, and floodplains across sub-Saharan Africa, with feral populations in parts of Europe.

animals.name: Quail
animals.summary: A quail is a small, plump ground-dwelling bird with mottled brown camouflage plumage, found in grasslands and farmland worldwide. The common quail is migratory and famous for its distinctive three-note call. Quails feed on seeds and insects, nest on the ground, and usually live 3 to 5 years.

sections.heading: Small, round, and hidden
sections.body: Quails are small, rounded birds that spend most of their lives on the ground, relying on streaky brown plumage to vanish into grass and crops. They prefer to run or crouch rather than fly, and when flushed they burst into a fast, low, whirring flight before dropping back into cover.

sections.heading: Calls and breeding
sections.body: The common quail is heard far more often than seen. Males give a distinctive repeated three-note call to attract mates across fields of tall grass. Females nest in a simple scrape on the ground and can lay large clutches, with chicks able to walk and feed soon after hatching.

sections.heading: Migration and diet
sections.body: Unusually for such a small game bird, the common quail is a long-distance migrant, traveling between Europe and Asia and wintering in Africa and southern Asia. Quails are omnivores that eat seeds, grain, and insects, foraging by scratching and pecking at the ground.

sections.heading: Quails and people
sections.body: Quails have been kept and hunted by people for thousands of years, and domesticated quail are raised worldwide for eggs and meat. Wild common quail remain widespread and are listed as Least Concern, though changes in farming affect their numbers.

faqs.question: What does a quail look like?
faqs.answer: A quail is a small, plump ground bird with short legs and mottled brown plumage that provides excellent camouflage in grass and crops.

faqs.question: Can quails fly?
faqs.answer: Yes, but quails prefer to run and hide. When startled they make a fast, low, whirring flight over a short distance before dropping back into cover.

faqs.question: What do quails eat?
faqs.answer: Quails are omnivores that feed on seeds, grain, and insects, foraging on the ground by pecking and scratching.

faqs.question: Where do quails live?
faqs.answer: Quails live in grasslands, meadows, and farmland. The common quail breeds across Europe and Asia and migrates to Africa and southern Asia for winter.

faqs.question: Are quails endangered?
faqs.answer: The common quail is listed as Least Concern and remains widespread, though intensive farming can reduce local populations.

range.nativeRange: Grasslands and farmland across Europe and Asia, migrating to Africa and southern Asia for winter.

animals.name: Vulture
animals.summary: A vulture is a large bird of prey that feeds mainly on carrion, soaring for hours on broad wings to find carcasses. Its often bald head stays cleaner while feeding. Vultures provide a vital sanitation service, can live 20 to 30 years, and several species are now Critically Endangered.

sections.heading: Masters of soaring
sections.body: Vultures are built to cover huge distances with almost no effort, riding rising columns of warm air called thermals on long, broad wings. From great height they scan the ground, and Old World vultures rely mainly on sharp eyesight to spot carcasses or the activity of other scavengers.

sections.heading: Why the bald head
sections.body: Many vultures have bare heads and necks. Feeding inside a carcass is messy, and bare skin is easier to keep clean and free of bacteria, while also helping the bird control its temperature. Powerful stomach acid lets vultures safely digest meat that would sicken other animals.

sections.heading: Nature's sanitation service
sections.body: By quickly consuming dead animals, vultures stop the spread of diseases such as rabies and anthrax and recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem. Where vultures have vanished, rotting carcasses and booming populations of feral dogs and rats have followed, harming public health.

sections.heading: A conservation crisis
sections.body: Several vulture species have suffered some of the steepest declines of any birds. In South Asia, the veterinary drug diclofenac in livestock carcasses poisoned vultures and crashed their numbers, and poisoning remains a major threat in Africa. Many species are now Endangered or Critically Endangered.

faqs.question: What do vultures eat?
faqs.answer: Vultures are scavengers that feed mainly on carrion, the bodies of dead animals. Their strong stomach acid lets them safely digest meat full of bacteria.

faqs.question: Why do vultures have bald heads?
faqs.answer: A bald head and neck stay cleaner when a vulture feeds inside a carcass and help the bird regulate its body temperature.

faqs.question: Are vultures endangered?
faqs.answer: It varies by species. Several, especially in South Asia and Africa, are Critically Endangered after poisoning and the veterinary drug diclofenac caused massive declines.

faqs.question: Why are vultures important?
faqs.answer: Vultures clean up dead animals quickly, which limits the spread of diseases like rabies and anthrax and recycles nutrients in the environment.

faqs.question: How do vultures find food?
faqs.answer: Old World vultures soar to great heights and use keen eyesight to spot carcasses and the movements of other scavengers below.

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Soars for hours; can dive faster

facts.label: Conservation status
facts.value: Varies by species; several Critically Endangered

range.nativeRange: Mountains, plains, and open country across Africa, southern Europe, and Asia (Old World vultures).

animals.name: Kiwi
animals.summary: The kiwi (Apteryx australis) is a flightless, nocturnal bird found only in New Zealand, roughly the size of a chicken with shaggy, hair-like feathers and no visible wings. Unique among birds, it has nostrils at the very tip of its long bill, which it uses to sniff out earthworms and insects in the soil. It weighs about 1.3 to 3.5 kg and can live 25 to 50 years. Several kiwi species are Vulnerable.

sections.heading: A bird like no other
sections.body: The kiwi is one of the world's most unusual birds, so distinctive that it is often described as an honorary mammal. About the size of a chicken and weighing 1.3 to 3.5 kg, it has loose, shaggy feathers that look more like coarse hair, and its wings are so tiny as to be invisible. It has no tail, strong muscular legs, and a body temperature lower than most birds. Kiwi are the smallest of the ratites, the flightless group that includes the ostrich and emu.

sections.heading: Smell and the tip-of-bill nostrils
sections.body: Alone among birds, the kiwi has nostrils at the very tip of its long, slender bill rather than at the base. This gives it an exceptional sense of smell, which it uses to detect earthworms, grubs, and insects hidden underground. Probing the soil, it sniffs out prey it cannot see and seizes it deep in the leaf litter. This reliance on smell, rare in the bird world, suits its nocturnal, ground-based way of life.

sections.heading: Diet and nocturnal habits
sections.body: The kiwi is an omnivore that feeds chiefly on earthworms and insect larvae, adding berries, seeds, and other invertebrates to its diet. It is strictly nocturnal, spending the day in a burrow and emerging after dark to forage across the forest floor. Sensitive whiskers around the bill and acute hearing help it move and feed in near-total darkness. Its poor eyesight matters little for a bird that lives by scent and touch.

sections.heading: The remarkable egg
sections.body: The kiwi lays one of the largest eggs relative to body size of any bird, an egg that can make up around a fifth of the female's weight. The male usually takes on the long task of incubation, sitting for around 70 to 80 days. Chicks hatch fully feathered and able to leave the burrow within days, feeding themselves without being fed by the parents. This huge investment in a single well-developed chick is another of the kiwi's mammal-like traits.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Kiwi are found only in New Zealand, living in native forest, scrubland, and rough farmland that offers dense cover. They are territorial and largely monogamous, and pairs may stay together for many years, calling to each other at night. The bird's loud, shrill call, especially the male's, carries far through the dark forest and gives the kiwi its name. Wild kiwi can live 25 to 50 years, a long lifespan for a bird of its size.

sections.heading: Why kiwi are threatened
sections.body: Kiwi are listed as Vulnerable, with several species declining and the status varying from one species to another. Their greatest threat comes from introduced predators such as stoats, dogs, and cats, which kill huge numbers of chicks and adults each year. Habitat loss has also shrunk their range since human settlement. Intensive conservation, including predator control and 'Operation Nest Egg', in which eggs are hatched in safety and chicks released once large enough to defend themselves, is central to saving them.

faqs.question: Can a kiwi fly?
faqs.answer: No. The kiwi is flightless, with wings so small they are hidden in its shaggy feathers. It lives entirely on the ground, using strong legs to run and forage across the forest floor.

faqs.question: Why does the kiwi have nostrils at the end of its beak?
faqs.answer: The kiwi is the only bird with nostrils at the tip of its bill. This gives it a superb sense of smell for detecting earthworms, grubs, and insects underground, which it probes for at night.

faqs.question: What does a kiwi eat?
faqs.answer: The kiwi is an omnivore that eats mainly earthworms and insect larvae, along with berries, seeds, and other invertebrates. It forages at night, sniffing prey out of the soil and leaf litter.

faqs.question: Where do kiwi live?
faqs.answer: Kiwi live only in New Zealand, in native forest, scrubland, and farmland with plenty of cover. They are nocturnal and spend the day hidden in burrows, emerging after dark to feed.

faqs.question: How long do kiwi live?
faqs.answer: Wild kiwi can live between 25 and 50 years, which is remarkably long for a bird of their size. Their slow reproduction, with just one or two large eggs at a time, is offset by this long life.

faqs.question: Why are kiwi endangered?
faqs.answer: Kiwi are Vulnerable mainly because of introduced predators such as stoats, dogs, and cats, which kill many chicks and adults. Habitat loss has added to the decline, and conservation now relies heavily on predator control and captive-rearing programmes.

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Native forest, scrubland, and farmland with cover

range.nativeRange: New Zealand only — native to both main islands and several offshore islands; found nowhere else on Earth.

animals.name: Northern Mockingbird
animals.summary: The northern mockingbird (Mimus polyglottos) is a medium-sized grey North American songbird famous for extraordinary vocal mimicry — it can learn and replicate 200 or more songs, calls, and sounds, including other birds, frogs, insects, and even car alarms. Unmated males may sing continuously through the night during breeding season.

sections.heading: The master mimic
sections.body: The northern mockingbird is one of the most accomplished vocal mimics in the animal kingdom. It can learn and perform more than 200 distinct songs, calls, and environmental sounds during its lifetime, adding new ones continuously. The Latin name Mimus polyglottos means 'many-tongued mimic.' It does not simply copy sounds once — it integrates them into long, complex sequences, cycling through its repertoire and repeating each phrase several times before switching to the next. Individuals with larger repertoires attract mates more successfully, so mimicry is a genuine fitness signal.

sections.heading: Night singing and territorial defence
sections.body: Mockingbirds are highly territorial and will vigorously defend their area against much larger birds and animals, sometimes dive-bombing cats, dogs, and people who approach their nest. Unmated males sing continuously through the night during breeding season — a behaviour admired by some and a source of sleep complaints from others. Once paired, night singing typically decreases. Their territoriality is intense enough that they will memorise and respond aggressively to specific individual people they identify as a threat.

sections.heading: Appearance and range
sections.body: The northern mockingbird is a slender songbird with grey upper parts, whitish underparts, and white patches on its wings that flash conspicuously in flight. It is widespread across the continental United States, southern Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean, and is a year-round resident in most of its range — it does not make long migrations. It is the official state bird of five US states.

sections.heading: Diet and wing-flashing
sections.body: Mockingbirds shift their diet by season. In summer they eat mainly insects; in autumn and winter they switch to berries, fruit, and seeds. They forage on the ground with a distinctive run-and-stop style, and often spread their wings open in a display that may startle insects into moving, making them easier to catch. This wing-flashing behaviour is also used in territorial displays.

faqs.question: How many songs can a mockingbird imitate?
faqs.answer: Individual northern mockingbirds can learn over 200 distinct songs and sounds during their lifetime, and they keep adding new ones. Males generally have larger repertoires than females and use their song range to attract mates and defend territory.

faqs.question: Why do mockingbirds sing at night?
faqs.answer: Unmated males sing at night — particularly under bright conditions like a full moon or near streetlights — to advertise their availability to females. Once paired, night singing usually stops. The behaviour peaks in spring and early summer.

faqs.question: Are mockingbirds aggressive?
faqs.answer: Yes — they are notably territorial and will dive-bomb and physically strike animals many times their size, including cats, dogs, hawks, and people, if they perceive a threat to their nest. The attacks are genuine and can include contact.

faqs.question: Which states have the mockingbird as their state bird?
faqs.answer: The northern mockingbird is the official state bird of Arkansas, Florida, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Texas.

faqs.question: What does the mockingbird eat?
faqs.answer: In warm months mockingbirds eat mainly insects; in autumn and winter they rely more on berries, fruit, and seeds. They are versatile omnivores that forage on the ground and in shrubs, and their diet shifts with seasonal availability.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Omnivore (insects in summer, berries in winter)

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Open woodland, gardens, parks, suburban areas, scrub

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: Up to 8 years in the wild

range.nativeRange: Widespread across the continental United States, southern Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean year-round.

animals.name: European Robin
animals.summary: The European robin (Erithacus rubecula) is a small, round garden bird instantly known by its orange-red breast and face. Found across woodland, gardens, parks, and hedgerows throughout Britain and Europe, it measures about 14 cm long and weighs just 16 to 22 g. This bold, territorial omnivore eats insects, worms, seeds, and berries, and though many die young it can live up to 8 years. It is listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Appearance and identification
sections.body: The robin is a plump little bird about 14 cm long with a wingspan of 20 to 22 cm and a weight of only 16 to 22 g. Its warm orange-red breast and face, bordered by soft blue-grey, make it one of the easiest garden birds to recognise. Males and females look alike, so the sexes cannot be told apart by plumage. Young robins lack the red altogether and are speckled brown, which helps protect them from territorial adults.

sections.heading: Territory and bold behaviour
sections.body: Robins are fiercely territorial and will defend a patch year-round, one of the few British birds to hold territory and sing through the winter. The red breast is a signal used in disputes, and males may fight vigorously, occasionally to the death, over boundaries. Their tameness towards people is famous: a robin will often follow a gardener closely to snatch worms and grubs turned up by the spade. This habit grew from a natural instinct to follow large animals such as wild boar that disturb the soil.

sections.heading: Song and communication
sections.body: The robin has a sweet, wistful, warbling song delivered from an exposed perch throughout much of the year. Both males and females sing in autumn and winter to hold feeding territories, which is unusual among songbirds. In spring the male's song becomes richer and more urgent as he advertises for a mate. Robins will even sing at night under streetlights, sometimes mistaken for a nightingale.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: The European robin is an omnivore that feeds heavily on insects, spiders, and earthworms, especially in the breeding season. In autumn and winter it turns more to seeds, fruit, and berries, and readily visits garden feeders and bird tables. It hunts by perching low, watching the ground, then dropping to seize prey. Robins are among the first birds to visit freshly dug soil in search of exposed invertebrates.

sections.heading: Nesting and breeding
sections.body: Robins nest low down in sheltered spots, from ivy and hedge banks to sheds, kettles, and old boots left in a garden. The female builds a cup of moss, leaves, and hair and lays a clutch of four to six eggs, often raising two or more broods a season. Chicks fledge after about two weeks but rely on their parents for a while longer. Many robins die in their first year, which is why the average lifespan is short even though individuals can reach 8 years.

sections.heading: Cultural role and status
sections.body: The robin is Britain's unofficial national bird and a fixture of Christmas cards, a link that dates to Victorian postmen in red coats nicknamed 'robins'. It is a common and widespread species listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. British robins are largely resident, while many from colder parts of Europe migrate south and west for winter. Continental robins tend to be shyer than the confiding birds of British gardens.

faqs.question: How long do European robins live?
faqs.answer: A robin can live up to about 8 years, but the average lifespan is only around 2 years. High mortality in the first year, from cold, predators, and territorial fights, keeps the typical lifespan short.

faqs.question: What do robins eat?
faqs.answer: Robins are omnivores that eat insects, spiders, and earthworms, along with seeds, fruit, and berries. In winter they rely more on seeds and readily visit garden feeders and bird tables.

faqs.question: Are male and female robins different?
faqs.answer: No, male and female robins look identical, both showing the same orange-red breast and face. They cannot be reliably told apart by appearance. Young robins are speckled brown and lack the red until their first autumn.

faqs.question: Why are robins so tame around people?
faqs.answer: Robins follow gardeners to grab worms and grubs turned up by digging. This comes from a natural habit of trailing large animals like wild boar that disturb the soil, which people have replaced in the garden.

faqs.question: Do robins sing in winter?
faqs.answer: Yes. Robins are one of the few British birds to sing throughout winter, when both males and females defend feeding territories. Their song can even be heard at night near streetlights.

faqs.question: Why is the robin linked to Christmas?
faqs.answer: The connection dates to Victorian Britain, when postmen wore red coats and were nicknamed 'robins'. The bird began appearing on Christmas cards delivered by these postmen, and the association has stuck ever since.

range.nativeRange: Woodland, gardens, and parks across Europe, parts of North Africa, and western Asia; resident throughout the UK year-round.

animals.name: Magpie
animals.summary: The magpie (Pica pica) is a bold, black-and-white member of the crow family found across farmland, woodland edges, parks, and suburbs. Around 45 cm long with a 52–60 cm wingspan and a long iridescent tail, it is one of the most intelligent of all birds. Magpies are opportunistic omnivores that typically live about five years, though some reach 21.

sections.heading: Intelligence and self-awareness
sections.body: Magpies are among the cleverest birds in the world, with a large brain relative to body size. In a famous experiment, magpies became one of the very few non-mammal species to pass the mirror self-recognition test, appearing to understand that the reflection was themselves. They solve problems, plan ahead, and remember complex social relationships within their flocks. Such cognitive skill puts them alongside their crow-family relatives as feathered problem-solvers.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: The magpie is an omnivore that eats insects, worms, seeds, fruit, carrion, scraps, and the eggs and chicks of other birds. This raiding of nests has given magpies an unfair reputation, though studies show it has little effect on overall songbird numbers. Their varied diet lets them thrive in farmland, hedgerows, parks, and gardens alike. Magpies readily exploit human food waste and often forage boldly around towns and roadsides.

sections.heading: The myth of the thieving magpie
sections.body: Magpies have long been accused of stealing and hoarding shiny objects, a belief cemented by opera and folklore. In reality, research suggests wild magpies are more wary than attracted when confronted with shiny items, and there is little evidence of genuine treasure-hoarding. The birds do cache food, hiding surplus to eat later, which may be the root of the legend. Their reputation as thieves is largely a human story rather than a fact of magpie behaviour.

sections.heading: Behaviour and social life
sections.body: Magpies are noisy, sociable birds that pair for the long term and defend a territory throughout the year. Non-breeding birds may gather in loose flocks, and large numbers sometimes assemble in dramatic communal displays known as "parliaments." They chatter with a distinctive rattling call and mob predators such as cats and birds of prey. Bold and curious, they are quick to investigate anything new in their surroundings.

sections.heading: Nesting and reproduction
sections.body: Breeding magpies build a large, domed nest of sticks with a roof to shelter the eggs and young from predators and weather. The female lays a clutch of around six eggs in spring, and both parents help feed the chicks once they hatch. Young magpies stay with their parents for several weeks after fledging before joining flocks of other juveniles. Magpies are listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, and populations across Europe are stable or increasing.

faqs.question: Are magpies really intelligent?
faqs.answer: Yes. Magpies are among the most intelligent birds known and are one of the few non-mammal species to pass the mirror self-recognition test. They solve problems, remember individuals, and navigate complex social relationships within their flocks.

faqs.question: Do magpies actually steal shiny things?
faqs.answer: Probably not in the way folklore suggests. Research indicates wild magpies are more cautious than attracted around shiny objects, and there is little evidence they hoard treasure. The legend may stem from their habit of caching food to eat later.

faqs.question: How long do magpies live?
faqs.answer: Most magpies live about five years, but some survive much longer, with the oldest recorded reaching around 21. Predation and harsh weather mean many young birds do not make it through their first year.

faqs.question: What do magpies eat?
faqs.answer: Magpies are omnivores that eat insects, worms, seeds, fruit, carrion, and food scraps, as well as the eggs and chicks of other birds. This varied diet helps them thrive in farmland, parks, and gardens.

faqs.question: Are magpies bad for other birds?
faqs.answer: Magpies do take eggs and chicks, which gives them a poor reputation, but large-scale studies have found no evidence that they cause declines in songbird populations. Habitat loss and other pressures have far greater effects on garden birds.

faqs.question: Why do magpies gather in groups?
faqs.answer: Outside the breeding season, non-breeding magpies form loose flocks, and they sometimes assemble in noisy gatherings called "parliaments." These groups may be linked to establishing territories and sorting out social rank among the birds.

range.nativeRange: Open countryside with trees, farmland, and towns across Europe, much of temperate Asia, and North Africa.

animals.name: Blackbird
animals.summary: The common blackbird (Turdus merula) is a familiar garden thrush across Europe, prized for its rich, fluting song. The male is glossy black with a bright orange-yellow bill and eye-ring, while the female is dark brown. About 27 cm (11 in) long and weighing 80 to 125 g, it forages for worms and berries in gardens, woodland, parks, and hedgerows. Most live only a few years, though some reach 20 or more, and the IUCN lists the species as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Appearance and sexes
sections.body: The blackbird shows clear differences between the sexes. The male is entirely glossy black with a striking orange-yellow bill and a matching ring around the eye, while the female is a warm dark brown, often with faint mottling on the breast. Young birds resemble the female but are more rufous and spotted. Measuring about 27 cm (11 in) long with a wingspan of 34 to 39 cm and weighing 80 to 125 g, it is a medium-sized, round-bodied thrush.

sections.heading: The blackbird's song
sections.body: The blackbird is one of the finest songsters of the European countryside and gardens, and its music is a large part of its fame. The male sings a rich, mellow, flute-like series of phrases, typically from a high perch, most intensely at dawn and dusk through the breeding season. The song is varied and improvised, with birds often weaving in imitations of other sounds. Alongside the song, blackbirds give sharp alarm calls and a low chuckling when disturbed.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: Blackbirds are omnivores with a diet that shifts through the year. In spring and summer they hunt earthworms and insects, running and hopping across lawns and cocking their heads to listen and watch for movement before pulling prey from the soil. In autumn and winter they turn to berries and fallen fruit, and they readily visit gardens for windfall apples and food put out for them. This flexible diet is one reason they thrive so well alongside people.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The common blackbird is widespread across Europe and into parts of Asia and North Africa, and has been introduced to Australia and New Zealand. Originally a woodland bird, it has adapted superbly to gardens, parks, and hedgerows, and is now one of the most familiar birds of towns and suburbs. It forages on the ground in open, grassy areas but retreats to shrubs and trees for cover and nesting. This adaptability has made it abundant across much of its range.

sections.heading: Nesting and breeding
sections.body: Blackbirds build a neat cup nest of grass, twigs, and mud, usually hidden in a shrub, hedge, or climbing plant. The female incubates a clutch of blue-green, speckled eggs, and both parents feed the chicks a steady supply of worms and insects. A pair often raises two or three broods in a single season, from early spring into summer. The young leave the nest before they can fly well and are fed by the parents for a while as they find their feet.

sections.heading: Lifespan and status
sections.body: Life is short for most blackbirds, with the average bird living only about three to four years, largely because young birds face many hazards. Those that survive their first year can live much longer, with the oldest individuals reaching 20 years or more. The species is abundant and adaptable, and the IUCN lists it as Least Concern. Its success in gardens and parks means people encounter it more often than almost any other thrush.

faqs.question: Why is the male blackbird black and the female brown?
faqs.answer: Only the male has the glossy all-black plumage with an orange-yellow bill and eye-ring. The female is dark brown, often with faint mottling on the breast, which gives her better camouflage while sitting on the nest.

faqs.question: What does a blackbird eat?
faqs.answer: Blackbirds are omnivores. In spring and summer they eat mainly earthworms and insects taken from the ground, and in autumn and winter they switch to berries and fallen fruit, including windfall apples in gardens.

faqs.question: Why do blackbirds sing so much?
faqs.answer: Males sing to defend a territory and attract a mate, especially through the breeding season. Their rich, flute-like song is most intense at dawn and dusk and is considered one of the finest of any European bird.

faqs.question: How long do blackbirds live?
faqs.answer: Most blackbirds live only about three to four years on average, as young birds face many hazards. Those that survive can live far longer, with the oldest reaching 20 years or more.

faqs.question: Where do blackbirds build their nests?
faqs.answer: They build a cup-shaped nest of grass, twigs, and mud, usually well hidden in a shrub, hedge, or climbing plant. A pair often raises two or three broods between early spring and summer.

faqs.question: Are blackbirds common?
faqs.answer: Yes. The common blackbird is abundant and highly adaptable, thriving in gardens, parks, woodland, and hedgerows across Europe and beyond. The IUCN lists it as Least Concern.

range.nativeRange: Gardens, woodland, and parks across Europe, North Africa, and western Asia; introduced to Australia and New Zealand.

animals.name: Crow
animals.summary: The American crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos) is a large, glossy-black songbird found across farmland, woodland, parks, and cities in North America. It weighs 300–600 g, spans 85–100 cm across the wings, and ranks among the most intelligent of all birds. Crows are opportunistic omnivores that live in tight family groups and typically survive 7–8 years in the wild, though some reach 16 or more.

sections.heading: Intelligence and problem-solving
sections.body: Crows are among the smartest animals on the planet, with problem-solving abilities that rival those of some primates. They fashion and use simple tools, remember individual human faces for years, and can hold what looks like a grudge against people who have threatened them. Captive and wild birds have both been recorded dropping hard-shelled nuts onto roads so that passing cars crack them open, then waiting for a safe gap in traffic to retrieve the food.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: The crow is a true generalist, eating grain, insects, earthworms, carrion, eggs, small animals, and human scraps. This flexible menu is a big reason the species thrives everywhere from remote fields to busy city centres. Crows cache surplus food, hiding it under leaves or in bark crevices to recover later, and they watch other birds closely to steal from poorly hidden stores. Around rubbish bins and car parks they have learned to exploit almost any edible waste people leave behind.

sections.heading: Family life and roosts
sections.body: Crows are highly social and often live in extended family groups, with young from previous years helping their parents raise the next brood. Outside the breeding season, thousands may gather at communal night roosts, streaming in from miles around at dusk. These roosts offer safety in numbers and may help birds share information about good feeding sites. Family members preen one another and defend a shared territory throughout the year.

sections.heading: Communication and calls
sections.body: The familiar harsh "caw" is only part of a crow's vocabulary, which includes rattles, clicks, and surprisingly soft, musical notes. Crows use different calls to raise the alarm, rally the group, or scold a predator, and they can recognise the individual voices of their relatives. When a hawk, owl, or cat appears, a mob of crows will gather to harass it noisily until it moves on. Some birds even mimic other species and mechanical sounds.

sections.heading: Range and adaptability
sections.body: American crows are found across most of North America, absent only from the far north and the driest deserts. They readily colonise farmland, woodland edges, suburbs, and city parks, and their numbers have grown as they exploit human landscapes. Crows are listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, reflecting a large and stable population. The species did suffer local declines from West Nile virus, but populations have largely recovered.

faqs.question: How intelligent are crows?
faqs.answer: Crows are among the most intelligent birds known, capable of using tools, solving multi-step puzzles, and recognising individual human faces. Their reasoning skills are often compared to those of great apes, and they can plan ahead and remember hidden food for long periods.

faqs.question: How long do crows live?
faqs.answer: Wild crows typically live about 7–8 years, though many survive well beyond that, with some reaching 16 or more. In captivity, protected from predators and disease, they can live even longer.

faqs.question: What do crows eat?
faqs.answer: Crows are omnivores with an extremely varied diet, including grain, insects, worms, carrion, eggs, small animals, and human food scraps. This adaptability lets them thrive in farmland, woodland, and cities alike.

faqs.question: Can crows really remember faces?
faqs.answer: Yes. Studies have shown that crows remember and react to specific human faces for years, especially people who have threatened or trapped them. They can even pass this recognition on to other crows, which then treat the same person as a threat.

faqs.question: Why do crows gather in large groups?
faqs.answer: Outside the breeding season, crows form huge communal roosts that can number in the thousands. Gathering together offers protection from predators, warmth on cold nights, and possibly a way to share information about good feeding sites.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a crow and a raven?
faqs.answer: Ravens are noticeably larger, with heavier bills, shaggy throat feathers, and a wedge-shaped tail in flight, while crows are slimmer with a fan-shaped tail. Ravens also give a deep croak rather than the crow's higher, sharper "caw."

range.nativeRange: Fields, woodlands, parks, and cities across the United States and Canada.

animals.name: Pigeon
animals.summary: The pigeon (Columba livia), also called the rock dove, is a familiar grey city bird found on every continent except Antarctica. Descended from wild cliff-dwelling doves, it weighs 300 to 500 g and can fly at 90 km/h (56 mph), even faster when racing. Pigeons are famed for an extraordinary homing sense that lets them navigate back over hundreds of miles, and they are listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Origins and appearance
sections.body: The city pigeon is a domesticated and feral form of the wild rock dove, a bird that naturally nests on sea cliffs and rocky ledges. That cliff heritage is why pigeons feel at home on the ledges and window sills of buildings, which mimic their ancestral crags. Typical birds are grey with two dark wing bars and a glossy green-and-purple neck, though centuries of domestication have produced many colours and patterns.

sections.heading: Homing and navigation
sections.body: Pigeons possess one of the most remarkable navigation abilities in the animal world, able to find their way home from hundreds of miles away in unfamiliar territory. They appear to combine several senses, including the Earth's magnetic field, the position of the sun, and even smell and low-frequency sound, to build a mental map. This talent made them prized racing and messenger birds, and homing pigeons carried vital messages in both World Wars.

sections.heading: Diet and city life
sections.body: Pigeons are granivores that naturally eat seeds and grain, but in towns they readily scavenge bread, scraps, and other human food. This adaptable diet is a key reason they thrive in cities across the world. They feed in flocks and can drink by sucking water up directly, unlike most birds that must tip their heads back to swallow.

sections.heading: Breeding and crop milk
sections.body: Pigeons breed year-round in mild conditions and usually lay two white eggs at a time. Both parents share incubation and feed their chicks, called squabs, on a rich secretion known as crop milk that is produced in the lining of the crop. This nutritious food lets pigeons raise young even when seeds are scarce, helping them nest repeatedly through the year.

sections.heading: Flight and speed
sections.body: Pigeons are powerful, fast fliers, cruising at around 90 km/h (56 mph) and reaching higher speeds when racing over long distances. Their strong flight muscles and streamlined build let them cover great distances with ease. Racing pigeons bred for speed and endurance can fly home across hundreds of miles in a single day.

sections.heading: Intelligence and lifespan
sections.body: Pigeons are surprisingly intelligent birds that can recognise individual human faces, learn to distinguish letters of the alphabet, and even tell apart paintings by different artists in laboratory tests. In the wild they usually live 3 to 5 years, but well-kept birds can reach around 15 years of age. Widespread and adaptable, the pigeon is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN.

faqs.question: How do pigeons find their way home?
faqs.answer: Pigeons combine several senses to navigate, including detecting the Earth's magnetic field, using the position of the sun, and relying on smell and low-frequency sound. Together these allow a homing pigeon to return from hundreds of miles away in unfamiliar country.

faqs.question: How fast can a pigeon fly?
faqs.answer: Pigeons typically fly at around 90 km/h (56 mph) and can go even faster when racing over long distances. Their strong flight muscles let them cover great distances quickly.

faqs.question: What do pigeons eat?
faqs.answer: Pigeons are seed and grain eaters by nature, but in cities they readily feed on bread, scraps, and other human food. This flexible diet is one reason they thrive in urban areas worldwide.

faqs.question: How long do pigeons live?
faqs.answer: Wild city pigeons usually live around 3 to 5 years, largely because of predators, traffic, and disease. Well-cared-for birds, including racing and pet pigeons, can live up to about 15 years.

faqs.question: Are pigeons intelligent?
faqs.answer: Yes, pigeons are notably intelligent. In laboratory studies they can recognise individual human faces, learn letters of the alphabet, and even distinguish between paintings by different artists.

faqs.question: Why are there so many pigeons in cities?
faqs.answer: City pigeons descend from wild rock doves that nest on cliffs, so building ledges suit them perfectly. Combined with a flexible diet of human food scraps and year-round breeding, this lets them flourish in towns everywhere.

range.nativeRange: The wild rock dove is native to Europe, North Africa, and southwest Asia; feral pigeons now live in cities on every continent except Antarctica.

animals.name: Swan
animals.summary: The mute swan (Cygnus olor) is a large white waterbird of lakes, rivers, ponds, and estuaries across Europe and beyond, and one of the heaviest flying birds. Adults weigh 10 to 12 kg (22 to 26 lb) with a wingspan of 2 to 2.4 m (6.5 to 8 ft), and are known for gliding gracefully on water and pairing for many years. Powerful fliers, they can reach around 80 km/h aloft and commonly live 10 years or more. The IUCN lists them as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Appearance and size
sections.body: The mute swan is unmistakable, with pure white plumage, a long S-curved neck, and an orange bill topped by a black fleshy knob that is larger in males. It is among the heaviest of all flying birds, with adults weighing 10 to 12 kg (22 to 26 lb) and spanning 2 to 2.4 m (6.5 to 8 ft) across the wings. Young birds, called cygnets, are greyish-brown and gradually turn white over their first year. Despite their bulk, adults are strong fliers once airborne.

sections.heading: Flight and movement
sections.body: Getting a bird this heavy into the air takes effort, so swans run and beat their wings across the water surface for a long stretch before lifting off. Once airborne they are surprisingly fast, reaching speeds of around 80 km/h, with slow, powerful wingbeats that produce a distinctive throbbing sound audible from a distance. On water they swim smoothly and can up-end to feed, while on land they walk with an ungainly waddle. Their large webbed feet make them at home on lakes, rivers, and coastal estuaries.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: Swans are herbivores that feed mainly on aquatic vegetation, reaching down with their long necks to graze plants on the bottom of shallow water. They also eat grasses on land and will take grain and other plant matter, and in many parks they readily accept bread, though it is poor nutrition for them. The long neck lets them reach food up to about a metre below the surface without diving. Cygnets feed on the small invertebrates stirred up by the adults as well as on plants.

sections.heading: Breeding and family life
sections.body: Mute swans form strong, long-lasting pair bonds and often stay with the same mate for many years. The pair builds a large mound of vegetation near water, where the female lays a clutch of eggs that both parents guard fiercely. Cygnets hatch able to swim and follow their parents closely, sometimes riding on an adult's back among the feathers for warmth and safety. The family stays together through the first winter before the young disperse to find territories of their own.

sections.heading: Behaviour and temperament
sections.body: Swans are highly territorial during the breeding season and will drive off intruders, including other swans and sometimes people who venture too close to a nest. A threatening bird raises its wings over its back in a display called busking and can deliver forceful blows with its wings and bill. Outside the breeding season they are more social and may gather in large flocks on open water. Their reputation for aggression is real but seasonal, tied mainly to protecting eggs and cygnets.

sections.heading: Range and status
sections.body: The mute swan is native across much of Europe and temperate Asia and has been introduced to North America and elsewhere, where it is now widespread. It thrives on lakes, slow rivers, ponds, and sheltered coasts, and adapts well to parks and other human-modified waters. Populations are generally healthy, and the IUCN lists the species as Least Concern. Individuals commonly live about 10 years in the wild, with some reaching 20 years or more.

faqs.question: How much does a swan weigh?
faqs.answer: Adult mute swans weigh about 10 to 12 kg (22 to 26 lb), making them one of the heaviest flying birds in the world. Males are typically a little larger than females.

faqs.question: Can swans fly, and how fast?
faqs.answer: Yes. Although they need a long running take-off across water to get airborne, swans are strong fliers and can reach speeds of around 80 km/h in flight, with wingbeats that produce a distinctive throbbing sound.

faqs.question: What do swans eat?
faqs.answer: Swans are herbivores. They feed mainly on aquatic plants reached with their long necks, along with grasses and grain. They readily take bread in parks, but it offers them little nutrition.

faqs.question: How long do swans live?
faqs.answer: Mute swans commonly live about 10 years in the wild, and some individuals reach 20 years or more. Well-protected birds in safe habitats tend to live longest.

faqs.question: Do swans mate for life?
faqs.answer: Mute swans form strong pair bonds and often stay with the same mate for many years, sometimes for life. Both parents defend the nest and raise the cygnets together.

faqs.question: Are swans aggressive?
faqs.answer: Swans can be very aggressive when defending a nest or cygnets, raising their wings and striking with wings and bill to drive off intruders. This behaviour is mostly seasonal, and outside breeding they are far more tolerant and often gather in flocks.

range.nativeRange: Lakes, rivers, and coasts across Europe and temperate Asia; widely introduced to North America. Resident across the UK.

animals.name: Goldfish
animals.summary: The goldfish is a small freshwater fish and the world's most popular pet fish, descended from wild carp domesticated in China more than a thousand years ago. Kept in ponds and aquariums, it commonly grows to 10 to 20 cm and swims slowly, cruising rather than darting. Hardy and long-lived, a well-cared-for goldfish often reaches 10 to 15 years and sometimes more than 20.

sections.heading: Origins and domestication
sections.body: Goldfish are a domesticated form of a plain grey-brown carp native to East Asia. Keepers in imperial China began selecting for unusually coloured individuals more than a thousand years ago, gradually fixing the orange and gold hues we recognise today. From there the fish spread to Japan and eventually to Europe, becoming a fixture of ornamental ponds and, later, the home aquarium. Every fancy goldfish traces back to that single ancestral species, Carassius auratus.

sections.heading: Breeds and varieties
sections.body: Centuries of selective breeding have produced a remarkable range of goldfish varieties. Common and comet goldfish keep the streamlined body of their wild ancestor, while fancy breeds such as the fantail, oranda, ryukin, and bubble-eye have rounded bodies, flowing fins, or dramatic head growths. Colours range from bright orange and red through white, black, and calico patterning. The more ornate breeds are generally slower swimmers and need calmer, warmer conditions than the hardy single-tailed types.

sections.heading: Feeding and care
sections.body: Goldfish are omnivores that do well on a varied diet of prepared flakes or pellets supplemented with vegetables, and small live or frozen foods. They have no true stomach and are prone to overfeeding, so small, regular portions suit them best. Because they are messy feeders that produce a lot of waste, they need a well-filtered, spacious tank or pond with good water quality. Contrary to a common myth, a cramped bowl is unsuitable; goldfish need far more space than most people assume.

sections.heading: Swimming and behaviour
sections.body: Goldfish are gentle, slow-moving swimmers that spend much of the day cruising and foraging along the bottom and among plants. They are social and often more active and confident when kept in groups. Surprisingly bright for a fish, goldfish can learn to recognise their owners, respond to feeding routines, and even be trained to perform simple tasks. Their memory is far better than the popular three-second myth suggests, spanning weeks or months.

sections.heading: Size and lifespan
sections.body: In a small aquarium a goldfish typically reaches 10 to 20 cm, but in a spacious pond it can grow considerably larger. Good conditions matter enormously for how long they live: a healthy goldfish commonly reaches 10 to 15 years, and some have passed 20 or even 30. Cool, clean, well-oxygenated water and a proper diet are the keys to a long life. Most goldfish that die young do so because of poor water quality or cramped housing rather than natural causes.

sections.heading: Goldfish in ponds
sections.body: Goldfish are popular garden pond fish because they are hardy and tolerate a wide range of temperatures. In a well-established outdoor pond they can survive cold winters by slowing their metabolism as the water cools, resting near the bottom below the ice. Pond-kept goldfish often grow larger and live longer than aquarium fish thanks to the extra space and natural food. Because they breed readily and can disrupt native wildlife, however, they should never be released into wild waterways.

faqs.question: How long do goldfish live?
faqs.answer: With good care, goldfish commonly live 10 to 15 years, and some reach 20 or more. Poor water quality and cramped housing, rather than old age, are the usual reasons they die young.

faqs.question: How big do goldfish get?
faqs.answer: In an aquarium goldfish usually grow to 10 to 20 cm, but in a spacious pond they can become considerably larger. Their final size depends heavily on the space, water quality, and diet they are given.

faqs.question: Do goldfish really have a three-second memory?
faqs.answer: No, that is a myth. Goldfish can remember things for weeks or months, learn feeding routines, and even recognise the person who feeds them.

faqs.question: Can a goldfish live in a bowl?
faqs.answer: A small bowl is not suitable for a goldfish. They produce a lot of waste and need a spacious, well-filtered tank or pond with plenty of oxygen to stay healthy.

faqs.question: What do goldfish eat?
faqs.answer: Goldfish are omnivores that thrive on prepared flakes or pellets supplemented with vegetables and small live or frozen foods. Because they have no true stomach, they should be fed small amounts regularly rather than one large meal.

faqs.question: Where do goldfish come from?
faqs.answer: Goldfish were domesticated in China from a wild grey-brown carp more than a thousand years ago. Selective breeding for colour and body shape produced the ornamental fish kept around the world today.

range.nativeRange: Domesticated from wild carp in East Asia and now kept in ponds and aquariums worldwide.

animals.name: Betta Fish
animals.summary: The betta, or Siamese fighting fish (Betta splendens), is a small, brilliantly coloured freshwater fish originally from the shallow ponds, rice paddies, and slow streams of Southeast Asia. Domesticated for centuries, it is now one of the world's most popular aquarium fish, prized for flowing fins and vivid colours. Bettas grow to about 6–8 cm and usually live 2–4 years in home aquariums.

sections.heading: Origins and domestication
sections.body: Betta splendens has been kept and bred in Thailand for well over a century, first for the sport of fish fighting and later for its ornamental beauty. Selective breeding has transformed the plain, dull-brown wild fish into hundreds of colour and fin varieties, from crimson veiltails to iridescent blue halfmoons. The name "Siamese fighting fish" comes from the males' natural aggression toward one another. Today the domesticated betta is a global aquarium staple, quite different in appearance from its wild ancestors in Southeast Asia. While the pet betta is everywhere, the wild Betta splendens is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, as the shallow wetlands it depends on are lost to farming and development.

sections.heading: The labyrinth organ and breathing air
sections.body: Bettas possess a special breathing structure called the labyrinth organ, which lets them gulp oxygen directly from the air at the water's surface. This adaptation evolved for life in warm, shallow, oxygen-poor water such as rice paddies and stagnant pools. It means a betta must have access to the surface to breathe and cannot rely on gills alone. The same trait allows the fish to survive in conditions that would suffocate many other species.

sections.heading: Temperament and territory
sections.body: Male bettas are famously territorial and will flare their gills and fins, or fight, when they meet another male. In an aquarium two males should never be housed together, as confrontations can be fatal. Bettas swim in short, darting bursts rather than long steady cruises, patrolling and defending their patch of water. Many become surprisingly responsive to their keepers, learning to follow a finger and rise to the surface at feeding time.

sections.heading: Feeding and care
sections.body: The betta is a carnivore that in the wild eats insects, larvae, and tiny aquatic invertebrates. In captivity it thrives on protein-rich pellets, frozen or live bloodworms, brine shrimp, and daphnia. Bettas need warm water, ideally around 24–27 °C, and do best in a heated, gently filtered tank rather than an unheated bowl. Good water quality and a varied diet are key to keeping the fish healthy through its 2–4 year lifespan.

sections.heading: Breeding and bubble nests
sections.body: Breeding bettas is a striking process centred on the bubble nest, a raft of saliva-coated air bubbles the male builds at the surface. After an elaborate courtship, the male wraps around the female to fertilise her eggs, then gathers them in his mouth and places each one in the nest. He alone guards the nest and tends the eggs and newly hatched fry, chasing the female away. This devoted paternal care is one of the most fascinating aspects of keeping the species.

faqs.question: How long do betta fish live?
faqs.answer: Betta fish usually live 2–4 years in a home aquarium. Good water quality, a heated tank, and a varied protein-rich diet give a betta the best chance of reaching the upper end of that range.

faqs.question: Can two betta fish live together?
faqs.answer: Two male bettas should never share a tank, as they are highly territorial and will fight, sometimes to the death. Females can sometimes be kept together in a group, but pairs are only brought together briefly for breeding.

faqs.question: Do betta fish really breathe air?
faqs.answer: Yes. Bettas have a special organ called the labyrinth that lets them gulp oxygen from the air at the surface. This is why they can survive in warm, shallow, low-oxygen water, but it also means they must be able to reach the surface to breathe.

faqs.question: What do betta fish eat?
faqs.answer: Bettas are carnivores. In the wild they eat insects and small aquatic invertebrates, and in aquariums they do best on high-protein betta pellets supplemented with frozen or live bloodworms, brine shrimp, and daphnia.

faqs.question: Do betta fish need a heater?
faqs.answer: Yes. Bettas are tropical fish that need warm, stable water of roughly 24–27 °C. An unheated bowl at room temperature is too cold and stressful, so a heated, gently filtered tank is far better for their health.

faqs.question: Why is the betta called a fighting fish?
faqs.answer: The name comes from the intense aggression male bettas show toward one another, flaring and fighting on sight. In Thailand this behaviour was once the basis of an organised betting sport, which drove the fish's early domestication and breeding.

range.nativeRange: Shallow rice paddies, ditches, and slow streams of Thailand, Cambodia, and neighboring Southeast Asia.

animals.name: Atlantic Salmon
animals.summary: The Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) is a powerful migratory fish of the North Atlantic, hatching in rivers, maturing at sea, and returning upstream to spawn. Adults typically weigh 3 to 15 kg (7 to 33 lb) and can swim in bursts of around 40 km/h (25 mph), leaping waterfalls on their way home. Wild salmon usually live 4 to 8 years and are listed as Least Concern, though many local populations are in serious decline.

sections.heading: The upstream migration
sections.body: Atlantic salmon are famous for returning from the ocean to spawn in the very river where they hatched, often the exact stretch of gravel. To reach the spawning grounds they swim upriver against strong currents and leap over waterfalls and rapids, reaching burst speeds of around 40 km/h (25 mph). They appear to navigate using the Earth's magnetic field on the open ocean and then their sense of smell to pick out their home river.

sections.heading: From freshwater to sea and back
sections.body: Salmon begin life in freshwater, where young fish called parr spend one to several years before a bodily transformation, called smolting, prepares them to survive in salt water. They then migrate downstream and out into the North Atlantic to feed and grow. After one or more years at sea they return as mature adults to spawn, completing a life cycle that spans both river and ocean.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: Atlantic salmon are carnivores whose diet changes with age. Young fish in rivers eat aquatic insects, larvae, and other small invertebrates. At sea, adults feed on small fish such as herring, sand eels, and capelin, along with crustaceans that help give their flesh its pink colour. Once they enter their home river to spawn, adults largely stop feeding and live off stored reserves.

sections.heading: Spawning and the next generation
sections.body: On the spawning grounds, the female uses her tail to dig a gravel nest called a redd, where she lays her eggs for the male to fertilise. Unlike Pacific salmon, some Atlantic salmon survive spawning and return to the sea to breed again in later years. The buried eggs hatch into tiny alevins that live off their yolk sac before emerging as fry to begin the cycle anew.

sections.heading: Size and lifespan
sections.body: Adult Atlantic salmon typically weigh 3 to 15 kg (7 to 33 lb) and can reach around 0.9 m (3 ft) in length, with the largest specimens considerably bigger. Their lifespan is usually 4 to 8 years, split between their years in the river and their time feeding at sea. Fish that survive to spawn more than once tend to be among the largest and oldest individuals.

sections.heading: Conservation and threats
sections.body: Although the Atlantic salmon is listed as Least Concern globally by the IUCN, many wild populations have fallen sharply. Dams that block migration routes, pollution, warming waters, overfishing, and interbreeding and disease from fish farms all put pressure on wild stocks. Removing river barriers, improving water quality, and managing fisheries are key to helping these iconic migratory fish recover.

faqs.question: Why do salmon swim upstream?
faqs.answer: Salmon swim upstream to return to the freshwater rivers where they hatched in order to spawn. Reaching clean, oxygen-rich gravel beds gives their eggs the best chance of survival, so the fish battle currents and leap waterfalls to get there.

faqs.question: How do salmon find their home river?
faqs.answer: Salmon are thought to navigate the open ocean using the Earth's magnetic field, then switch to their acute sense of smell as they near the coast. This lets them home in on the unique scent of the river, and often the exact stream, where they were born.

faqs.question: How big do Atlantic salmon get?
faqs.answer: Adult Atlantic salmon typically weigh 3 to 15 kg (7 to 33 lb) and grow to around 0.9 m (3 ft) long. The very largest fish, which have spent longer at sea, can be considerably heavier.

faqs.question: What do Atlantic salmon eat?
faqs.answer: They are carnivores. Young salmon in rivers eat insects and small invertebrates, while adults at sea feed on small fish such as herring and sand eels, plus crustaceans. Adults largely stop eating once they enter their home river to spawn.

faqs.question: How long do salmon live?
faqs.answer: Wild Atlantic salmon usually live 4 to 8 years, divided between their early years in freshwater and their feeding years at sea. Unlike Pacific salmon, some Atlantic salmon survive spawning and return to breed again.

faqs.question: Are Atlantic salmon endangered?
faqs.answer: Globally the Atlantic salmon is listed as Least Concern, but many individual wild populations have declined severely. Dams, pollution, warming rivers, overfishing, and impacts from fish farms are the main threats to wild stocks.

range.nativeRange: Rivers and coastal waters of the North Atlantic, from northeastern North America to Europe.
