animals.name: Boa Constrictor
animals.summary: The boa constrictor (Boa constrictor) is a large, heavy-bodied, non-venomous snake native to tropical forests, savannas, and deserts across Central and South America. It typically reaches 2 to 3 m and weighs around 10 to 15 kg, killing prey not with venom but by coiling around it and squeezing until it can no longer breathe. A slow-moving ambush hunter, the boa can live 20 to 30 years and is listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Size and appearance
sections.body: The boa constrictor is a thick, muscular snake that commonly grows to 2 to 3 m, with females larger than males and weighing up to around 15 kg. Its background colour ranges from tan and brown to grey, overlaid with distinctive dark saddle-shaped markings that deepen to reddish tones towards the tail, giving rise to the nickname red-tailed boa. This patterning is superb camouflage among leaf litter and dappled forest light. Unlike venomous snakes, it has a narrow head only slightly wider than its neck and no fangs.

sections.heading: How it kills by constriction
sections.body: The boa constrictor is non-venomous and kills entirely by constriction, as its name suggests. It seizes prey with backward-curving teeth, then throws several coils of its powerful body around the animal. Rather than crushing bones, the snake tightens its grip each time the prey exhales, cutting off blood flow and breathing until the animal quickly loses consciousness. It then swallows the meal whole, head first, its jaws stretching around prey far wider than its own head.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: Boas are carnivores that eat a wide range of warm-blooded prey, from rodents, birds, and bats to lizards and larger mammals such as opossums. They are ambush hunters, lying still and camouflaged before striking with a rapid lunge. Heat-sensitive scales around the mouth help them detect the body warmth of prey in darkness. After a large meal a boa may not need to feed again for weeks.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The boa constrictor ranges widely across Central and South America and some Caribbean islands, occupying a remarkable variety of habitats. It is found in tropical rainforest, dry woodland, savanna grassland, and semi-desert scrub, from sea level into the hills. Young boas often climb into trees and shrubs, while heavier adults spend more time on the ground, frequently near water. This adaptability across so many habitats is one reason the species remains widespread.

sections.heading: Reproduction and young
sections.body: Boa constrictors give birth to live young rather than laying eggs, a trait known as ovoviviparity. The female carries the developing embryos internally and delivers a litter that can number a couple of dozen fully formed babies, each around 40 to 50 cm long. The young are independent from birth, receiving no parental care, and begin hunting small prey almost at once. They grow steadily over several years before reaching breeding size.

sections.heading: Conservation and people
sections.body: The boa constrictor is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, reflecting its wide range and adaptability, though some local populations are pressured by hunting for the skin trade and collection for pets. It is one of the most familiar snakes in captivity, valued in the reptile hobby for its manageable temperament and striking pattern. Introduced boas have also established themselves in a few places outside their native range. Habitat loss is the main long-term concern for wild populations.

faqs.question: Are boa constrictors venomous?
faqs.answer: No. Boa constrictors are non-venomous and have no fangs or venom. They kill prey entirely by constriction, coiling around the animal and tightening until it can no longer breathe.

faqs.question: How big do boa constrictors get?
faqs.answer: Boa constrictors typically reach 2 to 3 m in length and weigh around 10 to 15 kg. Females grow noticeably larger and heavier than males, and exceptional individuals can be longer still.

faqs.question: What do boa constrictors eat?
faqs.answer: Boa constrictors are carnivores that eat warm-blooded prey such as rodents, birds, bats, lizards, and larger mammals like opossums. They ambush their prey, seize it, and kill it by constriction before swallowing it whole.

faqs.question: How does a boa constrictor kill its prey?
faqs.answer: It grips the prey with its teeth and wraps several coils of its body around it, then squeezes tighter each time the animal breathes out. This cuts off blood flow and breathing, and the prey loses consciousness within moments before being swallowed whole.

faqs.question: Do boa constrictors lay eggs?
faqs.answer: No. Boa constrictors give birth to live young rather than laying eggs. A female carries the developing babies internally and delivers a litter of up to a couple of dozen fully formed young, which are independent from birth.

faqs.question: How long do boa constrictors live?
faqs.answer: Boa constrictors commonly live 20 to 30 years. Well-kept animals in captivity often reach the upper end of that range, and some live even longer with good care.

range.nativeRange: Tropical forests, savannas, and deserts from Mexico through Central and South America.

animals.name: Gila Monster
animals.summary: The Gila monster is a large, slow-moving venomous lizard of the deserts and scrubland of the south-western United States and north-western Mexico. It grows to about 0.6 m (2 ft) and 0.7 kg, with black skin marbled by pink or orange beading. It walks with a heavy, deliberate gait and delivers venom by chewing rather than striking. Listed as Near Threatened, it can live 20 years or more.

sections.heading: Appearance and identification
sections.body: The Gila monster is unmistakable, its dark body covered in bead-like scales called osteoderms patterned in pink, orange, and salmon against black. It is one of the heaviest lizards native to the United States, reaching roughly 0.5 to 0.6 m (up to 2 ft) and about 0.7 kg. The thick, sausage-shaped tail acts as a fat store, swelling after good feeding and shrinking during lean months. Its bright colouring is a warning signal, advertising to predators that the animal is venomous.

sections.heading: Venom and its bite
sections.body: Unlike snakes that inject venom through hollow fangs, the Gila monster has grooved teeth in its lower jaw and works venom into a wound by chewing and holding on. The venom is a neurotoxin that causes intense pain, swelling, and a drop in blood pressure, but bites are rarely dangerous to healthy adults. Because the lizard is slow and reluctant to bite, almost all envenomations happen when people deliberately handle it. A compound first identified in its venom, exendin-4, inspired the diabetes drug exenatide.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: The Gila monster is a carnivore that feeds mainly on the eggs of birds and reptiles, along with nestling rodents, young rabbits, and the occasional small lizard. It relies on a keen sense of smell, flicking its forked tongue to track prey and raid nests. Because meals are seasonal and unpredictable, it eats enormously when food is available, consuming up to a third of its body weight in a single sitting. Fat stored in the tail and body then sustains it through long fasts.

sections.heading: Habitat and behaviour
sections.body: This lizard lives in the Sonoran, Mojave, and Chihuahuan deserts, favouring rocky foothills, scrubland, and areas near seasonal washes. It spends the great majority of its life underground in burrows, emerging for only a few weeks a year, mostly after spring rains. Active by day in the mild months and at dusk in the heat of summer, it walks slowly and rarely ventures far from shelter. Its low metabolism suits a life of long inactivity punctuated by brief bursts of feeding and breeding.

sections.heading: Lifespan and reproduction
sections.body: Gila monsters are long-lived for lizards, commonly reaching 20 years or more in the wild and longer in captivity. Mating takes place in spring, and the female lays a clutch of around two to twelve eggs in summer, burying them in a burrow. The eggs incubate underground over winter and hatch the following spring, with young emerging fully independent. This slow reproductive pace means populations recover only gradually from losses.

sections.heading: Conservation status
sections.body: The Gila monster is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN and is legally protected across much of its range, including in the state of Arizona. Its main threats are habitat loss from development, road deaths, and illegal collection for the exotic pet trade. Because it breeds slowly and occupies fragmented desert habitat, local populations are vulnerable to disturbance. Legal protection and habitat conservation are the main tools keeping numbers stable.

faqs.question: Is the Gila monster venomous?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is one of only a handful of venomous lizards and delivers a neurotoxic venom through grooved teeth in its lower jaw. The bite is very painful but rarely dangerous to a healthy adult, and the lizard is too slow to be a threat unless handled.

faqs.question: How big does a Gila monster get?
faqs.answer: Adults reach around 0.5 to 0.6 m (up to 2 ft) in total length and weigh about 0.7 kg. This makes the Gila monster one of the largest lizards native to the United States.

faqs.question: What do Gila monsters eat?
faqs.answer: They are carnivores that specialise in eggs, raiding the nests of birds and reptiles, and also eat young rodents and rabbits. Because meals are irregular, a Gila monster can eat up to a third of its body weight at once and store the energy as fat in its tail.

faqs.question: How long do Gila monsters live?
faqs.answer: In the wild they commonly live 20 years or more, and captive individuals can live even longer. Their slow metabolism and long periods spent underground contribute to this longevity.

faqs.question: Where do Gila monsters live?
faqs.answer: They inhabit the deserts and scrubland of the south-western United States and north-western Mexico, including parts of the Sonoran, Mojave, and Chihuahuan deserts. They spend most of their lives in burrows and emerge above ground for only a few weeks each year.

faqs.question: Are Gila monsters endangered?
faqs.answer: They are classified as Near Threatened by the IUCN and are legally protected in much of their range. Habitat loss, road deaths, and illegal collection for the pet trade are their main threats.

facts.label: Venom
facts.value: Venomous bite, rarely dangerous to humans

range.nativeRange: Deserts and scrubland of the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico.

animals.name: Nile Crocodile
animals.summary: The Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus) is Africa's largest crocodilian and one of the continent's most formidable predators, living in rivers, lakes, and wetlands across much of sub-Saharan Africa. Large adults reach up to 5 m (16 ft) and can weigh up to about 750 kg (1,650 lb), ambushing prey with an explosive lunge and one of the strongest bites in the animal kingdom. These long-lived reptiles can survive 70 to 100 years. The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Size and physical power
sections.body: The Nile crocodile is the largest freshwater predator in Africa, with big males reaching up to 5 m (16 ft) in length and weighing up to about 750 kg (1,650 lb). Its body is built around ambush and power: a heavily armoured back, a muscular tail that drives it through water, and jaws that deliver one of the strongest measured bites of any living animal. The eyes, ears, and nostrils sit on top of the head, letting the crocodile watch and breathe while almost fully submerged. Conical teeth grip rather than chew, holding struggling prey fast.

sections.heading: Hunting and diet
sections.body: Nile crocodiles are carnivores and opportunistic ambush hunters, lying still at the water's edge until prey comes within reach. They take fish, birds, and mammals, and large adults are capable of pulling down animals as big as zebra, buffalo, and wildebeest at river crossings. A crocodile grabs its victim and often drags it underwater, using a spinning "death roll" to subdue and dismember large prey. Because they cannot chew, they tear off chunks by twisting, and can go for long periods between meals thanks to a slow metabolism.

sections.heading: On land and in water
sections.body: Crocodiles are far more agile in water than on land, swimming with powerful sweeps of the tail and steering with their webbed feet. On land they usually move in a sprawling walk but can manage bursts of speed up to around 30 km/h over short distances, especially when lunging from the bank. They spend much of the day basking to regulate body temperature, mouth held open to shed heat, then become more active as ambush hunters around dawn, dusk, and night. Being cold-blooded, they rely on the sun and water to control their temperature.

sections.heading: Nesting and young
sections.body: Female Nile crocodiles dig nest holes in sandy banks and lay their eggs there, then guard the site closely for around three months until the young hatch. Unusually among reptiles, the mother responds to the calls of the hatchlings and helps them to the water, sometimes gently carrying them in her mouth. The temperature of the nest determines whether the eggs develop as males or females. Despite this care, hatchlings are tiny and vulnerable, and only a small fraction survive the many predators of their first years.

sections.heading: Danger to humans
sections.body: The Nile crocodile is responsible for a significant number of attacks on people each year, more than most other crocodilian species, because it is large, aggressive, and shares rivers and lakes where communities collect water. Its ambush strategy means victims often have no warning before the strike. Attacks are most frequent where people fish, bathe, or draw water at the same places crocodiles hunt. This conflict shapes how people living alongside them manage the risk.

sections.heading: Conservation and status
sections.body: After heavy hunting for skins reduced numbers through the twentieth century, the Nile crocodile has recovered across much of its range under protection and regulated management, and the IUCN now lists it as Least Concern. Populations remain healthy in many rivers, lakes, and wetlands of sub-Saharan Africa, though local declines persist where habitat is lost or conflict is intense. These long-lived reptiles can survive 70 to 100 years, growing slowly throughout their lives. Sustainable farming and trade of skins now supports conservation in several countries.

faqs.question: How big do Nile crocodiles get?
faqs.answer: Large Nile crocodiles reach up to 5 m (16 ft) in length and can weigh up to about 750 kg (1,650 lb). Males grow larger than females, and the biggest individuals are among the largest crocodiles in the world.

faqs.question: What do Nile crocodiles eat?
faqs.answer: They are carnivores that ambush prey from the water's edge. Their diet ranges from fish and birds to large mammals such as zebra, buffalo, and wildebeest caught at river crossings.

faqs.question: How fast can a Nile crocodile move?
faqs.answer: In water they are fast and agile, driven by the tail. On land they can manage short bursts of up to around 30 km/h, usually as a sudden lunge from the bank rather than a sustained chase.

faqs.question: How long do Nile crocodiles live?
faqs.answer: They are very long-lived, commonly surviving 70 to 100 years. They grow slowly throughout their lives, so the largest individuals are also among the oldest.

faqs.question: Are Nile crocodiles dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Nile crocodile is one of the most dangerous crocodilians to people and is responsible for many attacks each year, largely because it shares the rivers and lakes where communities fish, bathe, and collect water.

faqs.question: Are Nile crocodiles endangered?
faqs.answer: No. After past overhunting for their skins, populations have recovered under protection and regulated management, and the IUCN lists the species as Least Concern across most of its range.

range.nativeRange: Rivers, lakes, and wetlands across sub-Saharan Africa and the Nile basin.

animals.name: Corn Snake
animals.summary: The corn snake (Pantherophis guttatus) is a gentle, colourful North American rat snake and one of the most popular pet snakes in the world. Native to the fields, woodlands and farmland of the southeastern United States, it grows to around 1.4 m (up to about 1.8 m) and is a non-venomous constrictor that hunts rodents. Docile and easy to keep, corn snakes can live 15 to 20 years in captivity and are listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Appearance and colour
sections.body: The corn snake is named partly for the maize-like checkerboard pattern on its belly and partly for its habit of hunting around grain stores. Wild individuals are typically orange or reddish-brown with bold, black-edged red or orange blotches down the back. Decades of captive breeding have produced a huge range of colour and pattern variations, known as morphs, from snow-white to lavender. A slender adult reaches about 1.4 m long and weighs around 0.9 kg (2 lb).

sections.heading: A non-venomous constrictor
sections.body: The corn snake is completely harmless to people, with no venom and only tiny teeth. It kills its prey by constriction, coiling around a rodent and tightening its grip until the animal stops breathing before swallowing it whole. Corn snakes are carnivores that feed mainly on mice, rats and other small rodents, along with the occasional bird or egg. This appetite for rodents makes them welcome around farms and barns, where they help control pests.

sections.heading: Habitat and behaviour
sections.body: In the wild the corn snake ranges across the southeastern United States, favouring fields, woodlands, farmland and abandoned buildings. It slithers across the ground and is a capable climber, scaling trees and rafters in search of prey and shelter. Mostly active at dawn, dusk and night, it spends much of its time hidden under logs, rocks or debris. When alarmed it may vibrate its tail against dry leaves, mimicking a rattlesnake to bluff predators.

sections.heading: Why it is a popular pet
sections.body: The corn snake is often recommended as an ideal beginner's snake because it is calm, tolerant of handling and simple to care for. It stays a manageable size, feeds readily on frozen-thawed rodents, and rarely bites. Its wide array of colour morphs also makes it a favourite among keepers and breeders. With good care a pet corn snake can live 15 to 20 years.

sections.heading: Reproduction and life cycle
sections.body: Corn snakes breed in spring, after emerging from a cooler winter dormancy that helps trigger the cycle. The female lays a clutch of around a dozen eggs in a warm, humid, hidden spot such as rotting wood or leaf litter, then leaves them to develop on their own. The eggs hatch after about two months, and the young snakes are independent from birth. In the wild corn snakes generally live several years, but in captivity they commonly reach 15 to 20 years.

sections.heading: Conservation status
sections.body: The corn snake is listed as Least Concern and remains common across its native range in the southeastern United States. It is one of the most widely bred snakes in the world, so the pet trade draws overwhelmingly on captive-bred animals rather than wild ones. Habitat loss and road deaths affect some local populations, but the species as a whole is secure. Its adaptability to farmland and disturbed land has helped it persist alongside people.

faqs.question: Are corn snakes venomous or dangerous?
faqs.answer: No. Corn snakes are completely non-venomous and harmless to people. They kill prey by constriction, are very docile, and rarely bite, which is why they are considered one of the safest pet snakes.

faqs.question: How big do corn snakes get?
faqs.answer: Corn snakes typically grow to around 1.4 m long, with some reaching about 1.8 m (6 ft), and weigh roughly 0.9 kg (2 lb). They are a slender, moderately sized rat snake.

faqs.question: What do corn snakes eat?
faqs.answer: Corn snakes are carnivores that feed mainly on mice, rats and other small rodents, along with the occasional bird or egg. In captivity they are usually fed appropriately sized frozen-thawed rodents.

faqs.question: How long do corn snakes live?
faqs.answer: With good care a pet corn snake can live 15 to 20 years. Wild corn snakes generally live shorter lives because of predators and other hazards.

faqs.question: Why are corn snakes good pets for beginners?
faqs.answer: Corn snakes are calm, tolerant of handling and simple to care for. They stay a manageable size, feed readily on frozen-thawed rodents, rarely bite, and come in a wide range of attractive colour morphs.

faqs.question: Why is it called a corn snake?
faqs.answer: The name comes partly from the maize-like checkerboard pattern on the snake's belly and partly from its habit of hunting rodents around grain and corn stores. It is a type of North American rat snake.

range.nativeRange: Fields, woodlands, and farmland across the southeastern and central United States.

animals.name: Gharial
animals.summary: The gharial is a critically endangered crocodilian of the northern Indian subcontinent, instantly recognized by its extremely long, thin snout lined with sharp teeth. This shape is perfect for catching fish, its main food, with quick sideways sweeps of the jaws. Large males develop a bulbous growth on the snout and can reach 6 m (20 ft), and gharials may live 50 to 60 years.

sections.heading: Behavior and the long snout
sections.body: The gharial's slender snout has low water resistance, letting it whip sideways through the water to snap up fish with its many interlocking teeth. Poorly suited to walking on land, gharials are the most aquatic of the large crocodilians and usually only leave the water to bask and nest. They are not built to take large land prey and are essentially harmless to humans.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: Adult gharials feed almost entirely on fish, which they catch and manipulate to swallow head first. Young gharials also eat insects, tadpoles, and small frogs. The narrow jaws are fragile compared with those of other crocodilians, suiting them to small, slippery prey rather than large animals.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Gharials once lived across the rivers of the northern Indian subcontinent, from Pakistan to Myanmar. Today they survive in a few river systems in India and Nepal, especially the Chambal and its tributaries. They depend on clean, deep, fast-flowing rivers with sandbanks for basking and nesting.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: The gharial is Critically Endangered, having declined dramatically due to dam building, sand mining, fishing nets, and the loss of riverside nesting banks. Captive breeding and release programs, together with protected river stretches, have helped slow the decline. The species remains one of the most threatened large reptiles in the world.

faqs.question: What is a gharial?
faqs.answer: A gharial is a large, fish-eating crocodilian from the Indian subcontinent, recognized by its very long, narrow snout. It is one of the most aquatic and most endangered of the crocodilians.

faqs.question: Why does the gharial have such a thin snout?
faqs.answer: The slender snout slips through water with little resistance, letting the gharial sweep sideways and snap up fish. The narrow jaws are ideal for catching small, slippery prey.

faqs.question: Are gharials dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: No. Gharials are not adapted to take large prey and their fragile, fish-catching jaws make them essentially harmless to people, though males will defend nesting areas.

faqs.question: What do gharials eat?
faqs.answer: Adult gharials eat almost entirely fish, while young also take insects, tadpoles, and small frogs. They catch fish with quick sideways snaps of the jaws.

faqs.question: Are gharials endangered?
faqs.answer: Yes. The gharial is listed as Critically Endangered. Dams, sand mining, fishing nets, and lost nesting banks have caused steep declines, and only a few river populations remain.

faqs.question: Where do gharials live?
faqs.answer: Gharials live in deep, fast-flowing rivers of the northern Indian subcontinent, with the main surviving populations in India and Nepal, especially the Chambal River.

range.nativeRange: Deep, fast-flowing rivers of the northern Indian subcontinent, mainly in India and Nepal.

animals.name: Frilled Lizard
animals.summary: The frilled lizard (Chlamydosaurus kingii) is a tree-dwelling reptile of northern Australia and southern New Guinea, famous for the wide, leathery frill it snaps open around its neck when threatened. It grows up to about 0.9 m (3 ft) long including the tail and weighs around 0.5 kg (1.1 lb). When alarmed on the ground it sprints away on its hind legs, and it can live 10 to 20 years.

sections.heading: The famous frill and its bluff
sections.body: The frill is a fold of skin supported by long rods of cartilage attached to the jaw. Normally it lies flat against the shoulders, but when the lizard opens its mouth the frill springs out into a disc that can be up to 30 cm across. Combined with hissing, gaping, and tail-lashing, this display makes the animal look far larger and more dangerous than it really is. The bluff is meant to startle a predator long enough for the lizard to escape.

sections.heading: Running on two legs
sections.body: If the display fails, the frilled lizard turns and flees in a way few reptiles can match. It rears up and runs on its hind legs alone, tail held out for balance, in a comical upright sprint toward the nearest tree. This bipedal dash can reach around 30 km/h over short distances. Once it reaches a trunk it scrambles up and freezes against the bark, where its grey-brown colouring blends in.

sections.heading: Life in the trees
sections.body: Frilled lizards are strongly arboreal and spend most of the day clinging to trunks and branches in tropical woodland and dry forest. From this vantage point they watch the ground for movement and drop down to snatch prey. They are ambush hunters that stay motionless for long stretches, relying on camouflage rather than active searching. Height also keeps them clear of many ground predators.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: This lizard is a carnivore that feeds mainly on insects. Cicadas, beetles, ants, termites, and spiders make up the bulk of its diet, and larger individuals will also take small lizards and the occasional small mammal. It hunts by sitting still and ambushing anything that wanders within reach. Feeding activity rises sharply in the wet season, when insect numbers explode.

sections.heading: Seasons and breeding
sections.body: Northern Australia's climate swings between a hot wet season and a long dry season, and the frilled lizard's year is built around it. The animals are most active and breed during the wet, when food is abundant, and become far more sluggish and secretive through the dry months. Females lay clutches of roughly 8 to 23 eggs in shallow nests dug into soft soil. The eggs hatch after two to three months, and hatchlings are independent from birth.

sections.heading: Conservation status
sections.body: The frilled lizard is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and remains widespread across its northern Australian and New Guinean range. The main pressures it faces are habitat clearance, wildfire, and predation by introduced cats and foxes. It is also collected for the exotic pet trade, though wild populations are currently considered stable. Healthy tree cover is the single most important thing for its long-term survival.

faqs.question: Why does the frilled lizard have a frill?
faqs.answer: The frill is a defensive bluff. When a predator approaches, the lizard opens its mouth and flares the frill into a wide disc, making itself look much bigger and scarier so the attacker hesitates. It is not used for feeding and has no venom behind it.

faqs.question: Can a frilled lizard really run on two legs?
faqs.answer: Yes. When it flees on open ground the frilled lizard rears up and runs on its hind legs alone, holding its tail out for balance. This upright bipedal sprint carries it quickly to the nearest tree, where it climbs to safety.

faqs.question: How big does a frilled lizard get?
faqs.answer: A frilled lizard reaches up to about 0.9 m (3 ft) in total length, though most of that is its long tail. Body weight is only around 0.5 kg (1.1 lb), so it is a lightly built, agile climber rather than a heavy reptile.

faqs.question: What do frilled lizards eat?
faqs.answer: Frilled lizards are carnivores that eat mostly insects, including cicadas, beetles, ants, termites, and spiders. Larger individuals also take small lizards and occasionally small mammals. They hunt by ambush, staying still and grabbing prey that passes close by.

faqs.question: Are frilled lizards dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: No. Despite the dramatic threat display, frilled lizards are harmless to people. They have no venom, and a large one can deliver only a mild bite if handled. Their whole strategy is to frighten enemies off rather than to fight.

faqs.question: How long do frilled lizards live?
faqs.answer: Frilled lizards typically live between 10 and 20 years. Lifespan depends heavily on avoiding predators such as birds of prey, snakes, and introduced cats and foxes, especially while young and small.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Up to 0.9 m (3 ft) including tail

range.nativeRange: Tropical and warm-temperate woodlands of northern Australia and southern New Guinea.

animals.name: Snapping Turtle
animals.summary: The common snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina) is a large freshwater turtle native to ponds, lakes, and slow rivers across North America. It has a rugged shell up to about 0.5 m (20 in) long, powerful hooked jaws, and can weigh 4.5 to 16 kg (10 to 35 lb). An opportunistic omnivore, it often lives 30 to 50 years in the wild and is listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Appearance and anatomy
sections.body: Snapping turtles have a rough, ridged carapace that reaches up to about 0.5 m (20 in) in length, a long muscular tail, and a large head with a sharp, beak-like jaw. Unlike many turtles, they cannot fully withdraw into their shell, which leaves their limbs and neck exposed and helps explain their defensive temperament. Their skin is often coated in algae or mud, giving them excellent camouflage on the bottom of a pond. Adults typically weigh between 4.5 and 16 kg (10 to 35 lb).

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The species is widespread across eastern and central North America, from southern Canada down to the Gulf of Mexico. It favours freshwater habitats with soft, muddy bottoms, including ponds, lakes, marshes, and slow-moving rivers where it can bury itself and wait. Snapping turtles tolerate a wide range of conditions and are sometimes found in brackish water near the coast. They spend most of their time submerged, surfacing mainly to breathe.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: Snapping turtles are opportunistic omnivores that eat fish, frogs, invertebrates, small mammals, birds, carrion, and a surprising amount of aquatic plants. They hunt largely by ambush, lying still on the bottom and lunging with a fast strike of the neck when prey passes within reach. In water they are far less aggressive than on land and will usually swim away from a swimmer rather than attack. Their strong jaws let them tackle prey that many other freshwater turtles cannot.

sections.heading: Behaviour and temperament
sections.body: In their aquatic home snapping turtles are generally shy and prefer to slip quietly away from disturbance. On land, however, they become notably defensive because they cannot retreat into their shell, and will lunge, hiss, and snap to protect themselves. They are strong swimmers but move slowly and awkwardly on land, with a top speed of only around 5 km/h. Females may travel considerable distances overland during the nesting season.

sections.heading: Reproduction and lifespan
sections.body: Females nest in late spring and early summer, often travelling well away from water to dig a hole in sandy or loose soil. A typical clutch contains around 20 to 40 round, leathery eggs, which incubate for two to three months, and nest temperature helps determine the sex of the hatchlings. Many nests are lost to raccoons, foxes, and other predators, so survival to adulthood is low. Those that reach maturity are long-lived, commonly reaching 30 to 50 years in the wild.

faqs.question: How big do snapping turtles get?
faqs.answer: Common snapping turtles reach a shell length of about 0.5 m (20 in) and typically weigh between 4.5 and 16 kg (10 to 35 lb). Their long tail can add substantially to their overall length.

faqs.question: Are snapping turtles dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Snapping turtles have powerful jaws and can deliver a painful bite if handled or cornered on land, where they cannot hide in their shell. In the water they are shy and almost always swim away from people rather than confront them.

faqs.question: What do snapping turtles eat?
faqs.answer: They are omnivores that eat fish, frogs, insects, crayfish, small mammals, birds, carrion, and aquatic plants. Much of their hunting is done by ambush, waiting motionless on the bottom and striking quickly when prey comes near.

faqs.question: How long do snapping turtles live?
faqs.answer: In the wild snapping turtles commonly live 30 to 50 years. They grow slowly and mature late, so long individual lifespans are important for keeping populations stable.

faqs.question: Where do snapping turtles live?
faqs.answer: They live in freshwater habitats across eastern and central North America, including ponds, lakes, marshes, and slow rivers with muddy bottoms. They spend most of their time submerged and can occasionally tolerate brackish coastal water.

faqs.question: Are snapping turtles endangered?
faqs.answer: The common snapping turtle is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and remains widespread. Local populations can still be affected by road deaths, habitat loss, and collection, but the species overall is not threatened.

range.nativeRange: Freshwater ponds, lakes, and rivers across central and eastern North America.

animals.name: Garter Snake
animals.summary: The garter snake is one of the most common and widespread snakes in North America, found in meadows, marshes, woodlands, and gardens from Canada to Mexico. It is a slender snake, typically 0.5 to 1.3 m long and about 150 g, usually striped in yellow or green along a darker body. Harmless to people, it slithers actively by day hunting worms, amphibians, and fish, and lives around four to ten years.

sections.heading: Appearance and identification
sections.body: Garter snakes are best known for the long stripes that run the length of the body, usually one down the back and one along each side, in yellow, green, or cream against brown, grey, or black. Adults are slim and typically measure 0.5 to 1.3 m (about 1.5 to 4.3 ft) and weigh around 150 g. There are many regional colour forms, so patterning varies widely across the species' huge range. The keeled scales give the skin a slightly rough, matte look rather than a glossy sheen.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: The garter snake is a carnivore with a broad appetite, eating earthworms, slugs, amphibians, small fish, and the occasional rodent or nestling. It slithers actively through vegetation and shallow water by day, using sight and a flicking tongue to track prey rather than lying in wait. Some populations tolerate the toxins of newts and toads that would poison other predators. Prey is seized in the jaws and swallowed whole, as the snake has no venom potent enough to subdue large animals.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Few snakes are as adaptable, and the garter snake ranges from Canada through the United States into Mexico across an enormous variety of habitats. It thrives in damp meadows, marshes, pond edges, woodland, and suburban gardens, rarely far from water. This tolerance of cool climates lets it live farther north than almost any other North American snake. Its willingness to live alongside people makes it one of the reptiles most familiar to gardeners.

sections.heading: Reproduction and hibernation
sections.body: Garter snakes give birth to live young rather than laying eggs, producing litters that can number from a handful to several dozen. In colder regions they spend winter in communal dens called hibernacula, sometimes gathering by the hundreds or thousands in the same rocky shelter. When they emerge in spring, males may form writhing mating balls around a single female. The newborn snakes are fully independent from birth and receive no parental care.

sections.heading: Defence and predators
sections.body: When threatened, a garter snake first tries to flee, slithering quickly into cover. If cornered it may flatten its body, strike, or release a foul-smelling musk from glands near the tail to deter a predator. Its saliva contains a mild toxin that helps subdue small prey but is harmless to humans, causing at most minor irritation. Hawks, larger snakes, raccoons, and domestic cats are among its many predators.

sections.heading: Lifespan and conservation
sections.body: In the wild garter snakes typically live four to ten years, though predation means many do not survive their first year. The species is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and remains abundant across its range. A few localised subspecies, such as the San Francisco garter snake, are threatened by habitat loss and are protected. For the species as a whole, adaptability and a varied diet keep populations healthy.

faqs.question: Are garter snakes dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: No. Garter snakes are essentially harmless to people; they have only a very mild toxin in their saliva that helps them subdue small prey. A bite may cause minor irritation or swelling but is not medically dangerous.

faqs.question: What do garter snakes eat?
faqs.answer: They are carnivores that eat earthworms, slugs, amphibians such as frogs and toads, small fish, and occasionally rodents or nestlings. They hunt actively by day, tracking prey by sight and scent.

faqs.question: How big do garter snakes get?
faqs.answer: Most garter snakes are 0.5 to 1.3 m long (about 1.5 to 4.3 ft) and weigh around 150 g. They are slender snakes, so even the longest individuals stay lightweight.

faqs.question: Do garter snakes lay eggs?
faqs.answer: No, garter snakes give birth to live young rather than laying eggs. A single female can produce anywhere from a few to several dozen fully independent offspring in a litter.

faqs.question: How long do garter snakes live?
faqs.answer: In the wild they usually live four to ten years, although heavy predation means many die young. Individuals in captivity can live somewhat longer under stable conditions.

faqs.question: Where are garter snakes found?
faqs.answer: They range across North America from Canada to Mexico and live in meadows, marshes, woodlands, pond edges, and gardens. Their tolerance of cool climates lets them live farther north than almost any other North American snake.

range.nativeRange: Meadows, marshes, and gardens across North America, one of the most widespread snakes on the continent.

animals.name: Asian Water Monitor
animals.summary: The Asian water monitor (Varanus salvator) is one of the largest lizards in the world, reaching up to 3 m (10 ft) long and around 25 kg (55 lb). It lives across South and Southeast Asia in wetlands, rivers, mangroves, and coastal areas, where it walks powerfully on land and swims with ease using its muscular tail. A carnivore and scavenger, it eats almost anything it can catch and can live 10 to 20 years.

sections.heading: Size and build
sections.body: The water monitor is second only to the Komodo dragon among the world's heaviest lizards. Large adults stretch up to 3 m (10 ft) from snout to tail tip and weigh as much as 25 kg (55 lb), with the tail alone making up more than half the total length. The body is long and muscular, covered in dark scales flecked with yellow spots and bands. Strong limbs and sharp, curved claws make it an excellent climber and digger as well as a swimmer.

sections.heading: At home in the water
sections.body: As its name suggests, this monitor is closely tied to water and is rarely found far from it. Its flattened, oar-like tail drives it through rivers, swamps, and coastal shallows, and it can stay submerged for many minutes while hunting or hiding. On land it walks with a steady, side-to-side gait and can put on a surprising burst of speed of around 30 km/h when pressed. It readily crosses stretches of sea between islands, which is one reason it is so widespread.

sections.heading: Diet and scavenging
sections.body: Water monitors are opportunistic carnivores that eat an enormous range of prey. Fish, frogs, crabs, birds, rodents, snakes, turtles, and eggs are all on the menu, and they will raid nests and dig up buried food. They are also important scavengers, feeding readily on carrion and human refuse, which draws them into towns and villages. A keen sense of smell, aided by a forked tongue, helps them track food from a distance.

sections.heading: Living alongside people
sections.body: Few large predators tolerate human company as well as the water monitor. It thrives in canals, rice paddies, fishing ports, and even city parks across Southeast Asia, where scraps and rodents are plentiful. Generally shy, it prefers to slip into the water or flee rather than confront a person. This adaptability has allowed it to remain common in landscapes where many other big reptiles have vanished.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.body: Females lay clutches of up to around 40 eggs, often depositing them inside termite mounds or in holes dug into riverbanks and rotting logs. The termite mound provides steady warmth and humidity, and the insects reseal the chamber around the eggs. Incubation takes several months, after which the hatchlings emerge fully independent and immediately take to the water. Young monitors are brightly patterned and spend much of their early life in trees, out of reach of ground predators.

sections.heading: Conservation status
sections.body: The Asian water monitor is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and remains widespread and adaptable across its range. Even so, it is hunted in large numbers for its skin, which supplies the leather trade, and for meat and the pet market. Local populations can be depleted where hunting is intense, but its tolerance of disturbed and urban habitats has kept the species as a whole secure. Wetland protection helps sustain the healthiest populations.

faqs.question: How big do Asian water monitors get?
faqs.answer: Asian water monitors can reach up to 3 m (10 ft) in total length and weigh as much as 25 kg (55 lb). Much of that length is tail. This makes them one of the largest lizard species in the world, second only to the Komodo dragon by weight.

faqs.question: Can water monitors swim?
faqs.answer: Yes, they are superb swimmers. A flattened, paddle-like tail powers them through rivers, swamps, and coastal water, and they can stay submerged for several minutes. They even swim between islands across open sea, which has helped them spread across Southeast Asia.

faqs.question: What do water monitors eat?
faqs.answer: Water monitors are opportunistic carnivores. They eat fish, frogs, crabs, birds, rodents, snakes, turtles, and eggs, and they scavenge carrion and human refuse. A strong sense of smell helps them find both live prey and buried or hidden food.

faqs.question: Are water monitors dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: They are large and powerful but generally shy, and they usually flee into water rather than attack. Bites are rare and normally happen only when the animal is cornered or handled, though a big monitor can inflict a painful wound with its teeth and claws.

faqs.question: Where do Asian water monitors live?
faqs.answer: They live across South and Southeast Asia in wetlands, rivers, mangroves, and coastal areas. They are highly adaptable and also thrive in human landscapes such as canals, rice paddies, fishing ports, and city parks.

faqs.question: How long do water monitors live?
faqs.answer: Asian water monitors typically live between 10 and 20 years. Their long lifespan and adaptable, opportunistic lifestyle help them persist even in areas heavily altered by people.

range.nativeRange: Wetlands, rivers, mangroves, and coasts across South and Southeast Asia.

animals.name: Adder
animals.summary: The adder (Vipera berus) is Britain's only venomous snake, a stocky viper of heathland, moorland, woodland edges, and dunes across Europe and into Asia. It grows to about 60 to 90 cm and roughly 100 g, and is recognised by the dark zigzag stripe down its back. It slithers out to bask and hunt small mammals, lizards, and frogs. Its bite is venomous but rarely fatal, and adders live 10 to 15 years.

sections.heading: Appearance and identification
sections.body: The adder is a short, thick-set snake, usually 60 to 90 cm long and about 100 g, with a distinctive dark zigzag stripe running the length of its back. Colours range from silvery-grey in many males to reddish-brown in females, and some individuals are entirely black. A V or X marking often shows on the head, and the eyes have vertical, cat-like pupils typical of vipers. This bold dorsal pattern makes the adder one of Britain's most recognisable reptiles.

sections.heading: Venom and its bite
sections.body: As a true viper, the adder has hinged fangs that fold back against the roof of the mouth and swing forward to inject venom in a rapid strike. The venom is designed to subdue small prey and is only mildly dangerous to humans; bites cause pain and swelling but are very rarely fatal. Most bites occur when a snake is trodden on or handled, and it will always try to escape first. Anyone bitten should seek medical advice, as reactions can occasionally be severe.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: The adder is a carnivore that preys on small mammals such as voles and mice, along with lizards, frogs, and nestling birds. It hunts by ambush, striking prey with a venomous bite and then following the scent trail until the animal succumbs. After swallowing prey whole it may rest for days to digest. Young adders take smaller fare, including insects and slow-worms, until they are large enough for bigger prey.

sections.heading: Habitat and behaviour
sections.body: Adders favour open, sunny habitats including heathland, moorland, woodland edges, and coastal dunes across much of Europe and into Asia. Being cold-blooded, they rely on the sun and are often seen basking on banks or paths in spring to warm up. They are shy and secretive, quick to slither away into cover at the first sign of disturbance. Over winter they hibernate communally in sheltered spots, emerging around March to bask and breed.

sections.heading: Reproduction and lifespan
sections.body: Adders mate in spring, when males perform a swaying "dance" as they wrestle rivals for access to females. Females give birth to live young in late summer, producing a litter of roughly three to twenty, rather than laying eggs. This ability to incubate young inside the body helps the species breed successfully in cool northern climates. Adders can live 10 to 15 years, though females often breed only every two or three years.

sections.heading: Conservation status
sections.body: Globally the adder is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, but in Britain many local populations are declining and fragmented. Loss and disturbance of heathland, intensive land use, and the isolation of small colonies are the main pressures. In the UK the species is legally protected against being killed or injured. Sympathetic habitat management and the linking of isolated sites are key to reversing local declines.

faqs.question: How dangerous is an adder bite?
faqs.answer: An adder bite is venomous but rarely dangerous; it causes pain and swelling and is very seldom fatal to a healthy adult. Anyone bitten should still seek medical advice, as some people react more strongly and children and pets are more vulnerable.

faqs.question: How do you identify an adder?
faqs.answer: Look for a short, stocky snake 60 to 90 cm long with a dark zigzag stripe running down its back and vertical, cat-like pupils. Males are often silvery-grey and females reddish-brown, and a V or X mark frequently appears on the head.

faqs.question: What do adders eat?
faqs.answer: Adders are carnivores that hunt small mammals such as voles and mice, as well as lizards, frogs, and nestling birds. They ambush prey with a venomous bite and then track it down before swallowing it whole.

faqs.question: Where do adders live?
faqs.answer: They inhabit heathland, moorland, woodland edges, and coastal dunes across Europe and into Asia. As Britain's only venomous snake, the adder is often found basking in open, sunny spots in spring.

faqs.question: Do adders lay eggs?
faqs.answer: No. Adders give birth to live young, with a female producing a litter of around three to twenty in late summer. Incubating the young inside the body helps them breed in cool northern climates.

faqs.question: How long do adders live?
faqs.answer: Adders can live 10 to 15 years in the wild. Females often breed only once every two or three years, so populations recover slowly from losses.

facts.label: Venom
facts.value: Venomous; bites rarely fatal to humans

range.nativeRange: Heathland, moorland, and woodland across Europe and into East Asia, reaching within the Arctic Circle; the UK's only native venomous snake.

animals.name: African Wild Dog
animals.summary: The African wild dog is a lean, long-legged carnivore of sub-Saharan Africa, famous for its mottled coat of black, tan, and white patches. Weighing 20 to 30 kg and standing about 1.1 m in body length, it is one of the world's most efficient pack hunters, chasing prey at up to 60 km/h. Packs are intensely social and cooperative. With only a few thousand left, the IUCN lists the species as Endangered.

sections.heading: Appearance and identity
sections.body: Also called the painted wolf, the African wild dog wears a unique coat blotched with black, yellow-tan, and white, so no two individuals look alike. It has large, rounded 'satellite-dish' ears that help with hearing and shed heat, a lean frame built for endurance, and only four toes on each foot rather than five. Adults weigh between 20 and 30 kg, with males slightly larger than females. This is Africa's only member of its genus, distinct from wolves, jackals, and domestic dogs.

sections.heading: Pack life and social structure
sections.body: African wild dogs are among the most social of all carnivores, living in packs led by a dominant breeding pair. The whole pack cooperates to raise pups, hunt, and care for sick or injured members, sharing food by regurgitation. Rather than fighting over rank, they use elaborate greeting ceremonies of twittering calls and body contact to bond and coordinate. Packs even 'vote' on whether to set off hunting through a chorus of sneezes, with the majority deciding the move.

sections.heading: Hunting and diet
sections.body: These dogs are carnivores that hunt medium-sized antelope such as impala and kudu, along with warthog and smaller game. Instead of ambushing, they run their prey down in a sustained, coordinated chase, reaching speeds of up to 60 km/h and wearing quarry out over long distances. Their teamwork makes them extraordinarily successful, with hunts often ending in a kill far more reliably than those of lions or hyenas. After a kill, pups are allowed to eat first, an unusual mark of their cooperative nature.

sections.heading: Breeding and pups
sections.body: Normally only the dominant pair breeds, producing a large litter after a gestation of about 70 days. Litters can be exceptionally big, sometimes exceeding ten pups, which are raised in a den and guarded by the whole pack. Adults returning from a hunt regurgitate meat for the pups and for any pack members that stayed behind. Young dogs remain with the pack to help rear the next generation before some disperse to form new packs.

sections.heading: Why it is endangered
sections.body: The African wild dog is listed as Endangered, with only a few thousand individuals remaining across a fragmented range. Habitat loss and the break-up of large wild areas force packs into contact with people, leading to conflict with livestock farmers and deaths on roads. They are also highly vulnerable to diseases such as rabies and canine distemper caught from domestic dogs. Because they need vast territories, protecting connected landscapes and wildlife corridors is vital to their survival.

sections.heading: Range and habitat
sections.body: African wild dogs once roamed across much of the continent but now survive mainly in southern and eastern Africa. They favour savannas, grasslands, and open woodlands where there is room to run down prey. Some of the strongest populations persist in large protected areas such as those in Botswana, Zimbabwe, and Tanzania. Each pack ranges over a huge home area, which is why fragmented habitat hits them so hard.

faqs.question: Are African wild dogs actually dogs?
faqs.answer: African wild dogs belong to the dog family, Canidae, but they are not closely related to domestic dogs and cannot interbreed with them. They are the only living species in the genus Lycaon, set apart by having just four toes on each foot instead of five.

faqs.question: How fast can an African wild dog run?
faqs.answer: African wild dogs can reach speeds of up to 60 km/h (37 mph) and, crucially, sustain a fast pace over long distances. This endurance lets them wear down prey in extended chases rather than relying on a short ambush.

faqs.question: Why are African wild dogs endangered?
faqs.answer: They are Endangered mainly because of habitat loss, conflict with farmers, road deaths, and diseases such as rabies and distemper spread by domestic dogs. Because each pack needs a very large territory, the break-up of wild landscapes is especially damaging.

faqs.question: How successful are African wild dogs at hunting?
faqs.answer: African wild dogs are among the most successful large predators in Africa, with a high proportion of their coordinated hunts ending in a kill. Their success comes from teamwork and stamina rather than raw power or surprise.

faqs.question: Why do African wild dogs sneeze?
faqs.answer: Researchers have found that packs use sneezes as a kind of vote when deciding whether to leave a resting spot and hunt. If enough dogs sneeze during their social greeting rituals, the pack sets off, so the sneezes act as a group decision.

faqs.question: How long do African wild dogs live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, African wild dogs usually live about 10 to 11 years. Individuals in captivity, safe from disease, predators, and vehicles, can live somewhat longer.

animals.name: Wildebeest
animals.summary: The wildebeest, or blue wildebeest, is a large grazing antelope of the savannas and grasslands of East and southern Africa. Also called the gnu, it weighs 120 to 290 kg and can gallop at up to 80 km/h (50 mph) in short bursts. Wildebeest are famous for the annual Serengeti migration, live 15 to 20 years, and are listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: The great migration
sections.body: Wildebeest are best known for one of the largest overland migrations on Earth, in which more than a million animals travel a roughly circular route between Tanzania's Serengeti and Kenya's Maasai Mara. The herds follow seasonal rains in search of fresh grass, covering hundreds of kilometres each year. River crossings, especially of the crocodile-filled Mara, are the most dangerous stage of the journey. Zebra and other grazers often travel alongside them, forming vast mixed herds.

sections.heading: Grazing and diet
sections.body: Wildebeest are specialised grazers that feed almost entirely on short grasses and fresh green shoots. Their broad muzzles and wide rows of teeth are suited to cropping grass close to the ground, and they prefer swards kept short by other herbivores. Because they need to drink regularly, their movements are tightly tied to water and to the flush of new growth after rain. A herd can transform a landscape as it moves through, and its grazing helps maintain the open grasslands it depends on.

sections.heading: Appearance and build
sections.body: The blue wildebeest has a heavy, front-loaded body with a deep chest, sloping back, and slender legs built for endurance running. Adults stand around 1.2 to 1.4 metres at the shoulder, reach about 2.3 metres in body length, and weigh between 120 and 290 kg, with bulls noticeably heavier than cows. Both sexes carry curved horns and a dark, silvery-grey coat marked with faint vertical stripes on the shoulders. A shaggy mane and beard give the animal its distinctive, slightly unkempt profile.

sections.heading: Herd life and behaviour
sections.body: Wildebeest are intensely social and gather in herds that can swell into the tens of thousands during migration. Bulls establish and defend temporary territories, grunting and sparring to hold ground and attract cows during the rut. Outside the breeding season the herds are more loosely organised, relying on sheer numbers for safety from lions, hyenas, and wild dogs. Their constant lowing and grunting make a moving herd audible long before it comes into view.

sections.heading: Breeding and calves
sections.body: Most wildebeest calves are born within the same few weeks at the start of the rainy season, a burst of synchronised births that swamps predators with more young than they can take. A calf can stand and run within minutes of birth, an essential head start in open country. Cows give birth to a single calf after a gestation of around eight and a half months, and the young keep close to their mothers within the herd. In the wild wildebeest typically live 15 to 20 years.

sections.heading: Predators and conservation
sections.body: Wildebeest are a keystone prey animal for the big predators of the African plains, and lions, spotted hyenas, cheetahs, and crocodiles all rely heavily on them. The species is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, with the migratory Serengeti population remaining strong. Fences, roads, and expanding farmland are the main threats, because they can cut across the traditional routes the herds must follow. Where migration corridors stay open, wildebeest numbers have proven remarkably resilient.

faqs.question: What is a wildebeest?
faqs.answer: A wildebeest is a large African antelope, also called a gnu, that grazes the savannas and grasslands of East and southern Africa. Despite its ox-like head and shaggy mane, it is a true antelope and one of the most numerous large mammals on the continent.

faqs.question: How fast can a wildebeest run?
faqs.answer: A wildebeest can reach up to 80 km/h (50 mph) in short bursts. Combined with excellent stamina, this speed helps herds outrun or outlast predators such as lions and hyenas over open ground.

faqs.question: Why do wildebeest migrate?
faqs.answer: Wildebeest migrate to follow seasonal rains and the fresh grass that springs up after them. This drives the famous annual loop between the Serengeti and the Maasai Mara, with more than a million animals moving in search of grazing and water.

faqs.question: How much does a wildebeest weigh?
faqs.answer: Adult wildebeest weigh between 120 and 290 kg (260 to 640 lb), with bulls heavier than cows. They stand a little over a metre at the shoulder and measure about 2.3 metres in body length.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a wildebeest and a gnu?
faqs.answer: There is no difference; "gnu" and "wildebeest" are two names for the same animal. "Wildebeest" comes from Afrikaans meaning "wild beast", while "gnu" imitates the animal's grunting call.

faqs.question: Are wildebeest endangered?
faqs.answer: No, wildebeest are listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and remain abundant across their range. The main risks come from fences, roads, and farmland that block migration routes, rather than from any overall population decline.

animals.name: Springbok
animals.summary: The springbok is a medium-sized, fawn-and-white antelope of the arid grasslands of southern Africa, and the national animal of South Africa. Standing lightly built at around 1.5 m long and 30 to 50 kg, it is famous for pronking, a stiff-legged leap up to 2 m high. It grazes and browses on grasses, shrubs, and succulents, can sprint up to 88 km/h, and typically lives 10 to 12 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Pronking, the signature leap
sections.body: The springbok takes its name from its habit of pronking, also called stotting: a series of stiff-legged, arch-backed bounds that can carry it up to 2 m off the ground. When it pronks, the animal fans out a fold of white skin along its back, flashing a crest of long white hairs. Biologists think pronking signals fitness to predators, effectively telling a lion or cheetah that this individual is too alert and fit to be worth chasing. It may also serve to alarm the herd and confuse an attacker.

sections.heading: Speed and survival
sections.body: Springbok are among the fastest land animals, able to sprint at up to 88 km/h over open ground. That raw speed, combined with sharp senses and sudden changes of direction, is their main defence against cheetahs, lions, and hunting dogs. They are also remarkably agile, capable of leaping long distances at full gallop. Living in herds adds safety in numbers, with many eyes watching for danger across the open plains.

sections.heading: Diet and desert adaptation
sections.body: Springbok are mixed feeders that graze on grasses when they are green and browse on shrubs, leaves, and succulents when grass is scarce. This flexibility lets them thrive in the dry, unpredictable environment of the Karoo, Kalahari, and Namib fringes. They are well adapted to going without free-standing water, drawing much of their moisture from the plants they eat, and they often feed at dawn, dusk, and even at night to avoid the worst heat. Succulent tubers and roots dug from the ground provide extra water in the driest months.

sections.heading: Herds and social life
sections.body: Springbok are social animals that gather in herds ranging from small family groups to, historically, enormous aggregations. In the past, migrating herds numbering in the hundreds of thousands, known as treks, once swept across the South African interior in search of grazing. Today herds are far smaller, but the animals remain gregarious, with mixed groups of females and young and separate bachelor groups of males. Dominant rams hold territories during the breeding season and compete for access to females.

sections.heading: Breeding and young
sections.body: Breeding can occur at various times of year but often peaks to coincide with the rains, when food is most plentiful. After a gestation of around six months, a female gives birth to a single lamb, which she hides in vegetation for the first days of life. Lambs are up and running remarkably quickly, an essential ability in open country full of predators. Within a few weeks they join the herd, where the safety of numbers improves their chances of reaching adulthood.

sections.heading: Status and importance
sections.body: The springbok is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and remains common across much of southern Africa, particularly in South Africa, Namibia, and Botswana. It is farmed on private ranches and game reserves and hunted both for meat and as a game animal, which gives it strong economic value. As the national animal of South Africa, it lends its name to the country's rugby team, the Springboks. Well-managed populations on protected and private land help keep the species secure.

faqs.question: What is pronking?
faqs.answer: Pronking is the springbok's signature stiff-legged leap, in which it bounds up to 2 m into the air with an arched back and flared white crest. It is thought to signal fitness to predators and to alert the rest of the herd to danger.

faqs.question: How fast can a springbok run?
faqs.answer: Springbok can sprint at up to 88 km/h, making them one of the fastest land animals. Their speed and agility are their main defences against predators such as cheetahs and lions.

faqs.question: Where do springbok live?
faqs.answer: They inhabit the arid and semi-arid grasslands of southern Africa, especially South Africa, Namibia, and Botswana. They are well suited to dry areas like the Karoo and Kalahari, where they can survive with little standing water.

faqs.question: What do springbok eat?
faqs.answer: Springbok are mixed feeders that graze on grasses and browse on shrubs, leaves, and succulents. They can go long periods without drinking, getting much of their water from the plants they eat.

faqs.question: How much does a springbok weigh?
faqs.answer: Adult springbok weigh roughly 30 to 50 kg and measure about 1.5 m in length, with rams slightly heavier than ewes. They are lightly built, which helps them reach their high speeds.

faqs.question: Why is the springbok important to South Africa?
faqs.answer: The springbok is South Africa's national animal and lends its name to the national rugby team. It is also economically important, farmed and hunted for its meat across private reserves and ranches.

animals.name: Thomson's Gazelle
animals.summary: Thomson's gazelle (Eudorcas thomsonii) is a small, swift antelope of East Africa's grasslands and savannas, instantly known by the bold black stripe along its flanks. It grazes on short grasses and tender shoots, weighs 15 to 30 kg, and can sprint at up to 80 km/h while making sharp turns to escape cheetahs. Wild gazelles live around 10 to 12 years, and the IUCN lists the species as Near Threatened.

sections.heading: Speed and escaping predators
sections.body: Thomson's gazelle is built for open-country speed, reaching up to 80 km/h in a flat-out sprint. Because it cannot outrun a cheetah over the first hundred metres, its real defence is agility: it zig-zags and cuts at sharp angles that a heavier predator struggles to follow. This constant threat from cheetahs, lions, wild dogs, and hyenas shapes almost everything about how the gazelle lives and moves. Even at rest, herds stay alert and rarely let a predator approach unnoticed.

sections.heading: Grazing and diet
sections.body: Thomson's gazelles are grazers that feed mainly on short grasses and fresh green shoots. They follow the growth of new grass after rain and often move onto areas that larger grazers such as zebra and wildebeest have already cropped down. This preference for short, nutritious turf lets them extract enough moisture from their food to go long periods without drinking. When grass is scarce they will also browse on low herbs and foliage.

sections.heading: Range and the great migration
sections.body: The species is closely tied to the grasslands and savannas of East Africa, above all the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem. Large numbers travel alongside the wildebeest and zebra of the great migration, exploiting the flush of new grass that follows the herds and the rains. Outside migration, gazelles form loosely structured herds that shift across the plains as grazing conditions change. Males often hold small territories that they mark and defend during the breeding season.

sections.heading: Stotting behaviour
sections.body: One of the gazelle's most striking habits is stotting, sometimes called pronking, in which it springs stiffly into the air with all four legs held straight. This eye-catching leap is thought to signal to a predator that the gazelle is fit, alert, and not worth chasing. It may also warn the rest of the herd that danger is near. A cheetah that sees strong, energetic stotting will often break off before a chase even begins.

sections.heading: Reproduction and young
sections.body: Females can breed year-round, though births often peak with the rains when grazing is richest. After a gestation of roughly five to six months a single fawn is born and hidden in tall grass, lying motionless while its mother grazes nearby and returns to nurse. This hiding strategy keeps the vulnerable newborn out of sight of predators during its first weeks. Once strong enough, the fawn joins the herd and must quickly learn to run with the group.

sections.heading: Why it is Near Threatened
sections.body: Although still numerous, Thomson's gazelle is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN because its numbers have been falling. Expanding farmland, fences, and settlements break up the open plains it depends on and cut off migration routes. Competition with livestock for grazing and localised hunting add further pressure. Well-managed reserves in the Serengeti and Maasai Mara remain vital strongholds for the species.

faqs.question: How fast can a Thomson's gazelle run?
faqs.answer: A Thomson's gazelle can reach up to 80 km/h in a sprint. Just as important as raw speed is its agility: it makes sharp, sudden turns that help it shake off faster predators such as cheetahs.

faqs.question: What do Thomson's gazelles eat?
faqs.answer: They are herbivores that graze mainly on short grasses and tender green shoots. They favour the fresh regrowth that follows rain and grazing by larger animals, and will browse on low herbs when grass is scarce.

faqs.question: Why do gazelles jump straight up in the air?
faqs.answer: This stiff-legged leap is called stotting or pronking. It signals to a predator that the gazelle is healthy and hard to catch, and can warn the rest of the herd of danger. Predators often give up when they see strong stotting.

faqs.question: How big is a Thomson's gazelle?
faqs.answer: Adults weigh between 15 and 30 kg and stand only about knee-high to a person, roughly 1 m in body length. Males are similar in size to females but carry longer, more strongly ringed horns.

faqs.question: Where do Thomson's gazelles live?
faqs.answer: They live on the grasslands and savannas of East Africa, especially the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem. Many move with the great migration of wildebeest and zebra, following fresh grass across the plains.

faqs.question: Are Thomson's gazelles endangered?
faqs.answer: They are listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN. They remain common in protected areas, but numbers are declining as farmland, fences, and livestock fragment the open plains and block their migration routes.

facts.label: Diet

animals.name: Water Buffalo
animals.summary: The water buffalo is a large Asian bovine famous for wallowing in mud and water to stay cool. Domestic animals reach up to 700 kg and about 3 m in length, feeding on grasses and aquatic plants across wetlands, rice paddies, and floodplains. Domestic buffalo can live 20 to 25 years, while the truly wild population is small and scattered. The wild water buffalo is listed as Endangered.

sections.heading: Size and physical features
sections.body: The water buffalo is one of the heaviest of all bovines, with large bulls reaching up to 700 kg and a body length of around 3 m. Both sexes carry sweeping, backward-curving horns, which in wild animals are among the widest of any living cattle. Its wide, splayed hooves and flexible leg joints spread the animal's weight and stop it sinking in soft mud. A sparse coat and dark grey-black skin suit a life spent partly submerged in water.

sections.heading: Wallowing and habitat
sections.body: True to its name, the water buffalo depends on wetlands, rice paddies, and floodplains, and it wallows in mud and water for hours to cool down and shed parasites. It has few sweat glands, so submerging is essential for regulating body temperature in the tropical heat. Wallowing also coats the skin in mud, which dries into a protective layer against biting insects. This close tie to water shapes where the animal can live and how herds move through the landscape.

sections.heading: Diet and grazing
sections.body: Water buffalo are herbivores that graze on grasses, sedges, and a wide range of aquatic plants growing in and around water. Like other cattle they are ruminants, digesting tough vegetation in a multi-chambered stomach and chewing the cud to extract more nutrients. Their ability to thrive on coarse wetland plants that other livestock ignore makes them valuable in marshy farming regions. They usually feed in the cooler hours of morning and evening, resting in water through the midday heat.

sections.heading: Domestic buffalo and human use
sections.body: Domesticated for thousands of years, the water buffalo is a cornerstone of farming across South and Southeast Asia and beyond. It provides milk far richer than cow's milk, the basis for traditional mozzarella and many South Asian dairy products, as well as meat, hides, and dung used as fuel and fertiliser. As a draught animal it ploughs flooded rice fields where tractors struggle, earning the nickname "the living tractor of the East." Domestic buffalo commonly live 20 to 25 years.

sections.heading: Temperament and behaviour
sections.body: Despite their bulk, domestic water buffalo are generally calm and manageable, and they bond closely with the people who work with them. They are social animals that gather in herds, with strong ties between females and their calves. When threatened, however, they can charge at up to 48 km/h and are capable of driving off predators as large as tigers. Wild buffalo are far more wary and aggressive than their domesticated relatives.

sections.heading: Why wild water buffalo are endangered
sections.body: While hundreds of millions of domestic buffalo exist worldwide, the genuinely wild water buffalo is listed as Endangered by the IUCN, with only a few thousand animals left. Its numbers have crashed through habitat loss, hunting, and disease, but the greatest long-term threat is interbreeding with domestic and feral buffalo, which dilutes the wild gene pool. Remaining populations survive in scattered reserves in India, Nepal, and Southeast Asia. Protecting these isolated herds from crossbreeding is central to saving the wild form.

faqs.question: How much does a water buffalo weigh?
faqs.answer: Large water buffalo weigh up to about 700 kg (1,540 lb), with wild bulls being the biggest. They can reach roughly 3 m in body length.

faqs.question: Why do water buffalo wallow in mud?
faqs.answer: Water buffalo have very few sweat glands, so they wallow in mud and water to cool down. The mud also dries on their skin as a protective coat against biting insects and parasites.

faqs.question: What do water buffalo eat?
faqs.answer: They are herbivores that graze on grasses, sedges, and aquatic plants in and around wetlands. As ruminants they chew the cud, which helps them digest coarse vegetation that other livestock avoid.

faqs.question: Are water buffalo dangerous?
faqs.answer: Domestic water buffalo are usually calm and easy to handle. Wild buffalo are far more aggressive and can charge at up to 48 km/h, making them capable of fending off predators as large as tigers.

faqs.question: Are water buffalo endangered?
faqs.answer: Domestic water buffalo are extremely numerous, but the truly wild water buffalo is listed as Endangered by the IUCN. Only a few thousand wild animals remain, threatened mainly by habitat loss and interbreeding with domestic buffalo.

faqs.question: How long do water buffalo live?
faqs.answer: Domestic water buffalo typically live 20 to 25 years. Wild populations tend to have shorter lifespans because of predation, disease, and environmental pressures.
