animals.name: Ferret
animals.summary: The ferret is a small domesticated carnivore descended from the European polecat, kept for centuries as a working and companion animal. Slender and long-bodied, it typically weighs 0.7 to 2 kg and measures around half a metre including the tail, with males (hobs) noticeably larger than females (jills). Ferrets are famously playful and inquisitive, sleep much of the day, and live for about 6 to 10 years with good veterinary care.

sections.heading: Origins and domestication
sections.body: Ferrets are the domesticated form of the European polecat and have been kept by people for well over two thousand years. They were bred chiefly to bolt rabbits and rats from their burrows, a practice known as ferreting that is still carried out in parts of Britain today. Unlike wild mustelids, ferrets cannot survive well on their own and depend entirely on human care. Their scientific name, Mustela putorius furo, reflects this ancestry, with furo meaning 'thief' in Latin.

sections.heading: Body and physical traits
sections.body: A ferret has a long, tubular body, short legs, and a flexible spine that lets it squeeze through tight spaces and turn almost back on itself. Adults usually weigh between 0.7 and 2 kg, with hobs considerably heavier and longer than jills. Their coats come in a range of colours and patterns, from sable and albino to silver and cinnamon. Well-developed scent glands give ferrets a distinctive musky odour that many owners reduce through neutering and regular bathing.

sections.heading: Temperament and behaviour
sections.body: Ferrets are intensely curious, social, and playful, and are best known for the 'weasel war dance', a frenzied hopping display they perform when excited. They sleep for as much as 14 to 18 hours a day but are lively and energetic during their waking hours. Most enjoy the company of other ferrets and form strong bonds with their owners. Their inquisitive nature means they will investigate and often steal small objects, tucking them away in hidden caches.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: As obligate carnivores, ferrets need a meat-based diet rich in animal protein and fat, with very little carbohydrate or fibre. In practice this means whole prey, high-quality ferret kibble, or specially formulated raw diets. Their digestive systems are short and process food quickly, so they eat little and often throughout the day. Foods high in sugar or plant matter can cause serious health problems and should be avoided.

sections.heading: Care and lifespan
sections.body: With attentive care, ferrets live around 6 to 10 years. They need a secure enclosure, daily supervised exercise, and mental stimulation to stay healthy and content. Because they are prone to conditions such as adrenal disease and insulinoma, regular checks with a vet experienced in exotic pets are important. In many places ferrets are also given vaccinations against canine distemper and rabies, both of which can be fatal to them.

faqs.question: Are ferrets wild or domesticated animals?
faqs.answer: Ferrets are fully domesticated animals, bred from the European polecat over more than two thousand years. They are not a wild species and generally cannot survive without human care, which is why they are kept as pets and working animals rather than living in the wild.

faqs.question: How long do ferrets live?
faqs.answer: Pet ferrets typically live about 6 to 10 years with good veterinary care. Lifespan depends heavily on diet, housing, and access to a vet experienced with exotic pets, since ferrets are prone to several age-related illnesses.

faqs.question: What do ferrets eat?
faqs.answer: Ferrets are obligate carnivores and need a meat-based diet high in animal protein and fat. This usually means high-quality ferret kibble, whole prey, or a properly balanced raw diet. Sugary treats and foods high in plant fibre should be avoided because ferrets cannot digest them well.

faqs.question: Why do ferrets smell musky?
faqs.answer: Ferrets have scent glands in their skin that produce a natural musky odour. Neutering greatly reduces the smell, and regular cleaning of their bedding and enclosure keeps it manageable. Frequent bathing is not recommended, as it can actually make the odour worse by stimulating the glands.

faqs.question: Do ferrets get along with other pets?
faqs.answer: Ferrets are very social and usually thrive in the company of other ferrets. They can sometimes live alongside dogs and cats with careful introductions, but their strong prey drive makes them a danger to rabbits, rodents, and birds, which should always be kept well away from them.

faqs.question: How big do ferrets get?
faqs.answer: Adult ferrets usually weigh between 0.7 and 2 kg and measure around half a metre from nose to tail tip. Males, called hobs, are noticeably larger and heavier than females, known as jills.

animals.name: American Mink
animals.summary: The American mink (Neogale vison) is a sleek, semi-aquatic member of the weasel family, native to North America and widely introduced across Europe and Asia. About 60 cm long including the tail and weighing up to 1.6 kg, it has dark, water-repellent fur and hunts fish, birds, and small mammals along rivers and lakesides. An agile swimmer and climber, it lives up to ten years in the wild.

sections.heading: Semi-aquatic hunting
sections.body: The American mink is equally at home in water and on land, hunting fish, frogs, and crayfish beneath the surface and rodents, rabbits, and birds along the bank. It swims strongly and can dive to catch prey, using partially webbed feet and a streamlined body. On land it moves in a bounding gait at up to 25 km/h (16 mph) and readily climbs to reach nests. This versatility makes it one of the most effective small predators of wetland habitats.

sections.heading: Fur and body
sections.body: Mink are prized for their dense, glossy, water-repellent fur, which ranges from rich chocolate brown to nearly black, usually with a small white patch on the chin or chest. The coat traps a layer of air that keeps the animal warm and dry even in cold water. A long, low-slung body and short legs suit a life of squeezing into burrows and diving after prey. Males are noticeably larger and heavier than females.

sections.heading: Territory and behaviour
sections.body: American mink are solitary and territorial, marking the banks of their home range with a strong-smelling secretion from scent glands. Each individual patrols a stretch of waterway, often using several dens among tree roots, rocks, or abandoned burrows. They are active mainly at dawn and dusk and largely avoid one another except to breed. Females hold smaller territories that may overlap with a larger male's range.

sections.heading: Breeding and kits
sections.body: Mink breed in late winter and early spring, and after a variable gestation the female gives birth to a litter of around four to six kits in a sheltered den. The young are born blind and helpless and are cared for solely by the mother. They are weaned at roughly eight weeks and become independent by late summer, dispersing to establish territories of their own. Most are ready to breed by the following year.

sections.heading: An invasive species in Europe
sections.body: Although native to North America, the American mink has spread widely across Europe and parts of Asia after escaping and being released from fur farms. In these regions it is a damaging invasive species, preying heavily on ground-nesting birds, water voles, and other native wildlife that lack defences against it. In Britain it has been a major factor in the decline of the water vole. Control programmes now aim to protect vulnerable native species from its impact.

sections.heading: Distribution and status
sections.body: In its native North America the American mink is common and widespread along rivers, lakes, marshes, and coastlines, and the IUCN lists it as Least Concern. It tolerates a wide range of wetland habitats and is not threatened across its natural range. Wild mink live three to ten years, with survival often limited by harsh winters and larger predators. Its adaptability is exactly what makes it such a successful colonist elsewhere.

faqs.question: Is the American mink the same as the European mink?
faqs.answer: No, they are different species. The American mink (Neogale vison) is larger and now widespread in Europe as an invasive animal, while the native European mink is a separate, rarer species that has declined sharply, partly due to competition from its American relative.

faqs.question: What do American mink eat?
faqs.answer: American mink are carnivores that hunt fish, frogs, and crayfish in the water and rodents, rabbits, and birds on land. Their varied diet and willingness to hunt both in and out of water make them highly effective predators.

faqs.question: Can mink swim?
faqs.answer: Yes, mink are excellent swimmers and divers, with partly webbed feet and water-repellent fur. They regularly hunt underwater prey such as fish and crayfish.

faqs.question: Why are American mink a problem in Britain?
faqs.answer: American mink escaped and were released from fur farms and have since spread across Britain, where they are an invasive species. They prey heavily on native wildlife such as water voles and ground-nesting birds, contributing to serious declines.

faqs.question: How long do American mink live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, American mink typically live three to ten years, though many die younger. Captive animals tend to live longer thanks to steady food and shelter.

faqs.question: How big is an American mink?
faqs.answer: Including the tail, an American mink is about 60 cm long and weighs between 0.6 and 1.6 kg (1.3 to 3.5 lb). Males are considerably larger than females.

animals.name: Stoat
animals.summary: The stoat (Mustela erminea) is a small, slender carnivore of the weasel family found across the Northern Hemisphere in woodland, farmland, and tundra. Weighing just 200 to 400 g and about 30 cm long, it is a fierce, agile hunter of rabbits, rodents, birds, and eggs. In the far north its brown coat turns pure white in winter, when it is known as ermine. Stoats live 4 to 7 years and are listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Appearance and the ermine coat
sections.body: The stoat is a long, low-slung mammal about 30 cm in length, with chestnut-brown fur above, a creamy belly, and a distinctive black tip to its tail. It weighs only 200 to 400 g, with males noticeably larger than females. In colder regions the coat moults to pure white each winter, a form long prized in fur trade and heraldry as ermine, though the black tail-tip always remains. This seasonal change is triggered by shortening day length and provides camouflage against snow.

sections.heading: A ferocious hunter
sections.body: For its size the stoat is one of the boldest predators in the countryside, routinely killing rabbits several times its own weight. It hunts by scent and sight, following prey into burrows and dispatching it with a precise bite to the base of the skull. Stoats are famed for 'mesmerising' rabbits with a strange, hypnotic dance of leaps and twists, which may confuse the prey long enough to close in. Their long, thin bodies let them pursue rodents right into their tunnels.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: The stoat is a pure carnivore, feeding mainly on rabbits and small rodents such as voles and mice, along with birds and their eggs. It has a fast metabolism and must eat frequently, taking a large share of its body weight in food each day. When prey is plentiful a stoat will cache surplus kills to see it through leaner times. This appetite makes it a valuable natural check on rabbit and rodent numbers on farmland.

sections.heading: Speed, agility and senses
sections.body: Stoats are quick and tireless, moving in a bounding gait and reaching around 25 km/h in short bursts. They are excellent climbers and swimmers, able to follow prey up trees or across water. Sharp hearing and a keen sense of smell guide most of their hunting. Their slim build lets them squeeze through tiny gaps, but it also means they lose heat quickly and must remain active to keep feeding.

sections.heading: Breeding and life cycle
sections.body: Stoats have an unusual reproductive trick called delayed implantation, in which a fertilised egg pauses its development for many months before the young grow. This means females mate in summer but do not give birth until the following spring, timing the litter to the season of plenty. A litter usually numbers six to twelve kits, born blind and helpless in a den. Wild stoats generally live four to seven years, though many die much younger.

sections.heading: Range, status and impact
sections.body: The stoat ranges widely across the woodlands, farmland, and tundra of Europe, Asia, and North America, and is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. In its native range it is a natural part of the ecosystem and a useful control on rabbits. Where it has been introduced, however, notably in New Zealand, it has become a serious threat to ground-nesting native birds. There it is the target of intensive predator-control efforts.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a stoat and a weasel?
faqs.answer: A stoat is larger than a weasel and always has a black tip to its tail, while a weasel's tail is short and lacks the black tip. Stoats also move with a bounding gait and can turn white in winter, when they are called ermine.

faqs.question: Why does a stoat turn white in winter?
faqs.answer: In colder northern regions the stoat's brown coat moults to pure white each winter, triggered by shortening daylight. The white fur, known as ermine, camouflages it against snow, though the black tail-tip always stays.

faqs.question: What do stoats eat?
faqs.answer: Stoats are carnivores that mainly eat rabbits and small rodents such as voles and mice, along with birds and eggs. They regularly kill rabbits several times their own body weight.

faqs.question: How big is a stoat?
faqs.answer: A stoat is about 30 cm long and weighs only 200 to 400 g, with males larger than females. Despite this small size it is a bold predator capable of taking prey much bigger than itself.

faqs.question: Are stoats dangerous?
faqs.answer: Stoats pose no real danger to people and will avoid humans. They can, however, be serious predators of poultry, game birds, and, where introduced, native wildlife. In New Zealand they are a major threat to ground-nesting birds.

faqs.question: How long do stoats live?
faqs.answer: Wild stoats typically live 4 to 7 years, although many die much younger from predators and harsh conditions. Their reproduction uses delayed implantation, so young are born in spring when food is plentiful.

animals.name: Brown Lemming
animals.summary: The brown lemming is a small, stocky rodent of the Arctic and alpine tundra of Scandinavia and Russia. Weighing only 30 to 112 g and measuring about 15 cm, it feeds on grasses, sedges, moss, and bark and stays active all winter beneath the snow. Lemmings are famous for dramatic population booms and crashes, and they live just one to two years. The species is listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Size and appearance
sections.body: The brown lemming is a small, round-bodied rodent with dense fur, short legs, tiny ears, and a very short tail, all adaptations for conserving heat in the cold. It weighs only 30 to 112 g and measures around 15 cm long, with its weight varying through the seasons. Its thick coat and compact shape reduce heat loss in the harsh tundra climate. Strong claws help it dig burrows and tunnels through soil and snow.

sections.heading: Life on the tundra
sections.body: Lemmings live in the treeless Arctic and alpine tundra of Scandinavia and Russia, among the harshest habitats any mammal endures. Rather than hibernating, they stay active all winter, tunnelling through the insulating layer of snow where the temperature is far milder than the air above. There they build nests of grass and continue to feed and even breed in favourable years. This ability to exploit the space beneath the snow is key to surviving the long polar winter.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: The brown lemming is a herbivore that eats grasses, sedges, moss, and bark, feeding almost constantly to fuel its fast metabolism. Because tundra plants are low in nutrients, a lemming must consume large amounts of vegetation each day relative to its size. In winter it gnaws on roots, shoots, and bark reached through its snow tunnels. Its intense grazing can strip patches of tundra during years when the population is high.

sections.heading: Population booms and crashes
sections.body: Lemmings are best known for their dramatic population cycles, in which numbers explode roughly every three to five years and then collapse just as sharply. Their rapid breeding, with several litters a year, allows the population to multiply quickly when food and conditions are good. When numbers peak, food runs short and many lemmings disperse in large movements to find new ground. This boom-and-bust pattern ripples through the whole tundra ecosystem.

sections.heading: The myth of mass suicide
sections.body: Contrary to popular belief, lemmings do not deliberately hurl themselves off cliffs to their deaths. The myth was cemented by a 1958 Disney film in which the animals were pushed off a ledge for the camera. What really happens is that during population peaks, huge numbers migrate in search of food and some drown while trying to cross rivers or lakes. The truth is a story of desperate dispersal, not deliberate self-destruction.

sections.heading: Predators and conservation
sections.body: As a small, abundant rodent, the lemming is a crucial food source for tundra predators such as Arctic foxes, snowy owls, skuas, and stoats. The breeding success of many of these predators rises and falls in step with the lemming cycle. The brown lemming itself is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, being widespread and, in good years, extremely numerous. These short-lived rodents rarely survive beyond one to two years.

faqs.question: Do lemmings really commit mass suicide?
faqs.answer: No. The idea that lemmings deliberately jump off cliffs is a myth, popularised by a staged 1958 Disney film. In reality, large numbers migrate during population peaks and some accidentally drown while crossing rivers or lakes.

faqs.question: What do lemmings eat?
faqs.answer: Lemmings are herbivores that eat grasses, sedges, moss, and bark. They feed almost constantly to fuel a fast metabolism, and in winter they gnaw roots and shoots reached through their snow tunnels.

faqs.question: Where do lemmings live?
faqs.answer: The brown lemming lives in the Arctic and alpine tundra of Scandinavia and Russia. It stays active all winter, tunnelling beneath the snow where temperatures are milder than the freezing air above.

faqs.question: Why do lemming populations rise and fall so dramatically?
faqs.answer: Lemmings breed very fast, producing several litters a year, so their numbers can explode roughly every three to five years when conditions are good. When food runs short, the population crashes just as sharply.

faqs.question: How big is a lemming?
faqs.answer: The brown lemming is small, measuring about 15 cm long and weighing only 30 to 112 g. Its stocky body, dense fur, and short limbs all help it conserve heat in the cold tundra.

faqs.question: How long do lemmings live?
faqs.answer: Lemmings are short-lived rodents, typically surviving just one to two years in the wild. High predation and the boom-and-bust nature of their populations keep individual lifespans short.

animals.name: Common Shrew
animals.summary: The common shrew (Sorex araneus) is a tiny, insect-eating mammal found in woodlands, gardens, and grasslands across Europe. Weighing just 5–15 g and measuring around 8 cm, it is one of the continent's smallest mammals, with a pointed snout, velvety fur, and a ferocious appetite. Shrews live fast and die young, rarely surviving beyond one to two years in the wild.

sections.heading: A relentless appetite
sections.body: The common shrew has an extraordinarily fast metabolism and must eat almost constantly to stay alive. It consumes around 80–90 per cent of its own body weight in food every day and can starve to death in just a few hours without a meal. Shrews forage in short bursts around the clock, taking only brief naps between hunts. This punishing energy budget shapes almost everything about the animal's short, frantic life.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: Shrews are insectivores that hunt insects, earthworms, slugs, spiders, and other small invertebrates among leaf litter and soil. They rely heavily on smell, touch, and a fine sense of hearing rather than eyesight, which is poor. The common shrew has a mildly venomous bite, produced by its saliva, which helps subdue larger prey such as earthworms. Sharp, red-tipped teeth let it crunch through tough insect shells with ease.

sections.heading: Territory and behaviour
sections.body: Common shrews are solitary and fiercely territorial, defending their patch with loud, high-pitched squeaks when neighbours trespass. They spend much of their time in runways and tunnels through vegetation and leaf litter, moving with quick, restless energy at up to 8 km/h. Outside the brief breeding season, adults generally avoid one another. Their constant, twitchy activity reflects the need to keep finding food day and night.

sections.heading: Breeding and short lives
sections.body: Female shrews raise several litters between spring and late summer, each usually containing five to seven tiny young. The mother sometimes leads her weaned babies in a "caravan," each youngster gripping the tail of the one in front so the family moves as a chain. Young shrews grow quickly and are independent within weeks. Most adults die after a single breeding season, so few live more than a year or two.

sections.heading: Role in the ecosystem
sections.body: Despite its size, the common shrew is an abundant and important part of European woodland and grassland communities. As a voracious predator of insects, worms, and slugs, it helps keep invertebrate numbers in check across gardens and farmland. Shrews in turn are hunted by owls, weasels, and foxes, though many mammal predators reject them because of foul-tasting scent glands. The species is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and remains widespread and common.

faqs.question: Is a shrew a rodent?
faqs.answer: No. Although it looks a little like a mouse, the common shrew is not a rodent but an insectivore, belonging to a separate group of mammals. Its long pointed snout, tiny eyes, and sharp teeth set it apart from mice and voles.

faqs.question: Why do shrews eat so much?
faqs.answer: Shrews have an exceptionally fast metabolism and burn energy very quickly, so they must eat almost constantly. A common shrew eats around 80–90 per cent of its body weight each day and can starve within a few hours if it goes without food.

faqs.question: Are shrews venomous?
faqs.answer: The common shrew has a mildly venomous bite produced in its saliva, which helps it subdue prey such as earthworms. The venom is not dangerous to humans, though a bite from a handled shrew can sting.

faqs.question: How long do shrews live?
faqs.answer: Common shrews have very short lives, rarely surviving beyond one to two years in the wild. Most die after their first and only breeding season.

faqs.question: What do shrews eat?
faqs.answer: Shrews are insectivores that feed mainly on insects, earthworms, slugs, and spiders. They hunt almost constantly among leaf litter and soil, using smell and touch rather than sight to find prey.

faqs.question: Do cats kill shrews but not eat them?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Cats frequently catch shrews but leave them uneaten because the shrews' scent glands make them taste unpleasant. Many wild predators avoid eating shrews for the same reason.

animals.name: Banded Mongoose
animals.summary: The banded mongoose is a small, highly social carnivore-leaning omnivore of sub-Saharan Africa's savannas and open woodlands. Named for the dark bands across its back, it weighs 1.5 to 2.5 kg and measures around 0.45 m in body length. It lives in bustling groups that forage together and famously takes on snakes with speed and agility. The IUCN lists the banded mongoose as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Appearance and identity
sections.body: The banded mongoose is a compact, ground-dwelling mammal with coarse greyish-brown fur crossed by a series of dark bands running across its back, which give the species its name. It has a slender body, short legs, and strong claws well suited to digging out prey. Adults weigh between 1.5 and 2.5 kg and reach about 0.45 m in body length, plus a tapering tail. Its low, quick build lets it move with the darting agility for which mongooses are famous.

sections.heading: Social life and behaviour
sections.body: Banded mongooses are intensely social, living in colonies of a dozen to forty or more that forage, sleep, and defend territory together. They shelter in communal dens, often in old termite mounds or burrow systems, moving between several dens within their range. Group members keep in touch with a constant stream of calls, and researchers have shown these calls carry meaningful information about what an individual is doing. The whole group helps guard and raise the young, sharing the duties of babysitting and teaching.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: The banded mongoose is an omnivore, though most of its diet is animal prey. It feeds mainly on insects and their larvae, along with rodents, reptiles, eggs, and some fruit. Foraging groups spread out across the ground, sniffing and digging through leaf litter and soil to unearth beetles, millipedes, and grubs. They have learned clever tricks such as smashing eggs and hard-shelled prey against rocks to break them open.

sections.heading: Facing snakes and predators
sections.body: Mongooses are celebrated for their boldness against snakes, and the banded mongoose will mob and harry serpents that stray too close to the group. Their speed, agility, and thick fur help them dodge strikes, though they are not truly immune to venom in the way some myths suggest. Against larger predators such as birds of prey and jackals, safety lies in numbers, with sentries watching while others feed. When threatened, the whole group may bunch together and advance as one to appear larger and more dangerous.

sections.heading: Breeding and young
sections.body: Unusually, most females in a banded mongoose group often give birth around the same time, producing a communal litter of pups. The young are raised cooperatively, with adults taking turns to guard the den while others forage. Each pup may form a bond with a particular adult 'escort' that feeds, grooms, and protects it as it learns to find food. This shared care helps explain why so many pups survive in a busy, competitive group.

sections.heading: Range and conservation
sections.body: The banded mongoose is widespread across the savannas and open woodlands of sub-Saharan Africa, wherever there is cover, food, and den sites. It adapts well to a range of habitats and is not currently threatened, which is why the IUCN lists it as Least Concern. Its populations remain healthy and even thrive near human settlements in some areas. In the wild, banded mongooses live around 8 to 10 years.

faqs.question: Can a mongoose really kill a snake?
faqs.answer: Yes, mongooses are famous for taking on snakes, using their speed, agility, and quick reflexes to dodge strikes and deliver bites of their own. Banded mongooses often mob snakes as a group, though they are not fully immune to venom and rely mainly on avoiding being bitten.

faqs.question: What do banded mongooses eat?
faqs.answer: Banded mongooses are omnivores whose diet is mostly insects and their larvae, along with rodents, reptiles, eggs, and some fruit. They forage in groups, digging through soil and leaf litter and even smashing hard-shelled prey against rocks.

faqs.question: How big is a banded mongoose?
faqs.answer: A banded mongoose weighs between 1.5 and 2.5 kg (3.3 to 5.5 lb) and measures about 0.45 m in body length, plus its tail. It is a small, low-slung mammal built for quick, agile movement on the ground.

faqs.question: Do mongooses live in groups?
faqs.answer: Yes. Banded mongooses are highly social and live in colonies of a dozen to forty or more individuals that forage, sleep, and defend territory together. They share communal dens and cooperatively raise their young.

faqs.question: How long do banded mongooses live?
faqs.answer: Banded mongooses typically live around 8 to 10 years in the wild. Their cooperative group living, with sentries and shared care of pups, helps individuals survive predators and raise young successfully.

faqs.question: Are banded mongooses endangered?
faqs.answer: No, the banded mongoose is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. It is widespread and adaptable across sub-Saharan Africa, and its populations remain healthy, sometimes even thriving close to human settlements.

animals.name: Aye-aye
animals.summary: The aye-aye is a large nocturnal lemur found only in Madagascar, easily recognised by its bushy tail, rodent-like teeth and long, spindly middle finger. It weighs 2 to 3 kg (4.4 to 6.6 lb) and forages alone at night for insect larvae, fruit, nectar and fungi. Long-lived for a lemur, it can survive 20 to 23 years in the wild. The IUCN lists it as Endangered.

sections.heading: A unique way of finding food
sections.body: The aye-aye feeds using a method found in no other primate, sometimes called percussive foraging. It taps rapidly along a branch with its slender middle finger and listens for the hollow echo of a tunnel left by wood-boring grubs. Once it locates a cavity, it gnaws a hole with its ever-growing incisors and hooks the larva out with that same thin finger. This tap-and-listen technique fills the same ecological niche that woodpeckers occupy elsewhere in the world.

sections.heading: Diet beyond insects
sections.body: Although insect larvae are a signature food, the aye-aye is an omnivore with a varied menu. It also eats fruit, nectar and fungi, and is fond of the seeds inside ripe coconuts and ramy nuts, which it opens with its powerful teeth. This flexible diet allows it to survive in both native rainforest and human-planted coconut groves. Its taste for cultivated crops occasionally brings it into conflict with farmers.

sections.heading: Anatomy and senses
sections.body: The aye-aye grows to around 0.9 m (3 ft) including its long, bushy tail, which is often longer than its body. Its most extraordinary feature is the elongated, almost skeletal middle finger, fitted with a ball-and-socket joint that lets it swivel freely. Large, sensitive ears give it acute hearing for detecting grubs beneath bark, and its huge eyes are adapted to gathering light on moonlit nights. Unusually among primates, its front teeth never stop growing, like a rodent's.

sections.heading: Behaviour and lifestyle
sections.body: Aye-ayes are strictly nocturnal and spend the daylight hours asleep in a spherical nest of leaves and twigs high in the canopy. They are largely solitary, moving slowly through the trees and leaping between branches to cover their large home ranges. Males range more widely than females and their territories often overlap, though individuals usually forage alone. They are surprisingly long-lived for a lemur, reaching over two decades in the wild.

sections.heading: Why it is endangered
sections.body: The aye-aye is listed as Endangered by the IUCN, threatened chiefly by the clearing of Madagascar's forests for farming and timber. It also suffers from direct persecution, because some local traditions regard the animal as an omen of bad luck and kill it on sight. Its slow reproduction, with females raising a single infant every two to three years, makes it hard for populations to recover. Protected reserves and captive-breeding programmes now play a key role in safeguarding the species.

faqs.question: What is an aye-aye?
faqs.answer: The aye-aye is a nocturnal lemur native to Madagascar and the world's largest nocturnal primate. It is famous for its long, thin middle finger, which it uses to fish grubs out of tree bark.

faqs.question: Why does the aye-aye have such a long finger?
faqs.answer: Its elongated middle finger is a specialised feeding tool. The aye-aye taps on branches to find hollow tunnels made by insect larvae, gnaws a hole in the wood, then uses the thin finger to hook the grubs out.

faqs.question: What do aye-ayes eat?
faqs.answer: Aye-ayes are omnivores. They eat insect larvae, fruit, nectar and fungi, and are especially fond of coconut flesh and the seeds inside hard nuts, which they crack open with their strong, ever-growing teeth.

faqs.question: How long do aye-ayes live?
faqs.answer: Aye-ayes can live 20 to 23 years in the wild, which is unusually long for a lemur. In captivity, well-cared-for individuals may live even longer.

faqs.question: Are aye-ayes endangered?
faqs.answer: Yes. The aye-aye is classified as Endangered by the IUCN. Habitat loss across Madagascar and killing driven by local superstition are the main threats to its survival.

faqs.question: Where do aye-ayes live?
faqs.answer: Aye-ayes live only on the island of Madagascar. They inhabit rainforests and, increasingly, coconut plantations, where they spend the day sleeping in leaf nests high in the trees.

animals.name: Philippine Tarsier
animals.summary: The Philippine tarsier is a tiny nocturnal primate found only in the forests of the southern Philippines. Weighing just 80 to 160 g and small enough to fit in a human hand, it has enormous eyes, each larger than its brain, and can leap more than 40 times its own body length between branches. Tarsiers are strictly carnivorous, live around 10 to 12 years in the wild, and are classed as Near Threatened.

sections.heading: Enormous eyes and night vision
sections.body: The tarsier's most striking feature is its pair of huge, fixed eyes, each roughly the size of its brain, which give it superb vision in near-total darkness. Because the eyes cannot move in their sockets, the tarsier instead rotates its head almost 180 degrees in each direction, like an owl, to scan for prey. Large membranous ears and sensitive hearing complete a body built entirely around hunting at night.

sections.heading: A leaping specialist
sections.body: Tarsiers are extraordinary jumpers, with greatly elongated ankle bones (the tarsus that gives them their name) acting like springs. From a standing cling on a vertical trunk, a tarsier can launch itself more than 40 body lengths in a single leap, snatching insects out of the air or landing precisely on the next branch. In short bursts they move through the forest at speeds of up to 24 km/h (15 mph).

sections.heading: A purely carnivorous primate
sections.body: Unusually for a primate, the tarsier eats no plant matter at all. Its diet is entirely animal: insects such as crickets, beetles, and moths, plus the occasional small lizard, bird, or even snake. It hunts by sitting still and listening, then pouncing with both hands to seize prey and deliver a killing bite.

sections.heading: Habitat and behaviour
sections.body: The Philippine tarsier lives in the lowland and montane forests of islands such as Bohol, Samar, Leyte, and Mindanao, favouring dense secondary growth and tangled vegetation. It is nocturnal and largely solitary, resting by day clinging to a vertical stem in thick cover. Individuals mark territories with scent and keep in contact using high-pitched calls, some of them ultrasonic and inaudible to humans.

sections.heading: Conservation and threats
sections.body: The Philippine tarsier is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN, with numbers declining as its forest home is cleared. Habitat loss from logging and agriculture is the main pressure, compounded by capture for the pet trade and disturbance from tourism. Tarsiers are highly stress-prone in captivity, so protecting wild forest and well-managed sanctuaries are the most effective safeguards.

sections.heading: Lifespan and reproduction
sections.body: In the wild tarsiers live around 10 to 12 years. Females give birth to a single, well-developed baby after a long gestation of about six months, and the newborn can cling to fur and even climb within days. Mothers sometimes carry infants in their mouths or park them on a branch while foraging nearby.

faqs.question: How big is a Philippine tarsier?
faqs.answer: The Philippine tarsier is one of the smallest primates, weighing just 80 to 160 g (0.08 to 0.16 kg) and measuring around 15 cm in body length. It is small enough to sit comfortably in the palm of a human hand.

faqs.question: Why do tarsiers have such big eyes?
faqs.answer: Tarsiers are nocturnal and their huge eyes gather as much light as possible for hunting in near darkness. Each eye is about the size of the animal's brain, and because the eyes cannot move, the tarsier turns its head almost 180 degrees to look around.

faqs.question: What do tarsiers eat?
faqs.answer: Tarsiers are strictly carnivorous, feeding on insects such as crickets, beetles, and moths. They also catch small vertebrates including lizards, birds, and even small snakes, making them the only entirely meat-eating primates.

faqs.question: How far can a tarsier jump?
faqs.answer: A tarsier can leap more than 40 times its own body length in a single bound, thanks to its elongated ankle bones. This lets it cross wide gaps between trees and snatch flying insects in mid-air.

faqs.question: Are tarsiers endangered?
faqs.answer: The Philippine tarsier is currently listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN. Its numbers are falling mainly because of forest clearance, along with capture for the pet trade and disturbance from tourism.

faqs.question: How long do tarsiers live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, Philippine tarsiers live around 10 to 12 years. They are highly sensitive to stress, which makes them very difficult to keep alive in captivity.

animals.name: White-handed Gibbon
animals.summary: The white-handed gibbon (Hylobates lar) is a small, tailless ape of the rainforest canopy in Thailand, Malaysia, and Sumatra. Weighing only 5 to 7 kg, it swings through the treetops by its long arms and can move at up to 56 km/h. Pairs are famous for their loud, musical duets and can live 25 to 30 years in the wild. The species is listed as Endangered.

sections.heading: Life in the canopy
sections.body: White-handed gibbons spend almost their entire lives high in the rainforest canopy, rarely coming down to the ground. Their long arms, hook-like hands, and lightweight bodies of just 5 to 7 kg make them supremely agile among the branches. They are not monkeys but small apes, lacking a tail and instead relying on balance and their powerful shoulders to move. Their fur ranges from cream to dark brown, but the hands and feet are always pale, giving the species its name.

sections.heading: Brachiation: swinging through the trees
sections.body: Gibbons are the fastest and most acrobatic of the tree-swinging apes, moving by a hand-over-hand technique called brachiation. Swinging beneath the branches, a white-handed gibbon can travel at up to 56 km/h and clear gaps of several metres in a single leap. Its ball-and-socket wrist joint lets the hand rotate freely, so momentum carries it smoothly from one hold to the next. This graceful, gravity-defying travel is far more efficient than climbing for an animal living in the treetops.

sections.heading: Singing duets
sections.body: White-handed gibbons are among the most vocal of all apes, and mated pairs perform elaborate morning duets that ring through the forest. The female typically leads with a rising, whooping call known as the great call, while the male adds his own phrases. These songs advertise the pair's bond and warn rival gibbons away from their territory. A duet can carry for over a kilometre through dense rainforest, letting neighbours locate one another without meeting.

sections.heading: Diet and daily routine
sections.body: Gibbons are mainly frugivores, favouring ripe fruit and supplementing it with young leaves, flowers, and the occasional insect. They forage by day, moving through a familiar home range and often returning to favourite fruiting trees. Because they seek out ripe fruit scattered across the canopy, they range widely each day in search of the best food. In the cool of midday they rest high in the branches before feeding again in the afternoon.

sections.heading: Family life
sections.body: White-handed gibbons live in small family groups built around a bonded adult pair and their offspring. Both parents help defend the territory, and young gibbons stay with the family for several years before leaving to find mates of their own. A single infant is born after a long gestation and clings to its mother as she swings through the canopy. In the wild these apes can live 25 to 30 years, growing slowly and investing heavily in each youngster.

sections.heading: Why it is endangered
sections.body: The white-handed gibbon is listed as Endangered by the IUCN, and its numbers are falling. The greatest threat is the loss of tropical rainforest to logging, agriculture, and palm-oil plantations, which fragments the continuous canopy these apes depend on. Gibbons are also captured for the illegal pet trade, with infants often taken after their mothers are killed. Protecting large, connected areas of intact rainforest is essential to their survival.

faqs.question: Is a gibbon a monkey or an ape?
faqs.answer: A gibbon is an ape, not a monkey. Like other apes it has no tail, and it belongs to the group known as the lesser apes, which are smaller and more agile than the great apes such as gorillas and chimpanzees.

faqs.question: How fast can a gibbon move through the trees?
faqs.answer: A white-handed gibbon can swing through the canopy at up to 56 km/h (35 mph) using a hand-over-hand motion called brachiation. It can also leap several metres between branches in a single bound.

faqs.question: Why do gibbons sing?
faqs.answer: Mated pairs sing loud, musical duets to strengthen their bond and to warn rival gibbons away from their territory. The songs can carry more than a kilometre through the forest, allowing neighbouring pairs to locate each other.

faqs.question: What do white-handed gibbons eat?
faqs.answer: They are mainly frugivores, feeding on ripe fruit and adding young leaves, flowers, and the occasional insect to their diet. They travel widely through the canopy each day to reach fruiting trees.

faqs.question: How long do gibbons live?
faqs.answer: White-handed gibbons typically live 25 to 30 years in the wild. They mature slowly and raise their young over several years within a close family group.

faqs.question: Why are gibbons endangered?
faqs.answer: White-handed gibbons are Endangered mainly because of the loss and fragmentation of their rainforest habitat to logging, farming, and palm-oil plantations. They are also captured for the illegal pet trade, which further reduces wild populations.

animals.name: Olive Baboon
animals.summary: The olive baboon is a large, ground-dwelling monkey found across the savannas, woodlands, and rocky hills of equatorial Africa. Highly intelligent and adaptable, it lives in big social troops, eats almost anything, and can run at up to 45 km/h (28 mph). Males can weigh around 30 kg, roughly twice the size of females. Olive baboons live 25 to 30 years in the wild and are listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Troop life and social structure
sections.body: Olive baboons live in large, complex troops that can number from a dozen to well over a hundred individuals. These groups are built around a core of related females with a stable dominance hierarchy, while males move between troops and compete for rank and mating opportunities. Social bonds are reinforced through grooming, which soothes tension and cements alliances that can decide an individual's status. Life in a big troop offers protection from predators such as lions, leopards, and hyenas.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: Baboons are opportunistic omnivores that eat grasses, seeds, fruit, roots, insects, and small mammals, and they will readily raid crops and rubbish where people live nearby. Their varied appetite and clever foraging are a big part of why they thrive in so many habitats. They use their hands with great dexterity to dig up roots, strip seeds, and turn over stones for insects. Cheek pouches let them stuff food away quickly and chew it later in a safer spot.

sections.heading: Intelligence and communication
sections.body: Olive baboons are among the more intelligent monkeys, capable of learning, planning, and forming intricate social strategies. They communicate through a rich repertoire of grunts, screams, and barks, along with facial expressions and postures that signal threat, submission, or reassurance. A yawning male flashing his long canine teeth is issuing a clear warning to rivals. Their sharp memories help them track the shifting alliances and rivalries that run through troop life.

sections.heading: Appearance and build
sections.body: The olive baboon takes its name from the greenish-grey sheen of its coat, and it has a dog-like muzzle, powerful jaws, and a sloping body around 1.1 metres long. Males are far larger than females, weighing up to about 30 kg, roughly twice a female's size, and carry a mane of longer hair over the shoulders. Both sexes have formidable canine teeth that can rival a leopard's in length. Their strong limbs and calloused sitting pads suit a life spent largely on the ground.

sections.heading: Habitat and adaptability
sections.body: Olive baboons range widely across equatorial Africa, occupying savannas, open woodlands, and rocky hills from Mali to Ethiopia and south into Tanzania. They are one of the most adaptable primates, thriving everywhere from semi-desert to moist forest edges and increasingly around farms and towns. Access to water and to safe sleeping sites, usually tall trees or cliffs, shapes where a troop can settle. This flexibility is a key reason the species remains so widespread and numerous.

sections.heading: Breeding and young
sections.body: Female baboons signal their fertility with conspicuous swellings, and dominant males compete for the chance to mate, though females also form lasting "friendships" with particular males. A single infant is born after a gestation of about six months and clings to its mother's belly before later riding jockey-style on her back. Youngsters learn the troop's social rules through play and close observation over several years. In the wild olive baboons can live 25 to 30 years, and longer in captivity.

faqs.question: What do olive baboons eat?
faqs.answer: Olive baboons are omnivores that eat grasses, seeds, fruit, roots, insects, and small mammals. They are highly opportunistic and will also raid crops and rubbish near human settlements, which is a major part of their success as a species.

faqs.question: How big do olive baboons get?
faqs.answer: Males can weigh up to about 30 kg (66 lb) and measure around 1.1 metres in body length, while females are roughly half that size. This strong size difference between the sexes is typical of baboons.

faqs.question: Are baboons dangerous?
faqs.answer: Baboons are powerful animals with long canine teeth and can be aggressive, especially males defending a troop or habituated animals raiding for food. Serious attacks on people are uncommon, but baboons should be treated with respect and never fed, as this encourages bold and risky behaviour.

faqs.question: How long do baboons live?
faqs.answer: Olive baboons typically live 25 to 30 years in the wild, and can live longer in captivity. Their long lifespan allows the complex social relationships and hierarchies of the troop to develop over many years.

faqs.question: How fast can a baboon run?
faqs.answer: Olive baboons can run at up to 45 km/h (28 mph) on all fours. This speed, combined with their agility and ability to climb, helps them escape predators such as leopards and lions.

faqs.question: Do baboons live in groups?
faqs.answer: Yes. Olive baboons live in large troops that can range from a dozen to more than a hundred members, organised around related females and a hierarchy of males. Troop life provides safety in numbers and a web of grooming-based social bonds.

animals.name: Mandrill
animals.summary: The mandrill is the world's most colourful primate, a large forest-floor monkey native to the rainforests of central Africa. Dominant males are unmistakable, with a scarlet-and-blue face and rump, and can weigh up to about 35 kg, far more than the smaller females. Mandrills are omnivores that live in some of the largest groups of any primate, reach 20 to 25 years in the wild, and are listed as Vulnerable.

sections.heading: The most colourful primate
sections.body: The mandrill is the most vividly coloured of all mammals, and the colour is strongest in dominant adult males. Their faces carry a bright red central stripe flanked by ridged blue cheeks, and the same scarlet and blue appear on the rump. These signals grow more intense with rank and testosterone, advertising a male's status to rivals and females across the dim forest floor.

sections.heading: Size and striking sexual dimorphism
sections.body: Mandrills show some of the most extreme size differences between the sexes of any primate. Large males can weigh up to about 35 kg (77 lb) and are roughly three times the weight of females, which are typically around 12 to 15 kg. Males also carry long canine teeth, sometimes several centimetres long, which they bare in a wide "yawn" to intimidate rivals.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: Mandrills are omnivores that forage mainly on the forest floor, using their strong hands and cheek pouches to gather food as they travel. Their diet is dominated by fruit and seeds, supplemented with leaves, roots, fungi, insects, and small animals such as frogs and lizards. They will dig through leaf litter and turn over stones to reach hidden invertebrates.

sections.heading: Life in huge groups
sections.body: Mandrills form some of the largest stable groups of any primate, and central troops known as hordes can number in the hundreds. These groups are built around related females and their young, with males often living more peripherally and joining fully in the breeding season. In forest sprints a mandrill can move at up to 40 km/h (25 mph) when escaping danger or covering ground between feeding sites.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The mandrill lives in the tropical rainforests and gallery forests of west-central Africa, chiefly in Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, and the Republic of the Congo. It is largely terrestrial, foraging by day across the forest floor, but climbs trees to sleep safely at night. Its range is bounded by major rivers that separate it from its close relative, the drill.

sections.heading: Conservation and threats
sections.body: The mandrill is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, and its numbers are falling. The two biggest threats are hunting for bushmeat, made easier by their large, noisy groups, and the loss and fragmentation of rainforest to logging and agriculture. Because mandrills breed slowly and depend on large tracts of intact forest, protected reserves are important to their future.

faqs.question: Why are mandrills so colourful?
faqs.answer: Mandrills use their bright red and blue faces and rumps to signal status and health. The colours are most intense in dominant males, driven by testosterone, and help advertise rank to rivals and females on the shadowy forest floor.

faqs.question: How big do mandrills get?
faqs.answer: Male mandrills can weigh up to about 35 kg (77 lb), while females are much smaller at roughly 12 to 15 kg. This makes the mandrill one of the largest and most sexually dimorphic of all monkeys.

faqs.question: What do mandrills eat?
faqs.answer: Mandrills are omnivores whose diet is dominated by fruit and seeds. They also eat leaves, roots, fungi, insects, and small animals such as frogs and lizards, foraging mostly on the forest floor.

faqs.question: Are mandrills the same as baboons?
faqs.answer: No, though they are closely related and were once grouped with baboons. Mandrills belong to their own genus, Mandrillus, and are distinguished by their vivid colouring and their rainforest, forest-floor lifestyle.

faqs.question: How large are mandrill groups?
faqs.answer: Mandrills form some of the largest groups of any primate. Central troops, known as hordes, can contain several hundred individuals, built mainly around related females and their young.

faqs.question: Are mandrills endangered?
faqs.answer: Mandrills are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, and their numbers are declining. The main threats are hunting for bushmeat and the loss of rainforest habitat to logging and farming.

animals.name: Proboscis Monkey
animals.summary: The proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus) is a large, reddish leaf-eating monkey found only on the island of Borneo, where it lives in mangroves, peat swamps, and riverine forest. Males are unmistakable for their huge, drooping noses and can weigh up to 24 kg, far more than females. Strong swimmers, they cross rivers and can move at up to 24 km/h. They live around 15 to 20 years and are listed as Endangered.

sections.heading: The remarkable nose
sections.body: The proboscis monkey takes its name from the enormous, pendulous nose of adult males, which can hang down past the mouth. This oversized nose is thought to amplify the male's honking calls and to signal health and status to females. Females and young have much smaller, upturned noses by comparison. No other primate carries a nose quite like it, making the species instantly recognisable.

sections.heading: Found only on Borneo
sections.body: Proboscis monkeys live nowhere else on Earth but the island of Borneo, shared by Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brunei. They keep to lowland habitats close to water, favouring coastal mangroves, peat-swamp forest, and forest along rivers. Rarely straying far from the water's edge, they gather in the trees overhanging rivers and estuaries. This tight link to waterside forest makes them especially sensitive to the loss of these habitats.

sections.heading: Leaf-eating and the pot belly
sections.body: Proboscis monkeys are herbivores, feeding mainly on young leaves and unripe fruit, along with seeds and flowers. To digest this tough, leafy diet they have a large, chambered stomach full of bacteria that ferment the plant material, giving them a distinctly pot-bellied appearance. This specialised gut means they generally avoid sweet ripe fruit, which can ferment too quickly and upset their digestion. They feed mostly in the morning and late afternoon, resting during the heat of the day.

sections.heading: Swimming and moving through the forest
sections.body: Unusually among monkeys, proboscis monkeys are excellent swimmers, with partially webbed fingers and toes that help them cross rivers. They can move at up to 24 km/h and will leap dramatically from trees into the water to escape predators such as crocodiles or to reach the far bank. In the trees they travel by climbing and leaping through the canopy. This swimming ability lets them exploit the flooded, waterlogged forests that many other primates avoid.

sections.heading: Social structure
sections.body: Proboscis monkeys live in harem groups made up of one dominant male, several females, and their young, alongside separate bachelor groups of males. At night, many groups gather in trees along the same stretch of river, coming together in loose communities before dispersing to feed by day. Males are much larger than females, weighing up to around 24 kg, and use their size and honking calls to hold their group together. Young males eventually leave to join bachelor bands before trying to win a harem of their own.

sections.heading: Why it is endangered
sections.body: The proboscis monkey is listed as Endangered by the IUCN, and its population continues to fall. Its waterside forests are being cleared rapidly for palm-oil plantations, logging, and shrimp farming, destroying the mangroves and riverine trees it depends on. Because the species is confined to Borneo and tied to a narrow band of habitat, it has little room to retreat. Protecting mangrove and riverside forest is critical to its future.

faqs.question: Why do proboscis monkeys have such big noses?
faqs.answer: Only adult males have the huge nose, which is thought to amplify their honking calls and signal health and status to females. Females and young have much smaller, upturned noses.

faqs.question: Where do proboscis monkeys live?
faqs.answer: Proboscis monkeys are found only on the island of Borneo, in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brunei. They live in lowland habitats near water, including mangroves, peat-swamp forest, and forest along rivers.

faqs.question: Can proboscis monkeys swim?
faqs.answer: Yes. They are among the best-swimming of all monkeys, with partially webbed fingers and toes. They will leap from trees into rivers to cross to the other side or to escape predators such as crocodiles.

faqs.question: What do proboscis monkeys eat?
faqs.answer: They are herbivores that feed mainly on young leaves and unripe fruit, along with seeds and flowers. Their large, chambered stomach ferments this leafy diet, giving them a pot-bellied look.

faqs.question: How big do proboscis monkeys get?
faqs.answer: Males are much larger than females and can weigh up to around 24 kg (53 lb). This large size difference between the sexes is typical of the species.

faqs.question: Why are proboscis monkeys endangered?
faqs.answer: They are Endangered mainly because their waterside forests on Borneo are being cleared for palm-oil plantations, logging, and shrimp farming. Confined to a single island and a narrow band of habitat, they have little room to retreat.

animals.name: Howler Monkey
animals.summary: The howler monkey is a large, leaf-eating New World primate famous for having one of the loudest calls of any land animal in the Americas. Living in the tropical forests of Central and South America, it weighs around 5 to 10 kg and spends almost its whole life high in the canopy. Its booming dawn chorus, produced with the help of a specialised throat bone, can carry for several kilometres. Howlers live 15 to 20 years in the wild and are listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: The famous howl
sections.body: Howler monkeys are named for the deep, roaring calls that make them one of the loudest land animals in the Americas. Males produce these booming howls using an enlarged hyoid bone in the throat that acts as a resonating chamber. The calls carry for several kilometres through dense forest and are used to space out rival troops without the need to fight. Choruses are most striking at dawn and dusk, when neighbouring groups answer one another across the canopy.

sections.heading: Range and habitat
sections.body: Howler monkeys, of the genus Alouatta, live throughout the tropical forests of Central and South America, from southern Mexico to northern Argentina. They inhabit a range of woodland, including rainforest, dry forest, and mangrove, wherever there are enough tall trees. Almost their entire life is spent in the canopy, where they find food, sleep, and travel. They are among the most widespread of the New World monkeys.

sections.heading: Diet and slow metabolism
sections.body: Howlers are folivores, feeding mainly on leaves along with fruit, flowers, and buds. Leaves are low in energy and slow to digest, so the monkeys have an enlarged gut where bacteria ferment the tough plant material. To cope with this low-energy diet they rest for much of the day, sometimes for 15 hours or more. When fruit and young leaves are plentiful they take advantage of the richer food.

sections.heading: Movement through the canopy
sections.body: Howler monkeys move slowly and deliberately through the trees, rarely leaping and instead climbing carefully from branch to branch. Their strong, fully prehensile tail acts as a fifth limb, gripping branches and even supporting the animal's full weight while it reaches for food. Top speeds of around 16 km/h are reached only in short bursts, as their leaf-based diet leaves little energy to spare. They almost never come down to the ground, staying safe among the high branches.

sections.heading: Social structure
sections.body: Howlers live in troops of around 6 to 15 individuals, usually including several adults of both sexes along with juveniles and infants. Rather than fighting over territory, neighbouring groups rely on their loud calls to keep their distance. Within the troop, grooming and vocal exchanges help maintain social bonds. Males are larger than females and take the lead in the roaring contests that define howler society.

sections.heading: Reproduction and lifespan
sections.body: Females give birth to a single infant after a gestation of around six months, and the newborn clings to its mother as she moves through the trees. Young howlers are weaned gradually and learn which leaves and fruit are safe to eat by watching the adults. In the wild, howler monkeys live around 15 to 20 years. Their slow, energy-conserving lifestyle is reflected in their unhurried pace of breeding and growth.

faqs.question: Why are howler monkeys so loud?
faqs.answer: Male howler monkeys have an enlarged hyoid bone in the throat that acts as a resonating chamber, letting them produce deep, booming calls. These howls can carry for several kilometres and are used to advertise a troop's presence so that rival groups keep their distance without fighting.

faqs.question: What do howler monkeys eat?
faqs.answer: Howler monkeys are folivores, feeding mainly on leaves along with fruit, flowers, and buds. Leaves provide little energy and are slow to digest, so howlers have an enlarged gut to ferment them and spend much of the day resting to conserve energy.

faqs.question: Where do howler monkeys live?
faqs.answer: Howler monkeys live in the tropical forests of Central and South America, ranging from southern Mexico to northern Argentina. They occupy rainforest, dry forest, and mangroves, spending almost their entire lives high in the canopy.

faqs.question: How loud is a howler monkey's call?
faqs.answer: A howler monkey's call is among the loudest of any land animal in the Americas and can be heard several kilometres away through dense forest. The calls are loudest at dawn and dusk, when neighbouring troops answer one another across the canopy.

faqs.question: How long do howler monkeys live?
faqs.answer: Howler monkeys live around 15 to 20 years in the wild. Their slow, energy-conserving lifestyle, driven by a low-energy diet of leaves, is reflected in their unhurried pace of growth and breeding.

faqs.question: Are howler monkeys endangered?
faqs.answer: Howler monkeys are listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, meaning they are not currently at high risk of extinction. They remain widespread across the Americas, though habitat loss and hunting affect some populations more than others.

animals.name: Capuchin Monkey
animals.summary: The capuchin is a small, highly intelligent New World monkey found in the tropical forests of Central America and northwest South America. Weighing about 3 to 4 kg and measuring roughly half a metre in body length, it is an agile tree-dweller that uses its prehensile tail for balance. Capuchins are famous for their problem-solving and use of simple tools, and they can live for 20 to 25 years in the wild. The IUCN lists them as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Range and habitat
sections.body: White-faced capuchins live across the tropical forests of Central America and the north-western fringe of South America, from Honduras down to Colombia and Ecuador. They occupy a wide variety of woodland, from lowland rainforest to dry and mangrove forest, and are highly adaptable. Most of their lives are spent in the canopy and mid-levels of the forest, though they will descend to lower branches and occasionally the ground to forage. This flexibility has helped keep them widespread and common across their range.

sections.heading: Intelligence and tool use
sections.body: Capuchins are among the most intelligent of the New World monkeys, with large brains relative to their body size. They are well documented using simple tools, such as stones to crack open nuts and shellfish, and they rub crushed plants and insects into their fur, which may deter parasites. Their dexterity and learning ability have long made them a focus of scientific study into primate cognition. In captivity, this same cleverness has seen them trained to assist people with disabilities.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: As omnivores, capuchins eat a broad and opportunistic diet of fruit, insects, small vertebrates, and nuts. They are inventive foragers, tearing apart bark, prising open pods, and searching leaf litter for hidden prey. Their strong hands and problem-solving skills let them reach foods that many other monkeys cannot. By carrying and dropping seeds as they feed, capuchins help spread the plants of the forest they live in.

sections.heading: Social life
sections.body: Capuchins live in groups of around 10 to 35 individuals, led by a dominant male and female. These troops are noisy and cooperative, grooming one another and joining together to mob predators such as snakes and birds of prey. Communication relies on a rich mix of calls, facial expressions, and body postures. Young capuchins learn foraging techniques and social rules by closely watching the adults around them.

sections.heading: Movement through the trees
sections.body: Capuchins are agile, quadrupedal climbers that run and leap through the branches, reaching speeds of up to 24 km/h in the trees. Their semi-prehensile tail acts as a fifth limb, curling around branches to steady them and free their hands for feeding. They rarely make the long, arm-swinging leaps of larger primates, instead moving in quick, controlled bounds. On the ground they move less confidently and prefer to stay aloft where they are safer from predators.

sections.heading: Reproduction and lifespan
sections.body: Females usually give birth to a single infant after a gestation of about five to six months. The newborn clings to its mother's back and is cared for by her and, at times, other members of the troop. Capuchins mature slowly for a small monkey, reflecting their long lives of 20 to 25 years in the wild and often longer in captivity. This slow pace of life is closely tied to their large brains and lengthy learning period.

faqs.question: Why are capuchin monkeys considered so intelligent?
faqs.answer: Capuchins have unusually large brains for their body size and are among the few primates that use tools in the wild, such as stones to crack nuts. They learn quickly, solve novel problems, and pass foraging techniques between generations, which is why they feature so often in studies of primate cognition.

faqs.question: What do capuchin monkeys eat?
faqs.answer: Capuchins are omnivores with a varied diet of fruit, insects, small vertebrates, and nuts. They are resourceful foragers that tear open bark and pods and search leaf litter for hidden prey, adjusting their diet to whatever is available in their forest.

faqs.question: Where do capuchin monkeys live?
faqs.answer: The white-faced capuchin lives in the tropical forests of Central America and the north-west of South America, ranging from Honduras to Colombia and Ecuador. They occupy many forest types, from lowland rainforest to dry and mangrove woodland, spending most of their time in the canopy.

faqs.question: How long do capuchin monkeys live?
faqs.answer: Capuchins live around 20 to 25 years in the wild and often longer in captivity. This is a long lifespan for such a small monkey and is linked to their large brains and slow development.

faqs.question: Do capuchin monkeys make good pets?
faqs.answer: Capuchins are wild animals and generally make poor pets. They are long-lived, highly intelligent, and social, and in captivity they often become destructive or aggressive when their complex needs are not met. Their care is demanding and, in many places, keeping one is legally restricted.

faqs.question: Are capuchin monkeys endangered?
faqs.answer: The white-faced capuchin is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, meaning it is not currently at high risk of extinction. It remains widespread and adaptable, though like most rainforest animals it is affected by habitat loss and the pet trade in parts of its range.

animals.name: Black-tailed Prairie Dog
animals.summary: The black-tailed prairie dog is a burrowing ground squirrel of the shortgrass and mixed-grass plains of central North America, not a dog at all. It grows to about 40 cm long and 0.7 to 1.5 kg, and lives in vast underground colonies known as towns. Highly social and vocal, these rodents graze on grasses and forbs and typically live 3 to 8 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Life underground in the town
sections.body: Black-tailed prairie dogs live in sprawling colonies called towns, which are divided into family groups known as coteries. A coterie usually holds one adult male, several females, and their young, all sharing and defending a network of tunnels. Their burrows include separate chambers for sleeping, nurseries, and even listening posts near the entrance, along with raised mounds that keep out floodwater and serve as lookout platforms. Historically these towns could stretch for miles and hold thousands of animals.

sections.heading: Grazing and diet
sections.body: These rodents are strict herbivores that feed mainly on grasses, forbs, and the occasional root or seed. They clip vegetation short around their burrows, partly for food and partly to keep a clear line of sight for predators. This grazing and the constant reworking of the soil enrich the surrounding grassland and encourage fresh plant growth. In dry spells they can get much of the moisture they need directly from the plants they eat.

sections.heading: The famous alarm calls
sections.body: Prairie dogs have one of the most sophisticated warning systems known in any mammal. Sentries posted on mounds give sharp, chirping alarm calls that can carry different information about the type of predator approaching, whether a hawk, coyote, or human. Researchers have found that these calls even vary with the size, shape, and colour of an intruder. When danger passes, colony members often perform a distinctive jump-yip display, throwing their forelegs up and calling in a wave that ripples across the town.

sections.heading: A keystone species of the plains
sections.body: Black-tailed prairie dogs are considered a keystone species because so much of the grassland ecosystem depends on them. Their abandoned burrows shelter burrowing owls, snakes, and countless invertebrates, while the animals themselves are a vital food source for predators. The black-footed ferret, one of North America's rarest mammals, relies almost entirely on prairie dogs to survive. Where prairie dog towns vanish, many of these dependent species decline with them.

sections.heading: Breeding and family life
sections.body: Prairie dogs breed once a year, usually in late winter or early spring, with a gestation of roughly a month. Litters of three to five pups are born and raised underground, emerging above ground after about six weeks. Young of the year often stay within their birth coterie, and adults greet one another with a distinctive open-mouthed nuzzle that looks much like a kiss. Females are the stable core of the family group, while young males typically disperse to found or join other coteries.

sections.heading: Population and threats
sections.body: Although still listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, black-tailed prairie dogs occupy only a small fraction of their former range. Conversion of prairie to farmland, poisoning campaigns, and outbreaks of introduced sylvatic plague have all reduced their numbers dramatically over the last century. Because they can compete with livestock for forage, they have long been treated as pests by ranchers. Conservationists now work to protect surviving towns, recognising how many other prairie animals depend on them.

faqs.question: Is a prairie dog actually a dog?
faqs.answer: No. Despite the name, prairie dogs are burrowing rodents in the squirrel family. They earned the name from their sharp, bark-like alarm calls, which early settlers thought resembled a dog's yip.

faqs.question: How big do prairie dogs get?
faqs.answer: Black-tailed prairie dogs reach about 40 cm in length and weigh between 0.7 and 1.5 kg. Males are usually a little heavier than females, especially before winter.

faqs.question: What is a prairie dog town?
faqs.answer: A town is a large colony of prairie dogs made up of many family groups called coteries. Each coterie defends its own section of interconnected burrows, and historically some towns stretched for miles and held thousands of animals.

faqs.question: What do prairie dogs eat?
faqs.answer: They are herbivores that graze on grasses, forbs, roots, and seeds. They clip the vegetation around their burrows short, which helps them spot approaching predators as well as providing food.

faqs.question: How long do prairie dogs live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, black-tailed prairie dogs typically live 3 to 8 years. Predation, disease, and harsh winters mean many do not reach the upper end of that range.

faqs.question: Why are prairie dogs important to the ecosystem?
faqs.answer: They are a keystone species whose burrows and grazing support many other prairie animals. Burrowing owls, snakes, and the endangered black-footed ferret all depend on prairie dog colonies for shelter or food.

animals.name: Groundhog
animals.summary: The groundhog (Marmota monax) is a large ground-dwelling squirrel, or marmot, native to fields and woodland edges across much of North America. Also known as the woodchuck, it grows to about 65 cm long, weighs up to 6 kg before winter, and digs extensive burrows. Groundhogs are true hibernators, sleeping through the cold months, and live around four to six years in the wild.

sections.heading: Burrowing and daily life
sections.body: Groundhogs are among the most accomplished diggers of the rodent world, excavating burrow systems that can run several metres long with multiple chambers and escape exits. These tunnels provide shelter for sleeping, raising young, and hiding from predators such as foxes, coyotes, and hawks. A groundhog rarely strays far from a burrow entrance and will bolt underground at up to 16 km/h (10 mph) when alarmed. Discarded burrows also become homes for rabbits, foxes, and other wildlife.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: The groundhog is a dedicated herbivore, grazing on grasses, clover, dandelions, and a wide variety of wild and garden plants. In summer it feeds heavily to build up fat reserves, which is why it is such a familiar and unwelcome visitor to vegetable plots and allotments. An adult can eat well over a pound of vegetation in a single day during peak season. This intense feeding is essential preparation for the long hibernation ahead.

sections.heading: Hibernation
sections.body: Unlike many mammals that merely slow down in winter, the groundhog is a true hibernator. From roughly October to February it retreats to a deep burrow chamber, where its heart rate drops to just a few beats per minute and its body temperature falls close to that of the surrounding soil. It survives entirely on the fat it stored during autumn, emerging thin but alive in early spring. This deep dormancy is what inspired the folklore behind Groundhog Day.

sections.heading: Groundhog Day and folklore
sections.body: The groundhog owes much of its fame to the North American tradition of Groundhog Day, held on 2 February, when a waking groundhog is said to predict the arrival of spring. According to the custom, if the animal sees its shadow, six more weeks of winter follow. The tradition has no real forecasting value but reflects the groundhog's genuine role as an early-spring riser. It has made this otherwise ordinary marmot one of the continent's best-known wild mammals.

sections.heading: Breeding and young
sections.body: Groundhogs breed in early spring, soon after emerging from hibernation, and females give birth to a litter of two to six blind, hairless pups after about a month. The young are weaned within roughly six weeks and leave to establish their own burrows by midsummer. Mothers raise the litter alone, as groundhogs are largely solitary outside the breeding season. Most young disperse before their first winter to dig burrows of their own.

sections.heading: Distribution and status
sections.body: Groundhogs are widespread across the eastern and central United States and much of Canada, thriving in farmland, meadows, and the edges of suburbs. Their adaptability to human-altered landscapes has kept their numbers healthy, and the IUCN lists them as Least Concern. In the wild they usually live four to six years, though protected captive individuals have reached fourteen. Their tunnelling can damage crops and foundations, so they are sometimes treated as agricultural pests.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a groundhog and a woodchuck?
faqs.answer: There is no difference — groundhog and woodchuck are two common names for the same animal, Marmota monax. The name woodchuck has nothing to do with wood or chucking; it comes from a Native American word for the animal.

faqs.question: Do groundhogs really hibernate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Groundhogs are true hibernators, spending roughly October to February in a deep burrow. Their heart rate and body temperature drop dramatically, and they survive on fat reserves built up over the summer.

faqs.question: What do groundhogs eat?
faqs.answer: Groundhogs are herbivores that feed mainly on grasses, clover, dandelions, and other leafy plants. They are also fond of garden vegetables, which often brings them into conflict with gardeners and farmers.

faqs.question: How long do groundhogs live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, groundhogs typically live four to six years. In captivity, with no predators and a steady food supply, some have lived up to fourteen years.

faqs.question: Are groundhogs dangerous?
faqs.answer: Groundhogs are not dangerous to people and prefer to flee underground when threatened. Their main impact is on gardens and farmland, where their feeding and burrowing can cause damage.

faqs.question: How big do groundhogs get?
faqs.answer: Adult groundhogs reach about 65 cm (26 inches) in length and weigh between 2 and 6 kg (4.4 to 13 lb). They are noticeably heaviest in autumn, when they have fattened up for hibernation.
