animals.name: Pine Marten
animals.summary: The pine marten (Martes martes) is an agile, cat-sized member of the weasel family found in the conifer and mixed forests of Europe and western Asia. About 55 cm long with rich brown fur and a cream-coloured throat patch, it is an expert climber that hunts small mammals, birds, and eggs, and also eats fruit. Largely nocturnal and solitary, it can live up to ten years in the wild.

sections.heading: Life in the trees
sections.body: The pine marten is superbly adapted to an arboreal life, with a long body, sharp semi-retractable claws, and a bushy tail that helps it balance as it bounds through the canopy. It can leap between branches and descend tree trunks head-first, hunting squirrels and birds far above the ground. Much of its life is spent in dense woodland, where it dens in tree hollows, old nests, and rocky crevices. This agility sets it apart from most other members of the weasel family.

sections.heading: Varied diet
sections.body: Although a member of the carnivore family, the pine marten is an opportunistic omnivore. It hunts small mammals such as voles, mice, and squirrels, along with birds and their eggs, but also eats large quantities of berries and fruit, especially in late summer and autumn. This flexible diet helps it survive lean periods when prey is scarce. In parts of its range, its fondness for grey squirrels may even help native red squirrels recover.

sections.heading: Territory and behaviour
sections.body: Pine martens are solitary and strongly territorial, marking their range with droppings, known as scats, left in prominent places. Each animal patrols a large home range that it defends against others of the same sex. Mostly active at night and around dawn and dusk, martens move quickly and quietly through the forest at up to 25 km/h (16 mph). They rely on scent and keen senses to navigate and communicate across their wooded territory.

sections.heading: Breeding and delayed implantation
sections.body: Pine martens mate in summer, but the female's body delays the development of the embryos until the following spring, a strategy known as delayed implantation. This ensures the young, usually two or three kits, are born in spring when conditions are best. The kits are raised in a secure den, often a tree hollow, and are cared for by the mother alone. They become independent by autumn and reach breeding age in their second or third year.

sections.heading: Decline and recovery in Britain
sections.body: Pine martens were once widespread across Britain but were driven to near extinction by habitat loss and persecution, surviving mainly in the Scottish Highlands. Legal protection and, more recently, reintroduction projects in Wales and England have begun to reverse this decline. The species is slowly reclaiming former woodlands where it had long been absent. Its return is also of interest to conservationists because of its potential to suppress invasive grey squirrels.

sections.heading: Range and status
sections.body: Across Europe and western Asia as a whole, the pine marten remains widespread in suitable forest, and the IUCN lists it as Least Concern. It favours conifer and mixed woodland but can also use scrub and rocky ground where cover is good. Wild pine martens typically live eight to ten years. Continued forest cover and the easing of past persecution are key to its ongoing recovery in areas where it had declined.

faqs.question: What does a pine marten look like?
faqs.answer: A pine marten is about the size of a cat, roughly 55 cm long, with rich chestnut-brown fur, large rounded ears, and a bushy tail. Its most distinctive feature is a creamy-yellow patch on the throat and chest.

faqs.question: What do pine martens eat?
faqs.answer: Pine martens are omnivores that hunt voles, mice, squirrels, and birds and raid nests for eggs. They also eat a lot of berries and fruit, particularly in late summer and autumn.

faqs.question: Are pine martens good for red squirrels?
faqs.answer: Evidence suggests they can be. Pine martens catch grey squirrels more easily than the lighter, more agile native red squirrels, so their return may help suppress invasive greys and give reds a chance to recover.

faqs.question: Where do pine martens live?
faqs.answer: Pine martens live in conifer and mixed forests across Europe and western Asia. In Britain their stronghold has long been the Scottish Highlands, though reintroductions are helping them return to Wales and England.

faqs.question: How long do pine martens live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, pine martens usually live eight to ten years. They are listed as Least Concern across their wider European and Asian range, even though they became rare in parts of Britain.

faqs.question: Are pine martens rare in the UK?
faqs.answer: They became very rare in Britain after centuries of habitat loss and persecution, surviving mainly in Scotland. Thanks to legal protection and reintroduction projects, they are now slowly recovering in Wales and parts of England.

animals.name: Northern Elephant Seal
animals.summary: The northern elephant seal (Mirounga angustirostris) is a huge deep-diving seal of the eastern Pacific, breeding on beaches in California and Mexico and feeding far offshore. Bulls are enormous, reaching around 3.5 m long and weighing anywhere from 400 to 2,300 kg, far heavier than females. They dive for squid and deep-sea fish and typically live 11 to 13 years. The species is listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Size and the elephant-like nose
sections.body: Northern elephant seals are named for the large, inflatable snout of adult males, which resembles a short trunk and hangs over the mouth. Bulls are among the largest of all seals, growing to roughly 3.5 m and weighing from 400 kg up to about 2,300 kg, while females are far smaller. Males use the trunk-like proboscis as a resonating chamber, producing deep, clattering roars that carry across a crowded breeding beach. This dramatic size difference between the sexes is one of the most extreme of any mammal.

sections.heading: Record-breaking diving
sections.body: Few mammals dive as deeply or for as long as the northern elephant seal. Individuals routinely descend hundreds of metres and can reach depths beyond 1,500 m, staying submerged for 20 minutes or more between short breaths at the surface. They spend most of the year at sea, diving almost continuously day and night to hunt in the cold, dark water column. Special adaptations, including large blood volume and oxygen-rich muscle, let them stay under far longer than their lung capacity alone would allow.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting at depth
sections.body: Elephant seals are carnivores that feed mainly on squid, deep-sea fish, and occasionally rays and small sharks. They hunt in the twilight and dark zones of the open ocean, using sensitive whiskers and large eyes to detect prey where little light reaches. Because they feed far offshore and deep down, they rarely compete with coastal fisheries. A foraging seal may travel thousands of kilometres across the Pacific during a single trip to sea.

sections.heading: Breeding beaches and battles
sections.body: Each winter, northern elephant seals haul out on beaches in California and Baja California, Mexico, to breed. Dominant bulls fight for control of harems of females, rearing up and slamming their chests and necks together in bloody clashes. Females give birth to a single pup and nurse it on extremely rich milk for about a month before returning to sea. Only the largest, most dominant males win the right to mate, so the winners father a large share of the pups.

sections.heading: Recovery from near-extinction
sections.body: The northern elephant seal is a rare conservation success story. Hunted relentlessly for its blubber oil in the nineteenth century, the species was reduced to perhaps fewer than 100 animals before protection began. Given legal protection by Mexico and later the United States, the population has rebounded into the hundreds of thousands and is now listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. Because all living individuals descend from that tiny remnant, however, the species carries very low genetic diversity.

sections.heading: Time on land and moulting
sections.body: Although superb swimmers, elephant seals are ungainly on land, hauling themselves along at up to about 16 km/h in short bursts. They come ashore twice a year: once to breed and again to moult, when they shed skin and fur in large patches during a so-called catastrophic moult. During these weeks on land they fast, living off stored blubber rather than feeding. Between these visits they are almost entirely oceanic, returning to the same beaches year after year.

faqs.question: How big is a northern elephant seal?
faqs.answer: Bulls reach around 3.5 m in length and can weigh anywhere from 400 kg to about 2,300 kg (880 to 5,070 lb). Females are much smaller, which makes the northern elephant seal one of the most size-differentiated mammals between the sexes.

faqs.question: How deep can elephant seals dive?
faqs.answer: Northern elephant seals are among the deepest-diving mammals, routinely reaching several hundred metres and sometimes exceeding 1,500 m. They can stay underwater for 20 minutes or more, thanks to large blood volume and oxygen-storing muscle.

faqs.question: What do elephant seals eat?
faqs.answer: They are carnivores that feed mainly on squid and deep-sea fish, along with the occasional ray or small shark. They hunt in the dark, deep layers of the open Pacific rather than in shallow coastal waters.

faqs.question: Where do northern elephant seals live?
faqs.answer: They spend most of the year far offshore in the eastern North Pacific and come ashore to breed and moult on beaches in California and Baja California, Mexico. Well-known haul-out sites include Año Nuevo and Piedras Blancas.

faqs.question: Why are they called elephant seals?
faqs.answer: The name comes from the large, inflatable snout of adult males, which resembles a short elephant's trunk. Bulls use it to amplify their roaring calls during the breeding season.

faqs.question: Are northern elephant seals endangered?
faqs.answer: No. Although they were hunted almost to extinction in the 1800s, they have recovered strongly and are now listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. The whole population descends from a tiny surviving group, so genetic diversity remains low.

animals.name: Grey Seal
animals.summary: The grey seal (Halichoerus grypus) is a large North Atlantic seal named for its long, horse-like muzzle. It swims after fish, squid, and crustaceans along rocky coasts, islands, and ice edges, and a big bull can weigh up to 230 kg. Powerful swimmers, grey seals reach about 24 km/h in the water and can live 25 to 35 years. The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Swimming and diving
sections.body: Grey seals are strong, agile swimmers, driving themselves through the water with their hind flippers at speeds of up to 24 km/h. They routinely dive to depths of tens of metres and can stay submerged for well over ten minutes while hunting on or near the seabed. A thick layer of blubber keeps them warm in cold Atlantic water and stores energy for the breeding season. On land they are far clumsier, hauling out onto rocks and beaches to rest, moult, and breed.

sections.heading: Diet and hunting
sections.body: As carnivores, grey seals take a wide range of fish, along with squid and crustaceans. Sandeels, cod, and other bottom-dwelling fish feature heavily in the diet, and prey choice shifts with the seasons and what is locally abundant. Sensitive whiskers help them detect the movements of fish in dark or murky water. A large adult may eat several kilograms of food each day to fuel its bulk.

sections.heading: Telling grey seals apart
sections.body: Grey seals are easily confused with the smaller common (harbour) seal, but a few features set them apart. The grey seal has a long, straight, horse-like muzzle with nostrils that sit almost parallel, whereas the common seal has a shorter, dog-like face and V-shaped nostrils. Grey seals are also noticeably bigger, with bulls far larger than cows. Coat patterns are blotchy rather than neatly spotted.

sections.heading: Breeding colonies and pups
sections.body: Grey seals gather in large, noisy colonies to breed, with bulls competing to control stretches of beach and the females on them. Each cow gives birth to a single pup with a fluffy white coat, which she nurses on extremely rich milk. The pup piles on weight rapidly over about three weeks, then is weaned abruptly and left to moult its white fur and take to the sea on its own. Adults may live 25 to 35 years, so a colony contains many long-established animals.

sections.heading: Where grey seals live
sections.body: Grey seals are animals of North Atlantic coasts, islands, and ice edges, on both the European and North American sides of the ocean. The coasts of Britain and Ireland are a global stronghold, holding a large share of the world's grey seals, which makes them a familiar sight to UK sea-watchers. They favour remote rocky shores, sandbanks, and offshore islands where they can haul out undisturbed. Individuals may range widely at sea between these haul-out sites.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: The grey seal is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, and numbers in the North Atlantic have generally been stable or increasing. In Britain the species is legally protected, and its populations have grown since the days of heavy hunting. Entanglement in fishing gear, disturbance at breeding beaches, and conflict with fisheries remain the main concerns. Careful monitoring of colonies helps track the health of the wider population.

faqs.question: How fast can a grey seal swim?
faqs.answer: Grey seals can swim at up to about 24 km/h, propelling themselves with their hind flippers. They are agile in the water and can dive to considerable depths, but they move slowly and awkwardly on land.

faqs.question: What do grey seals eat?
faqs.answer: Grey seals are carnivores that feed on fish, squid, and crustaceans. Sandeels, cod, and other bottom-living fish are important, and their diet shifts with the seasons and local abundance. A large adult eats several kilograms a day.

faqs.question: How can you tell a grey seal from a common seal?
faqs.answer: A grey seal has a long, straight, horse-like muzzle with near-parallel nostrils and is noticeably larger. The common (harbour) seal has a shorter, dog-like face with V-shaped nostrils. Grey seals also have blotchy rather than neatly spotted coats.

faqs.question: How big do grey seals get?
faqs.answer: Grey seals weigh from around 100 kg up to 230 kg, with bulls much larger than cows. They reach roughly 2.3 m in length, making them one of the largest seals in the North Atlantic.

faqs.question: Where do grey seals live in the UK?
faqs.answer: Grey seals breed all around the coasts of Britain and Ireland, favouring remote rocky shores, sandbanks, and offshore islands. The UK holds a large share of the world's grey seals, so they are a common sight for coastal wildlife watchers.

faqs.question: How long do grey seals live?
faqs.answer: Grey seals typically live 25 to 35 years in the wild. Females often live longer than the heavily competing bulls, and long-established colonies contain many older, experienced animals.

animals.name: Leopard Seal
animals.summary: The leopard seal is a large, solitary predator of the Antarctic pack ice, named for the dark spots scattered across its silvery-grey coat. It grows to about 3.5 m (11.5 ft) long and weighs 200 to 450 kg (440 to 990 lb), with females larger than males. A formidable hunter, it eats penguins, seals, fish and krill and can reach 40 km/h (25 mph) in the water. Wild leopard seals live 20 to 26 years and are listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Antarctica's apex predator
sections.body: The leopard seal sits near the top of the Antarctic food chain, with only the killer whale as a serious rival. It is one of the very few seals that regularly hunts other warm-blooded animals, including penguins and smaller seals. Armed with a wide gape, powerful jaws and long canine teeth, it is a bold and effective ambush predator. Its reputation is fearsome, yet it plays a central role in keeping Antarctic prey populations in balance.

sections.heading: A surprisingly varied diet
sections.body: Despite its predatory image, the leopard seal is a flexible feeder that takes penguins, seals, fish and krill. Much of its diet, especially in summer, is actually made up of tiny shrimp-like krill, which it strains from the water using specially shaped cheek teeth. When hunting penguins, it often waits at the ice edge and seizes them as they enter the sea, then thrashes the catch to break it apart. This mix of hunting and filter-feeding lets it thrive across the changing Antarctic seasons.

sections.heading: Built for cold water
sections.body: The leopard seal is superbly adapted to the freezing Southern Ocean. A thick layer of blubber insulates its long, muscular body and streamlines it for fast, agile swimming. Unusually for a seal, it relies mainly on its powerful front flippers to drive itself through the water, giving it bursts of speed up to 40 km/h. Its large head and serpentine neck let it strike quickly at fast-moving prey.

sections.heading: A solitary life on the ice
sections.body: Leopard seals live alone across a vast range of Antarctic and sub-Antarctic pack ice and water. Outside the brief breeding season they rarely tolerate company, hauling out on isolated ice floes to rest between hunts. They communicate over long distances with haunting underwater calls, which males produce for hours during the summer. This solitary, wide-ranging lifestyle makes the species difficult to study in the wild.

sections.heading: Breeding and life cycle
sections.body: Mating takes place in the water during the Antarctic summer, and females give birth on the ice after a gestation of around eleven months. A mother nurses her single pup on rich milk for about a month before leaving it to fend for itself. Females grow larger than males, reaching lengths of around 3.5 m, and both sexes can live for 20 to 26 years in the wild. Young seals must learn to hunt quickly once their mother departs.

sections.heading: Conservation status
sections.body: The leopard seal is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, and its remote Antarctic home has so far shielded it from most direct human pressures. Its numbers are hard to count precisely because the animals are scattered and spend much of their time on remote ice. The greatest long-term concern is climate change, which is reducing the sea ice the seals and their prey depend on. Shrinking krill stocks in a warming ocean could affect the whole Antarctic food web on which the leopard seal sits.

faqs.question: How big is a leopard seal?
faqs.answer: Leopard seals grow to around 3.5 m (11.5 ft) long and weigh between 200 and 450 kg (440 to 990 lb). Unusually, females are larger than males.

faqs.question: What do leopard seals eat?
faqs.answer: Leopard seals eat penguins, other seals, fish and krill. They are one of the few seals that hunt warm-blooded prey, but a large part of their diet is actually tiny krill strained from the water.

faqs.question: Are leopard seals dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Leopard seals are powerful predators and should be treated with respect, and there have been rare serious incidents. Encounters are uncommon, however, because the seals live in remote Antarctic waters far from most people.

faqs.question: How fast can a leopard seal swim?
faqs.answer: A leopard seal can swim at up to 40 km/h (25 mph). It uses its long front flippers, rather than its hind flippers, to power through the water in fast, agile bursts.

faqs.question: How long do leopard seals live?
faqs.answer: Leopard seals live around 20 to 26 years in the wild. Females tend to grow larger than males, and both sexes reach maturity after a few years.

faqs.question: Are leopard seals endangered?
faqs.answer: No. Leopard seals are listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, largely because they live in remote Antarctic waters. The main long-term threat is climate change, which is reducing the sea ice and krill they depend on.

animals.name: Beluga Whale
animals.summary: The beluga is a small, sociable white whale of the Arctic and sub-Arctic seas, easily recognised by its rounded forehead and lack of a dorsal fin. Adults grow to about 4.5 m and weigh between 700 and 1,400 kg, with males the larger sex. Belugas swim in tight-knit pods, feed on fish and invertebrates, and can live 35 to 50 years. The IUCN lists the species as Near Threatened.

sections.heading: Appearance and adaptations
sections.body: Belugas are unmistakable: pure white as adults, with a bulbous 'melon' on the forehead and no dorsal fin. That flat back is an adaptation to life among sea ice, letting them swim close beneath the surface and break through thin ice to breathe. Unlike most whales, belugas have unfused neck vertebrae, so they can turn and nod their heads. A thick layer of blubber, up to 40 percent of body weight, insulates them in near-freezing water.

sections.heading: Habitat and seasonal movements
sections.body: Belugas live in the cold coastal waters, estuaries, and pack ice of the Arctic and sub-Arctic. Many populations migrate with the ice, moving into river mouths and shallow bays in summer and retreating toward the open sea as winter ice advances. They are remarkably at home under ice, using sound and agility to find breathing holes across vast frozen expanses. Some populations gather in warm estuaries each summer to moult their outer skin.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: Belugas are carnivores with a varied menu of fish such as cod and salmon, along with crustaceans, marine worms, and cephalopods like squid and octopus. They forage on the seabed as well as in open water, using their flexible necks and pursed lips to root out and suck up prey. An adult may eat many kilograms of food a day to fuel its warm-blooded body in icy seas. They often hunt cooperatively, herding schooling fish into tight balls.

sections.heading: Communication and intelligence
sections.body: Nicknamed 'the canaries of the sea', belugas are among the most vocal of all whales, producing an extraordinary range of clicks, whistles, chirps, and squeals. They rely on echolocation to navigate and hunt in dark or ice-covered waters, reading the echoes of their own clicks. Belugas are highly intelligent and social, living in pods that can merge into gatherings of hundreds. They can even mimic sounds, and captive individuals have been recorded imitating human speech patterns.

sections.heading: Reproduction and life cycle
sections.body: Females give birth to a single calf after a gestation of roughly 14 to 15 months, usually in warmer summer estuaries. Calves are born grey or brownish and only gradually turn white, reaching the adult colour at around five to nine years of age. A mother nurses her calf for up to two years, and the strong bond keeps young belugas close to the pod. With slow reproduction, belugas can live 35 to 50 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Conservation and threats
sections.body: The beluga is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN, though some local populations, such as those in Canada's Cook Inlet and St Lawrence estuary, are far more imperilled. Key threats include pollution, industrial noise that disrupts their sound-based world, shipping traffic, and the loss of sea ice to a warming climate. Historic hunting reduced several stocks, and subsistence hunting continues in parts of the Arctic. Reducing contaminants and underwater noise is central to protecting the species.

faqs.question: Why are beluga whales white?
faqs.answer: Adult belugas are pure white, a colour thought to camouflage them against sea ice and snow-lit water, helping them avoid predators such as polar bears and orcas. Calves are born grey or brown and only turn fully white at around five to nine years old.

faqs.question: How big do beluga whales get?
faqs.answer: Belugas reach about 4.5 m in length and weigh between 700 and 1,400 kg (1,540 to 3,090 lb). Males are noticeably larger than females, making belugas one of the smaller whale species.

faqs.question: How long do beluga whales live?
faqs.answer: Beluga whales typically live 35 to 50 years in the wild. They mature slowly and raise a single calf at a time, so populations recover only gradually from losses.

faqs.question: What do beluga whales eat?
faqs.answer: Belugas are carnivores that eat fish such as cod and salmon, plus crustaceans, marine worms, and cephalopods like squid and octopus. They forage on the seabed and in open water, often herding schooling fish cooperatively.

faqs.question: Why are belugas called the canaries of the sea?
faqs.answer: Belugas earned the nickname because they are exceptionally vocal, producing clicks, whistles, chirps, and squeals that carry through the water. They use these sounds to communicate within their pods and to echolocate prey and breathing holes beneath the ice.

faqs.question: How fast can a beluga whale swim?
faqs.answer: Belugas can swim at up to about 22 km/h (14 mph) in short bursts, though they usually cruise much more slowly. Their flexible bodies and lack of a dorsal fin make them especially agile beneath the ice rather than fast in open water.

animals.name: Emu
animals.summary: The emu is a large flightless bird native to Australia, second only to the ostrich in height among living birds. It stands up to 1.9 m tall, weighs around 40 kg, and roams grassland, woodland, and scrub as an omnivore. Emus can run at up to 50 km/h on their powerful legs and typically live 10 to 20 years. The species is listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Size and appearance
sections.body: The emu is Australia's tallest native bird and the second-largest bird alive, reaching about 1.9 m in height and weighing roughly 40 kg. Its shaggy grey-brown plumage hangs loosely and helps insulate the body against both desert heat and cold nights. The wings are reduced to tiny stubs, useless for flight, but the long, three-toed legs are exceptionally strong. Bare blue skin on the neck becomes more vivid during the breeding season.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: Emus are omnivores that wander widely in search of food, eating seeds, fruit, flowers, fresh shoots, and a range of insects and other small invertebrates. They follow seasonal rainfall across the continent, timing their movements to reach areas where plants are fruiting and seeding. Like many birds, they swallow small stones that sit in the gizzard and help grind up tough plant matter. An emu can go for long stretches without water but will drink heavily when it finds a source.

sections.heading: Movement and speed
sections.body: Although it cannot fly, the emu is built for travel across open country and can sprint at up to 50 km/h. Its long stride lets it cover great distances at an economical pace, and populations may move hundreds of kilometres over a year in response to food and rain. The muscular legs also deliver a powerful forward kick, the bird's main defence against predators such as dingoes. Emus are strong swimmers and will cross rivers when needed.

sections.heading: Breeding and the role of the male
sections.body: Emu breeding reverses the usual roles: the female lays a clutch of large dark-green eggs and then often leaves to mate again, while the male takes over incubation. The sitting male barely eats or drinks for around eight weeks, living off stored body fat until the chicks hatch. He then guards and raises the striped youngsters for up to eighteen months, teaching them where to find food. This intense paternal care is one of the emu's most distinctive traits.

sections.heading: Emus and people
sections.body: The emu is a national symbol of Australia and appears on the country's coat of arms alongside the kangaroo. Farmed populations are raised for lean meat, oil, and leather, and the bird features prominently in Aboriginal stories and star lore. Wild emus are sometimes seen as pests where they enter farmland, and the famous 1932 "Emu War" saw soldiers struggle to control large flocks. Despite this, the species remains widespread and abundant across most of the mainland.

sections.heading: Conservation status
sections.body: The emu is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, with a large and stable population across mainland Australia. It adapts well to farmland and disturbed country, which has helped it thrive where more specialised species have declined. Several smaller island subspecies were driven to extinction after European settlement, but the mainland bird is in no danger. Wild emus typically live 10 to 20 years.

faqs.question: How tall is an emu?
faqs.answer: An emu stands up to about 1.9 m tall, making it the tallest bird native to Australia and the second-tallest living bird after the ostrich. Adults weigh roughly 40 kg.

faqs.question: Can emus fly?
faqs.answer: No. Emus are flightless, with wings reduced to small stubs. Instead of flying they rely on their long, powerful legs, which let them run at up to 50 km/h and deliver a strong defensive kick.

faqs.question: What do emus eat?
faqs.answer: Emus are omnivores. They feed on seeds, fruit, flowers, and fresh plant shoots, along with insects and other small invertebrates, and they swallow small stones to help grind food in the gizzard.

faqs.question: How fast can an emu run?
faqs.answer: An emu can reach speeds of up to 50 km/h (31 mph) over open ground. Its long stride also lets it travel long distances at a steady, energy-efficient pace.

faqs.question: Do male or female emus raise the chicks?
faqs.answer: The male does almost all the work. After the female lays the eggs, the male incubates them for around eight weeks with little food or water, then guards and raises the chicks for up to eighteen months.

faqs.question: How long do emus live?
faqs.answer: Wild emus typically live 10 to 20 years. Birds in captivity or on farms, protected from predators, often reach the upper end of that range or beyond.

animals.name: Southern Cassowary
animals.summary: The southern cassowary is a large, flightless rainforest bird of Queensland and New Guinea, often called the world's most dangerous bird. It stands up to 1.8 m (6 ft) tall, weighs 40 to 60 kg (88 to 132 lb) and carries a dagger-like claw on each foot. It feeds mainly on fallen fruit and can sprint through dense forest at up to 50 km/h (31 mph). Though listed as Least Concern globally, its Australian population is under pressure, and wild birds live 30 to 40 years.

sections.heading: A powerful and dangerous bird
sections.body: The southern cassowary has earned a reputation as the most dangerous bird in the world, thanks to the long, dagger-like inner claw on each of its powerful feet. When cornered or defending chicks, it can deliver a forward kick strong enough to cause serious injury. Most attacks, however, involve birds that have been fed by people and have lost their natural wariness. Left alone in the forest, cassowaries are shy and prefer to avoid humans altogether.

sections.heading: The rainforest gardener
sections.body: As a frugivore, the cassowary lives almost entirely on fruit that has fallen to the rainforest floor, along with some fungi. It swallows large fruits whole and passes the seeds unharmed, spreading them far from the parent tree. Many rainforest plants have seeds so big that the cassowary is one of the only animals able to move them, making the bird vital to the forest's regeneration. Some tree species depend on it so heavily that they struggle to spread where cassowaries have vanished.

sections.heading: Casque and appearance
sections.body: The most striking feature of the cassowary is the tall, helmet-like casque on top of its head, made of a spongy material over a bony core. Its function is still debated, with theories ranging from a tool for pushing through undergrowth to a resonating chamber for deep calls. The bird's glossy black plumage contrasts with vivid blue and red skin on its bare neck and dangling wattles. Females are larger and more brightly coloured than males, the reverse of the pattern seen in many birds.

sections.heading: Breeding and fatherhood
sections.body: In the cassowary's world it is the male that raises the young. After a female lays a clutch of large green eggs, she leaves to mate with other males, and the father takes over completely. He incubates the eggs for about 50 days, barely eating, then guards and leads the striped chicks for up to nine months. During this time the normally solitary male becomes fiercely protective and will charge anything that threatens his brood.

sections.heading: Speed and movement
sections.body: Despite its bulk, the cassowary is remarkably fast and agile in thick forest. It can run at up to 50 km/h (31 mph), weaving between trees, and is also a capable jumper and a strong swimmer. When threatened it usually flees rather than fights, crashing through dense undergrowth that would stop a person. Its stout, three-toed feet give it both the traction to sprint and the weaponry to defend itself.

sections.heading: Conservation and threats
sections.body: Globally the southern cassowary is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, but its situation in Australia is far more precarious. Clearing of tropical rainforest, collisions with vehicles, dog attacks and feeding by tourists all threaten the northern Queensland population. Because the species reproduces slowly and needs large tracts of connected forest, local declines are hard to reverse. Protecting rainforest corridors and keeping wild birds from becoming used to people are key to their future in Australia.

faqs.question: Why is the cassowary called the most dangerous bird?
faqs.answer: The cassowary has a long, dagger-like claw on the inner toe of each foot and can deliver a powerful kick. It earns the title because a defensive cassowary can seriously injure a person, though attacks are rare and usually involve birds fed by humans.

faqs.question: How big is a southern cassowary?
faqs.answer: Southern cassowaries stand up to 1.8 m (6 ft) tall and weigh between 40 and 60 kg (88 to 132 lb). Females are noticeably larger and more brightly coloured than males.

faqs.question: What do cassowaries eat?
faqs.answer: Cassowaries are frugivores that feed mainly on fruit fallen to the rainforest floor, along with some fungi. By swallowing large fruits whole and passing the seeds, they play a vital role in spreading rainforest plants.

faqs.question: How fast can a cassowary run?
faqs.answer: A cassowary can run at up to 50 km/h (31 mph) even through dense forest. It is also an agile jumper and a strong swimmer, and usually chooses to flee rather than fight.

faqs.question: What is the casque on a cassowary's head for?
faqs.answer: The tall, helmet-like casque is made of spongy tissue over bone, and its exact purpose is still uncertain. Suggested roles include pushing through undergrowth, signalling to other cassowaries, and helping the bird produce its deep, booming calls.

faqs.question: Are cassowaries endangered?
faqs.answer: The southern cassowary is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN overall, but its Australian population is threatened. Rainforest clearing, vehicle collisions and dog attacks are the main dangers in northern Queensland.

animals.name: Brown Pelican
animals.summary: The brown pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) is a large coastal seabird of the Americas, found from the United States down through the Caribbean and around the Galápagos. It is famous for plunge-diving from up to 20 m to catch fish such as anchovies and sardines in its stretchy throat pouch. Adults weigh 2 to 5 kg, span roughly 1.4 m, and can live 20 to 25 years. The IUCN lists it as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Plunge-diving and feeding
sections.body: The brown pelican is the only pelican that hunts by plunge-diving, folding its wings and dropping from as high as 20 m to hit the water. The impact stuns small schooling fish, which the bird scoops up along with several litres of seawater in its expandable pouch. Before swallowing, it tips its bill down to drain the water, then jerks its head back to gulp the catch. Anchovies and sardines make up most of its diet, and a hunting bird may dive dozens of times a day.

sections.heading: The throat pouch
sections.body: The pelican's most recognisable feature is the loose, elastic pouch of skin slung beneath its long bill. It works as a dip-net rather than a storage bag, briefly holding water and fish before the water is squeezed out. The pouch also helps the bird cool down in hot coastal weather, fluttering the bare skin to release heat. During courtship the pouch and bill can flush with bright colours.

sections.heading: Where brown pelicans live
sections.body: Brown pelicans are birds of warm, shallow seas and rarely stray far from the coast. Their range runs along both coasts of the Americas, through the Caribbean, and out to the Galápagos Islands. They favour estuaries, bays, sandbars, and rocky islets where fish are plentiful and safe roosting sites are close by. Unlike most seabirds, they are equally at home resting on piers, jetties, and mangrove branches.

sections.heading: Flight and flocking
sections.body: For such a heavy bird, the brown pelican is a superb and economical flier, cruising at up to 48 km/h. Flocks travel in tidy single-file lines or V-formations, alternating a few slow wingbeats with long glides. They are experts at ground-effect soaring, skimming just centimetres above the waves to ride the cushion of air pushed up by the swell. This saves energy on long coastal commutes between feeding and roosting grounds.

sections.heading: Breeding and nesting
sections.body: Brown pelicans nest in colonies on islands and in mangroves, safe from ground predators. Depending on the location, a pair builds a stick platform in a tree or a simple scrape on the ground, where the female lays two or three eggs. Both parents share incubation, warming the eggs with the blood-rich skin of their feet. Chicks are naked and helpless at first and depend on regurgitated fish for several weeks before they can fledge.

sections.heading: Recovery and conservation
sections.body: The brown pelican is one of conservation's great comeback stories. Through the mid-20th century the pesticide DDT thinned their eggshells so badly that colonies collapsed across much of their range. After DDT was banned, populations rebounded strongly, and the species is now listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. Oil spills, fishing-line entanglement, and disturbance at nesting islands remain the main local threats.

faqs.question: How does a brown pelican catch fish?
faqs.answer: It plunge-dives, dropping from as high as 20 m and folding its wings to hit the water. The dive stuns small fish, which the pelican scoops into its throat pouch before draining the water and swallowing the catch. It is the only pelican species that hunts this way.

faqs.question: What does a brown pelican eat?
faqs.answer: Brown pelicans are piscivores, feeding almost entirely on small schooling fish such as anchovies and sardines. They occasionally take other fish and the odd crustacean. An adult may make dozens of dives a day to meet its needs.

faqs.question: How big is a brown pelican?
faqs.answer: Adults weigh between 2 and 5 kg and measure around 1.4 m in length, with males slightly larger than females. Despite that bulk they have a broad wingspan that makes them buoyant, energy-efficient fliers.

faqs.question: How long do brown pelicans live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, brown pelicans typically live 20 to 25 years. Survival is lowest in the first year, when young birds are still learning to dive and feed efficiently.

faqs.question: Are brown pelicans endangered?
faqs.answer: No. The brown pelican is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. It was once devastated by the pesticide DDT, but populations recovered strongly after the chemical was banned, making it a well-known conservation success.

faqs.question: What is the pelican's throat pouch for?
faqs.answer: The pouch is a dip-net for catching fish, not a place to store them. It briefly holds water and prey, then the water is drained before the bird swallows. It also helps the pelican shed heat in warm coastal weather.

facts.value: Piscivore — mainly fish such as anchovies and sardines

animals.name: White Stork
animals.summary: The white stork is a tall, long-legged wading bird of wet meadows, farmland, and wetlands across Eurasia, instantly recognisable by its white plumage, black wing tips, and bright red bill and legs. Standing over a metre tall and weighing up to about 4.5 kg, it is a powerful soaring migrant that winters in Africa. It feeds on frogs, insects, rodents, and fish, and can live 20 to 25 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Appearance and flight
sections.body: The white stork is a striking bird with snow-white body feathers, black flight feathers, and a long, straight red bill matched by long red legs. It stands well over a metre tall with a wingspan approaching two metres, yet in the air it is graceful, soaring on broad wings with its neck outstretched and legs trailing behind. Rather than flap continuously, storks ride rising columns of warm air called thermals, gliding for long distances to save energy. On thermals they cruise at around 45 km/h.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: Storks are carnivores that hunt a wide variety of small animals, including frogs, insects, earthworms, lizards, rodents, and fish. They forage by striding slowly through meadows, marshes, and shallow water, watching the ground and snapping up prey with a quick jab of the bill. Freshly mown or ploughed fields are a favourite hunting ground, where disturbed insects and small mammals are easy to catch. Their varied, opportunistic diet lets them thrive alongside farming across much of their range.

sections.heading: Nesting on rooftops
sections.body: White storks are famous for building their large stick nests on chimneys, rooftops, church towers, and specially provided platforms in towns and villages. These bulky nests are reused and added to year after year, sometimes growing to a huge size and lasting for decades. The birds have a long tradition of nesting close to people, and in much of Europe a stork's nest on the house is regarded as a sign of good luck. Because they lack a true voice box, storks communicate at the nest mainly by loudly clattering their bills.

sections.heading: Migration
sections.body: White storks are long-distance migrants that breed in Europe and western Asia and spend the winter in Africa, some reaching as far south as the southern tip of the continent. Because they rely on thermals that form over land, they avoid long sea crossings and funnel through narrow points such as the Strait of Gibraltar and the Bosphorus. The round trip can cover thousands of kilometres each year. In recent decades some populations, particularly in Spain and Portugal, have begun wintering closer to home, feeding at landfills instead of migrating all the way to Africa.

sections.heading: Breeding and chicks
sections.body: Pairs typically return to the same nest each spring, greeting one another with elaborate bill-clattering displays. The female lays a clutch of around three to five eggs, which both parents take turns to incubate for roughly a month. The chicks are fed regurgitated food and remain in the nest for about two months before they can fly. Not all survive, as parents may fail to feed the weakest chicks when food is short, but successful young join the autumn migration south.

sections.heading: Status and folklore
sections.body: The white stork is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, and after mid-century declines many European populations have recovered thanks to protection and nest platforms. Loss of wet meadows and feeding habitat, along with collisions with power lines, remain the main pressures on the species. Culturally, the stork is one of Europe's most beloved birds, tied to the age-old legend that storks deliver babies. Its return each spring has long been welcomed as a herald of the changing season.

faqs.question: How big is a white stork?
faqs.answer: White storks stand over a metre tall with a wingspan of nearly two metres, and weigh up to about 4.5 kg. Their long red legs and bill make them look even taller as they wade through meadows and marshes.

faqs.question: What do white storks eat?
faqs.answer: They are carnivores that eat frogs, insects, earthworms, lizards, rodents, and fish. Storks hunt by walking slowly through fields and shallow water, snapping up prey with a quick jab of the bill.

faqs.question: Where do white storks migrate?
faqs.answer: White storks breed in Europe and western Asia and winter in Africa, some travelling all the way to the south of the continent. They rely on thermals over land, so they funnel through narrow crossings like Gibraltar and the Bosphorus rather than fly over open sea.

faqs.question: Why do storks nest on chimneys and rooftops?
faqs.answer: Rooftops, chimneys, and towers offer tall, stable platforms for their heavy stick nests, safe from ground predators. Storks have nested near people for centuries, and in many parts of Europe a nest on the house is thought to bring good luck.

faqs.question: How long do white storks live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, white storks typically live 20 to 25 years. Their longevity, combined with their habit of returning to the same nest each year, means individual birds can become well known in a village.

faqs.question: Do storks make any sound?
faqs.answer: White storks have almost no voice because they lack a proper syrinx, or bird voice box. Instead they communicate by loudly clattering their bills, especially during greeting displays at the nest.

animals.name: Sandhill Crane
animals.summary: The sandhill crane is a tall grey wading bird of North America and eastern Siberia, known for its elaborate courtship dancing and bugling calls. It stands with a long neck and legs, reaches about 1.2 m in length, and weighs 3 to 6 kg. An omnivore of wetlands and prairies, it can fly at up to 56 km/h and live 20 to 25 years. The species is listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Appearance and identification
sections.body: The sandhill crane is a large, elegant bird with slate-grey plumage, a long neck, and long dark legs, standing over a metre tall. A patch of bare red skin caps the forehead and crown, one of its most reliable field marks. Adults measure around 1.2 m in length and weigh between 3 and 6 kg, with a wingspan wide enough to make their flight unmistakable. Many birds show a rusty wash on the body, stained by the iron-rich mud they preen into their feathers.

sections.heading: Dancing and courtship
sections.body: Sandhill cranes are celebrated for their dramatic dances, in which pairs leap into the air with wings spread, bow, and toss tufts of grass and sticks. Although dancing peaks during courtship, birds of all ages dance throughout the year, and it helps strengthen the bond between mates. Cranes form long-lasting pair bonds and often stay together for many years. Their loud, rattling bugle carries far across open country and is a signature sound of northern wetlands.

sections.heading: Migration and flocks
sections.body: Many sandhill cranes are long-distance migrants, breeding across the northern United States, Canada, and Siberia and wintering as far south as the southern United States and Mexico. They fly at speeds up to 56 km/h, riding rising columns of warm air to save energy on their journeys. Each spring, hundreds of thousands gather along Nebraska's Platte River in one of North America's greatest wildlife spectacles. Not all populations migrate; some in the far south stay in one area year-round.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: The sandhill crane is an omnivore with a broad diet that shifts with the seasons and habitat. It probes soil and mud for plant tubers, seeds, and waste grain, and also takes insects, snails, amphibians, and small mammals. On migration and in winter, waste corn and other grains in farm fields become an important food source. This flexibility lets the crane thrive across a wide range of wetland and grassland habitats.

sections.heading: Nesting and chicks
sections.body: Sandhill cranes nest on the ground, building a large mound of plant material in or beside shallow wetlands. The female usually lays two eggs, and both parents share incubation for around a month. Newly hatched chicks, known as colts, can leave the nest and follow their parents within a day of hatching. Typically only one chick survives to fledge, and young birds stay with their parents through their first migration.

sections.heading: Conservation status
sections.body: The sandhill crane is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, and most populations are healthy or increasing thanks to wetland protection and careful management. This marks a strong recovery from the early twentieth century, when hunting and habitat drainage had reduced some populations sharply. A few small, isolated populations in the far south remain vulnerable and receive special protection. Wild sandhill cranes can live 20 to 25 years.

faqs.question: How big is a sandhill crane?
faqs.answer: Sandhill cranes stand over a metre tall, measure about 1.2 m in length, and weigh between 3 and 6 kg. Their broad wingspan makes them easy to recognise in flight.

faqs.question: Why do sandhill cranes dance?
faqs.answer: Dancing helps sandhill cranes court mates and reinforce their long-term pair bonds. Birds of all ages dance year-round, leaping, bowing, and tossing vegetation into the air.

faqs.question: What do sandhill cranes eat?
faqs.answer: They are omnivores. Their diet includes plant tubers, seeds, and waste grain, along with insects, snails, amphibians, and small mammals, depending on the season and location.

faqs.question: Where do sandhill cranes migrate?
faqs.answer: Many breed across Canada, the northern United States, and Siberia and winter in the southern United States and Mexico. Huge numbers stop over along Nebraska's Platte River each spring.

faqs.question: How fast do sandhill cranes fly?
faqs.answer: Sandhill cranes fly at speeds of up to 56 km/h (35 mph). They often ride rising columns of warm air, gliding to conserve energy on long migrations.

faqs.question: How long do sandhill cranes live?
faqs.answer: Sandhill cranes can live 20 to 25 years in the wild. They are long-lived birds that form lasting pair bonds, with pairs often staying together for many breeding seasons.

animals.name: Grey Heron
animals.summary: The grey heron (Ardea cinerea) is a tall, long-legged wading bird found in wetlands, rivers, and coasts across Eurasia and Africa. Standing up to a metre tall with grey, white, and black plumage, it hunts by standing motionless before spearing fish, amphibians, and small mammals with its dagger-like bill. A patient and adaptable predator, it can live up to 25 years and is listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Patient hunting technique
sections.body: The grey heron is the archetypal ambush hunter, standing frozen at the water's edge for long stretches before striking with astonishing speed. When a fish or frog moves within reach, the bird uncoils its S-shaped neck and spears or seizes the prey with its long, sharp bill. Fish form the bulk of its diet, but it also takes amphibians, small mammals, insects, and even ducklings. This patient, energy-efficient style lets it hunt successfully in almost any shallow water.

sections.heading: Appearance and flight
sections.body: Grey herons are unmistakable, with pale grey upperparts, a white head and neck marked by a black eye-stripe and crest, and a long yellowish bill. In flight they fold the neck back into a distinctive S-shape and trail their long legs behind, beating broad wings slowly and steadily at up to 40 km/h (25 mph). Standing nearly a metre tall, they are among the largest and most familiar wetland birds of Europe. Their unhurried, deliberate movements make them easy to recognise even at a distance.

sections.heading: Wetland habitat
sections.body: The grey heron occupies almost any body of water with fish, from rivers, lakes, and marshes to estuaries, coastlines, and even garden ponds. This adaptability has allowed it to thrive across a vast range spanning Eurasia and Africa. In many towns and cities it has become a bold and familiar sight, patrolling park lakes and raiding ornamental fish ponds. It needs only shallow water for hunting and nearby trees or reedbeds for roosting and nesting.

sections.heading: Nesting in colonies
sections.body: Grey herons breed in colonies known as heronries, typically building large stick nests high in tall trees. The same sites are used year after year and may hold dozens of nests, making a noisy, conspicuous spectacle in early spring. The female usually lays three to five pale blue eggs, and both parents share incubation and feeding of the growing chicks. Young herons fledge after around seven to eight weeks but often return to be fed for a time afterwards.

sections.heading: Behaviour and lifespan
sections.body: Outside the breeding season grey herons are largely solitary, defending favoured fishing spots and often standing hunched and motionless for hours. They are long-lived for a bird of their size, surviving 15 to 25 years in the wild, though many young birds do not make it through their first hard winter. Cold spells that freeze their hunting waters are one of the main causes of death. Their patience and adaptability otherwise make them resilient survivors.

sections.heading: Range and status
sections.body: The grey heron is widespread and common throughout its enormous range across Europe, Asia, and Africa, and the IUCN lists it as Least Concern. Legal protection in many countries and its ease with human-altered habitats have helped keep populations healthy. It is one of the most familiar large birds of British and European waterways. Numbers can dip after severe winters but generally recover quickly.

faqs.question: What do grey herons eat?
faqs.answer: Grey herons eat mainly fish, which they catch by standing still and spearing prey with their sharp bill. They also take amphibians, small mammals, insects, and occasionally ducklings and other small birds.

faqs.question: How tall is a grey heron?
faqs.answer: A grey heron stands up to about a metre (roughly 3 feet) tall, making it one of the largest wetland birds in Europe. Despite its size it weighs only 1 to 2 kg, as birds have lightweight bones.

faqs.question: Why do herons stand so still?
faqs.answer: Herons stand motionless to ambush prey without alarming it. By waiting patiently at the water's edge, they can strike the instant a fish or frog comes within reach of their long neck and bill.

faqs.question: Do herons nest together?
faqs.answer: Yes, grey herons nest in colonies called heronries, usually high in tall trees. The same sites are reused each year and can hold dozens of large stick nests.

faqs.question: How long do grey herons live?
faqs.answer: Grey herons can live 15 to 25 years in the wild, which is long for a bird of their size. Many young birds, however, die during their first winter if freezing weather locks up their fishing waters.

faqs.question: Are grey herons a threat to garden ponds?
faqs.answer: They can be, as herons readily raid ornamental ponds for fish. Pond netting, cover, and hiding places for fish are the usual ways to deter them without harming the bird.

animals.name: Great Spotted Woodpecker
animals.summary: The great spotted woodpecker (Dendrocopos major) is a striking black-and-white bird with a red patch beneath the tail, found in woodlands and parks across Eurasia and North Africa. About 24 cm long and weighing only 70 to 100 g, it is best known for its rapid drumming on tree trunks. It feeds on insects, larvae, and seeds, and can live up to eleven years in the wild.

sections.heading: Drumming and communication
sections.body: The great spotted woodpecker is famous for its drumming — a rapid burst of hammering against a dead branch or trunk that can reach around ten to twenty strikes in less than a second. Unlike pecking for food, drumming is a form of communication used to claim territory and attract a mate, ringing out most often in late winter and spring. Both sexes drum, and the sound can carry a long way through quiet woodland. It is one of the defining sounds of a European forest in early spring.

sections.heading: Feeding and foraging
sections.body: This woodpecker uses its powerful, chisel-like bill to excavate insects and grubs from beneath tree bark and rotten wood. Its long, sticky tongue can reach deep into crevices to extract larvae, while its stiff tail feathers brace it upright against the trunk. In autumn and winter it turns increasingly to seeds and nuts, often wedging a pine cone into a bark crevice — a favoured spot known as an anvil — to hammer it open. It will also raid nest boxes and take the eggs and chicks of smaller birds.

sections.heading: How it avoids brain injury
sections.body: Hammering into solid wood thousands of times a day generates forces that would concuss most animals, yet the woodpecker is remarkably well protected. Its skull has spongy, shock-absorbing bone, and a specialised bone structure called the hyoid wraps around the skull to help cushion impacts. The brain is small, tightly packed, and oriented to spread the force of each blow. These adaptations let the bird drum and excavate without harming itself.

sections.heading: Nesting and breeding
sections.body: Great spotted woodpeckers excavate a fresh nest hole each spring, chiselling a neat cavity into a tree trunk over one to three weeks. The female lays a clutch of around four to seven white eggs, which both parents incubate before feeding the noisy chicks. Young birds fledge after roughly three weeks and can be recognised by a full red cap, which they lose as they mature. The abandoned nest holes later provide shelter for other birds and small mammals.

sections.heading: Appearance and identification
sections.body: About the size of a blackbird, the great spotted woodpecker has bold black-and-white plumage, large white shoulder patches, and a crimson patch under the tail. Males also carry a small red patch on the back of the head, which females lack, while juveniles have an entirely red crown. Its flight is distinctively undulating, rising and dipping as it bounds between trees at up to 24 km/h (15 mph). This combination makes it one of the most recognisable woodland birds in its range.

sections.heading: Range and status
sections.body: The species is widespread across the woodlands, parks, and gardens of Eurasia and North Africa, and it readily visits garden feeders in winter. It has adapted well to human-altered landscapes and its population is stable or increasing across much of its range. The IUCN lists it as Least Concern, and wild birds can live up to eleven years. Mature woodland with plenty of dead timber is its ideal habitat.

faqs.question: Why do woodpeckers drum on trees?
faqs.answer: Drumming is mainly a form of communication, not feeding. Woodpeckers hammer rapidly on resonant dead wood to advertise their territory and attract a mate, especially in late winter and spring.

faqs.question: How do woodpeckers not get concussed?
faqs.answer: Woodpeckers have spongy, shock-absorbing skull bone and a specialised hyoid bone structure that wraps around the skull to cushion impacts. Their small, tightly packed brain also helps spread the force of each blow.

faqs.question: What do great spotted woodpeckers eat?
faqs.answer: They eat mainly insects and larvae dug from bark and dead wood, extracted with a long, sticky tongue. In winter they switch to seeds and nuts, and they will also take the eggs and chicks of other birds.

faqs.question: How can you tell a male great spotted woodpecker from a female?
faqs.answer: Males have a small red patch on the back of the head, which females lack. Juveniles of both sexes have a full red crown that they lose as they mature.

faqs.question: How long do great spotted woodpeckers live?
faqs.answer: In the wild they typically live around eight to eleven years. They are widespread and their numbers are stable, so the IUCN lists them as Least Concern.

faqs.question: Do great spotted woodpeckers visit garden feeders?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially in autumn and winter, when they are drawn to peanuts, fat, and seeds. They are a familiar and welcome sight at garden feeding stations across their range.

animals.name: Chicken
animals.summary: The chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) is the world's most common bird, a domesticated descendant of the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia. Kept worldwide for eggs, meat, and companionship, a typical bird weighs 1.5 to 3 kg (3.3 to 6.6 lb) depending on breed. Chickens are ground-feeding omnivores that can flutter for short bursts at up to 15 km/h (9 mph). Well-kept backyard birds commonly live 5 to 10 years.

sections.heading: Origin and domestication
sections.body: The chicken descends primarily from the red junglefowl, a colourful pheasant-like bird of the forest edges of Southeast Asia, with some genetic input from related junglefowl species. People began keeping these birds thousands of years ago, initially as much for cockfighting and ritual as for food. From this single wild ancestor, selective breeding has produced the enormous variety of chickens kept today. The species now lives on every inhabited continent and is by far the most numerous bird on Earth.

sections.heading: Breeds and appearance
sections.body: There are hundreds of chicken breeds, ranging from tiny bantams weighing under a kilogram to heavy birds of 4 kg or more, though most fall between 1.5 and 3 kg (3.3 to 6.6 lb). Breeds are often grouped by purpose: layers such as the Leghorn are prized for eggs, table breeds for meat, and dual-purpose birds like the Rhode Island Red for both. Ornamental and heritage breeds come in a striking range of colours, comb shapes, and feather patterns. Both sexes carry a fleshy comb and wattles, which are usually larger and redder in the cockerel.

sections.heading: Behaviour and social life
sections.body: Chickens are sociable, inquisitive birds that live in flocks organised by a clear dominance ranking, the original "pecking order". They spend much of the day scratching and foraging, dust-bathing to keep their feathers clean, and roosting off the ground at night for safety. Hens and cockerels use a wide vocabulary of calls, including distinct alarm calls for aerial and ground threats. Far from being simple, chickens can recognise many individual flock-mates and remember them over time.

sections.heading: Eggs and reproduction
sections.body: A productive laying hen can produce well over 250 eggs a year, though she will lay whether or not a cockerel is present. When she does go broody, she incubates a clutch of eggs for about 21 days before they hatch. Newly hatched chicks are covered in down and able to walk and feed almost at once, following the mother hen closely. The hen protects and warms her brood, teaching them to forage until they are old enough to fend for themselves.

sections.heading: Care and husbandry
sections.body: Chickens are hardy and adaptable, which is part of why they are kept so widely, but they still need thoughtful care. They require a secure, well-ventilated coop that protects them from foxes and other predators, clean water, and a balanced feed supplemented by grain, insects, vegetation, and kitchen scraps. Access to grit helps them grind food in the gizzard, and space to roam keeps them active and content. With good husbandry, backyard chickens commonly live 5 to 10 years.

faqs.question: How long do chickens live?
faqs.answer: Well-kept backyard chickens commonly live 5 to 10 years, and some reach even older. Commercial laying and meat birds are usually kept for much shorter periods, so lifespan depends heavily on how a chicken is raised.

faqs.question: Can chickens fly?
faqs.answer: Chickens can only manage brief, fluttering flights rather than true sustained flight. They may flap up to a perch, over a low fence, or across a yard at up to about 15 km/h (9 mph), but their heavy bodies keep them mostly on the ground.

faqs.question: What are chickens descended from?
faqs.answer: Chickens are descended mainly from the red junglefowl, a wild bird of the forest edges of Southeast Asia, with some genetic input from related junglefowl. Thousands of years of domestication and selective breeding turned this wild bird into today's farmyard chicken.

faqs.question: Do hens need a rooster to lay eggs?
faqs.answer: No. A hen will lay eggs whether or not a cockerel is present, and a healthy layer can produce well over 250 eggs a year. A rooster is only needed if you want the eggs to be fertile and hatch into chicks.

faqs.question: What do chickens eat?
faqs.answer: Chickens are omnivores that eat grain, insects, worms, vegetation, and kitchen scraps. Backyard flocks are usually given a balanced feed alongside what they forage, plus grit to help them grind food in the gizzard.

faqs.question: How much does a chicken weigh?
faqs.answer: Most chickens weigh between 1.5 and 3 kg (3.3 to 6.6 lb), though it varies widely by breed. Small bantams weigh under a kilogram, while heavy table breeds can reach 4 kg or more.

animals.name: Wild Turkey
animals.summary: The wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo) is a large ground-dwelling bird native to the forests and fields of North America and the ancestor of the familiar farmyard turkey. Toms can weigh up to 8 kg and are known for their bald, colourful heads and fanned tail displays. They forage on acorns, seeds, insects, and berries, run at up to 40 km/h, and manage strong short bursts of flight. The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern.

sections.heading: Appearance and displays
sections.body: The wild turkey is a big, heavy-bodied bird with dark, iridescent feathers that gleam bronze and green in sunlight. Males, called toms or gobblers, have a bald head that can flush red, white, and blue, a fleshy snood over the bill, and a dangling wattle at the throat. In courtship a tom fans his broad tail, puffs out his body feathers, and struts while gobbling to attract hens and warn off rivals. Females, or hens, are smaller and more drably coloured for camouflage while nesting.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: Wild turkeys are omnivores that spend much of the day walking and scratching the ground for food. Acorns and other nuts, seeds, and berries form the bulk of their diet, supplemented by insects, and they will scratch through leaf litter to expose hidden morsels. Young poults rely heavily on protein-rich insects in their first weeks of life. Diet shifts with the seasons, leaning on hard mast such as acorns through autumn and winter.

sections.heading: Behaviour and flocks
sections.body: Wild turkeys are social birds that live in flocks for much of the year, with hens and young forming groups separate from bands of males outside the breeding season. They communicate with a wide range of calls, from the male's carrying gobble to soft yelps and clucks that keep a flock in contact. A pecking order sets which birds feed and roost in the best spots. Sharp eyesight and wariness make them surprisingly difficult to approach in the wild.

sections.heading: Roosting and flight
sections.body: Although wild turkeys feed on the ground and can run at up to 40 km/h, they are far from flightless. When alarmed they can burst into powerful, short flights to clear obstacles or reach safety. Each evening they fly up to roost in trees, which keeps them out of reach of ground predators through the night. At first light they glide back down to resume feeding.

sections.heading: From wild bird to domestic turkey
sections.body: The wild turkey is the wild ancestor of the domestic turkey raised for meat around the world. Indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica domesticated turkeys long before European contact, and the domestic bird was later carried to Europe and beyond. Centuries of selective breeding produced the heavier, broad-breasted farm turkey, which looks and behaves quite differently from its lean, agile wild cousin. The wild bird remains fully capable of flight and long days of foraging that farm breeds have largely lost.

sections.heading: Conservation and recovery
sections.body: The wild turkey is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, but it was not always secure. Overhunting and forest clearance drove wild populations to very low numbers across much of North America by the early 20th century. Reintroduction programmes, habitat protection, and regulated hunting have since restored the bird to much of its former range and beyond. It is now a common sight in woodlands and on field edges once more.

faqs.question: Can wild turkeys fly?
faqs.answer: Yes. Wild turkeys feed and run on the ground but are strong short-distance fliers, bursting into the air to escape danger. Each evening they fly up into trees to roost safely overnight, gliding back down at dawn.

faqs.question: What do wild turkeys eat?
faqs.answer: Wild turkeys are omnivores. Their diet is built around acorns and other nuts, seeds, and berries, along with insects, and they scratch through leaf litter to find food. Young poults depend heavily on insects for protein early in life.

faqs.question: How fast can a wild turkey run?
faqs.answer: Wild turkeys can run at up to about 40 km/h on the ground. Combined with strong short bursts of flight, this speed makes them surprisingly hard to catch despite their bulk.

faqs.question: How big do wild turkeys get?
faqs.answer: Wild turkeys weigh roughly 3 to 8 kg, with toms considerably larger than hens. They measure around 1.2 m in length, making them one of the largest ground birds in North America.

faqs.question: Are wild turkeys the same as farm turkeys?
faqs.answer: They are the same species, but not the same bird. The wild turkey is the lean, agile ancestor of the domestic turkey, which has been selectively bred for centuries into a much heavier, broad-breasted farm animal that can barely fly.

faqs.question: What is the fleshy bit on a turkey's head called?
faqs.answer: The flap of skin hanging over the bill is the snood, and the loose skin at the throat is the wattle. Both are most developed in males and can flush with bright colour during courtship displays.

animals.name: Canada Goose
animals.summary: The Canada goose is a large, adaptable waterbird native to North America, easily recognised by its black head and neck, white chinstrap, and loud honking call. It grazes on grasses and grain around lakes, fields, and parks, weighs 3 to 6 kg, and famously flies in V-formation, reaching up to 90 km/h (56 mph). Canada geese live up to 24 years and are listed as Least Concern.

sections.heading: The V-formation and migration
sections.body: Canada geese are celebrated for flying in a distinctive V-formation during their long seasonal migrations. Each bird flies slightly above the one in front, catching the uplift from its wingtips so the whole flock saves energy, and the lead position is rotated as birds tire. Migrating flocks can travel hundreds of kilometres in a day and reach speeds of up to 90 km/h with a following wind. Their honking calls help the flock stay together across great distances and in poor visibility.

sections.heading: Grazing and diet
sections.body: Canada geese are herbivores that feed mainly on grasses, sedges, grain, and aquatic plants. On land they graze like small livestock, cropping lawns, pastures, and playing fields with their serrated bills, while in water they up-end to reach submerged vegetation. In autumn and winter they switch heavily to waste grain in harvested fields, building fat reserves for migration and cold weather. This flexible, plant-based diet is one reason the species does so well around farmland and towns.

sections.heading: Appearance and identification
sections.body: The Canada goose is instantly recognisable by its long black neck and head marked with a broad white "chinstrap" across the throat. The body is greyish-brown above and paler below, ending in a white rump band and black tail. Adults typically weigh 3 to 6 kg and measure about a metre long, with the so-called giant subspecies growing heavier still. Males and females look alike, though ganders are usually a little larger than geese.

sections.heading: Nesting and goslings
sections.body: Canada geese pair for life and both parents share in raising the brood. The female builds a nest of grass and down on the ground near water and incubates a clutch of usually four to seven eggs for about four weeks, while the gander stands guard nearby. The fluffy yellow-and-grey goslings can walk, swim, and feed within a day of hatching and follow their parents closely. Families often merge into large groups called crèches, and the young stay with their parents through their first migration.

sections.heading: Behaviour and defence
sections.body: Canada geese are bold, social birds that gather in noisy flocks outside the breeding season. During nesting, however, a gander will defend his mate and eggs fiercely, hissing, spreading his wings, and charging at intruders many times his size, including people and dogs. This aggression around nests is a common source of conflict in parks and gardens. Their alertness and willingness to sound the alarm also make them effective early-warning sentinels for other wildlife.

sections.heading: Adaptability and status
sections.body: The Canada goose is listed as Least Concern and has become one of North America's great conservation success stories, rebounding strongly after historic overhunting. It thrives in human-altered landscapes such as parks, golf courses, reservoirs, and farmland, and many populations have stopped migrating where winters are mild and food is plentiful. Introduced birds have also established themselves in the UK and parts of Europe. In some areas they are now so numerous that they are considered a nuisance, with lifespans reaching up to 24 years in the wild.

faqs.question: Why do Canada geese fly in a V-formation?
faqs.answer: Geese fly in a V so that each bird can ride the uplift created by the wingtips of the one ahead, which saves energy across long flights. The lead bird works hardest and is swapped out as it tires, and the formation also helps the flock keep track of one another.

faqs.question: What do Canada geese eat?
faqs.answer: Canada geese are herbivores that eat grasses, sedges, grain, and aquatic plants. They graze on lawns and fields, feed on waste grain after harvest, and up-end in water to reach submerged plants.

faqs.question: How fast can a Canada goose fly?
faqs.answer: Canada geese can fly at up to 90 km/h (56 mph), especially with a helpful tailwind during migration. Their normal cruising speed is lower, but they can cover hundreds of kilometres in a single day.

faqs.question: How long do Canada geese live?
faqs.answer: Canada geese commonly live 10 to 24 years in the wild, and some individuals live even longer. Their long lifespan and lifelong pair bonds mean established pairs can return to the same breeding sites for many years.

faqs.question: Are Canada geese aggressive?
faqs.answer: Canada geese are usually calm but become highly protective during the nesting season. A gander guarding eggs or goslings will hiss, spread its wings, and charge at people or animals it sees as a threat, which is why nesting geese are best given a wide berth.

faqs.question: Why are there so many Canada geese?
faqs.answer: Canada geese have boomed because they adapt easily to human landscapes such as parks, farms, and reservoirs, where food is plentiful and natural predators are few. Many populations have also stopped migrating in mild areas, so numbers stay high year-round and can even be seen as a nuisance.
