animals.name: Domestic Sheep
animals.summary: The domestic sheep is one of the oldest and most widespread of all livestock, kept for wool, meat, and milk on pasture across every inhabited continent. A gentle, flock-living herbivore that grazes on grasses, forbs, and hay, it weighs anywhere from 45 to 160 kg depending on breed and stands about 1.2 m long. Domestic sheep usually live 10 to 12 years, and pet animals can live longer.

sections.heading: Origins and domestication
sections.body: The domestic sheep was one of the first animals humans ever tamed, descended from wild mouflon in the Near East around 10,000 years ago. Early flocks were kept mainly for meat, milk, and skins, with woolly fleeces developing gradually through selective breeding. From these beginnings the sheep spread with farming peoples across Europe, Asia, and eventually the whole world. Today it is one of the most numerous livestock animals on the planet, raised on pasture and rangeland everywhere people farm.

sections.heading: Breeds and their uses
sections.body: Centuries of selective breeding have produced more than a thousand sheep breeds suited to different climates and purposes. Wool breeds such as the Merino are prized for fine, soft fleece, while others like the Suffolk are bred mainly for meat and some, such as East Friesians, for milk. Sizes vary enormously, from small primitive breeds to heavy rams reaching up to 160 kg. This diversity lets sheep farming succeed everywhere from lowland pastures to rugged upland moors.

sections.heading: Grazing and diet
sections.body: Sheep are herbivores that graze on grasses, clover and other forbs, and hay, using a specialised digestive system to break down fibrous plants. As ruminants they ferment food in a four-chambered stomach and chew the cud, extracting nutrients from vegetation people cannot eat. Their narrow muzzles let them graze plants very close to the ground, which is why grazing must be managed to avoid over-cropping a pasture. Rotating sheep between fields keeps both the flock and the grassland healthy.

sections.heading: Flock behaviour and temperament
sections.body: Sheep are strongly social animals with a powerful instinct to stay together, and an isolated sheep quickly becomes stressed. This flocking behaviour is a natural defence, since staying in a group makes it harder for a predator to single out one individual. Far from being simple, sheep can recognise the faces of many other sheep and of people, and they remember them for years. They are generally docile and easily herded, which is exactly why they were among the first animals to be domesticated.

sections.heading: Wool, husbandry, and the farming year
sections.body: Most wool breeds are sheared once a year, usually in spring, both to harvest the fleece and to keep the animals comfortable through summer. The farming calendar revolves around lambing, when ewes give birth after a gestation of about five months, typically to one or two lambs. Shepherds also manage feeding, foot care, and protection from parasites and predators throughout the year. Well-cared-for sheep live around 10 to 12 years, and pet or hobby-farm animals often live longer.

sections.heading: Sheep and people
sections.body: Few animals have shaped human life as deeply as the sheep, providing clothing, food, and even parchment across thousands of years of history. Wool built major trading economies, and sheep farming still defines the landscape and culture of upland regions in Britain and beyond. Beyond farming, sheep appear throughout religion, language, and folklore, from nursery rhymes to proverbs. As a fully domesticated animal, the sheep depends on human care rather than living wild.

faqs.question: How long have sheep been domesticated?
faqs.answer: Sheep were among the first animals to be domesticated, tamed from wild mouflon in the Near East around 10,000 years ago. Early flocks were kept for meat, milk, and skins before woolly fleeces were bred over time.

faqs.question: What do sheep eat?
faqs.answer: Sheep are herbivores that graze on grasses, clover and other forbs, and hay. As ruminants, they ferment plant matter in a four-chambered stomach and chew the cud to extract nutrients.

faqs.question: How much does a sheep weigh?
faqs.answer: Weight varies enormously by breed, from around 45 kg in smaller breeds to up to 160 kg in the largest rams. This range reflects the more than a thousand sheep breeds developed for different climates and purposes.

faqs.question: Are sheep intelligent?
faqs.answer: Sheep are smarter than their reputation suggests. They can recognise and remember the faces of dozens of other sheep and of humans for years, and they show clear emotional responses and strong social bonds.

faqs.question: Why do sheep stay in flocks?
faqs.answer: Flocking is a natural defence: staying together makes it harder for predators to pick off a single animal. The instinct is so strong that an isolated sheep becomes stressed, which is also what makes sheep easy to herd.

faqs.question: How long do sheep live?
faqs.answer: Domestic sheep usually live about 10 to 12 years. Pet sheep and those on hobby farms, spared the pressures of commercial farming, often live longer.

animals.name: Domestic Goat
animals.summary: The domestic goat is a hardy, agile ruminant kept around the world for its milk, meat, fibre, and skins. Descended from the wild bezoar ibex of the Middle East, it was one of the earliest animals to be domesticated, around ten thousand years ago. A typical goat weighs 30 to 80 kg depending on the breed and stands out for its remarkable climbing ability and curious, sociable nature. Well cared-for goats commonly live 12 to 15 years.

sections.heading: Origins and domestication
sections.body: Goats were among the first livestock animals to be domesticated, tamed from the wild bezoar ibex in the mountains of the Middle East roughly ten thousand years ago. Their hardiness and willingness to eat a wide range of plants made them invaluable to early farmers, and they spread with people across Asia, Africa, and Europe. Today there are hundreds of breeds adapted to climates from desert to alpine. Their scientific name is Capra hircus.

sections.heading: Breeds and uses
sections.body: Domestic goats are bred for many purposes, and different breeds specialise in milk, meat, or fibre. Dairy breeds such as the Saanen and Nubian are prized for their milk, which is also made into cheese, while Boer goats are raised chiefly for meat. Fibre breeds like the Angora and Cashmere produce mohair and cashmere wool. Weights range widely, from around 30 kg in smaller breeds to 80 kg or more in the largest.

sections.heading: Diet and browsing
sections.body: Unlike sheep and cattle, which mainly graze grass, goats are browsers that prefer shrubs, leaves, bark, and weeds. This taste for woody and coarse plants lets them thrive on rough land that would not support other livestock, and makes them useful for clearing overgrown vegetation. As ruminants, they ferment their food in a four-chambered stomach and chew the cud to extract nutrients. Their agility helps them reach leaves and branches well above head height.

sections.heading: Climbing and agility
sections.body: Goats are exceptional climbers, able to scale steep, rocky slopes and even lean tree trunks in search of food. Their hooves have hard outer rims and soft, grippy inner pads that give them sure footing on precarious ledges. They can move at up to 16 km/h and balance on remarkably narrow footholds. This sure-footedness is inherited from their wild mountain ancestors and remains one of the goat's most striking traits.

sections.heading: Behaviour and intelligence
sections.body: Goats are social, curious, and surprisingly clever animals that live naturally in herds. They form strong bonds within the group, establish clear pecking orders, and can recognise the faces and voices of their companions and handlers. Research has shown they can learn to solve simple puzzles for food and remember the solutions for months. Their inquisitive, mischievous nature means they are quick to test fences and explore anything new.

faqs.question: How long do goats live?
faqs.answer: Domestic goats typically live 12 to 15 years, and pet goats that are well cared for can live even longer. Lifespan depends on breed, diet, and access to veterinary care.

faqs.question: What do goats eat?
faqs.answer: Goats are browsers rather than grazers, preferring shrubs, leaves, bark, and weeds over grass. As ruminants they ferment their food in a four-chambered stomach, and their taste for coarse, woody plants lets them thrive on rough land other livestock cannot use.

faqs.question: Why are goats such good climbers?
faqs.answer: Goats have hooves with hard outer rims and soft, grippy inner pads that give them excellent traction on steep and rocky ground. Combined with a strong sense of balance inherited from their wild mountain ancestors, this lets them scale cliffs and even lean tree trunks to reach food.

faqs.question: What are goats used for?
faqs.answer: Goats are kept worldwide for their milk, meat, fibre, and skins. Dairy breeds provide milk and cheese, meat breeds such as the Boer are raised for their meat, and fibre breeds like the Angora and Cashmere produce mohair and cashmere wool.

faqs.question: Are goats intelligent animals?
faqs.answer: Yes, goats are notably clever and social. They can recognise the faces and voices of their companions and handlers, solve simple puzzles for food, and remember the solutions for months. Their curiosity and problem-solving often lead them to test fences and escape enclosures.

faqs.question: How much does a goat weigh?
faqs.answer: A goat's weight depends heavily on its breed, ranging from around 30 kg in smaller breeds to 80 kg or more in the largest. Males are generally heavier and more muscular than females.

animals.name: Domestic Pig
animals.summary: The domestic pig is a highly intelligent farm mammal descended from the Eurasian wild boar and kept worldwide for meat, and increasingly as a pet. A typical pig weighs 60 to 150 kg, stands on four short legs, and lives 10 to 15 years, though commercial pigs are raised for far shorter periods. Pigs are social, curious, and among the smartest of all domesticated animals.

sections.heading: Origins and domestication
sections.body: The domestic pig descends from the wild boar, Sus scrofa, and was domesticated independently in several parts of Eurasia at least 9,000 years ago. Centuries of selective breeding have produced hundreds of breeds, from the pink Large White and Landrace of commercial farms to hardy traditional types such as the Tamworth and Gloucestershire Old Spots. Compared with their wild ancestors, farm pigs tend to be larger, faster-growing, and less hairy. Feral pigs that escape captivity readily revert to a boar-like appearance within a few generations.

sections.heading: Intelligence and behaviour
sections.body: Pigs are widely regarded as one of the most intelligent domestic animals, often ranked alongside dogs and above cats in problem-solving tests. They can learn their names, respond to commands, use simple tools, and even manipulate levers or joysticks in laboratory experiments. They are naturally social, living in stable groups and communicating through an extensive range of grunts, squeals, and barks. Far from being dirty, pigs are clean animals that keep separate areas for sleeping and toileting when given the space.

sections.heading: Diet and rooting
sections.body: Pigs are omnivores with a famously varied appetite, eating grain, vegetables, forage, roots, and kitchen scraps. Their most distinctive feeding behaviour is rooting, in which they use a tough, mobile snout tipped with a special prenasal bone to dig through soil for tubers, worms, and grubs. This rooting instinct is strong even in pampered pet pigs and helps them turn over and aerate ground. On farms their diet is usually a carefully balanced feed to support steady growth.

sections.heading: Wallowing and keeping cool
sections.body: Pigs cannot sweat effectively, so they wallow in mud or water to regulate their body temperature in warm weather. A coating of mud also shields their skin from sunburn and helps deter biting insects and parasites. This need to cool down, rather than any love of filth, is the real reason pigs seek out wet ground. Providing shade, water, and a place to wallow is an important part of good pig husbandry.

sections.heading: Farming and human uses
sections.body: Pork is one of the most widely eaten meats in the world, and pigs are farmed on every inhabited continent. A domestic pig typically weighs 60 to 150 kg and can live 10 to 15 years, although commercial pigs are usually raised for only a matter of months. Beyond meat, pigs provide leather, and their physiology is close enough to ours that they are used in medical research and even as organ-transplant donors. Miniature breeds are increasingly kept as household pets.

sections.heading: Piglets and reproduction
sections.body: A sow can produce two or more litters a year, each typically containing eight to twelve piglets after a gestation of about three months, three weeks, and three days. Piglets are born with their eyes open and quickly establish a "teat order", each returning to its own preferred nipple. They grow rapidly on their mother's rich milk and are usually weaned within a few weeks. Sows are attentive mothers and build nests from straw or vegetation before farrowing when allowed to do so.

faqs.question: Are pigs really intelligent?
faqs.answer: Yes, pigs are among the most intelligent domestic animals, often compared to dogs and young children in cognitive tests. They can learn their names, solve puzzles, remember locations, and even operate simple joystick-controlled tasks in research settings.

faqs.question: How long do pigs live?
faqs.answer: Pet and breeding pigs commonly live 10 to 15 years, and some reach beyond that with good care. Commercial pigs raised for meat, however, are kept for only a few months before slaughter.

faqs.question: Why do pigs roll in mud?
faqs.answer: Pigs roll in mud to cool down, because they cannot sweat effectively to lose heat. The mud also protects their skin from sunburn and helps keep biting insects and parasites away, so wallowing is a sign of a healthy, well-adapted pig rather than a dirty one.

faqs.question: What do pigs eat?
faqs.answer: Pigs are omnivores and eat grain, vegetables, forage, roots, and scraps. On farms they are given balanced feed, while in the wild or free-range settings they root through soil for tubers, worms, and grubs with their strong snouts.

faqs.question: How much does a pig weigh?
faqs.answer: A typical domestic pig weighs between 60 and 150 kg (130 to 330 lb), depending on breed and age. Some large commercial boars grow considerably heavier, while miniature pet breeds stay much smaller.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a pig and a wild boar?
faqs.answer: The domestic pig is a bred descendant of the wild boar and belongs to the same species. Farm pigs are generally larger, less hairy, and faster-growing, whereas wild boar are leaner, bristly, and equipped with prominent tusks.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Omnivore — grain, vegetables, forage, and scraps

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Farms worldwide; wild boar ancestry in Eurasia

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 17 km/h (11 mph) over short distances

animals.name: Wandering Albatross
animals.summary: The wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans) is a giant seabird of the Southern Ocean, boasting the widest wingspan of any living bird. It weighs around 8 to 12 kg (18 to 26 lb) and glides across the waves at up to 80 km/h (50 mph) with barely a wingbeat. Feeding on squid, fish, and carrion snatched from the sea surface, it is one of the longest-lived birds, reaching 40 to 50 years. The IUCN lists it as Vulnerable.

sections.heading: The widest wings on Earth
sections.body: The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird, with the longest individuals stretching over three metres from tip to tip. Its body measures around 1.3 m (over 4 ft) in length and weighs roughly 8 to 12 kg (18 to 26 lb), with males larger than females. Adults are mostly white with black-tipped wings, growing whiter with age, while young birds start out chocolate brown. Those enormous, narrow wings are built not for flapping but for effortless gliding.

sections.heading: Masters of gliding flight
sections.body: Wandering albatrosses are among the most efficient fliers in the animal kingdom, riding ocean winds for hours or even days with barely a wingbeat. Using a technique called dynamic soaring, they harvest energy from the difference in wind speed near the sea surface, sweeping up and down across the waves at up to 80 km/h (50 mph). A special tendon can lock the wing in the outstretched position, so holding it open costs almost no muscular effort. A single foraging trip can cover thousands of kilometres of open ocean.

sections.heading: Feeding at sea
sections.body: Wandering albatrosses are carnivores that feed mainly on squid, fish, and carrion taken from the surface of the sea. They forage over vast stretches of the Southern Ocean, seizing prey while sitting on the water or in shallow surface dives. Their keen sense of smell helps them locate food across huge distances, and they will readily follow ships and fishing boats for scraps. This scavenging habit, however, exposes them to one of their greatest dangers.

sections.heading: Breeding and long life
sections.body: Wandering albatrosses breed on remote sub-Antarctic islands, where pairs form lasting bonds reinforced by elaborate courtship dances. A pair raises just a single chick, and because the chick takes so long to fledge, successful pairs breed only once every two years. Birds do not begin breeding until they are around a decade old, and they are among the longest-lived of all birds, reaching 40 to 50 years. This slow, unhurried life history is possible only because adults face few natural predators at sea.

sections.heading: Why it is vulnerable
sections.body: The IUCN classifies the wandering albatross as Vulnerable, largely because of longline fishing. Birds diving for baited hooks are dragged under and drowned in large numbers, a toll their slow breeding cannot easily replace. Introduced predators such as mice and rats on some breeding islands, along with plastic pollution at sea, add further pressure. Seabird-friendly fishing measures, such as weighting lines and setting them at night, have helped reduce deaths where they are used.

faqs.question: How big is a wandering albatross's wingspan?
faqs.answer: The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird, with the longest individuals exceeding three metres from wingtip to wingtip. Its body is around 1.3 m long, and it weighs roughly 8 to 12 kg (18 to 26 lb).

faqs.question: How long do wandering albatrosses live?
faqs.answer: Wandering albatrosses are among the longest-lived birds, typically reaching 40 to 50 years of age. They mature slowly and do not usually begin breeding until they are around ten years old.

faqs.question: How fast can a wandering albatross fly?
faqs.answer: Wandering albatrosses can glide at up to about 80 km/h (50 mph) when wind conditions are favourable. They use a technique called dynamic soaring to travel vast distances with barely a wingbeat.

faqs.question: What do wandering albatrosses eat?
faqs.answer: Wandering albatrosses are carnivores that feed mainly on squid, fish, and carrion taken from the sea surface. They forage over huge areas of the Southern Ocean and often follow ships and fishing boats to scavenge scraps.

faqs.question: Why are wandering albatrosses endangered?
faqs.answer: Wandering albatrosses are listed as Vulnerable, chiefly because of longline fishing, in which birds are hooked and drowned. Introduced predators on breeding islands and plastic pollution add further pressure, and their slow breeding makes recovery difficult.

faqs.question: How often do wandering albatrosses breed?
faqs.answer: A successful pair of wandering albatrosses breeds only once every two years, because their single chick takes so long to raise. They nest on remote sub-Antarctic islands and form long-lasting pair bonds.

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 80 km/h (50 mph) wind-assisted gliding

range.nativeRange: Southern Ocean — breeding on sub-Antarctic islands including South Georgia, Crozet, Kerguelen, and Macquarie.

animals.name: Thresher Shark
animals.summary: The thresher shark (Alopias vulpinus) is an open-ocean predator famous for its enormously long, whip-like tail, which can be almost as long as its body. Found in temperate and tropical seas worldwide, it can reach about 5 m in length including the tail and weigh 150 to 250 kg. It swims at up to 48 km/h and uses its tail to stun small fish and squid. The species lives up to 25 years and is listed as Vulnerable.

sections.heading: The whip-like tail
sections.body: The thresher shark's most striking feature is its upper tail lobe, which is drawn out into a long, scythe-like whip that can be almost as long as the rest of the body. Counting the tail, an adult can measure around 5 m from nose to tip. Far from being decorative, this tail is a precision hunting tool honed for a single, remarkable technique. It gives the thresher a silhouette unlike any other shark in the open ocean.

sections.heading: Tail-slap hunting
sections.body: Thresher sharks hunt in a way seen in almost no other fish: they use the tail as a weapon. Swimming into a school of small fish, the shark throws its long tail forward over its head like a whip, striking and stunning several prey at once. It then circles back to swallow the dazed fish before they can recover. This overhead tail-slap is fast enough to create a crack in the water and lets a single shark disable many fish in one pass.

sections.heading: Diet and open-ocean life
sections.body: Thresher sharks are carnivores that feed mainly on small schooling fish such as mackerel, herring, and sardines, along with squid. They roam the temperate and tropical open oceans worldwide, often far from land, and can swim at speeds of up to 48 km/h in pursuit of prey. Powerful, warm-muscled swimmers, they sometimes leap clear of the surface. They tend to follow the movements of the baitfish schools on which they depend.

sections.heading: Slow growth and reproduction
sections.body: Like many large sharks, threshers grow slowly, mature late, and produce few young, which makes their populations slow to recover. Females give birth to a small litter of well-developed live pups rather than laying eggs. Unusually, the developing embryos practise oophagy, feeding on unfertilised eggs inside the mother before they are born. This life history means a thresher may live up to 25 years but replaces its numbers only gradually.

sections.heading: Why it is vulnerable
sections.body: The thresher shark is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN because its numbers have declined across much of its range. It is caught both deliberately and as bycatch in commercial fisheries, valued for its meat, fins, and liver oil. Its distinctive long tail also makes it a target for sport fishing. Because threshers breed so slowly, populations struggle to rebuild once they have been overfished.

sections.heading: Threshers and people
sections.body: Despite their size and speed, thresher sharks pose very little danger to people and are considered timid, rarely approaching divers. They are far more threatened by humans than the other way around. Anglers prize them for their leaping fights when hooked, and they are an important food and fin species in many fisheries. Encouraging sustainable fishing and reducing bycatch are the key steps to safeguarding them.

faqs.question: Why does the thresher shark have such a long tail?
faqs.answer: The thresher shark uses its long, whip-like tail to hunt. It swings the tail overhead to strike and stun schools of small fish, then circles back to eat the dazed prey, making the tail a specialised feeding tool rather than just a means of swimming.

faqs.question: How big do thresher sharks get?
faqs.answer: Thresher sharks can reach about 5 m in total length, with the tail making up roughly half of that. They typically weigh between 150 and 250 kg (330 to 550 lb).

faqs.question: What do thresher sharks eat?
faqs.answer: They are carnivores that feed mainly on small schooling fish such as mackerel, herring, and sardines, as well as squid. They stun their prey with a whip of the tail before swallowing them.

faqs.question: How fast can a thresher shark swim?
faqs.answer: Thresher sharks can swim at speeds of up to 48 km/h (30 mph). They are powerful, warm-muscled swimmers that sometimes leap clear of the water when hunting.

faqs.question: Are thresher sharks dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: No. Thresher sharks are timid and pose very little threat to people, rarely approaching divers. They are far more endangered by human fishing than they are a danger to us.

faqs.question: Are thresher sharks endangered?
faqs.answer: Thresher sharks are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN. They are slow to breed and are caught for their meat, fins, and liver oil, so their populations recover slowly once overfished.

facts.value: Temperate and tropical open oceans worldwide

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 48 km/h (30 mph); tail slap stuns prey

range.nativeRange: Circumglobal in temperate and tropical open oceans — common threshers in Atlantic and Pacific.

animals.name: Nurse Shark
animals.summary: The nurse shark is a slow-moving, bottom-dwelling shark of warm Atlantic and eastern Pacific coral reefs and sand flats. Reaching about 3 metres long and up to around 100 kg, it is known for its docile nature and habit of resting motionless on the seabed by day. It feeds at night on fish, crustaceans, molluscs, and stingrays, using powerful suction to draw prey from crevices. Nurse sharks live 20 to 25 years and are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN.

sections.heading: Appearance and identification
sections.body: The nurse shark has a broad, flattened head, a rounded body, and a long tail that can make up much of its total length of around 3 metres. Its colour is usually a plain yellowish-brown to grey-brown, helping it blend with sandy and reef bottoms. Two distinctive barbels hang below the snout, fleshy whisker-like organs it uses to taste and feel for hidden prey. Large adults can weigh up to about 100 kg, and exceptional individuals reach roughly 150 kg.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Nurse sharks live in warm, shallow waters of the western and eastern Atlantic and the eastern Pacific, favouring coral reefs, rocky ledges, and sand flats. They are strongly associated with the seabed and are rarely found far from the bottom. By day they often gather in groups, resting in caves, under ledges, or piled together on the sand. Their preference for shallow inshore waters brings them into regular contact with divers and snorkellers.

sections.heading: Feeding and hunting
sections.body: Nurse sharks are nocturnal carnivores that hunt after dark for fish, crustaceans, molluscs, and stingrays. Rather than chasing prey, they use a powerful, rapid suction to vacuum animals out of crevices and from beneath the sand. Their small mouths and rows of tightly packed, crushing teeth are well suited to breaking open hard-shelled prey such as crabs and conch. During the day they mostly rest and digest, conserving energy for the night's foraging.

sections.heading: Behaviour and movement
sections.body: Despite their size, nurse sharks are among the most sluggish and docile of sharks, spending much of the day lying still on the seabed. When they do swim, they move with slow, sinuous beats of the tail and can put on a burst of up to 40 km/h if threatened. Unlike many sharks, they can pump water over their gills while stationary, so they do not need to keep swimming to breathe. This ability is what allows them to rest motionless for long periods.

sections.heading: Reproduction and life cycle
sections.body: Nurse sharks are ovoviviparous, meaning the eggs hatch inside the mother and she gives birth to live, fully formed pups. Litters can number around 20 to 30 young after a gestation of roughly six months. The pups are independent from birth and shelter among reefs and seagrass to avoid predators. Nurse sharks grow slowly and are long-lived, reaching 20 to 25 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Conservation and threats
sections.body: The nurse shark is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, with numbers declining in several parts of its range. Its shallow, inshore habits make it easy to catch, and it is taken for its meat, fins, and skin, as well as being caught accidentally in other fisheries. Coastal development and reef damage further reduce the habitats it depends on. Its slow growth and modest litter sizes mean populations recover only slowly once depleted.

faqs.question: Are nurse sharks dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Nurse sharks are generally docile and pose little threat to people, and they are among the calmest of sharks. Bites are rare and almost always the result of a shark being grabbed, stepped on, or otherwise provoked, as they have strong jaws and can clamp down hard if disturbed.

faqs.question: What do nurse sharks eat?
faqs.answer: Nurse sharks are carnivores that feed at night on fish, crustaceans, molluscs, and stingrays. They use powerful suction to draw prey out of crevices and from under the sand, and their crushing teeth are ideal for breaking open hard-shelled animals such as crabs and conch.

faqs.question: How big do nurse sharks get?
faqs.answer: Adult nurse sharks reach about 3 metres in length and commonly weigh up to around 100 kg, with the largest individuals reaching roughly 150 kg. Much of their length is made up of a long tail.

faqs.question: Why do nurse sharks lie still on the bottom?
faqs.answer: Nurse sharks are nocturnal and rest on the seabed during the day to conserve energy for night-time hunting. Unlike many sharks, they can actively pump water over their gills while stationary, so they do not need to keep swimming to breathe and can lie motionless for long periods.

faqs.question: How long do nurse sharks live?
faqs.answer: Nurse sharks are long-lived, reaching 20 to 25 years in the wild. They grow slowly and mature relatively late, which is part of why their populations are slow to recover from overfishing.

faqs.question: Are nurse sharks endangered?
faqs.answer: Nurse sharks are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, meaning they face a real risk of decline in the wild. Their shallow, inshore habits make them easy to catch, and slow growth combined with fishing pressure and habitat loss has reduced numbers in several regions.

facts.value: Carnivore — fish, crustaceans, molluscs, and stingrays

animals.name: Sand Tiger Shark
animals.summary: The sand tiger shark is a large, slow-moving coastal shark found in warm and temperate seas worldwide, often seen hovering motionless in aquariums. Despite a mouthful of jagged teeth and a fierce appearance, it is docile and rarely dangerous to people. It grows to about 3 metres, weighs 90 to 190 kg, lives 12 to 15 years, and is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN.

sections.heading: Appearance and teeth
sections.body: The sand tiger shark has a stout, brownish-grey body, a pointed snout, and small eyes, often speckled with reddish or dark spots along the flanks. Its most striking feature is its mouth, which stays slightly open to reveal rows of long, narrow, backward-curving teeth even when relaxed. These needle-like teeth are perfect for gripping slippery fish but are not designed for cutting, which is why the shark swallows most prey whole or in large pieces. This toothy grin gives it a menacing look that belies its calm nature.

sections.heading: The gulping-air trick
sections.body: Sand tiger sharks are the only sharks known to gulp air at the surface and hold it in their stomachs to achieve near-perfect buoyancy. This lets them hang almost motionless in the water, hovering silently above the seabed as they wait for prey. The ability makes them energy-efficient ambush hunters and is one reason they thrive in aquariums, where they can be seen suspended in mid-water. No other shark uses this method of controlling its depth.

sections.heading: Hunting and diet
sections.body: As a carnivore, the sand tiger shark preys on bony fish, squid, rays, and smaller sharks. It is mainly a nocturnal hunter, using its buoyancy and slow, deliberate swimming to sneak up on prey before a quick lunge. Sand tigers sometimes cooperate to herd schools of fish into tighter groups, making them easier to catch. Despite the fearsome dentition, their diet is dominated by fish they can swallow rather than large struggling prey.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Sand tiger sharks live in warm and temperate coastal waters around much of the world, favouring sandy nearshore zones, rocky reefs, and submerged ledges. They are typically found from the surf line down to depths of around 190 metres and often shelter in caves and gullies by day. Individuals may undertake seasonal migrations, moving toward the poles in summer and back toward the equator in winter. Their preference for shallow coastal water brings them into frequent contact with divers, who generally find them placid.

sections.heading: Reproduction and embryo rivalry
sections.body: Sand tiger sharks have one of the most extraordinary reproductive strategies in the animal kingdom, known as intrauterine cannibalism. The first embryo to develop in each of the two uteruses eats its smaller siblings before birth, so a female typically gives birth to just two well-developed pups. Each pup emerges around a metre long and ready to fend for itself. This low reproductive rate means populations recover very slowly from any decline.

sections.heading: Why it is vulnerable
sections.body: The sand tiger shark is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, largely because it produces so few young. Overfishing, accidental capture in nets, and historic culls near beaches have driven serious declines in several regions. With a wild lifespan of only about 12 to 15 years and just two pups per litter, the species cannot quickly replace lost numbers. Protective legislation now shields it in a number of countries, including much of its range in Australia and the United States.

faqs.question: Are sand tiger sharks dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Sand tiger sharks look intimidating but are generally docile and pose little threat to people. They are not considered man-eaters, and unprovoked attacks are extremely rare, which is why they are among the most common sharks kept in public aquariums.

faqs.question: Why do sand tiger sharks gulp air?
faqs.answer: Sand tiger sharks gulp air at the surface and store it in their stomachs to fine-tune their buoyancy. This allows them to hover almost motionless in the water without swimming, saving energy and helping them ambush prey. They are the only sharks known to do this.

faqs.question: How big do sand tiger sharks get?
faqs.answer: Sand tiger sharks typically reach about 3 metres in length and weigh 90 to 160 kg, with the largest individuals approaching 190 kg. Despite this size, they are slow, unhurried swimmers.

faqs.question: What do sand tiger sharks eat?
faqs.answer: Sand tiger sharks are carnivores that feed mainly on bony fish, squid, rays, and smaller sharks. They hunt mostly at night, using stealth and their long gripping teeth to seize prey, which they usually swallow whole.

faqs.question: Why are sand tiger sharks endangered?
faqs.answer: Sand tiger sharks are listed as Vulnerable because they breed extremely slowly, producing only two pups per litter. Overfishing, bycatch, and beach-protection culls have caused steep declines that the species struggles to recover from.

faqs.question: Do sand tiger shark embryos eat each other?
faqs.answer: Yes. In a process called intrauterine cannibalism, the largest embryo in each uterus consumes its smaller siblings before birth. As a result, a female usually gives birth to just two large, fully developed pups.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Carnivore — fish, squid, and smaller sharks

range.nativeRange: Coastal warm temperate waters worldwide — sandy nearshore from Japan to Australia and both Atlantic coasts.

animals.name: Ocean Sunfish
animals.summary: The ocean sunfish, or mola, is the heaviest bony fish in the world, reaching up to about 2,000 kg and 3 m across in the largest specimens. Found in temperate and tropical oceans worldwide, it is a harmless drifter that swims slowly at up to 5 km/h and feeds mostly on jellyfish. Molas are famous for basking flat at the surface, live around 8 to 10 years, and are classed as Vulnerable.

sections.heading: The heaviest bony fish
sections.body: The ocean sunfish holds the record as the heaviest bony fish on Earth, with the largest individuals weighing up to about 2,000 kg (4,400 lb) and measuring around 3 m from fin tip to fin tip. Its body looks like a giant swimming head that ends abruptly, because it never develops a normal tail. In place of a tail it has a rounded rudder called a clavus, formed from the back of the body.

sections.heading: A slow, gentle swimmer
sections.body: Despite its bulk, the sunfish is a harmless, placid animal that poses no danger to people. It swims slowly, reaching only about 5 km/h (3 mph), by sculling its tall dorsal and anal fins from side to side rather than beating a tail. Molas often let currents carry them and glide gently through open water in search of food; they never run, because they are fish and move only by swimming.

sections.heading: Feeding on jellyfish
sections.body: The ocean sunfish feeds mainly on jellyfish and other gelatinous drifters such as salps and comb jellies, supplemented by small fish, squid, and crustaceans. Because this prey is mostly water and low in energy, a mola must eat huge quantities to sustain its size. It uses beak-like fused teeth to bite off chunks and a throat lined with spiny projections to break the slippery food apart.

sections.heading: Basking and parasites
sections.body: Sunfish are often seen lying flat on their sides at the ocean surface, seemingly sunbathing. This basking behaviour helps them re-warm after deep dives into cold water and lets seabirds and cleaner fish pick parasites from their skin. Molas carry an exceptional parasite load, and they will even leap clear of the water, perhaps to dislodge unwanted hitchhikers.

sections.heading: Reproduction and record fertility
sections.body: Female ocean sunfish are among the most fecund of all vertebrates, capable of carrying hundreds of millions of tiny eggs at once. The larvae hatch as spiny, spherical specks barely a few millimetres long, then grow through one of the largest size increases of any animal. Only a minute fraction survive the journey to adulthood.

sections.heading: Conservation and threats
sections.body: The ocean sunfish is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN. Large numbers are caught accidentally as bycatch in gillnet and longline fisheries, where their slow, surface-bound habits make them easy to snag. Floating plastic bags, which resemble jellyfish, are also mistaken for prey, adding to the pressures on this ocean giant.

faqs.question: How big is an ocean sunfish?
faqs.answer: The ocean sunfish is the heaviest bony fish in the world, with the largest specimens weighing up to about 2,000 kg (4,400 lb) and reaching around 3 m across. Typical adults are smaller, in the range of a few hundred kilograms.

faqs.question: Are ocean sunfish dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: No. Ocean sunfish are harmless, gentle animals with no interest in people and no ability to harm them. They swim slowly and feed on jellyfish, so divers can watch them at close range safely.

faqs.question: What do ocean sunfish eat?
faqs.answer: Ocean sunfish feed mainly on jellyfish and other gelatinous animals such as salps, along with some small fish, squid, and crustaceans. Because this prey is low in energy, they must eat large amounts to maintain their enormous size.

faqs.question: Why do sunfish lie on their side at the surface?
faqs.answer: Sunfish bask flat at the surface to re-warm their bodies after diving into cold, deep water. Basking also lets seabirds and cleaner fish remove the many parasites that collect on their skin.

faqs.question: How fast can an ocean sunfish swim?
faqs.answer: Ocean sunfish are slow swimmers, reaching only about 5 km/h (3 mph). They move by waving their tall dorsal and anal fins from side to side and often drift with the current.

faqs.question: Are ocean sunfish endangered?
faqs.answer: Ocean sunfish are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN. Their main threat is accidental capture as bycatch in fishing nets and longlines, and they can also die from swallowing floating plastic mistaken for jellyfish.

animals.name: Loggerhead Sea Turtle
animals.summary: The loggerhead is a large sea turtle found in temperate and tropical oceans worldwide, named for its exceptionally big, powerful-jawed head. Adults reach about 1 m in shell length and weigh 80 to 200 kg, using their strong jaws to crush hard-shelled prey like crabs and molluscs. They are long-lived, reaching 45 to 50 years, but mature only at 20 to 30 years old. The IUCN lists the loggerhead as Vulnerable.

sections.heading: Appearance and adaptations
sections.body: The loggerhead takes its name from its unusually large head and thick, muscular jaws, which give it a bite powerful enough to crush shellfish. Its heart-shaped shell is a warm reddish-brown above and paler yellow beneath, typically reaching around 1 m in length. Adults weigh between 80 and 200 kg, making the loggerhead one of the larger hard-shelled sea turtles. Powerful, flipper-like front limbs propel it through the water at speeds of up to 24 km/h in short bursts.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: Loggerheads are carnivores whose strong jaws are built for a diet of hard-bodied prey. They eat crabs, molluscs such as whelks and clams, jellyfish, and fish, crushing shells that would defeat most other turtles. Young loggerheads drifting in the open ocean feed near the surface, while adults forage along the seabed of coastal shelves. Their feeding even helps recycle nutrients and shells across the seafloor.

sections.heading: Migration and life at sea
sections.body: Loggerheads are ocean wanderers that undertake some of the longest migrations of any sea turtle, crossing entire ocean basins between feeding and nesting grounds. Hatchlings ride ocean currents for years in what biologists call the 'lost years', drifting among floating seaweed before returning to coastal waters as juveniles. Adults navigate thousands of kilometres using the Earth's magnetic field as a built-in compass. Remarkably, females return to nest on or near the very beach where they themselves hatched.

sections.heading: Nesting and reproduction
sections.body: Female loggerheads come ashore on sandy beaches at night, dig a nest with their rear flippers, and lay around a hundred leathery eggs before returning to the sea. A single female may nest several times in a season, then skip several years before breeding again. The temperature of the sand determines the sex of the hatchlings, with warmer nests producing more females. Loggerheads grow slowly and do not reach breeding age until 20 to 30 years old.

sections.heading: Why it is vulnerable
sections.body: The loggerhead is listed as Vulnerable, having declined across much of its range. Many drown after being caught accidentally in fishing gear such as trawls and longlines, one of the biggest threats to the species. Coastal development and artificial light disorient nesting females and hatchlings, while plastic pollution is often swallowed by mistake. Their slow maturity means populations recover only very slowly from these losses.

sections.heading: Range and habitat
sections.body: Loggerheads live in temperate and tropical oceans around the world, from the Atlantic and Mediterranean to the Indian and Pacific. They spend most of their lives at sea, occupying open water as juveniles and shallower continental shelves as adults. Major nesting concentrations occur on beaches in places such as the south-eastern United States, Oman, and the Mediterranean. Because they range so widely, their conservation depends on cooperation across many nations.

faqs.question: Why is it called a loggerhead turtle?
faqs.answer: The name comes from the turtle's unusually large, block-like head. That big head houses powerful jaw muscles that give the loggerhead a bite strong enough to crush the shells of crabs and molluscs.

faqs.question: How big do loggerhead turtles get?
faqs.answer: Adult loggerheads reach about 1 m in shell length and weigh between 80 and 200 kg (175 to 440 lb). This makes them one of the larger hard-shelled sea turtles, second among them mainly to the green turtle.

faqs.question: How long do loggerhead turtles live?
faqs.answer: Loggerheads typically live 45 to 50 years. They grow slowly and do not reach breeding age until they are 20 to 30 years old, so each generation takes decades to replace itself.

faqs.question: What do loggerhead turtles eat?
faqs.answer: Loggerheads are carnivores that eat crabs, molluscs such as clams and whelks, jellyfish, and fish. Their powerful jaws let them crush hard shells that most other sea turtles cannot manage.

faqs.question: Why are loggerhead turtles endangered?
faqs.answer: Loggerheads are Vulnerable, threatened mainly by accidental capture in fishing gear, coastal development, artificial lighting on nesting beaches, and plastic pollution. Because they mature so slowly, their populations recover only gradually from these pressures.

faqs.question: How do loggerhead turtles find their nesting beaches?
faqs.answer: Loggerheads navigate using the Earth's magnetic field like a built-in compass, allowing them to cross ocean basins. Females often return to nest on or near the same beach where they hatched decades earlier.

animals.name: Leatherback Sea Turtle
animals.summary: The leatherback is the largest sea turtle in the world and one of the widest-ranging reptiles, swimming across every ocean from the tropics to the cold edges of the Arctic. It reaches 1.8 m (6 ft) long, weighs 250 to 700 kg (550 to 1,540 lb) and feeds almost entirely on jellyfish. A strong swimmer, it can move at up to 35 km/h (22 mph) and lives around 40 to 45 years. The IUCN lists it as Vulnerable.

sections.heading: A shell like no other turtle
sections.body: Unlike every other sea turtle, the leatherback has no hard bony shell. Instead its back is covered by a layer of tough, rubbery, oil-saturated skin over a mosaic of tiny bones, giving the animal its name. Seven raised ridges run the length of this teardrop-shaped body, streamlining it for a life of constant swimming. This flexible design lets the leatherback dive deeper than any other turtle, plunging beyond 1,000 m in search of prey.

sections.heading: The giant jellyfish specialist
sections.body: The leatherback feeds almost exclusively on jellyfish and their relatives, the salps. Its throat is lined with backward-pointing spines that trap this slippery, gelatinous food and stop it slipping back out. Because jellyfish are mostly water, an adult must eat a huge volume every day to fuel its enormous body. This narrow diet leaves the turtle dangerously vulnerable to floating plastic bags, which it easily mistakes for a jellyfish and swallows.

sections.heading: Warm-blooded among reptiles
sections.body: The leatherback is unusually good at keeping warm for a reptile, which is how it can feed in near-freezing water off Canada and Norway. Its large body, thick insulating fat and heat-generating muscles let it hold a core temperature well above the surrounding sea. This ability, sometimes called gigantothermy, makes it the most cold-tolerant of all turtles. It is one of the few reptiles regularly found in sub-polar waters.

sections.heading: Nesting and reproduction
sections.body: Females return to tropical beaches every two to three years to nest, often crossing entire oceans to reach them. Over a single season a female may come ashore several times, each time digging a deep pit and laying around 80 fertile eggs. The temperature of the sand determines the sex of the hatchlings, with warmer nests producing more females. After about two months, palm-sized hatchlings dig their way out and scramble to the sea, where only a tiny fraction survive to adulthood.

sections.heading: An ocean traveller
sections.body: Leatherbacks are among the most migratory of all animals, tracking blooms of jellyfish across thousands of kilometres of open ocean. Individuals tagged in the tropical Atlantic have been recorded feeding off the coasts of Canada and Europe within the same year. Powerful front flippers, which can span more than 2.5 m tip to tip, drive them along at speeds of up to 35 km/h. This wandering lifestyle spreads the species across a wider range than almost any other reptile.

sections.heading: Why it is threatened
sections.body: The leatherback is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, and several regional populations have collapsed dramatically. The main threats are the harvesting of eggs, accidental capture in fishing gear, and the loss of nesting beaches to development and rising seas. Swallowed plastic and warming sand that skews hatchling sex ratios add further pressure. Protecting key nesting beaches and reducing bycatch are the most important steps for the species' recovery.

faqs.question: How big is a leatherback turtle?
faqs.answer: Leatherbacks are the largest turtles on Earth. They reach about 1.8 m (6 ft) in length and weigh between 250 and 700 kg (550 to 1,540 lb), far heavier than any hard-shelled sea turtle.

faqs.question: What do leatherback turtles eat?
faqs.answer: Leatherbacks eat almost nothing but jellyfish and their relatives, the salps. Backward-pointing spines in their throat help them grip and swallow this soft, slippery prey.

faqs.question: Why is it called a leatherback?
faqs.answer: Unlike other sea turtles, it has no hard bony shell. Its back is covered by tough, leathery, rubbery skin over a layer of small bones, which is where the name comes from.

faqs.question: How long do leatherback turtles live?
faqs.answer: Leatherbacks are thought to live around 40 to 45 years in the wild. Their exact lifespan is hard to measure because they spend almost their whole lives far out at sea.

faqs.question: How fast can a leatherback turtle swim?
faqs.answer: Leatherbacks are powerful swimmers and can reach speeds of up to 35 km/h (22 mph). Their large front flippers, spanning over 2.5 m, propel them across entire oceans.

faqs.question: Are leatherback turtles endangered?
faqs.answer: Leatherbacks are classified as Vulnerable by the IUCN, and some regional populations have declined sharply. Egg harvesting, accidental capture in fishing nets and the loss of nesting beaches are the biggest threats.

animals.name: Hawksbill Sea Turtle
animals.summary: The hawksbill is a small sea turtle of tropical coral reefs worldwide, named for its narrow, bird-like beak. It grows to about 0.9 m (3 ft) and 45 to 90 kg, feeds mainly on sponges, and can swim at up to 24 km/h (15 mph). Hawksbills live 30 to 50 years in the wild and are Critically Endangered, largely because their beautiful shells were harvested for tortoiseshell.

sections.heading: Appearance and the tortoiseshell shell
sections.body: The hawksbill is instantly recognised by its overlapping, amber-and-brown scutes, which form the patterned shell long prized as "tortoiseshell". Its jaws taper to a sharp, hooked beak that works like a pair of scissors, and the rear of the shell is serrated like the teeth of a saw. Adults reach around 0.9 m (3 ft) in shell length and 45 to 90 kg, making them smaller than the bulky loggerhead.

sections.heading: A sponge specialist
sections.body: Hawksbills are one of the very few animals that eat sponges as the core of their diet, using that narrow beak to reach into reef crevices. They also take jellyfish, sea anemones, and algae, and are tolerant of toxins that would poison most predators. By grazing sponges that would otherwise overgrow corals, hawksbills help keep reef surfaces open for reef-building coral.

sections.heading: Coral reef habitat
sections.body: Hawksbills favour tropical coral reefs, rocky areas, lagoons, and mangrove estuaries across the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans. They are strong, agile swimmers that reach speeds of up to 24 km/h (15 mph) and squeeze into tight reef spaces where larger turtles cannot follow. Individuals often show strong fidelity to particular reefs, returning to the same feeding grounds year after year.

sections.heading: Nesting and reproduction
sections.body: Females come ashore on remote tropical beaches, usually at night, digging a pit and laying clutches that can exceed 100 eggs. The sex of the hatchlings is set by nest temperature, with warmer sand producing more females. Hatchlings emerge after about two months and scramble to the sea, but only a tiny fraction survive to adulthood, and females may not breed until they are decades old.

sections.heading: Why it is Critically Endangered
sections.body: The hawksbill is listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN, and its population has fallen sharply over the last century. The main driver was the tortoiseshell trade, which killed vast numbers for jewellery and ornaments, and demand persists illegally today. Habitat loss, coral-reef decline, egg collection, and entanglement in fishing gear continue to threaten the species despite international protection.

sections.heading: Lifespan and slow maturity
sections.body: Hawksbills are long-lived, reaching 30 to 50 years in the wild, but they mature slowly and reproduce late. This slow life history means populations recover very gradually, so losses from hunting or bycatch take decades to replace. Protecting nesting beaches and reducing illegal shell trade are therefore central to any recovery.

faqs.question: Why is the hawksbill turtle endangered?
faqs.answer: Hawksbills are Critically Endangered mainly because of the historic tortoiseshell trade, which killed huge numbers for their patterned shells. Ongoing threats include illegal shell sales, loss of coral-reef habitat, egg poaching, and accidental capture in fishing gear.

faqs.question: What do hawksbill turtles eat?
faqs.answer: Hawksbills are specialists that feed mainly on sponges, which most animals avoid. They also eat jellyfish, sea anemones, and algae, using their narrow, beak-like jaws to reach prey inside reef crevices.

faqs.question: How big do hawksbill turtles get?
faqs.answer: Adult hawksbills reach about 0.9 m (3 ft) in shell length and weigh roughly 45 to 90 kg (100 to 200 lb). They are noticeably smaller than loggerhead and green turtles.

faqs.question: How long do hawksbill turtles live?
faqs.answer: In the wild hawksbills live around 30 to 50 years. They mature slowly and breed late in life, which makes their populations slow to recover from losses.

faqs.question: Why is it called a hawksbill turtle?
faqs.answer: The name comes from its narrow, pointed beak, which curves like a hawk's bill. This sharp beak lets it reach into tight crevices in the reef to pull out sponges and other prey.

faqs.question: How fast can a hawksbill turtle swim?
faqs.answer: Hawksbills can swim at up to about 24 km/h (15 mph) in short bursts. They are agile in the water and can twist through narrow reef spaces that larger turtles cannot enter.

facts.value: Carnivore — sponges, jellyfish, algae, and anemones

animals.name: Eastern Box Turtle
animals.summary: The eastern box turtle (Terrapene carolina) is a small, land-dwelling turtle of the eastern United States, known for the hinged shell it can close like a box for protection. It lives in woodlands, meadows, and wetlands, eating insects, fruit, mushrooms, and carrion. Barely 15 cm long and weighing around half a kilogram, it is a famously slow, long-lived reptile that can survive 50 to 100 years. The IUCN lists it as Vulnerable.

sections.heading: The hinged shell
sections.body: The box turtle takes its name from the hinge across its lower shell, or plastron, which lets it fold the front and back sections tightly shut. Pulled into its high-domed shell, the turtle can seal itself completely inside, leaving no soft parts exposed to a predator. This living armour is its main defence, since it is far too slow to flee from danger. The shell also bears colourful yellow or orange markings that vary from turtle to turtle.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: Eastern box turtles are omnivores with a varied appetite that changes as they grow. Young turtles lean heavily towards animal prey such as insects, worms, and snails, while adults eat more plant matter, including fruit and mushrooms. They will also scavenge carrion when they find it. Remarkably, box turtles can eat certain fungi that are toxic to humans without coming to harm.

sections.heading: Habitat and home range
sections.body: The species lives in the woodlands, meadows, and wetlands of the eastern United States, favouring moist, leafy ground with plenty of cover. Individual turtles are strongly tied to a small home range, often only a few hectares, which they may occupy for their entire lives. This deep attachment to home means a turtle moved far away will try to travel back, frequently dying on roads in the attempt. On hot days they shelter in leaf litter, logs, or shallow pools to stay cool and moist.

sections.heading: Longevity and reproduction
sections.body: Box turtles are among the longest-lived of small reptiles, commonly reaching 50 years and sometimes approaching a century. They mature slowly, often taking several years to reach breeding age. After mating, the female digs a nest in soft soil and lays a small clutch of eggs, then leaves them to incubate unattended. Only a few hatchlings survive to adulthood, so the loss of even a handful of breeding adults can hurt a population.

sections.heading: Hibernation
sections.body: In the colder parts of its range, the eastern box turtle spends winter in a state of dormancy. As temperatures drop it burrows into loose soil, leaf litter, or the mud of pond edges and slows its body down to survive the freeze. It can even tolerate small amounts of ice forming in its tissues without dying. When the ground warms in spring, the turtle emerges to resume feeding and breeding.

sections.heading: Why it is Vulnerable
sections.body: The eastern box turtle is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, and its slow life history makes it hard to recover from losses. Habitat destruction, road deaths, and collection for the pet trade all take a steady toll on wild populations. Because the turtles breed slowly and rely on many years of adult survival, even modest ongoing losses cause long-term decline. Keeping woodland habitats connected and leaving wild turtles where they are found both help the species persist.

faqs.question: Why is it called a box turtle?
faqs.answer: It is named for the hinge across its lower shell, which lets the turtle fold the shell shut like a box. Sealed inside its high-domed shell, it can hide every soft part from predators, its main defence against attack.

faqs.question: What do eastern box turtles eat?
faqs.answer: They are omnivores. Young turtles eat mostly insects, worms, and snails, while adults take more fruit and mushrooms, and both will scavenge carrion. They can safely eat some fungi that are poisonous to people.

faqs.question: How long do box turtles live?
faqs.answer: Eastern box turtles are remarkably long-lived, commonly reaching 50 years and sometimes nearing 100. They grow and mature slowly, so a wild population depends on adults surviving for many decades.

faqs.question: How big do eastern box turtles get?
faqs.answer: They are small turtles, only about 15 cm long and weighing roughly 0.3 to 0.6 kg. Their shell is distinctively high and domed, marked with variable yellow or orange patterns.

faqs.question: Why should you not move a box turtle?
faqs.answer: Box turtles are strongly attached to a small home range they may keep for life. A turtle carried away will try to return, often dying on roads in the attempt, so wild ones are best left exactly where they are found.

faqs.question: Are eastern box turtles endangered?
faqs.answer: They are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN. Habitat loss, road deaths, and collection for the pet trade steadily reduce their numbers, and their very slow breeding makes recovery from these losses difficult.

animals.name: Painted Turtle
animals.summary: The painted turtle is a small, colourful freshwater turtle of ponds, lakes, and slow rivers across North America, named for the bright yellow and red markings on its skin and shell edges. It reaches about 18 cm and 0.2 to 0.4 kg, and is often seen basking in rows on logs. An omnivore that eats aquatic plants, insects, and small fish, it swims at up to 5 km/h and can live 25 to 35 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Appearance and markings
sections.body: The painted turtle earns its name from the vivid pattern of yellow and red stripes on its head, neck, legs, and tail, set against a smooth, dark olive-to-black upper shell. The underside, or plastron, is often bright yellow, sometimes marked with a bold dark blotch depending on the subspecies. The shell is low and streamlined, an ideal shape for slipping easily through the water. At around 18 cm long, it is a modest-sized turtle, with females generally growing a little larger than males.

sections.heading: Basking and body temperature
sections.body: As a cold-blooded reptile, the painted turtle relies on the sun to warm its body, and basking is a central part of its daily routine. On warm days many turtles haul out onto logs, rocks, and banks, often stacked together in rows to soak up the heat. Basking raises their body temperature to aid digestion and helps rid the shell of algae and parasites. At the first sign of danger they slide quickly back into the safety of the water.

sections.heading: Diet and feeding
sections.body: Painted turtles are omnivores whose diet shifts with age and season. Young turtles tend to be more carnivorous, eating aquatic insects, tadpoles, small fish, and other invertebrates, while adults eat a greater share of aquatic plants and algae. They feed entirely in the water, where they can swallow and manoeuvre their food. This flexible, opportunistic diet allows them to thrive in a wide range of ponds, lakes, and quiet river backwaters.

sections.heading: Swimming and life in the water
sections.body: Painted turtles are strong, graceful swimmers, using their webbed feet to paddle through the water at up to 5 km/h. They spend most of their lives in or near water, hauling out mainly to bask or, for females, to lay eggs. On land their pace is slow and deliberate, but in water they move with ease and can stay submerged for long periods. They favour shallow, slow-moving water with a soft bottom and plenty of aquatic vegetation.

sections.heading: Surviving the winter
sections.body: In the cold northern parts of their range, painted turtles endure freezing winters by hibernating at the bottom of ponds beneath the ice. During this time their metabolism slows dramatically, and they can survive for months with little or no oxygen, absorbing what they need through their skin and the lining of the throat and cloaca. Painted turtle hatchlings are especially remarkable, often spending their first winter in the nest and tolerating partial freezing of their body tissues. This cold-hardiness lets the species range farther north than most other turtles.

sections.heading: Reproduction and lifespan
sections.body: In late spring and early summer, females leave the water to dig nests in sandy or soft soil, laying a clutch of several elongated eggs before covering them and returning to the pond. As in many reptiles, the temperature of the nest determines the sex of the hatchlings, with warmer nests producing more females. The eggs hatch after roughly two to three months, and the young make their own way to water. Painted turtles are long-lived, commonly reaching 25 to 35 years in the wild.

faqs.question: Why is it called a painted turtle?
faqs.answer: It is named for the bright yellow and red markings that decorate its head, legs, tail, and shell edges, which look as though they were painted on. These colours stand out against its smooth, dark upper shell.

faqs.question: How big do painted turtles get?
faqs.answer: Painted turtles grow to about 18 cm in shell length and weigh roughly 0.2 to 0.4 kg. Females are generally a little larger than males.

faqs.question: What do painted turtles eat?
faqs.answer: They are omnivores that eat aquatic plants, algae, insects, tadpoles, and small fish. Young turtles eat more animal prey, while adults take a larger share of plants.

faqs.question: How long do painted turtles live?
faqs.answer: In the wild, painted turtles commonly live 25 to 35 years. Their long lifespan and hardy nature make them one of North America's most widespread and successful turtles.

faqs.question: How do painted turtles survive winter?
faqs.answer: They hibernate at the bottom of ponds beneath the ice, slowing their metabolism dramatically. They can survive for months with very little oxygen, absorbing what they need through their skin and other tissues.

faqs.question: Why do painted turtles bask on logs?
faqs.answer: As cold-blooded reptiles, they bask in the sun to warm their bodies, which aids digestion and helps clear algae and parasites from the shell. They often pile onto logs in rows and slide into the water at the first sign of danger.

animals.name: Brown Bear
animals.summary: The brown bear is one of the world's largest land carnivores, found across North America, Europe, and Asia. Adults typically weigh 130–360 kg (290–800 lb), run up to 56 km/h (35 mph), and hibernate through winter in dens. Coastal populations that feed heavily on salmon can grow much larger than inland grizzlies.

sections.heading: Diet and seasonal feeding
sections.body: Brown bears are omnivores whose diet shifts with the seasons. In spring they graze on sedges and roots; summer brings berries and insects; autumn is dominated by hyperphagia as bears pack on fat before winter. Coastal bears gather at salmon runs, while inland populations rely more on plants and small mammals.

sections.heading: Hibernation and reproduction
sections.body: Pregnant females enter dens in late autumn and give birth during hibernation, usually to one to three cubs that nurse and grow inside the den until spring. Hibernation slows heart rate and metabolism dramatically, allowing bears to survive months without eating, drinking, or passing waste.

sections.heading: Range and subspecies
sections.body: Brown bears once ranged across much of western North America, Europe, and temperate Asia. Today they persist in Scandinavia, the Carpathians, the Rockies, Alaska, and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The North American grizzly and the Kodiak bear are well-known subspecies of Ursus arctos.

sections.heading: Conservation and human conflict
sections.body: Globally listed Least Concern, brown bears nevertheless face local declines from habitat fragmentation, poaching, and conflict with livestock. Responsible bear-country practices — securing food, carrying deterrents, and giving mothers with cubs space — reduce dangerous encounters.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a brown bear and a grizzly bear?
faqs.answer: Grizzly bears are a subspecies of brown bear (Ursus arctos horribilis) found mainly in inland North America. Coastal brown bears that eat more salmon tend to grow larger. All grizzlies are brown bears, but not all brown bears are grizzlies.

faqs.question: How big do brown bears get?
faqs.answer: Most adult males weigh 180–360 kg (400–800 lb), while females are smaller. Exceptional coastal males in Alaska and Kamchatka can exceed 600 kg when salmon is abundant.

faqs.question: Do brown bears hibernate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Brown bears enter a deep winter dormancy for several months, living off stored body fat. Their heart rate and body temperature drop, and females may give birth inside the den during this period.

faqs.question: Are brown bears dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: Brown bears usually avoid people, but surprise encounters, food-conditioned bears, and mothers defending cubs can be dangerous. Wildlife agencies advise making noise on trails, storing food properly, and never running from a bear.

faqs.question: What do brown bears eat?
faqs.answer: They are omnivores. Plants — especially berries, roots, and grasses — often make up most of the diet, supplemented by fish, insects, small mammals, and carrion depending on location and season.

animals.name: American Black Bear
animals.summary: The American black bear is the most common bear in North America, found from Canada to Mexico in forests, swamps, and even suburbs. Despite the name, colours range from jet black to cinnamon, blonde, and the rare white Kermode or 'spirit bear' of British Columbia. Adults typically weigh 45–250 kg and are skilled tree climbers.

sections.heading: Adaptability and range
sections.body: Black bears thrive in a wider variety of habitats than grizzlies, including eastern hardwood forests, western conifer woods, Florida swamps, and desert margins where food and cover exist. Their ability to climb trees and tolerate human-altered landscapes helps explain their continued abundance across the continent.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: Black bears are opportunistic omnivores. Spring diet includes emerging plants and carrion; summer brings berries and insects; autumn is a feeding frenzy on acorns, beechnuts, and apples where available. In some areas they raid cornfields or bird feeders, which can lead to habituation and removal.

sections.heading: Behaviour and reproduction
sections.body: Solitary for much of the year, females raise cubs for about 17 months before driving them off. Cubs are born in winter dens while the mother is in torpor. Black bears communicate through scent marking, vocalisations, and body posture; they are generally shy of humans unless food-trained.

sections.heading: Conservation and coexistence
sections.body: Listed Least Concern with an estimated North American population exceeding 600,000, black bears still face road mortality, habitat loss, and illegal trade in bile and paws in some markets. Securing garbage, removing bird feeders, and using bear-resistant bins in overlap areas keeps both bears and people safer.

faqs.question: Are black bears always black?
faqs.answer: No. Colour phases include cinnamon, blonde, brown, and the rare white Kermode bear on Canada's Pacific coast. All are the same species, Ursus americanus.

faqs.question: What should I do if I see a black bear?
faqs.answer: Stay calm, do not run, make yourself look large, and back away slowly. If a black bear attacks defensively, fight back. If it is a predatory encounter — extremely rare — fight back aggressively.

faqs.question: Can black bears climb trees?
faqs.answer: Yes. Black bears are excellent climbers and often escape danger or reach food by climbing, even as adults — unlike most large brown bears.

faqs.question: How big are black bears compared to grizzlies?
faqs.answer: Black bears are generally smaller. Large male black bears may reach 250 kg, while grizzlies commonly exceed that. Black bears also lack the prominent shoulder hump of brown bears.

faqs.question: What is a spirit bear?
faqs.answer: The Kermode or spirit bear is a white colour phase of the American black bear found on a few islands in British Columbia. It is not a separate species or albino — the pale coat comes from a recessive gene.

animals.name: Elk
animals.summary: The elk, or wapiti, is one of the largest deer species in the world, with bulls weighing up to 450 kg (990 lb) and carrying impressive antlers shed each year. Elk herds graze open meadows and forest edges across western North America, and males produce a famous autumn bugle during the rut.

sections.heading: The rut and bugling
sections.body: Each autumn bull elk gather harems and bugle — a piercing call that carries across valleys to attract cows and warn rivals. Bulls clash antlers in shoving matches that can leave scars or broken tines. After the rut, bulls lose weight and shed their antlers in winter.

sections.heading: Migration and herd life
sections.body: Many elk populations migrate seasonally between high summer range and lower winter range, sometimes crossing busy roads and development corridors. Cows, calves, and yearlings form herds for much of the year, while mature bulls are often solitary outside the breeding season.

sections.heading: Antlers and growth
sections.body: Only males grow antlers, which begin as velvet-covered bone in spring, harden by autumn, and are shed after the rut. Antler size reflects age, nutrition, and genetics. Elk antlers are among the fastest-growing bone structures in the animal kingdom.

sections.heading: Conservation and reintroduction
sections.body: Elk were nearly extirpated from much of the United States by the early 1900s but recovered through hunting regulation and reintroduction, including the famous Yellowstone herds. Today they are Least Concern globally, though local herds face habitat fragmentation and chronic wasting disease in some regions.

faqs.question: What is the difference between elk and moose?
faqs.answer: Moose are much larger, have palm-shaped antlers and a bulbous nose, and prefer wetland browse. Elk are smaller, bugle during the rut, and carry tall, branching antlers.

faqs.question: Why do elk bugle?
faqs.answer: Bulls bugle during the autumn rut to attract females and intimidate rival males. The sound combines a high whistle with a low grunt and can carry several kilometres in open country.

faqs.question: How fast can an elk run?
faqs.answer: Elk can reach about 72 km/h (45 mph) in short bursts — faster than any human — and maintain a steady gallop to escape wolves and other predators.

faqs.question: Where do elk live?
faqs.answer: Native to North America and eastern Asia (where related red deer occur). In North America they range from Canada through the western United States, with reintroduced herds in several eastern states.

faqs.question: Are elk dangerous?
faqs.answer: Elk generally flee from people, but bulls during the rut and cows with calves can charge if approached too closely. Parks advise keeping at least 25 metres distance.

animals.name: Walrus
animals.summary: Walruses are massive pinnipeds of the Arctic, with males weighing up to 1,700 kg (3,750 lb) and sporting elongated canine tusks used for hauling out on ice, fighting, and sensing the seafloor. They feed mainly on clams and molluscs on shallow seabeds and gather in huge haul-outs on ice or land.

sections.heading: Tusks and feeding
sections.body: Walrus tusks are elongated upper canines that can exceed one metre in large males. They are used to pull the body onto ice, establish dominance, and help the walrus 'feel' the seabed while foraging. A walrus may consume thousands of clams in a day, using powerful lips to suck meat from shells.

sections.heading: Social haul-outs
sections.body: Walruses rest in dense groups on sea ice or rocky beaches, vocalising with bell-like calls and whistles. Pacific walruses depend heavily on floating ice over shallow feeding grounds; when ice retreats beyond reach of feeding areas, animals haul out on land in enormous, sometimes dangerous crowds.

sections.heading: Pacific vs Atlantic populations
sections.body: Two recognised subspecies — Atlantic and Pacific — differ in size, tusk shape, and population trends. Pacific walruses number in the low hundreds of thousands; Atlantic walruses are far fewer and more fragmented across Canada, Greenland, and Arctic Europe.

sections.heading: Climate and conservation
sections.body: Listed Vulnerable, walruses face mounting pressure from sea-ice loss, shipping disturbance, and hunting in some regions. Reduced ice forces longer swims to feeding grounds and crowded land haul-outs where stampedes can kill calves.

faqs.question: How long are walrus tusks?
faqs.answer: Tusks typically measure 50–100 cm in large males, with record specimens slightly longer. Females also have tusks, but they are smaller.

faqs.question: What do walruses eat?
faqs.answer: Mainly bivalve molluscs such as clams, which they locate on the seafloor using their sensitive whiskers and tusks. They also eat worms, snails, and occasionally seals or seabirds.

faqs.question: Are walruses endangered?
faqs.answer: The IUCN lists walruses as Vulnerable. Pacific populations are large but declining in some areas; Atlantic walruses face greater pressure from climate change and limited habitat.

faqs.question: Do walruses attack humans?
faqs.answer: Walruses are generally wary but powerful and can be aggressive if cornered or if a haul-out is disturbed. Arctic travellers keep a safe distance from groups on ice or shore.

faqs.question: Why do walruses need sea ice?
faqs.answer: Ice provides resting platforms near shallow feeding grounds. Without it, walruses must swim farther and may crowd onto land, increasing energy costs and stampede risk.
