animals.name: Channel Catfish
animals.summary: The channel catfish is one of the most popular sport and farmed fish in North America, recognised by barbels ('whiskers'), smooth scaleless skin, and a forked tail. Native to central and eastern rivers and lakes, it grows to 10–25 kg (22–55 lb), tastes mild, and uses taste buds across its body to find food.

sections.heading: Barbels and taste
sections.body: Channel catfish have four pairs of barbels around the mouth plus taste buds covering the body — especially the whiskers — allowing them to locate food in murky water at night. They are opportunistic bottom feeders eating insects, crayfish, small fish, and plant matter.

sections.heading: Spines and defence
sections.body: Sharp spines in the dorsal and pectoral fins can lock in place and inject mild venom, deterring predators and unwary anglers. Handling from below and using lip grips reduces sting risk. Spines also help catfish lock into crevices.

sections.heading: Aquaculture and sport fishing
sections.body: Channel catfish are the top farmed fish species in the United States, raised in ponds across the South for food markets. Anglers target them with stink baits, chicken liver, and cut bait — they fight hard and tolerate low oxygen better than many game fish.

sections.heading: Range and introductions
sections.body: Native from southern Canada through the Great Lakes and Mississippi basin to Mexico, channel catfish have been stocked widely for fishing and farming. They can outcompete native species where introduced outside their range, requiring careful management.

faqs.question: Are catfish whiskers dangerous?
faqs.answer: The barbels are harmless feelers. The danger comes from sharp fin spines that can puncture skin — not from the whiskers themselves.

faqs.question: What do channel catfish eat?
faqs.answer: Almost anything on the bottom — insects, worms, crayfish, small fish, and plant material. They hunt mainly at night using taste and smell.

faqs.question: How big do channel catfish get?
faqs.answer: Most caught fish are 1–5 kg, but large river fish can exceed 20 kg. The record is over 25 kg.

faqs.question: Can catfish sting you?
faqs.answer: Fin spines can puncture and cause pain and swelling from mild venom. Handle carefully or use pliers to remove hooks.

faqs.question: Where are channel catfish found?
faqs.answer: Native to central and eastern North America; farmed and stocked in ponds across the United States and introduced in Europe and elsewhere.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Omnivore — insects, fish, plants, and bottom detritus

facts.label: Habitat

animals.name: Rainbow Trout
animals.summary: Rainbow trout are salmonid fish native to Pacific North America, named for the pink lateral stripe along silver sides. Stocked worldwide for sport fishing and aquaculture, they grow to 50 cm or more in rivers, leap at flies, and include steelhead populations that migrate to sea before returning to spawn.

sections.heading: Fly fishing icon
sections.body: Rainbow trout rise to dry flies on the surface, making them the quintessential fly-fishing species. Clear mountain streams of the American West — Montana, Idaho, Colorado — built a global angling culture around wild rainbow and cutthroat trout.

sections.heading: Steelhead life history
sections.body: Some coastal populations ('steelhead') migrate to the ocean and return to natal rivers to spawn, growing larger and more silvery than resident river fish. Dams, water extraction, and warming streams threaten these anadromous runs across the Pacific Northwest.

sections.heading: Global stocking
sections.body: Rainbow trout have been introduced to every continent except Antarctica for food and sport. They can hybridise with native trout and outcompete local species, making introductions controversial in places like New Zealand, Chile, and the Appalachian Mountains.

sections.heading: Aquaculture and wild genetics
sections.body: Farm-raised rainbow trout supply supermarkets worldwide. Hatchery supplementation of wild streams raises questions about genetic dilution of native strains. Wild populations in the Pacific Northwest remain the evolutionary heartland of the species.

faqs.question: Rainbow trout vs salmon?
faqs.answer: Rainbow trout are in the same genus as Pacific salmon. Steelhead are sea-run rainbow trout. Salmon typically die after spawning; many trout survive to spawn again.

faqs.question: What is a steelhead?
faqs.answer: A rainbow trout that migrates to the ocean and returns to freshwater to spawn — larger and more silvery than river-resident rainbows.

faqs.question: What do rainbow trout eat?
faqs.answer: Aquatic insects, terrestrial insects that fall on the water, crustaceans, and small fish — diet shifts with size and habitat.

faqs.question: Where are rainbow trout native?
faqs.answer: Pacific drainages from Alaska through California and inland to Idaho and Nevada — not the eastern United States, where they are introduced.

faqs.question: How big do rainbow trout get?
faqs.answer: Stream fish often 30–40 cm; lake and steelhead forms can exceed 90 cm and 9 kg in rich waters.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Carnivore — insects, crustaceans, and small fish

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Cold rivers, lakes, and streams; anadromous steelhead in coastal rivers

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: 4–11 years in the wild (varies by population)

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: 0.5–9 kg (1–20 lb); steelhead and lake fish larger

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Strong swimmer; leaps waterfalls during spawning runs

animals.name: Sulphur-crested Cockatoo
animals.summary: The sulphur-crested cockatoo is a large white parrot with a bright yellow crest, powerful bill, and raucous calls, common across Australia and New Guinea. Highly intelligent and long-lived — up to 80 years in captivity — it forages in flocks, damages crops, and is a popular but demanding pet.

sections.heading: Crest signals and flock life
sections.body: The yellow crest rises when the bird is alarmed, excited, or displaying — a visible signal across open woodland. Cockatoos feed in noisy flocks, screeching as they move between roost trees and feeding grounds. Strong pair bonds last years or life.

sections.heading: Intelligence and problem solving
sections.body: Cockatoos open bin lids, dismantle lawn ornaments, and solve multi-step puzzles in research settings. Wild birds learn to exploit human food sources, becoming familiar sights in Sydney and Canberra suburbs where they chew decking and window frames.

sections.heading: Agricultural conflict
sections.body: Large flocks damage grain, fruit, and nut crops, leading to culling permits in some Australian states despite Least Concern status. Their intelligence makes deterrence difficult — scare devices often fail after brief habituation.

sections.heading: Pet trade demands
sections.body: Cockatoos are charismatic pets but need decades of attention, large enclosures, and mental stimulation. Feather plucking and screaming result from neglect. Captive breeding supplies most pets; wild export is restricted under CITES.

faqs.question: How long do cockatoos live?
faqs.answer: Often 40–60 years in captivity, sometimes over 80 with excellent care — a lifetime commitment for owners.

faqs.question: Why do cockatoos scream?
faqs.answer: Flock communication, alarm calls, and attention-seeking. Loud vocalisations are normal — not a sign of distress alone, but constant screaming can indicate boredom.

faqs.question: Are sulphur-crested cockatoos smart?
faqs.answer: Among the most intelligent birds, solving puzzles, using tools in experiments, and learning to manipulate human-made objects.

faqs.question: Where do cockatoos live?
faqs.answer: Eastern and northern Australia, Tasmania, and New Guinea — also common in urban parks and farmland.

faqs.question: Can cockatoos talk?
faqs.answer: They mimic sounds and some words, though not as clearly as African grey parrots. They are better known for loud natural calls than speech.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Omnivore — seeds, nuts, fruit, roots, and insects

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Woodlands, farmland, and urban parks of Australia and New Guinea

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: 40–80 years in captivity; 20–40 in the wild

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Strong flier; agile climber using bill and feet

range.nativeRange: Woodlands and urban areas of eastern and northern Australia, Tasmania, and New Guinea; also kept as pets on other continents.

animals.name: Rhinoceros Hornbill
animals.summary: The rhinoceros hornbill is a huge black-and-white bird with a dramatic orange-red casque atop an enormous bill, found in rainforests of Southeast Asia. Females seal themselves inside tree-cavity nests while males deliver food, and the species is listed Vulnerable from logging and hunting.

sections.heading: Casque and bill
sections.body: The hollow casque is thought to amplify calls that carry through dense forest — males announce territory with resonant honking. The massive bill is used to pluck fruit and capture lizards and nestling birds, yet the hornbill's centre of gravity is adjusted by hollow bone structure.

sections.heading: Nest sealing ritual
sections.body: Females enter a tree hollow and seal the entrance with mud, droppings, and fruit pulp, leaving only a slit for the male to pass food. She moulted flight feathers during incubation and depends entirely on the male for weeks — one of bird world's most extreme breeding commitments.

sections.heading: Seed dispersers
sections.body: Hornbills swallow fruit whole and regurgitate or defecate seeds far from parent trees, making them vital gardeners of tropical forests. Loss of hornbills reduces regeneration of large-seeded trees such as figs and durians.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Listed Vulnerable from deforestation, poaching for casques and tail feathers used in traditional dress, and capture for the pet trade. Protected areas in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand support populations, but lowland forest loss continues across the range.

faqs.question: What is the horn on a hornbill?
faqs.answer: The casque is a hollow keratin structure atop the bill, used in displays and calls — not a true horn like a rhino's.

faqs.question: Why do hornbills seal the nest?
faqs.answer: Females wall themselves in to protect eggs and chicks from predators such as monitor lizards and snakes, relying on the male to deliver all food.

faqs.question: Where do rhinoceros hornbills live?
faqs.answer: Lowland rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, Thailand, and Sumatra — Borneo is a stronghold.

faqs.question: Are hornbills endangered?
faqs.answer: Rhinoceros hornbills are Vulnerable, not yet Endangered, but declining as lowland rainforest is logged and fragmented.

faqs.question: What do hornbills eat?
faqs.answer: Mostly fruit, especially figs, plus insects, lizards, and small vertebrates when available.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Omnivore — fruit, small animals, and insects

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Lowland and hill rainforests of Southeast Asia

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Powerful flier through forest gaps; heavy wingbeats

range.nativeRange: Lowland and hill rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, Thailand, and Sumatra — Borneo is a stronghold for rhinoceros hornbills.

animals.name: Cow
animals.summary: Domestic cattle descend from the aurochs and number over one billion worldwide, providing milk, meat, leather, and draft power. Dairy and beef breeds vary enormously — from 400 kg Jerseys to massive Chianina bulls — and cattle farming shapes landscapes, economies, and climate debates globally.

sections.heading: Domestication from aurochs
sections.body: Cattle were domesticated from wild aurochs in the Middle East and South Asia roughly 10,000 years ago, independently in some regions. Selective breeding produced dairy breeds optimised for milk, beef breeds for muscle, and draught breeds for pulling ploughs and carts.

sections.heading: Ruminant digestion
sections.body: Cattle are ruminants with four-chambered stomachs that ferment tough plant fibre through regurgitation and re-chewing ('chewing the cud'). Microbes in the rumen break down cellulose humans cannot digest — but also produce methane, a potent greenhouse gas.

sections.heading: Dairy and beef systems
sections.body: Modern dairy cows may produce 30+ litres of milk daily through selective breeding and nutrition. Beef cattle graze rangelands from the American West to the Brazilian cerrado. Welfare debates focus on feedlots, calf separation, and slaughter practices.

sections.heading: Environmental footprint
sections.body: Cattle farming uses more land and water than most crops and contributes significantly to methane emissions. Sustainable grazing can sequester carbon on some grasslands, but rainforest clearing for beef pasture remains a major conservation issue in the Amazon.

faqs.question: Cow vs bull vs steer?
faqs.answer: Cow is an adult female; bull is an intact adult male; steer is a castrated male raised for beef. Heifer is a young female that has not calved.

faqs.question: How much milk does a cow produce?
faqs.answer: Modern dairy breeds average 25–35 litres per day at peak lactation, far more than a calf needs — the result of centuries of selective breeding.

faqs.question: Are cows intelligent?
faqs.answer: Cattle show learning, memory, social bonds, and emotional responses. They recognise individual herd mates and humans and prefer familiar companions.

faqs.question: How many cows are there?
faqs.answer: Over one billion domestic cattle worldwide — among the most numerous large mammals on Earth.

faqs.question: What did cows evolve from?
faqs.answer: The wild aurochs (Bos primigenius), hunted to extinction in the 1600s but preserved genetically in domestic cattle.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Herbivore — grass, hay, silage, and grain supplement

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Farms and rangelands on every inhabited continent

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 35 km/h (22 mph) when frightened

range.nativeRange: Domesticated from the aurochs in the Middle East and South Asia; over one billion cattle on farms and rangelands on every inhabited continent.

animals.name: Reindeer
animals.summary: Reindeer — called caribou in North America — are Arctic deer where both sexes grow antlers, undertaking the longest land migrations of any terrestrial mammal. Herds cross tundra from Alaska to Scandinavia, support Indigenous herding cultures, and are listed Vulnerable from climate change and disturbance.

sections.heading: Epic migration
sections.body: Some barren-ground caribou herds travel over 5,000 km annually between calving grounds and winter range — the longest terrestrial migration on Earth. Calving synchrony on Arctic tundra overwhelms predators, but warming disrupts timing and insect harassment increases.

sections.heading: Antlers on females
sections.body: Reindeer are the only deer where females commonly grow antlers. Cows retain theirs through winter, while bulls shed after the rut. Antlers are used for digging through snow for lichens — critical winter food called reindeer moss.

sections.heading: Indigenous herding
sections.body: Sámi, Nenets, and other Arctic peoples have herded domestic reindeer for centuries, following migrations and relying on meat, hides, and transport. Wild caribou remain vital subsistence resources for Alaska Native communities.

sections.heading: Climate vulnerability
sections.body: Listed Vulnerable, reindeer and caribou face rain-on-snow events that ice over food, increased parasitic flies in warmer summers, and industrial disturbance of migration routes from mining and roads in the Arctic.

faqs.question: Reindeer vs caribou?
faqs.answer: Same species — Rangifer tarandus. 'Reindeer' usually means domesticated or Eurasian populations; 'caribou' refers to wild North American forms.

faqs.question: Why do reindeer noses turn red?
faqs.answer: Rich blood flow in nasal passages warms frigid air before it reaches the lungs — physiology that inspired festive folklore, though real noses are not bright red.

faqs.question: Do female reindeer have antlers?
faqs.answer: Yes — females grow antlers, unlike most other deer, and keep them longer through winter.

faqs.question: What do reindeer eat?
faqs.answer: Lichens (reindeer moss), grasses, sedges, leaves, and mushrooms — diet shifts between summer greenery and winter lichens dug from snow.

faqs.question: Are reindeer endangered?
faqs.answer: Listed Vulnerable globally. Some herds are declining sharply from climate change and habitat disturbance, though total numbers remain in the millions.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Herbivore — lichens, grasses, leaves, and mushrooms

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Arctic tundra, boreal forest, and mountain plateaus

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 80 km/h (50 mph) in flight

range.nativeRange: Arctic tundra and boreal forest from Scandinavia and Russia through Alaska and Canada to Greenland; wild caribou in North America, herded reindeer in Eurasia.

animals.name: Ocelot
animals.summary: The ocelot is a medium-sized spotted cat of Latin American forests, thorn scrub, and Texas borderlands, weighing 8–16 kg (18–35 lb) with a beautiful rosetted coat once prized by the fur trade. Nocturnal and solitary, it hunts rabbits, rodents, and birds and persists in a small Texas breeding population.

sections.heading: Rosettes and camouflage
sections.body: Chain rosettes and streaks break up the ocelot's outline in dappled understory — similar patterning to leopards but on a cat roughly twice the size of a house cat. Each coat is unique, like a fingerprint.

sections.heading: Nocturnal hunter
sections.body: Ocelots hunt mainly at night, stalking rodents and opossums on the forest floor and occasionally climbing for monkeys or birds. Excellent vision and hearing suit them to dense cover where they travel along game trails.

sections.heading: Texas population
sections.body: A small breeding population persists in southern Texas shrubland — the only U.S. breeding ocelots outside captivity. Habitat loss to agriculture and roads threatens this isolated group, linked genetically to Mexican populations.

sections.heading: Fur trade legacy
sections.body: Ocelots were heavily trapped for fur until international protection; coat patterns were mimicked in fashion. Listed Least Concern globally, they still lose forest to soy, cattle, and palm expansion across the Amazon and Atlantic Forest.

faqs.question: Ocelot vs leopard?
faqs.answer: Ocelots are much smaller — about 12 kg versus 60+ kg for leopards — and live only in the Americas. Patterning looks similar but they are unrelated species.

faqs.question: Are ocelots in the United States?
faqs.answer: Yes — a few dozen wild ocelots breed in southern Texas. They are also kept in zoos but are not native pets.

faqs.question: Can ocelots be pets?
faqs.answer: No — they are wild cats with specialised needs and are illegal to own in most places. Celebrity ownership in the past harmed conservation awareness.

faqs.question: What do ocelots eat?
faqs.answer: Rodents, rabbits, opossums, birds, reptiles, and fish — varied small prey taken by stalking and pouncing.

faqs.question: Are ocelots endangered?
faqs.answer: Globally Least Concern, but the Texas population is Endangered under U.S. law, and some regional populations are declining from habitat loss.

facts.value: Carnivore — rodents, rabbits, birds, reptiles, and fish

facts.label: Habitat

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 55 km/h (34 mph) in ambush pursuit

animals.name: Serval
animals.summary: The serval is a slender African wild cat with the longest legs relative to body size of any felid, huge ears, and a high vertical pounce that plucks birds and rodents from tall grass. Weighing 9–18 kg (20–40 lb), it hunts in savannas and wetlands and is Least Concern across sub-Saharan Africa.

sections.heading: Vertical pounce hunting
sections.body: Servals locate prey by sound in tall grass, then leap straight up and strike down with forepaws — catching more than 50% of targets in some studies. This spectacular hunting style is unique among cats and inspired the domestic savannah cat breed.

sections.heading: Acute hearing
sections.body: Enormous ears with sharp localisation help servals detect rodents rustling underground or birds moving in grass. Large ear bones and tight skull attachment maximise sensitivity — servals often hunt with eyes closed, relying entirely on sound.

sections.heading: Territory and water
sections.body: Servals need grassland near water and cover for denning. Territories overlap minimally between same-sex adults. They are mainly crepuscular and solitary, though pairs may associate briefly during breeding.

sections.heading: Conservation and hybridisation
sections.body: Least Concern across much of Africa, servals face wetland drainage and bushmeat snares locally. Hybridisation with domestic cats occurs in captivity for the pet trade — controversial and illegal in many countries because wild servals do not make suitable pets.

faqs.question: How high can a serval jump?
faqs.answer: Over 3 metres vertically — higher relative to body size than almost any other cat — to pin birds and rodents.

faqs.question: Serval vs cheetah?
faqs.answer: Servals are much smaller and hunt by listening and pouncing, not sprinting. Cheetahs chase prey at high speed in open savanna.

faqs.question: Are servals legal as pets?
faqs.answer: Laws vary by country and state. They are wild cats with spray, claw, and dietary needs far beyond domestic cats — generally unsuitable as pets.

faqs.question: Where do servals live?
faqs.answer: Sub-Saharan Africa in savanna, grassland, and marsh — absent from rainforest interiors and the Sahara.

faqs.question: What do servals eat?
faqs.answer: Mainly rodents and vlei rats, plus birds, frogs, insects, and occasionally small antelope fawns.

facts.value: Carnivore — rodents, birds, frogs, and insects

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: African savannas, grasslands, and wetlands near water

facts.value: Up to 80 km/h (50 mph); pounces 3+ metres vertically

animals.name: North American Porcupine
animals.summary: The North American porcupine is a slow, nearsighted rodent armed with roughly 30,000 barbed quills covering its back and tail. It climbs trees to eat bark and leaves, defends by backing into predators, and lives across forests and tundra from Alaska to Mexico.

sections.heading: Quill defence
sections.body: Quills are modified hairs with barbed tips that embed and migrate in attackers — painful and difficult to remove. Porcupines cannot shoot quills; predators must contact the raised tail. Fishers are skilled porcupine hunters, attacking the unquilled face.

sections.heading: Arboreal herbivore
sections.body: Strong claws and rough soles let porcupines spend days in trees eating inner bark, especially in winter. Their salt craving draws them to road salt, tool handles, and plywood glue — sometimes bringing them near human structures.

sections.heading: Slow reproduction
sections.body: Females bear a single precocial young after seven months gestation — long for a rodent. Baby porcupines ('porcupettes') have soft quills that harden within hours. Adults are solitary except during breeding.

sections.heading: Forest role and conflict
sections.body: Porcupines girdle trees, sometimes damaging timber operations, but also create habitat for other species through bark stripping. Least Concern globally, they remain common across Canada and the western United States.

faqs.question: Can porcupines shoot quills?
faqs.answer: No — quills detach when touched. The porcupine swings its tail at predators, and barbed tips embed on contact.

faqs.question: What eats porcupines?
faqs.answer: Fishers are the main specialist predators, attacking the face where quills are sparse. Cougars, wolves, and bobcats occasionally succeed.

faqs.question: Are porcupines rodents?
faqs.answer: Yes — among the largest rodents in North America, in the family Erethizontidae, separate from Old World porcupines.

faqs.question: Why do porcupines climb trees?
faqs.answer: To feed on bark, leaves, and buds — especially in winter when ground forage is scarce.

faqs.question: Are porcupines dangerous to dogs?
faqs.answer: Very — curious dogs often receive quills in the face and mouth. Veterinary removal is usually required; quills do not dissolve.

facts.value: Herbivore — tree bark, leaves, buds, and green plants

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Forests, shrublands, and tundra across North America

animals.name: Malayan Tapir
animals.summary: The Malayan tapir is the largest tapir species and the only one native to Asia, with a striking black front and white rear that breaks up its outline in dappled rainforest. Weighing 250–320 kg (550–700 lb), it browses leaves and fruit, disperses seeds, and is Endangered from deforestation and snaring.

sections.heading: Living fossil
sections.body: Tapirs have changed little in 20 million years — short prehensile snouts grasp leaves and fruit, and splayed toes suit soft forest floor. Malayan tapirs are odd-toed ungulates related to horses and rhinos, not pigs.

sections.heading: Disruptive coloration
sections.body: The black front and white saddle confuse predators in moonlit forest — a large dark mass splits into less recognisable shapes. Calves are spotted and striped like watermelon for camouflage, losing adult patterning by six months.

sections.heading: Seed dispersal
sections.body: Tapirs swallow fruit whole and deposit seeds kilometres away in dung, earning them the title 'gardeners of the forest'. Loss of tapirs reduces regeneration of large-seeded trees in Southeast Asian rainforests.

sections.heading: Endangered status
sections.body: Listed Endangered from habitat loss to palm oil and logging, plus snaring in wire traps set for other species. Road kills fragment populations in Malaysia and Sumatra. Protected areas and wildlife corridors are urgent priorities.

faqs.question: Are tapirs related to pigs?
faqs.answer: No — tapirs are perissodactyls (odd-toed ungulates), related to horses and rhinos. Pigs are artiodactyls (even-toed).

faqs.question: Why is the Malayan tapir two-coloured?
faqs.answer: Disruptive camouflage — the contrast breaks up the body outline in dappled forest light, confusing predators.

faqs.question: Are tapirs dangerous?
faqs.answer: Usually shy, but can bite if cornered. Their size and powerful jaws demand respect in the wild.

faqs.question: Where do Malayan tapirs live?
faqs.answer: Peninsular Malaysia, southern Thailand, and Sumatra — in lowland and hill rainforest.

faqs.question: Are tapirs endangered?
faqs.answer: Malayan tapirs are Endangered. All four tapir species worldwide are threatened to some degree.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Herbivore — leaves, shoots, fruit, and aquatic plants

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Tropical rainforests of Malaysia, Thailand, and Sumatra

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 48 km/h (30 mph) on forest paths

range.nativeRange: Tropical rainforests of peninsular Malaysia, southern Thailand, and Sumatra — the only tapir species native to Asia.

animals.name: Giant Anteater
animals.summary: The giant anteater is a unmistakable mammal with a long snout, bushy tail, and front claws used to tear open termite mounds. Its tongue extends up to 60 cm and flicks 150 times per minute into insect nests. Listed Vulnerable, it walks on knuckles to protect claws and carries single offspring on its back.

sections.heading: Tongue mechanics
sections.body: The sticky tongue is attached to the sternum and can extend 60 cm — longer than the skull — with no teeth in the tubular mouth. A giant anteater consumes up to 30,000 insects daily but spends only seconds at each nest to avoid soldier ant stings.

sections.heading: Knuckle walking and claws
sections.body: Front claws up to 10 cm long tear concrete-hard termite mounds but would wear on pavement-like ground, so anteaters walk on their knuckles. When threatened, they rear up on hind legs and slash — capable of deterring jaguars and killing humans in rare encounters.

sections.heading: Mother and riding young
sections.body: Females bear a single offspring that clings to the mother's back for up to a year, camouflaged by matching striping. Mothers are protective and may carry the young even while foraging.

sections.heading: Roadkill and habitat loss
sections.body: Listed Vulnerable, giant anteaters are killed by vehicles crossing roads in Brazil's cerrado and by habitat conversion to soy and cattle pasture. Fire in grassland savannas also kills slow-moving individuals.

faqs.question: Do anteaters eat all ants?
faqs.answer: They avoid certain species with painful stings and move between nests, taking only seconds at each to limit bites.

faqs.question: Are giant anteaters endangered?
faqs.answer: Vulnerable — declining from habitat loss, road mortality, and hunting in parts of Central America.

faqs.question: Giant anteater vs aardvark?
faqs.answer: Similar ecological niche but unrelated — anteaters are from the Americas (Xenarthra); aardvarks are African. Both eat ants but differ in anatomy.

faqs.question: Can anteaters fight jaguars?
faqs.answer: They can deter jaguars with slashing claws when standing on hind legs — jaguars sometimes prey on them but respect the defence.

faqs.question: Where do giant anteaters live?
faqs.answer: From Honduras and Guatemala south through Brazil, Paraguay, and Bolivia — mainly savanna and open woodland.

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Grasslands, savannas, and forests of Central and South America

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 30 km/h (19 mph) in gallop

range.nativeRange: Grasslands, savannas, and open forests from Guatemala and Honduras south through Brazil, Paraguay, and Bolivia.

animals.name: Muskrat
animals.summary: The muskrat is a semi-aquatic rodent weighing 0.6–2 kg (1.3–4.4 lb) with a scaly tail and webbed hind feet, found in wetlands across North America and introduced to Europe and Asia. It builds dome lodges from cattails, feeds on aquatic plants, and is trapped for fur while listed Least Concern globally.

sections.heading: Wetland engineer
sections.body: Muskrats excavate burrows into pond banks and build conical lodges from cattails and mud — structures that create habitat for ducks, turtles, and fish. Their feeding opens channels through dense vegetation, maintaining open water in marshes that might otherwise silt over.

sections.heading: Semi-aquatic adaptations
sections.body: Partially webbed hind feet, a laterally flattened tail used as a rudder, and dense waterproof underfur let muskrats swim efficiently and stay warm in icy water. They can remain submerged for 15 minutes, closing ear flaps and using stored oxygen.

sections.heading: Fur trade and introductions
sections.body: Muskrat fur ('musquash') supported a major trapping industry across North America for centuries. Deliberate and accidental introductions established populations in Europe and Asia, where they sometimes damage dikes and compete with native water voles.

sections.heading: Ecology and management
sections.body: Listed Least Concern, muskrats remain abundant in suitable wetlands but face habitat loss from drainage and pollution. In some areas they are managed as pests when burrowing undermines levees; elsewhere they are valued as wetland indicators and fur-bearer resources.

faqs.question: Is a muskrat a rat?
faqs.answer: Despite the name, muskrats are not true rats — they belong to the vole and lemming family (Cricetidae), adapted for aquatic life with webbed feet and a scaly tail.

faqs.question: What do muskrats eat?
faqs.answer: Mainly aquatic plants such as cattails, pondweed, and roots; they occasionally eat mussels, snails, and small fish.

faqs.question: Where do muskrats live?
faqs.answer: Native to North America from Alaska and Canada through the United States and into northern Mexico; introduced to Europe and parts of Asia.

faqs.question: Do muskrats build dams?
faqs.answer: Muskrats build lodges and burrows, not dams like beavers. Their structures use cattails and mud rather than felled trees.

faqs.question: Are muskrats dangerous?
faqs.answer: They generally avoid people and are not aggressive, though they may bite if handled. They can carry tularemia and other diseases in some regions.

facts.label: Habitat

animals.name: Mountain Gorilla
animals.summary: The mountain gorilla is a subspecies of eastern gorilla living in the cloud forests of the Virunga volcanoes and Bwindi Impenetrable Forest, with fewer than 1,100 individuals remaining. Adult silverback males weigh 140–220 kg (310–485 lb), live in stable family groups, and are listed Endangered despite decades of conservation success.

sections.heading: Silverback society
sections.body: Each group centres on a dominant silverback male who leads, protects, and mediates disputes among females and younger males. Groups typically contain 5–30 individuals with strong bonds — grooming, play, and vocalisations maintain cohesion in dense forest where visibility is limited.

sections.heading: High-altitude foraging
sections.body: Mountain gorillas spend much of the day eating bulky vegetation — wild celery, bamboo shoots, thistles, and nettles — requiring hours of continuous feeding to meet energy needs at cold elevations. They rarely drink standing water, obtaining moisture from plants.

sections.heading: Conservation turnaround
sections.body: Famously studied by Dian Fossey, mountain gorillas fell to roughly 250 individuals in the 1980s from poaching, habitat loss, and war. Intensive anti-poaching patrols, veterinary care, and ecotourism revenue helped numbers recover past 1,000 — one of conservation's rare success stories.

sections.heading: Ongoing threats
sections.body: Listed Endangered, mountain gorillas remain confined to two small forest blocks straddling Rwanda, Uganda, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Political instability, snares set for antelope, disease transmission from humans, and climate-driven habitat shifts still pose risks.

faqs.question: How many mountain gorillas are left?
faqs.answer: Roughly 1,000–1,100 individuals in two populations — the Virunga Massif and Uganda's Bwindi Impenetrable Forest — up from about 250 in the 1980s.

faqs.question: Are mountain gorillas dangerous?
faqs.answer: Wild gorillas are generally peaceful herbivores. Silverbacks charge to intimidate threats but rarely attack unless provoked or if a group feels cornered.

faqs.question: Where can you see mountain gorillas?
faqs.answer: Guided treks in Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park, Uganda's Bwindi and Mgahinga parks, and DRC's Virunga National Park — permits are limited and expensive to fund protection.

faqs.question: Mountain gorilla vs lowland gorilla?
faqs.answer: Mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei beringei) live at high elevation with longer fur and smaller range. Western and eastern lowland gorillas inhabit lowland rainforests and are separate subspecies.

faqs.question: Why are mountain gorillas endangered?
faqs.answer: Small range, habitat encroachment, snares, disease from human contact, and historical poaching — though numbers are slowly increasing thanks to sustained protection efforts.

animals.name: Javan Rhino
animals.summary: The Javan rhinoceros is the rarest of all rhino species, with roughly 70 individuals surviving in a single national park on Java, Indonesia. Smaller than the Indian rhino at 900–2,300 kg (2,000–5,000 lb), it has a single horn and nearly hairless grey skin, and is Critically Endangered from historic hunting and tiny range.

sections.heading: Last population on Java
sections.body: All surviving Javan rhinos live in Ujung Kulon National Park at the western tip of Java — a peninsula isolated by the 1883 Krakatau eruption and tsunami. No Javan rhinos remain in their former range across Southeast Asia, Vietnam, or India.

sections.heading: Forest browser
sections.body: Unlike grass-grazing white rhinos, Javan rhinos browse woody vegetation in dense rainforest, using a pointed upper lip to strip shoots and fallen fruit. They follow regular trails through undergrowth and wallow in mud to cool and deter insects.

sections.heading: Extreme rarity
sections.body: With fewer than 80 individuals, the Javan rhino is the rarest large mammal on Earth. The last Javan rhino in Vietnam was poached in 2010. Every birth in Ujung Kulon is monitored by camera traps — the population is too small to survive a disease outbreak or natural disaster.

sections.heading: Recovery challenges
sections.body: Plans to establish a second population on Java or elsewhere have progressed slowly due to habitat requirements, tsunami risk at Ujung Kulon, and the invasive Arenga palm crowding out rhino food plants. Anti-poaching success means natural threats now dominate.

faqs.question: How many Javan rhinos are left?
faqs.answer: Roughly 70–75 individuals, all in Ujung Kulon National Park on Java, Indonesia — the rarest rhino species and one of the rarest mammals on Earth.

faqs.question: Javan rhino vs Indian rhino?
faqs.answer: Javan rhinos are smaller, nearly hairless, and have a single horn. Indian (greater one-horned) rhinos are larger with armour-like skin folds and number over 4,000 in India and Nepal.

faqs.question: Why are Javan rhinos Critically Endangered?
faqs.answer: Historic hunting for horn and habitat loss eliminated them across Asia. The entire species now depends on one small park vulnerable to tsunami, disease, and invasive plants.

faqs.question: Do Javan rhinos have two horns?
faqs.answer: Usually one horn, rarely two — unlike African rhinos which typically have two horns (though black rhinos also have one primary horn).

faqs.question: Can you see Javan rhinos?
faqs.answer: No public tourism is permitted — the population is too fragile. Researchers rely on camera traps and footprints for monitoring.

animals.name: Largemouth Bass
animals.summary: The largemouth bass is a top predator in North American lakes and rivers, named for a jaw extending past the eye. Prized by anglers worldwide, it strikes lures aggressively, grows to 10 kg (22 lb) in rich waters, and has been stocked on every continent except Antarctica for sport fishing.

sections.heading: Ambush predator
sections.body: Largemouth bass hide among lily pads, fallen timber, and weed beds, exploding forward to engulf prey with a cavernous mouth that gives the species its name. They are visual hunters, striking artificial lures that mimic wounded minnows, frogs, and worms.

sections.heading: Nest guarding males
sections.body: Male bass build and defend circular nests in shallow gravel or sand during spring. They fan silt away, guard eggs against sunfish and crayfish, and protect fry for days after hatching — one of the most dedicated parental behaviours among popular game fish.

sections.heading: Global sport fishing icon
sections.body: Bass tournaments across the United States draw millions of participants and television audiences. Stocking programmes introduced largemouth bass to Japan, South Africa, and Europe, where they sometimes disrupt native fish communities in warm still waters.

sections.heading: Management and ecology
sections.body: Native and Least Concern in North America, largemouth bass regulate populations of smaller fish and crayfish. Fisheries managers adjust size and bag limits to maintain trophy fisheries. Invasive where introduced outside their native warm-water range.

faqs.question: How big do largemouth bass get?
faqs.answer: Most angler catches are 1–3 kg, but fish over 5 kg are trophies and the world record exceeds 10 kg from a California reservoir.

faqs.question: What do largemouth bass eat?
faqs.answer: Fish, crayfish, frogs, insects, and even small birds or mice near the surface — opportunistic predators that prefer live prey.

faqs.question: Where are largemouth bass native?
faqs.answer: Eastern and central North America from southern Canada through the Great Lakes and Mississippi basin to Florida and northeastern Mexico.

faqs.question: Largemouth vs smallmouth bass?
faqs.answer: Largemouth have a jaw extending past the eye and prefer weedy warm water. Smallmouth bass have a jaw that stops at the eye and favour clearer, cooler rocky streams and lakes.

faqs.question: Are largemouth bass good to eat?
faqs.answer: Yes — firm white flesh is popular in the American South, though catch-and-release sport fishing dominates in many trophy fisheries.

animals.name: Atlantic Cod
animals.summary: Atlantic cod is a cold-water groundfish that shaped the economies of Newfoundland, Iceland, and New England for centuries before overfishing collapsed many stocks. Growing to 40 kg (88 lb) and living 25 years, it supports fisheries where recovered and remains Vulnerable in the northwest Atlantic.

sections.heading: Historic fishery collapse
sections.body: Northwest Atlantic cod stocks crashed in 1992 when Canada's Grand Banks fishery closed — one of history's most famous fishery collapses after centuries of seemingly unlimited harvest. Recovery has been partial and slow, illustrating how even prolific species can be depleted.

sections.heading: Barbel and bottom feeding
sections.body: A whisker-like barbel on the chin helps cod detect prey on the seafloor — worms, crabs, and smaller fish. Cod migrate between shallow spawning grounds and deeper feeding areas, historically forming dense shoals that made them easy targets for trawlers.

sections.heading: Cultural and culinary importance
sections.body: Fish and chips, bacalao, and lutefisk all depend on cod. Basque and Viking fishermen pursued cod across the Atlantic for centuries before modern industrial trawling. Cod liver oil supplied vitamin D to generations of children.

sections.heading: Modern management
sections.body: Listed Vulnerable, Atlantic cod fisheries are now regulated with quotas, closed areas, and gear restrictions. Icelandic and Northeast Arctic stocks are healthier than Northwest Atlantic populations. Climate change shifts spawning grounds northward, complicating recovery.

faqs.question: Why did cod collapse?
faqs.answer: Decades of industrial trawling removed fish faster than they could reproduce, combined with poor management and environmental shifts — the 1992 moratorium on Canada's Grand Banks is the landmark example.

faqs.question: Is cod still overfished?
faqs.answer: Some stocks remain depleted or Vulnerable, especially in the northwest Atlantic. Northeast Atlantic and Icelandic fisheries are more sustainable under strict quotas.

faqs.question: What is bacalao?
faqs.answer: Salted and dried cod — a staple of Portuguese, Spanish, and Caribbean cuisine preserved for centuries before refrigeration.

faqs.question: How big do Atlantic cod get?
faqs.answer: Typically 2–8 kg in fisheries, but individuals can exceed 40 kg and live 25 years in unfished populations.

faqs.question: Where do Atlantic cod live?
faqs.answer: Cold waters of the North Atlantic from North America to Greenland, Iceland, Norway, and the Barents Sea — on continental shelves and banks.

animals.name: Peach-faced Lovebird
animals.summary: Peach-faced lovebirds are small colourful parrots from southwestern Africa, named for strong pair bonds and affectionate behaviour. Wild birds have green bodies with peach faces; captive colour mutations are popular pets. They weigh 40–60 g (1.4–2 oz), live in flocks at waterholes, and are Least Concern in the wild.

sections.heading: Pair bonding
sections.body: Lovebirds form strong monogamous pairs that preen, feed, and roost together year-round. In captivity a lone bird may bond with a human or mirror if no partner is available. Wild flocks gather at waterholes in dry country, splitting into pairs during breeding.

sections.heading: Nest building in captivity
sections.body: Females tuck nesting material into tail feathers and carry it to a cavity — a behaviour famous among pet owners who provide paper strips. In the wild they nest in tree holes and rock crevices, laying 4–6 eggs per clutch.

sections.heading: Pet trade and colour morphs
sections.body: Selective breeding produced lutino, pied, and orange-faced colour varieties far removed from wild green plumage. Lovebirds are social, noisy, and need companionship — unsuitable for owners who cannot provide daily interaction or a same-species partner.

sections.heading: Wild populations and crops
sections.body: Least Concern across Namibia, Angola, and South Africa, peach-faced lovebirds sometimes damage millet and sunflower crops. Escaped pets establish feral colonies in Arizona and other warm regions outside native range.

faqs.question: Do lovebirds need a partner?
faqs.answer: They are highly social — wild birds pair for life. Pet lovebirds do best with a companion bird or extensive daily human interaction to prevent loneliness and feather plucking.

faqs.question: How long do lovebirds live?
faqs.answer: About 10–15 years in the wild and 15–20 years in captivity with good diet and veterinary care.

faqs.question: Where are lovebirds from?
faqs.answer: Southwestern Africa — arid woodlands and savannas of Namibia, Angola, and South Africa, often near water in dry country.

faqs.question: Are lovebirds parrots?
faqs.answer: Yes — small parrots in the family Psittaculidae. They have curved beaks, zygodactyl feet, and the intelligence typical of parrots.

faqs.question: Can lovebirds talk?
faqs.answer: They mimic whistles and some words but are not among the best talkers. Their loud chirps and social chatter are more characteristic than speech.

animals.name: Canary
animals.summary: Canaries are domesticated songbirds descended from wild Atlantic canaries of the Canary Islands, Madeira, and the Azores. Bred for centuries for colour and song, they weigh 15–25 g (0.5–0.9 oz) and are kept in millions of households — while wild populations on their native islands remain Least Concern.

sections.heading: Domestication for song
sections.body: Spanish and European breeders selected canaries for song quality from the 1500s onward, producing roller, timbrado, and American singer varieties with distinct melodies. Male canaries sing to defend territory and attract mates — hens chirp but typically do not produce elaborate song.

sections.heading: Wild Atlantic canary
sections.body: Wild Serinus canaria on the Canary Islands, Madeira, and the Azores are streaky greenish-yellow finches of open woodland and coast. They were trapped and exported until captive breeding supplanted wild collection. Island populations remain secure.

sections.heading: Coal mine sentinel
sections.body: Canaries were used in British coal mines until 1986 to detect carbon monoxide — birds succumb to toxic gas faster than humans, giving miners warning to evacuate. The phrase 'canary in a coal mine' now means an early warning indicator for any danger.

sections.heading: Modern pet care
sections.body: Pet canaries need spacious cages, varied seed diet with fresh greens, and safe flying time. Colour-fed red factors require dietary carotenoids. They are hardy but sensitive to drafts, fumes, and sudden diet changes — popular beginner birds when basic needs are met.

faqs.question: Do only male canaries sing?
faqs.answer: Yes — male canaries sing elaborate songs to mark territory and attract females. Females make short chirps and calls but not sustained song.

faqs.question: Where do wild canaries live?
faqs.answer: The Canary Islands, Madeira, and the Azores in the eastern Atlantic — open woodland, scrub, and coastal gardens.

faqs.question: Why were canaries used in coal mines?
faqs.answer: Canaries are sensitive to carbon monoxide and methane. If a bird stopped singing or died, miners knew to evacuate before gas levels became lethal to humans.

faqs.question: How long do canaries live?
faqs.answer: Typically 7–12 years in captivity with good care — longer than many small pet birds but shorter than large parrots.

faqs.question: Are canaries finches?
faqs.answer: Yes — they belong to the finch family Fringillidae, related to goldfinches and siskins, not true parrots despite their popularity as cage birds.

animals.name: Common Pheasant
animals.summary: The common pheasant is a large colourful game bird native to Asia, with the cock's iridescent green head, red face wattles, and long barred tail familiar across European and American hunting estates. Introduced worldwide for sport shooting, it weighs 0.8–1.5 kg (1.8–3.3 lb) and is Least Concern globally.

sections.heading: Game bird introductions
sections.body: Romans and later medieval hunters spread pheasants from Asia across Europe. Mass releases on shooting estates in Britain, the United States, and New Zealand sustain populations far beyond what natural reproduction alone would support — millions are released annually for sport.

sections.heading: Sexual dimorphism
sections.body: Cocks are spectacularly coloured with iridescent plumage and long tails; hens are mottled brown for camouflage while incubating ground nests. Cocks crow and beat wings in display, sometimes fighting viciously during the breeding season.

sections.heading: Ecological impact
sections.body: Released pheasants compete with native ground-nesting birds, eat crop seed, and spread disease to wild galliformes. In Britain they are among the most numerous birds in autumn after releases. In native Asia, wild populations occupy forest edges and agricultural mosaic.

sections.heading: Hunting culture
sections.body: Driven pheasant shoots on European and American estates are a traditional autumn sport. Bag limits and release regulations vary. Wild Asian populations remain Least Concern, though local declines occur from habitat loss and overhunting.

faqs.question: Are pheasants native to the UK?
faqs.answer: No — common pheasants originate from Asia. They were introduced to Britain by the Romans and Normans and are now naturalised, especially on shooting estates.

faqs.question: What do pheasants eat?
faqs.answer: Seeds, grain, insects, berries, and green shoots — diet shifts seasonally between farmland foraging and woodland edge browsing.

faqs.question: Can pheasants fly?
faqs.answer: Yes — they burst into strong short flight when flushed, then prefer running through cover. Sustained flight is limited compared with migratory birds.

faqs.question: Male vs female pheasant?
faqs.answer: Males (cocks) are colourful with long tails and a white neck ring in the common subspecies. Females (hens) are cryptic brown for nest camouflage.

faqs.question: Where are pheasants originally from?
faqs.answer: Asia — from the Caucasus and Black Sea region through China. Most introduced populations derive from Chinese and ring-necked subspecies.

range.nativeRange: Native to forest edges and farmland from the Caucasus through China; introduced to Europe, North America, New Zealand, and elsewhere for game shooting on managed estates.

animals.name: Rooster
animals.summary: Roosters are adult male domestic chickens, descended from red junglefowl of Southeast Asia and bred for thousands of years for crowing, flock protection, and breeding. Weighing 2–4 kg (4.4–9 lb) with spurs and colourful plumage in many breeds, they guard hens from predators and announce dawn with loud crows.

sections.heading: Flock guardian
sections.body: Roosters watch for hawks and foxes, calling alarms and confronting threats with spurs on their legs. They find food and call hens to share, maintaining order in the pecking hierarchy through display and occasional fights with rival males.

sections.heading: Crowing and circadian rhythm
sections.body: Crows mark territory and respond to light — roosters often crow before dawn and throughout the day when challenged by distant rivals. The internal clock drives anticipation of sunrise even in constant light, though social cues from other roosters matter too.

sections.heading: Breeds and cockfighting legacy
sections.body: Hundreds of breeds vary from bantam show birds to massive Brahmas. Historically bred for cockfighting — now illegal in most countries — modern roosters serve backyard egg flocks, meat production, and exhibition. Spurs can injure handlers and other birds if not managed.

sections.heading: Urban and suburban controversy
sections.body: Backyard chicken keeping revives rooster ownership, but crowing brings noise complaints and many municipalities ban roosters while allowing hens. Hatchery chicks are often sexed, yet crowing adolescents still surprise urban keepers.

faqs.question: Why do roosters crow at dawn?
faqs.answer: Light triggers their circadian clock, but they also crow to announce territory and respond to other roosters — not only at dawn but most prominently at daybreak.

faqs.question: Are roosters aggressive?
faqs.answer: Some breeds and individual cocks defend flocks fiercely and may attack people or pets. Handling from chickhood and breed selection reduce aggression.

faqs.question: Rooster vs hen?
faqs.answer: Roosters are males with larger combs, spurs, and often colourful plumage. Hens are females that lay eggs and are typically less aggressive and quieter.

faqs.question: Can you keep a rooster in the city?
faqs.answer: Many cities prohibit roosters because of noise while allowing hens. Check local ordinances before hatching or buying chicks.

faqs.question: What did chickens evolve from?
faqs.answer: Red junglefowl (Gallus gallus) of Southeast Asia — domesticated roughly 8,000 years ago in multiple regions for meat and eggs.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Omnivore — grain, insects, scraps, and forage

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: 5–8 years (breeding cocks often kept fewer years)

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Capable short flight over fences; fast runner

range.nativeRange: Domesticated from red junglefowl of Southeast Asia; roosters kept on farms and in villages on every inhabited continent.

animals.name: Bed Bug
animals.summary: The common bed bug is a small flat insect that feeds exclusively on blood, mainly from humans at night while they sleep. Roughly 5 mm long and reddish-brown, it hides in mattress seams and furniture, resists many pesticides, and has resurged globally in hotels and homes — listed Not Evaluated by IUCN.

sections.heading: Nocturnal blood feeding
sections.body: Bed bugs emerge from hiding in darkness, attracted by carbon dioxide and body heat. They pierce skin with elongated mouthparts, feed for 5–10 minutes, then retreat to cracks. Bites often appear in lines or clusters but reactions vary — some people show no marks.

sections.heading: Resurgence and resistance
sections.body: Bed bugs nearly disappeared in wealthy countries after DDT use mid-century but resurged since the 1990s with international travel, pesticide resistance, and reduced use of broad-spectrum insecticides. They spread via luggage, furniture, and clothing.

sections.heading: Detection and treatment
sections.body: Signs include rusty spots (faecal stains), shed skins, and a sweet musty odour in heavy infestations. Heat treatment above 50°C kills all life stages. Professional extermination often combines heat, steam, encasements, and targeted insecticides.

sections.heading: Health impacts
sections.body: Bed bugs are not known to transmit disease to humans despite blood feeding. Bites cause itching, allergic reactions, and psychological distress — anxiety and sleep loss are common during infestations. Not Evaluated by IUCN as a human-associated pest.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs spread disease?
faqs.answer: No confirmed disease transmission to humans — unlike ticks or mosquitoes. The main harm is itching, allergic reaction, and psychological stress.

faqs.question: How do you get bed bugs?
faqs.answer: They hitchhike on luggage, used furniture, and clothing from infested hotels, homes, or public transport. They do not arrive from poor hygiene alone.

faqs.question: Can bed bugs fly?
faqs.answer: No — they have no wings and cannot jump. They crawl between rooms and spread through walls and pipes in multi-unit buildings.

faqs.question: How do you kill bed bugs?
faqs.answer: Professional heat treatment, steam, mattress encasements, and targeted pesticides. Washing bedding at high heat helps but rarely eliminates infestation alone.

faqs.question: What do bed bugs look like?
faqs.answer: Flat oval reddish-brown insects about apple-seed size (4–7 mm). After feeding they swell and darken. Nymphs are smaller and paler.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Blood — primarily human; also bats and birds in wild settings

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Human dwellings, hotels, dormitories, and bedding worldwide

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: 6–12 months; can survive months without feeding

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Crawls ~1 m per minute; does not fly or jump

range.nativeRange: Cosmopolitan human commensal found wherever people sleep — hotels, homes, and dormitories worldwide; likely originated as bat parasites in caves.

animals.name: Blacklegged Tick
animals.summary: The blacklegged tick, also called the deer tick, is a tiny arachnid that attaches to hosts and feeds on blood, transmitting Lyme disease and other pathogens in eastern North America. Unfed nymphs are poppy-seed sized; adults are larger and most active in fall. Listed Not Evaluated by IUCN.

sections.heading: Three-host life cycle
sections.body: Blacklegged ticks feed once at each life stage — larva, nymph, and adult — dropping off between hosts to moult. White-tailed deer are critical adult hosts that distribute ticks, while mice and birds infect nymphs with Lyme bacteria during larval and nymphal feeds.

sections.heading: Questing behaviour
sections.body: Ticks climb vegetation and extend front legs to latch onto passing hosts — a behaviour called questing. They detect carbon dioxide, heat, and vibration. Permethrin-treated clothing and DEET repellents reduce attachment during hiking.

sections.heading: Lyme disease transmission
sections.body: Ixodes scapularis is the primary vector of Borrelia burgdorferi, the bacterium causing Lyme disease in the United States. Nymphs — active in late spring and summer — cause most human infections because they are small and easily overlooked. Prompt tick removal within 24–36 hours reduces transmission risk.

sections.heading: Expanding range
sections.body: Climate warming and reforestation expand tick range northward and into Canada. Not Evaluated by IUCN, blacklegged ticks are a major public health concern rather than a conservation species. Landscape management and deer control can reduce local abundance.

faqs.question: What is a deer tick?
faqs.answer: Another name for the blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis) — named because white-tailed deer are important hosts for adult ticks, though deer do not transmit Lyme bacteria.

faqs.question: How do you remove a tick?
faqs.answer: Use fine tweezers to grasp the tick close to the skin and pull steadily upward without twisting. Clean the bite area and monitor for rash or fever.

faqs.question: Do all ticks carry Lyme disease?
faqs.answer: No — only some blacklegged ticks are infected, and rates vary by region. Other tick species carry different diseases.

faqs.question: When are ticks most active?
faqs.answer: Nymphs peak in May–July; adults in fall. Ticks can be active whenever temperatures exceed roughly 4°C (40°F).

faqs.question: Where are blacklegged ticks found?
faqs.answer: Eastern and midwestern United States and southeastern Canada — deciduous forest and edge habitat from Virginia to Minnesota and into New England.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Blood — feeds on mammals, birds, and reptiles

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Deciduous forests, leaf litter, and grassy edges of eastern North America

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: 2–3 years across larva, nymph, and adult stages

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Slow crawler; waits on vegetation with legs outstretched

range.nativeRange: Deciduous forest and grassy edges of eastern and midwestern United States and southeastern Canada — expanding northward with climate warming.

animals.name: Brown Recluse Spider
animals.summary: The brown recluse is a small venomous spider named for a violin-shaped mark on its cephalothorax and its shy, reclusive habits. Found mainly in the central and southern United States, it bites rarely but can cause necrotic skin lesions. Adults are 6–20 mm long and listed Not Evaluated by IUCN.

sections.heading: Reclusive habits
sections.body: Brown recluses avoid open spaces and daylight, spinning irregular webs in undisturbed corners rather than catching prey in orb webs. They hunt small insects at night and tolerate crowding — dozens may share a hidden void in infested buildings.

sections.heading: Violin marking and identification
sections.body: The dark violin-shaped mark on the cephalothorax helps identification, though similar marks occur on harmless species. Six eyes in three pairs (most spiders have eight) is a diagnostic feature. Misidentification is common outside their native range.

sections.heading: Venom and necrosis
sections.body: Bites occur when spiders are trapped against skin in clothing or bedding — they do not chase people. Venom contains enzymes that can cause necrotic wounds in some victims, though many bites heal without serious tissue damage. Medical attention is advised for suspected bites.

sections.heading: Geographic limits and myths
sections.body: Brown recluses are native to the south-central United States and rarely found outside this range despite frequent misidentifications elsewhere. Not Evaluated by IUCN. Reducing clutter, shaking out stored clothing, and sealing entry points limit indoor encounters.

faqs.question: Are brown recluse bites deadly?
faqs.answer: Death is extremely rare. Most bites cause mild irritation; some develop necrotic ulcers requiring medical care. Many suspected bites are misdiagnosed.

faqs.question: Where do brown recluse spiders live?
faqs.answer: South-central United States from Nebraska to Georgia and Texas — not on the West Coast or Northeast despite common misidentifications.

faqs.question: How do you identify a brown recluse?
faqs.answer: Uniform brown colour, violin mark on the back, six eyes in three pairs, and no stripes on the legs. Professional identification is recommended.

faqs.question: Do brown recluse spiders jump?
faqs.answer: No — they run briefly when disturbed but do not jump or actively attack people.

faqs.question: How do you prevent brown recluse bites?
faqs.answer: Shake out shoes and stored clothing, reduce clutter in garages and attics, use sticky traps in infested buildings, and seal cracks where spiders enter.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Carnivore — insects and other small arthropods

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Dark undisturbed spaces — attics, closets, sheds, and woodpiles

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: 2–4 years; slow-growing and long-lived for a spider

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Quick short bursts when threatened; otherwise sedentary

range.nativeRange: South-central United States from Nebraska and Iowa south to Texas and Georgia — rarely found outside this native range despite frequent misidentifications elsewhere.

animals.name: Tasmanian Devil
animals.summary: The Tasmanian devil is the world's largest surviving carnivorous marsupial, weighing 6–14 kg (13–31 lb) with powerful jaws that can crush bone. Found only on Tasmania, it is Endangered after devil facial tumour disease (DFTD) wiped out most of the population — captive insurance groups and a vaccine offer hope for recovery.

sections.heading: Jaw power and scavenging
sections.body: Tasmanian devils have one of the strongest bites relative to body size of any mammal — their wide jaws and thick teeth let them consume entire carcasses including bone and fur. They are primarily scavengers, locating dead wallabies and other animals by smell across kilometres of forest, though they also hunt small prey.

sections.heading: Nocturnal habits and vocalisations
sections.body: Devils are active mainly at night, resting in dens by day in hollow logs, burrows, or dense scrub. Their eerie screeches, growls, and coughs during communal feeding gave them the 'devil' name — settlers found the night-time squabbles over carcasses unsettling.

sections.heading: Devil facial tumour disease
sections.body: DFTD is a contagious cancer spread when devils bite each other during feeding and mating. Tumours on the face prevent eating and kill within months. The disease caused an estimated 80% population crash since the 1990s. Captive insurance populations, fenced disease-free areas, and vaccine trials are central to recovery efforts.

sections.heading: Conservation and recovery
sections.body: Listed Endangered, devils are now found only on Tasmania — extinct on mainland Australia for thousands of years, likely outcompeted by dingoes. Roadkill, habitat loss, and DFTD remain threats. Tourism and the Save the Tasmanian Devil Programme fund research and captive breeding.

faqs.question: Are Tasmanian devils dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: They avoid people and attacks are extremely rare. Devils may defend a food source aggressively if cornered but do not hunt humans.

faqs.question: Why are they called Tasmanian devils?
faqs.answer: Early European settlers named them for loud night screams and fierce squabbles when feeding on carcasses — not because they are evil, but because the sounds were eerie in the bush.

faqs.question: What is devil facial tumour disease?
faqs.answer: A contagious cancer transmitted through biting that causes fatal facial tumours. It devastated wild populations but captive insurance groups and research programmes aim to restore numbers.

faqs.question: How strong is a Tasmanian devil's bite?
faqs.answer: Devils can generate bite force disproportionate to their size — enough to crush bone and consume entire carcasses that other scavengers leave.

faqs.question: Where do Tasmanian devils live?
faqs.answer: Only on the island of Tasmania, Australia — in forests, coastal scrub, and farmland. They are extinct on the mainland.

facts.value: Carnivore — carrion, small mammals, birds, and insects

facts.label: Habitat

animals.name: Osprey
animals.summary: The osprey (Pandion haliaetus) is a fish-specialist raptor with reversible outer toes and spiny foot pads for gripping slippery prey. It nests on coasts, rivers, and lakes nearly worldwide — from the United States and Canada to the UK, Scandinavia, and Australia — and is listed Least Concern after recovering from mid-century pesticide declines.

sections.heading: Built for catching fish
sections.body: Ospreys are the only living members of the family Pandionidae. Their outer toe can swing backward like an owl's, creating a two-and-two grip, while barbed pads on the soles stop fish from wriggling free. Adults typically weigh about 1.6 kg with a wingspan near 1.5–1.8 m, and they often plunge feet-first from 10–40 m above the water.

sections.heading: Almost exclusively piscivorous
sections.body: Roughly 99% of an osprey's diet is live fish — mullet, flounder, trout, perch, and other surface-feeding species depending on region. They take both freshwater and saltwater fish and will travel several kilometres from the nest to productive shallows. Prey is usually carried head-first for aerodynamic flight.

sections.heading: Cosmopolitan waterside nests
sections.body: Breeding pairs occupy coastal bays, large lakes, reservoirs, and slow rivers across every continent except Antarctica. In North America and Europe they favour stick nests on channel markers, dead trees, and purpose-built platforms. Northern populations migrate; many Australian and tropical birds stay year-round near good fishing grounds.

sections.heading: DDT collapse and recovery
sections.body: Osprey numbers crashed in the 1950s–70s when DDT thinned eggshells and wrecked nesting success in North America and Europe. Bans on organochlorine pesticides, nest platforms, and legal protection drove a strong rebound, and the species is now Least Concern — though local threats still include entanglement in fishing line and disturbance at busy marina nests.

faqs.question: Can ospreys eat saltwater fish?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ospreys hunt in both fresh and salt water and commonly take coastal species such as mullet and flounder as well as inland trout and perch.

faqs.question: Why do ospreys dive feet-first?
faqs.answer: Their talons and reversible outer toes are specialised for gripping fish; diving feet-first protects the head and lets them snatch prey near the surface without swimming underwater like a cormorant.

faqs.question: Are ospreys related to eagles?
faqs.answer: They are raptors in Accipitriformes but sit in their own family, Pandionidae, separate from true eagles and hawks — a reflection of their extreme fish-hunting specialisation.

faqs.question: How fast can an osprey fly?
faqs.answer: In level flight they often cruise around 40–50 km/h, and stoops toward prey can approach roughly 80 km/h.

faqs.question: Do ospreys migrate?
faqs.answer: Many northern breeders migrate to warmer coasts and inland waters for winter, while some tropical and Australian populations remain resident where fish are available year-round.

animals.name: Short-beaked Echidna
animals.summary: The short-beaked echidna (Tachyglossus aculeatus) is a spiny, egg-laying monotreme that eats ants and termites across Australia and coastal New Guinea. Adults weigh about 5 kg, dig with powerful claws, and can live around 40 years. It is listed Least Concern, though some island populations face local pressures.

sections.heading: A mammal that lays eggs
sections.body: Echidnas belong to Monotremata with the platypus — mammals that lay leathery eggs. A single egg incubates in a temporary pouch; the hatchling, called a puggle, laps milk from specialised skin patches rather than nipples. Dense spines cover the back, and when threatened the animal digs in or curls to present only spines.

sections.heading: Ant and termite specialist
sections.body: A long, sticky tongue flicks into nests while electroreceptors in the snout help detect prey underground. They lack teeth; grit in the stomach grinds insects. Short-beaked echidnas take ants, termites, and other soil invertebrates rather than large prey.

sections.heading: From Tasmania to New Guinea
sections.body: They occupy forests, woodland, scrub, and arid inland Australia, plus Tasmania and coastal New Guinea. Individuals may roam widely, sheltering in hollows, under logs, or self-dug burrows. They cope with heat by being largely crepuscular or nocturnal in hot districts.

sections.heading: Roadkill and feral predators
sections.body: The species is Least Concern overall, but vehicle strikes, habitat fragmentation, and foxes or cats on some islands reduce local numbers. In colder regions they may enter deep torpor lasting days to weeks when food and temperatures drop.

faqs.question: Why do echidnas lay eggs?
faqs.answer: They are monotremes — an ancient mammal lineage that retained egg-laying. The egg hatches into a tiny puggle that continues developing on milk, combining reptile-like reproduction with mammalian care.

faqs.question: Are echidnas related to hedgehogs?
faqs.answer: No. Spines evolved independently; echidnas are Australian monotremes, while hedgehogs are placental mammals from Eurasia and Africa.

faqs.question: What is a baby echidna called?
faqs.answer: A puggle — the same informal name sometimes used for baby platypuses — that is the usual English name for a young short-beaked echidna.

faqs.question: Do echidnas have venom?
faqs.answer: Male echidnas have spurs on the hind ankles, but unlike platypuses they are not considered dangerously venomous to humans.

faqs.question: How long do echidnas live?
faqs.answer: Wild adults often reach several decades; captive records approach or exceed 40 years, unusually long for a small mammal.

animals.name: Sugar Glider
animals.summary: Sugar gliders (Petaurus breviceps) are nocturnal marsupials that glide between eucalypt trees on a membrane stretching from wrist to ankle. Native to eastern and northern Australia, New Guinea, and nearby islands, they eat nectar, sap, pollen, and insects, weigh about 120 g, and are listed Least Concern.

sections.heading: Wrist-to-ankle gliding membrane
sections.body: The patagium lets sugar gliders sail 50 m or more between trunks, steering with the tail and limbs. Soft grey fur, a dark dorsal stripe, and huge eyes suit night foraging. Social groups share tree hollows and use scent glands to mark territory and group members.

sections.heading: Sap, nectar, and insects
sections.body: They lap eucalypt and acacia sap, take nectar and pollen from blossoms, and catch moths, beetles, and spiders. Incisors help strip bark to reach gum flows. Seasonal flowering and insect pulses shift how much sugar versus protein they eat.

sections.heading: Canopy life in Oceania
sections.body: Eastern and northern Australia, New Guinea, and adjacent islands hold wild populations in eucalypt forests and woodland. They need connected canopy and hollow-bearing trees; cleared farmland can isolate colonies.

sections.heading: Pet trade versus wild needs
sections.body: Wild populations remain Least Concern, but hollow loss and fragmentation shrink local groups. As pets they need specialised diets and social housing — poor captive care, not IUCN status, is the usual welfare issue people encounter.

faqs.question: How far can a sugar glider glide?
faqs.answer: Documented glides often reach 50 m between trees when launching from height, using the membrane and tail for steering.

faqs.question: Are sugar gliders flying squirrels?
faqs.answer: No. They are marsupials; flying squirrels are placental rodents. Similar gliding membranes evolved independently.

faqs.question: What do wild sugar gliders eat at night?
faqs.answer: Nectar, pollen, tree sap and gum, plus insects and spiders — not a fruit-only diet.

faqs.question: Do sugar gliders live in groups?
faqs.answer: Yes. Small colonies share nests in hollows and communicate with scent and soft calls.

faqs.question: Is a baby sugar glider called a joey?
faqs.answer: Yes — like other marsupials, young are joeys and spend early life in the mother's pouch.

facts.label: Weight

animals.name: Tuatara
animals.summary: The tuatara (Sphenodon punctatus) is New Zealand's living rhynchocephalian — a lizard-like reptile lineage otherwise known only from fossils. It survives on predator-free offshore islands and sanctuaries, eats invertebrates, grows slowly to about 1 kg, and can live 60 years or more. IUCN lists it Least Concern under intensive management.

sections.heading: Not a lizard — a rhynchocephalian
sections.body: Tuatara are the sole survivors of Rhynchocephalia, separated from lizards and snakes for roughly 200 million years. They have a parietal "third eye" under skin on the forehead, two rows of upper teeth that shear against one lower row, and remarkably slow metabolism even for reptiles.

sections.heading: Nocturnal invertebrate hunter
sections.body: Adults take beetles, spiders, weta, snails, and occasionally lizard eggs or chicks. They forage mainly at night in cool coastal forest and scrub. Juveniles may be more diurnal to avoid cannibalistic adults.

sections.heading: Islands after mainland extinction
sections.body: Pacific rats (kiore), dogs, and other introduced mammals wiped tuatara from mainland New Zealand. Remaining wild groups live on managed offshore islands; reintroductions to fenced sanctuaries are expanding secure habitat.

sections.heading: Temperature-dependent sex and rats
sections.body: Eggs incubated cooler tend to produce females; warmer nests yield more males — a climate concern for nesting sites. Eradicating rats and restoring islands remain the core conservation tools that keep the species Least Concern today.

faqs.question: Is a tuatara a dinosaur?
faqs.answer: No. It is a living rhynchocephalian reptile — a cousin lineage to lizards and snakes, not a dinosaur.

faqs.question: Why do tuatara have a third eye?
faqs.answer: The parietal eye senses light and may help regulate circadian and seasonal cycles; it does not form sharp images like the lateral eyes.

faqs.question: How long can tuatara live?
faqs.answer: Decades are normal; well-documented individuals exceed 60 years, and some captive animals are thought to be older.

faqs.question: Where can you see tuatara in the wild?
faqs.answer: Almost only on protected New Zealand offshore islands and mainland sanctuaries free of introduced mammalian predators.

faqs.question: Do tuatara hibernate?
faqs.answer: In cooler months they become inactive and may remain in burrows for long periods, matching their slow metabolism.

animals.name: Shoebill
animals.summary: The shoebill (Balaeniceps rex) is a towering East African wetland bird named for its massive, shoe-shaped bill used to seize lungfish and other large aquatic prey. It stands about 1.2 m tall, weighs around 5.5 kg, and nests in papyrus swamps of South Sudan, Uganda, and Zambia. IUCN lists it Vulnerable because swamp drainage and disturbance shrink suitable habitat.

sections.heading: The shoe-shaped bill
sections.body: The bill can exceed 20 cm and ends in a sharp hook for gripping slippery fish. Shoebills hunt with statue-still patience, then strike in a sudden lunge. Broad wings and a slow wingbeat suit short flights over dense swamp vegetation.

sections.heading: Lungfish and swamp ambush
sections.body: Preferred prey includes African lungfish, catfish, frogs, and young crocodiles. Birds often stand motionless in shallow water or on floating vegetation until prey surfaces, then tip forward to clamp it.

sections.heading: Papyrus strongholds
sections.body: Core range covers freshwater swamps of East-Central Africa — especially South Sudan's Sudd, Uganda's Lake Victoria basin wetlands, and Zambian Bangweulu swamps. They need large, quiet tracts of papyrus and seasonal floodplain.

sections.heading: Vulnerable swamp specialist
sections.body: Drainage for agriculture, burning of papyrus, and nest disturbance keep the species Vulnerable. Low clutch size (often one chick fledged) means populations recover slowly even where habitat remains.

faqs.question: Why is the shoebill's bill so large?
faqs.answer: The deep, hooked bill lets it seize and crush large, slippery prey such as lungfish in dense swamp vegetation.

faqs.question: Do shoebills eat baby crocodiles?
faqs.answer: Yes — they occasionally take young crocodiles along with lungfish, catfish, and frogs.

faqs.question: Are shoebills related to storks?
faqs.answer: They look stork-like but sit in their own family, Balaenicipitidae, closer to pelicans in modern classifications.

faqs.question: Where do shoebills live?
faqs.answer: Freshwater papyrus swamps in East-Central Africa, notably South Sudan, Uganda, and Zambia.

faqs.question: Why are shoebills Vulnerable?
faqs.answer: Their specialised swamp habitat is being drained, burned, and disturbed, and they raise few chicks per year.
