animals.name: Porbeagle
animals.summary: The porbeagle (Lamna nasus) is a stocky mackerel shark of cool temperate seas, warm-blooded like its great white relatives. Adults reach 2.5 m and 135 kg, and are listed Vulnerable.

sections.heading: Warm-blooded tuna hunter
sections.body: Counter-current heat exchangers keep muscles warm for fast pursuit in cold water. A white flank patch and crescent tail distinguish porbeagles from similar sharks.

sections.heading: Mackerel, squid, and cod
sections.body: Schooling fish and squid dominate the diet. Pups are born live in nursery areas on continental shelves.

sections.heading: North Atlantic and southern oceans
sections.body: Northwest Atlantic, Northeast Atlantic, and South Pacific temperate waters. Seasonal migrations follow prey concentrations.

sections.heading: Vulnerable to targeted fishing
sections.body: IUCN lists porbeagle Vulnerable. Decades of sport and commercial harvest for meat and fins depleted stocks; recovery is slow due to late maturity.

faqs.question: Is the porbeagle related to great white sharks?
faqs.answer: Yes — both are lamnid sharks with partial warm-blooded physiology for fast swimming.

faqs.question: What is the white patch on a porbeagle?
faqs.answer: A pale mark on the rear flank helps separate porbeagles from mako sharks.

faqs.question: Are porbeagles dangerous?
faqs.answer: Bites to humans are extremely rare; they are offshore fish-eaters.

faqs.question: Why is the porbeagle Vulnerable?
faqs.answer: Slow reproduction and heavy fishing pressure collapsed populations in the Atlantic and elsewhere.

faqs.question: Where are porbeagle nurseries?
faqs.answer: Shallow continental shelf waters where females bear live young.

range.nativeRange: Cool temperate oceans of both hemispheres.

animals.name: Cookiecutter Shark
animals.summary: The cookiecutter shark (Isistius brasiliensis) is a small deep-sea shark that bites round plugs of flesh from whales, tuna, and submarines. Adults reach 50 cm, glow with bioluminescence, and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Living melon baller
sections.body: Lower teeth fuse into a saw-like plate that scoops cylindrical plugs of meat from much larger animals. Photophores on the belly hide the silhouette from below.

sections.heading: Squid, fish, and flesh bites
sections.body: Whole small prey are swallowed, but adults also ambush large animals — whales, dolphins, tuna — leaving crater scars. Even sonar domes and rubber seals get sampled.

sections.heading: Tropical oceanic midwaters
sections.body: Worldwide in warm deep water, rising vertically at night toward surface prey. Migration follows the deep scattering layer.

sections.heading: Tiny terror, stable numbers
sections.body: Least Concern with vast habitat and no fishery. Famous bite scars on submarines and whales document their bold parasitic feeding.

faqs.question: How does a cookiecutter shark bite?
faqs.answer: It latches on and spins, carving a round plug of flesh with serrated lower teeth.

faqs.question: Why do whales have round scars?
faqs.answer: Many come from cookiecutter sharks and similar species taking plug bites at night.

faqs.question: Do cookiecutter sharks glow?
faqs.answer: Yes — belly photophores match downwelling light, hiding the shark's silhouette.

faqs.question: How big is a cookiecutter shark?
faqs.answer: About 40–50 cm — tiny compared with the whales they scar.

faqs.question: Have cookiecutters damaged submarines?
faqs.answer: Yes — they have bitten rubber sonar domes and cables on navy vessels.

range.nativeRange: Tropical oceans worldwide.

animals.name: Lanternfish
animals.summary: The spotted lanternfish (Myctophum punctatum) is a keystone mesopelagic fish whose daily vertical migration moves carbon through ocean food webs. Adults reach 8 cm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Lights of the twilight zone
sections.body: Photophores along the flank produce species-specific glow patterns for schooling and camouflage. Huge eyes and silver sides suit life 200–1000 m deep.

sections.heading: Zooplankton commuter
sections.body: Nightly ascents to surface waters harvest copepods and krill; daytime descent hides from predators. Billions of individuals make this the world's most abundant vertebrate migration.

sections.heading: Temperate Atlantic midwaters
sections.body: Myctophum punctatum ranges the temperate and subtropical North Atlantic mesopelagic zone. The wider lanternfish family dominates deep oceans globally.

sections.heading: Invisible backbone of fisheries
sections.body: Least Concern with astronomical numbers. They transfer surface production to tuna, squid, and deep-diving whales — supporting commercial fisheries indirectly.

faqs.question: Why are they called lanternfish?
faqs.answer: Bioluminescent photophores dotted along the body resemble tiny lanterns in the deep sea.

faqs.question: Do lanternfish migrate daily?
faqs.answer: Yes — they rise toward the surface at night and sink hundreds of metres by day.

faqs.question: How important are lanternfish to oceans?
faqs.answer: They are among the most abundant vertebrates and channel plankton energy to larger predators.

faqs.question: How big is a spotted lanternfish?
faqs.answer: About 6–8 cm — small but extraordinarily numerous.

faqs.question: What eats lanternfish?
faqs.answer: Tuna, squid, dolphins, and deep-diving seabirds depend on lanternfish migrations.

range.nativeRange: Temperate and subtropical Atlantic mesopelagic zone.

animals.name: Viperfish
animals.summary: The Sloane's viperfish (Chauliodus sloani) is a fang-toothed deep-sea predator with a hinged skull for swallowing large prey. Adults reach 30 cm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Needle teeth and hinged skull
sections.body: Enormous fangs fold inward; the skull rotates to swallow fish nearly as long as the viperfish. Green photophores along the side may lure prey in darkness.

sections.heading: Fish and squid in the midnight zone
sections.body: Ambush and pursuit in mesopelagic and bathypelagic depths. Vertical migration places them in feeding layers at night.

sections.heading: Deep oceans worldwide
sections.body: Chauliodus sloani occurs across Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Ocean deep basins. Larvae rise nearer surface before adopting deep adult habits.

sections.heading: Abundant deep predator
sections.body: Least Concern with vast habitat and no fishery. Night trawls regularly capture viperfish where few other vertebrates venture.

faqs.question: How long are viperfish teeth?
faqs.answer: Fangs can exceed half the fish's head length — so long they fold beside the brain.

faqs.question: Do viperfish light up?
faqs.answer: Yes — photophores along the body may attract prey in the black bathypelagic zone.

faqs.question: How deep do viperfish live?
faqs.answer: Hundreds to thousands of metres down, rising higher only at night to feed.

faqs.question: Can viperfish swallow big fish?
faqs.answer: A hinged skull and elastic stomach let them take prey nearly their own length.

faqs.question: Are viperfish dangerous to humans?
faqs.answer: No — they live in deep water and are small; contact with divers is essentially nil.

range.nativeRange: Deep oceans worldwide.

animals.name: Gulper Eel
animals.summary: The gulper eel (Eurypharynx pelecanoides) is a bathypelagic fish with a pelican-like expandable mouth and whip-thin tail. Adults reach 1 m and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Pelican mouth in the abyss
sections.body: The head can balloon enormously to engulf squid and fish whole. A whip-like tail tip glows with photophores — possibly a lure. Body is black, fragile, and ribbon-thin.

sections.heading: Squid and deep fish
sections.body: Opportunistic gulps of whatever fits the expandable jaws. Metabolism is slow; meals may be infrequent in food-sparse depths.

sections.heading: Global bathypelagic zone
sections.body: Found roughly 500–3000 m deep in tropical and temperate oceans worldwide. Larvae look very different — transparent and ribbon-like near surface.

sections.heading: Rarely seen, widely distributed
sections.body: Least Concern despite few observations. Deep trawls and ROV footage confirm a broad range with no targeted harvest.

faqs.question: Why is it called a gulper eel?
faqs.answer: Its huge loosely hinged jaws can open wide like a pelican pouch to swallow large prey.

faqs.question: Is a gulper eel a true eel?
faqs.answer: It is a deep-sea fish in its own family — eel-like but not a typical anguillid eel.

faqs.question: What is the glowing tail tip?
faqs.answer: A photophore at the tail end may lure prey close to the mouth in darkness.

faqs.question: How deep do gulper eels live?
faqs.answer: Mainly bathypelagic depths from about 500 m to nearly 3000 m.

faqs.question: How big is a gulper eel mouth?
faqs.answer: The head can expand to many times the body width when feeding.

range.nativeRange: Deep oceans worldwide.

animals.name: Bonnethead
animals.summary: The bonnethead (Sphyrna tiburo) is the smallest hammerhead shark and the only shark known to eat substantial seagrass. Adults reach 1.5 m, inhabit warm shallows, and are listed Endangered.

sections.heading: Shovel-headed omnivore
sections.body: A rounded cephalofoil — not the classic T-hammer — houses electroreceptors for finding prey buried in sand. Digestive enzymes process both crustaceans and seagrass.

sections.heading: Crabs, shrimp, and seagrass
sections.body: Blue crabs and shrimp dominate carnivorous meals, but gut studies show significant seagrass digestion — rare plant-eating among sharks.

sections.heading: Western Atlantic and eastern Pacific shallows
sections.body: Estuaries, mangroves, and seagrass beds from New England to Brazil and in the Gulf of California. Warm, coastal nursery fidelity defines ecology.

sections.heading: Endangered in bycatch nets
sections.body: IUCN lists bonnethead Endangered. Gillnets and shrimp trawls kill large numbers; seagrass loss removes feeding habitat.

faqs.question: Do bonnethead sharks eat plants?
faqs.answer: Yes — they digest seagrass with enzymes, making them the only known omnivorous shark.

faqs.question: How is a bonnethead head shaped?
faqs.answer: A smooth, rounded hammer — narrower than great hammerheads — like a shovel.

faqs.question: Where do bonnetheads live?
faqs.answer: Warm shallow coastal waters of the western Atlantic and eastern Pacific.

faqs.question: Why is the bonnethead Endangered?
faqs.answer: Heavy bycatch in coastal fisheries and seagrass habitat degradation.

faqs.question: Are bonnetheads dangerous?
faqs.answer: Bites are very rare; they are small coastal sharks focused on crabs and seagrass.

range.nativeRange: Shallow coastal waters of the western Atlantic and eastern Pacific.

animals.name: Common Guitarfish
animals.summary: The common guitarfish (Rhinobatos rhinobatos) is a shark-ray hybrid shape hunted on Mediterranean and Atlantic sands. Adults reach 1 m and 7 kg, and are listed Critically Endangered.

sections.heading: Half shark, half ray
sections.body: A ray-like flattened front with shark-like tail and dorsal fins. Eyes on top scan for prey while camouflaged against sand.

sections.heading: Crabs, worms, and small fish
sections.body: Bottom-dwelling invertebrates and fish are crushed or speared on sandy shallows. Slow reproduction makes populations fragile.

sections.heading: Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic
sections.body: Coastal sands from the Bay of Biscay into the Mediterranean and along West Africa. Shallow habitat overlaps trawl fisheries.

sections.heading: Critically Endangered on the sand
sections.body: IUCN lists common guitarfish Critically Endangered. Bottom trawling and targeted harvest for meat devastated numbers across its range.

faqs.question: Is a guitarfish a shark or a ray?
faqs.answer: It is a rhinobatid — related to rays with a shark-like tail; common name reflects the guitar outline.

faqs.question: Why is the common guitarfish Critically Endangered?
faqs.answer: Intense bottom trawling and coastal fishing removed most individuals from sandy habitat.

faqs.question: Where do guitarfish live?
faqs.answer: Sandy coastal shallows of the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic.

faqs.question: What do guitarfish eat?
faqs.answer: Crabs, worms, molluscs, and small fish dug from the seabed.

faqs.question: Can guitarfish sting?
faqs.answer: They lack the venomous barb of stingrays; defence relies on camouflage and flight.

range.nativeRange: Coastal Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic.

animals.name: Common Torpedo
animals.summary: The common torpedo (Torpedo torpedo) is a Mediterranean electric ray that stuns prey with up to 220 volts. Adults reach 60 cm and 8 kg, and are listed Vulnerable.

sections.heading: Living battery on the seabed
sections.body: Modified muscle organs generate electric shocks to stun fish and deter predators. A rounded disc and small eyes suit buried ambush on sand and mud.

sections.heading: Stunned fish and crustaceans
sections.body: Buried rays discharge when prey approaches, then swallow immobilised fish whole. Shocks also protect against sharks and divers who step on them.

sections.heading: Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic
sections.body: Coastal sands from Norway to South Africa, common in the Mediterranean. Slow movement relies on camouflage and electric defence.

sections.heading: Vulnerable to trawling
sections.body: IUCN lists common torpedo Vulnerable. Bottom trawls capture buried rays; low reproduction limits recovery.

faqs.question: How strong is an electric ray shock?
faqs.answer: Common torpedo can deliver roughly 200+ volts — enough to stun fish and startle humans.

faqs.question: Can electric rays kill people?
faqs.answer: Shocks are painful and can cause injury, but fatalities are extremely rare.

faqs.question: Why is the common torpedo Vulnerable?
faqs.answer: Bottom trawling and coastal fishing mortality outweigh slow breeding capacity.

faqs.question: Do electric rays bury in sand?
faqs.answer: Yes — they hide under sand with eyes exposed, ambushing prey electrically.

faqs.question: Is torpedo named after the ray?
faqs.answer: Yes — naval torpedoes took their name from the Latin for electric ray.

range.nativeRange: Coastal Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic.

animals.name: Red Abalone
animals.summary: Red abalone (Haliotis rufescens) is a large marine snail prized for its mother-of-pearl shell along the California coast. Adults reach 25 cm and 1 kg, graze kelp, and are listed Critically Endangered.

sections.heading: Ear-shaped kelp grazer
sections.body: The shell bears a row of respiratory pores and iridescent nacre inside. A broad foot clamps to rocks while the head grazes drift kelp and algae.

sections.heading: Kelp forest lawnmower
sections.body: Adults feed mainly on giant kelp and other macroalgae. Slow growth and late maturity make populations vulnerable to overharvest.

sections.heading: Pacific California to Baja
sections.body: Rocky subtidal reefs from southern Oregon through California to Baja. Cold upwelling and kelp beds define prime habitat.

sections.heading: Critically Endangered after collapse
sections.body: IUCN lists red abalone Critically Endangered. Withering foot disease, poaching, and kelp loss crashed fisheries closed since the 1990s.

faqs.question: What are the holes in an abalone shell?
faqs.answer: Respiratory pores that release water after gills extract oxygen — a hallmark of abalones.

faqs.question: Why is red abalone Critically Endangered?
faqs.answer: Disease, illegal harvest, and kelp forest decline devastated California populations.

faqs.question: What do abalones eat?
faqs.answer: Mainly kelp and other macroalgae scraped with a rasping radula.

faqs.question: Is abalone shell mother-of-pearl?
faqs.answer: Yes — the inner shell layer is iridescent nacre used in jewellery and inlay.

faqs.question: Can you legally harvest red abalone?
faqs.answer: California fisheries are largely closed; check current state regulations before any collection.

range.nativeRange: Pacific coasts of California and Baja California.

animals.name: Sea Cucumber
animals.summary: The edible sea cucumber (Holothuria edulis) is a soft-bodied echinoderm that vacuums sandy reef flats in the Indo-Pacific. Adults reach 30 cm, recycle sediment, and are listed Least Concern.

sections.heading: Living sand conveyor
sections.body: Leathery bodies lack armour; tentacles around the mouth shovel sediment to extract organic film. Some species eject sticky threads or organs when threatened.

sections.heading: Detritus and reef recycling
sections.body: Sediment processing releases nutrients back to the ecosystem. In aquaculture ponds they improve water quality similarly.

sections.heading: Indo-Pacific reefs and flats
sections.body: Holothuria edulis ranges from East Africa to Polynesia on reef flats and sand patches. Daytime hiding under rubble is common.

sections.heading: Beche-de-mer pressure
sections.body: Least Concern for this species, but global sea-cucumber fisheries have crashed others. Dried beche-de-mer trade drives overharvest in many regions.

faqs.question: Are sea cucumbers animals or plants?
faqs.answer: Animals — they are echinoderms related to sea stars and urchins.

faqs.question: What happens when a sea cucumber is stressed?
faqs.answer: Some eject sticky Cuvierian tubules or expel organs to distract predators, then regenerate.

faqs.question: Why are sea cucumbers harvested?
faqs.answer: Dried beche-de-mer is a luxury food in East Asia, driving intensive fisheries.

faqs.question: What do sea cucumbers eat?
faqs.answer: Organic film and detritus sifted from sand and mud with oral tentacles.

faqs.question: Do sea cucumbers have brains?
faqs.answer: They have a simple nerve ring — enough to coordinate movement and feeding.

range.nativeRange: Indo-Pacific reefs and sand flats.

animals.name: Sand Dollar
animals.summary: The eccentric sand dollar (Echinarachnius parma) is a flat sea urchin that burrows in North Atlantic sand, filtering plankton with spine currents. Adults reach 8 cm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Flat urchin under the sand
sections.body: A rigid test with a five-petal flower pattern on top hides a skirt of spines that move food toward the mouth on the underside. Live animals are purple, not white like beach shells.

sections.heading: Plankton from sediment flows
sections.body: Spines create currents that deliver diatoms and detritus to mouth grooves. Burrowing keeps the animal just below the sand surface.

sections.heading: North Atlantic coastal sands
sections.body: Echinarachnius parma lives from Labrador to Massachusetts on subtidal and low-tide sands. Dense beds can cover hectares offshore.

sections.heading: Beachcombing versus live beds
sections.body: Least Concern with extensive habitat. Bleached tests wash ashore after storms; collecting live dollars from shallow beds can locally thin populations.

faqs.question: Are sand dollars alive when white?
faqs.answer: White discs are usually dead tests; live sand dollars are purple and covered in tiny spines.

faqs.question: What is the flower on a sand dollar?
faqs.answer: A five-part petal pattern where tube feet and respiratory pores align on the upper surface.

faqs.question: How do sand dollars eat?
faqs.answer: Spine currents pass sand grains to mouth grooves that extract organic film and plankton.

faqs.question: Where are eccentric sand dollars found?
faqs.answer: North Atlantic sandy seabeds from Canada to New England.

faqs.question: Are sand dollars related to sea urchins?
faqs.answer: Yes — they are flattened irregular echinoids in the same phylum.

range.nativeRange: North Atlantic coastal sands of North America.

animals.name: Gumboot Chiton
animals.summary: The gumboot chiton (Cryptochiton stelleri) is the largest chiton in the world, with a reddish leathery girdle on North Pacific rocks. Adults reach 30 cm and 1 kg and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Leathery coat over eight plates
sections.body: Unlike smaller chitons with visible armour rings, the gumboot's plates are hidden under a thick reddish mantle. A broad foot grips wave-swept boulders.

sections.heading: Algae scraper of surf zones
sections.body: A rasping radula scrapes diatoms and macroalgae from rock surfaces. Slow movement suits intertidal and shallow subtidal zones.

sections.heading: North Pacific rocky shores
sections.body: From Alaska to California and across to Asia on exposed coasts. Large size makes it a tidepool landmark.

sections.heading: Sturdy on the rocks
sections.body: Least Concern across a long coastline. Collection for curiosity and localized pollution are minor compared with habitat extent.

faqs.question: What is a chiton?
faqs.answer: A marine mollusc with eight overlapping shell plates and a muscular foot — like a armoured slug.

faqs.question: Why is it called gumboot chiton?
faqs.answer: The thick leathery girdle resembles a reddish rubber boot covering the shell plates.

faqs.question: How big is a gumboot chiton?
faqs.answer: Up to about 30 cm — the world's largest chiton species.

faqs.question: What do gumboot chitons eat?
faqs.answer: Algae and biofilm scraped from rocks with a radula.

faqs.question: Where can you find gumboot chitons?
faqs.answer: Rocky North Pacific shores from Alaska to California.

range.nativeRange: North Pacific rocky shores from Alaska to California and Asia.

animals.name: Feather Star
animals.summary: The common feather star (Antedon bifida) is a crinoid that walks on cirri while waving feathered arms to filter plankton. Adults reach 15 cm arm span and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Walking flower of the reef
sections.body: Feather stars are crinoids — ancient echinoderms with many branched arms lined in tube feet for filtering. Hooked cirri on the stalk let them crawl and re-anchor.

sections.heading: Plankton from passing currents
sections.body: Arms form a fan in current, trapping particles moved toward the mouth at the arm base. Some species host tiny shrimp among the pinnules.

sections.heading: Northeast Atlantic rocky reefs
sections.body: Antedon bifida lives from Norway to the Mediterranean on rocks and wrecks. Daytime they cling in current-swept sites.

sections.heading: Living fossil, stable stock
sections.body: Least Concern with broad range. Crinoids dominated Paleozoic seas; feather stars are their reduced, mobile descendants.

faqs.question: Are feather stars related to starfish?
faqs.answer: Both are echinoderms, but crinoids sit on a separate branch with filter-feeding arms on a stalk base.

faqs.question: Can feather stars swim?
faqs.answer: Some species pulse arms to swim short distances, but Antedon usually crawls with cirri.

faqs.question: What do feather stars eat?
faqs.answer: Plankton and organic particles filtered from water currents.

faqs.question: Why are crinoids called living fossils?
faqs.answer: Their body plan dates back hundreds of millions of years with few changes.

faqs.question: Where do common feather stars live?
faqs.answer: Rocky subtidal habitats in the northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean.

range.nativeRange: Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean rocky subtidal.

animals.name: Brittle Star
animals.summary: The common brittle star (Ophiothrix fragilis) forms dense carpets on northeast Atlantic gravel, arms raised to filter feed. Adults reach 15 cm arm span and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Arms that break to escape
sections.body: Long flexible arms detach easily when grabbed, regenerating later. A central disc hides the mouth; tube feet lack suckers unlike true starfish.

sections.heading: Filter feeding in aggregations
sections.body: Arms are held vertical in current to trap plankton. Winter aggregations can cover thousands per square metre on gravel bottoms.

sections.heading: Northeast Atlantic gravel beds
sections.body: From Norway to the Mediterranean on rocky and gravel seabeds. Trawling disturbance can break arms but populations rebound by regeneration.

sections.heading: Swarm engineer
sections.body: Least Concern and often superabundant. Dense mats alter sediment chemistry and provide food for fish and crustaceans.

faqs.question: Why are they called brittle stars?
faqs.answer: Arms snap off easily under predator attack and regrow over time.

faqs.question: How do brittle stars feed?
faqs.answer: Many species filter plankton with raised arms; others scavenge detritus on the seabed.

faqs.question: Are brittle stars the same as starfish?
faqs.answer: They are related echinoderms in class Ophiuroidea with thinner, more flexible arms.

faqs.question: Can brittle stars regrow arms?
faqs.answer: Yes — lost arms regenerate if the central disc survives.

faqs.question: Why do brittle stars form dense beds?
faqs.answer: Current-fed gravel offers ideal filter-feeding conditions, triggering huge aggregations.

range.nativeRange: Northeast Atlantic rocky and gravel seabeds.

animals.name: Box Jellyfish
animals.summary: The box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri) is the most venomous marine animal, with cube-shaped bells and trailing tentacles in northern Australian waters. Adults reach 30 cm bell height and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Cube bell, deadly tentacles
sections.body: Four-sided bells and up to 15 tentacles each carry millions of nematocysts. Complex eyes on stalks may help navigate mangrove channels toward prey.

sections.heading: Shrimp and fish in shallows
sections.body: Fast pulsating swimming lets them hunt in tropical shallows rather than drifting like many jellyfish. Venom can kill fish instantly and humans within minutes.

sections.heading: Northern Australian coasts
sections.body: Shallow tropical waters from Western Australia through Queensland. Seasonal stinger nets protect popular beaches in Cairns and Townsville.

sections.heading: Dangerous but not endangered
sections.body: IUCN lists Chironex fleckeri Least Concern. Public health measures — vinegar, nets, education — manage risk; populations remain robust.

faqs.question: How venomous is Chironex fleckeri?
faqs.answer: Its sting can cause cardiac arrest within minutes — among the deadliest venoms known.

faqs.question: Do box jellyfish have eyes?
faqs.answer: Yes — clusters of eyes on the bell may support navigation toward light gaps and prey.

faqs.question: What should you do for a box jelly sting?
faqs.answer: Pour vinegar to disable undischarged stingers and seek emergency medical care immediately.

faqs.question: When are box jellyfish most common?
faqs.answer: Warm wet-season months in northern Australia — stinger nets are seasonal.

faqs.question: Are box jellyfish endangered?
faqs.answer: No — IUCN lists them Least Concern despite their medical danger to humans.

range.nativeRange: Northern Australian coastal waters.

animals.name: Moon Jellyfish
animals.summary: The moon jellyfish (Aurelia aurita) is a translucent pulsing disc common in harbours worldwide, harmless to most swimmers. Bell diameter reaches 40 cm and the species is Least Concern.

sections.heading: Four rings in a glass bell
sections.body: Transparent bells show four horseshoe gonads. Short fine tentacles carry mild stinging cells. Rhythmic pulsation drives slow cruising in weak currents.

sections.heading: Plankton and mollusc larvae
sections.body: Cilia on oral arms move food to the mouth. They thrive in nutrient-rich harbours where zooplankton blooms.

sections.heading: Coastal seas nearly worldwide
sections.body: Harbours, bays, and shelf seas in temperate and tropical waters. Aurelia aurita is a complex of similar species globally.

sections.heading: Bloom and bust cycles
sections.body: Least Concern and often superabundant. Warm water, aquaculture nutrients, and reduced predators trigger spectacular blooms that clog power plant intakes.

faqs.question: Are moon jellyfish dangerous?
faqs.answer: Stings are mild for most people — a tingle rather than the medical emergency of box jellyfish.

faqs.question: What are the pink shapes inside the bell?
faqs.answer: Horseshoe-shaped gonads — reproductive organs visible through the transparent tissue.

faqs.question: Why do moon jellyfish bloom?
faqs.answer: Nutrient runoff, warming water, and fewer predators can trigger huge seasonal swarms.

faqs.question: Do moon jellyfish have brains?
faqs.answer: They have a diffuse nerve net — enough to pulse and orient but not for complex thought.

faqs.question: Where are moon jellyfish found?
faqs.answer: Coastal waters worldwide, especially harbours and sheltered bays.

range.nativeRange: Coastal waters nearly worldwide.

animals.name: Pistol Shrimp
animals.summary: The pistol shrimp (Alpheus digitalis) snaps its claw to create a cavitation bubble that stuns prey and communicates with mates. Adults reach 5 cm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Cavitation snap
sections.body: The enlarged claw closes so fast it vaporises water, producing a bubble that collapses with a snap up to 210 decibels — stunning prey and generating a flash of heat and light.

sections.heading: Worms, fish, and goby partners
sections.body: Small fish and invertebrates are stunned then eaten. Many species share burrows with gobies that watch for danger while shrimp maintain the tunnel.

sections.heading: Indo-Pacific reef sand
sections.body: Alpheus digitalis inhabits burrows in tropical reef flats and rubble. Snapping choruses audible on quiet reefs come from colonies.

sections.heading: Noisy but secure
sections.body: Least Concern across extensive reef habitat. Symbiosis with gobies and cryptic burrows protect them from many predators.

faqs.question: How loud is a pistol shrimp snap?
faqs.answer: The cavitation pop can exceed 200 decibels — louder than a gunshot at close range.

faqs.question: Why do pistol shrimp have one big claw?
faqs.answer: The major claw is specialised for the high-speed snap that stuns prey.

faqs.question: Do pistol shrimp partner with gobies?
faqs.answer: Yes — gobies stand guard while shrimp dig; both retreat into the shared burrow when threatened.

faqs.question: Can pistol shrimp break glass?
faqs.answer: Colonies in aquariums can crack thin glass with repeated snaps — a known hobby hazard.

faqs.question: What do pistol shrimp eat?
faqs.answer: Small fish, worms, and crustaceans stunned by the cavitation snap.

range.nativeRange: Indo-Pacific reefs and burrows.

animals.name: Japanese Spider Crab
animals.summary: The Japanese spider crab (Macrocheira kaempferi) is the world's largest arthropod, with leg spans reaching 3.7 m in deep Pacific waters off Japan. Adults weigh 20 kg and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Leg span of a small car
sections.body: Spindly legs and a relatively small knobby carapace create record arthropod span. Slow metabolism suits cold deep water on continental slopes.

sections.heading: Scavenger of the deep slope
sections.body: Dead fish, molluscs, and plant debris are picked from the seabed. Adults migrate seasonally to shallower depths for breeding.

sections.heading: Deep waters off Japan
sections.body: Pacific slopes around Honshu and nearby depths of 200–800 m. Larvae develop in plankton before settling to the abyssal fringe.

sections.heading: Protected giant
sections.body: Least Concern with fishing restrictions in Japan. Aquarium displays and cultural fame support conservation awareness.

faqs.question: How wide is a Japanese spider crab?
faqs.answer: Leg span can reach about 3.7 m — the largest known arthropod span.

faqs.question: Are Japanese spider crabs dangerous?
faqs.answer: They are slow deep-water scavengers; claws can pinch but they are not predators of humans.

faqs.question: Where do Japanese spider crabs live?
faqs.answer: Deep Pacific continental slopes primarily around Japan.

faqs.question: What do Japanese spider crabs eat?
faqs.answer: Carrion, molluscs, and plant material scavenged on the seabed.

faqs.question: Can you eat Japanese spider crab?
faqs.answer: Yes — it is a delicacy in Japan under regulated fisheries.

range.nativeRange: Deep waters off Japan.

animals.name: Vampire Squid
animals.summary: The vampire squid (Vampyroteuthis infernalis) is a deep-sea cephalopod that turns its cape inside out and eats marine snow, not blood. Adults reach 30 cm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Cape of cirri, not a bloodsucker
sections.body: A dark webbing between arms can invert like a vampire cloak, exposing soft cirri tipped with suckers. Red-blue photophores dot the skin. It is not a true squid or octopus but its own order.

sections.heading: Marine snow specialist
sections.body: Detritus, dead plankton, and gel particles are collected with sticky filaments on cirri — unusual among cephalopods that usually hunt live prey.

sections.heading: Oxygen-minimum zones worldwide
sections.body: Temperate and tropical deep midwaters with low oxygen. Vertical migration places it in food-rich layers at night.

sections.heading: Secure in the abyss
sections.body: Least Concern with huge deep habitat and no fishery. ROV footage made it an icon of deep-sea biology despite the scary name.

faqs.question: Do vampire squids drink blood?
faqs.answer: No — they eat marine snow (detritus and dead plankton); the name refers to their dark cape-like webbing.

faqs.question: What happens when a vampire squid is threatened?
faqs.answer: It inverts its webbed arms to expose spiny cirri and can release bioluminescent mucus.

faqs.question: Is a vampire squid a true squid?
faqs.answer: It sits in its own order Vampyromorphida, separate from squids and octopuses.

faqs.question: How deep do vampire squids live?
faqs.answer: Hundreds to about 900 m in oxygen-poor midwaters worldwide.

faqs.question: What is marine snow?
faqs.answer: Slowly sinking detritus and dead plankton that feeds many deep animals.

range.nativeRange: Oxygen-minimum zones of deep oceans worldwide.

animals.name: Dumbo Octopus
animals.summary: The dumbo octopus (Grimpoteuthis spp.) glides on ear-like fins above abyssal soft bottoms worldwide. Adults reach 30 cm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Fins like elephant ears
sections.body: Flapping lateral fins and webbed arms let dumbo octopuses hover just above sediment. Pale gelatinous bodies suit crushing-pressure depths.

sections.heading: Worms and crustaceans on mud
sections.body: Prey is engulfed or picked from the seabed; hunting is slow and opportunistic in food-sparse abyss.

sections.heading: Abyssal plains worldwide
sections.body: Grimpoteuthis species occur globally on soft bottoms roughly 1000–7000 m deep. ROV encounters are rare but widespread.

sections.heading: Beyond fishery reach
sections.body: Least Concern with no harvest and vast habitat. Deep mining and climate impacts are future concerns, not present drivers.

faqs.question: Why is it called a dumbo octopus?
faqs.answer: Ear-like fins flapping as it swims resemble Disney's Dumbo the elephant.

faqs.question: How deep do dumbo octopuses live?
faqs.answer: Typically abyssal depths from about 1000 m to 7000 m on soft sediment.

faqs.question: Do dumbo octopuses have ink?
faqs.answer: Many deep species lack ink sacs; defence relies on gelatinous bodies and depth.

faqs.question: What do dumbo octopuses eat?
faqs.answer: Small worms, crustaceans, and other benthic invertebrates on the abyssal floor.

faqs.question: Are dumbo octopuses intelligent?
faqs.answer: Like other octopuses they show curiosity in ROV footage, though little is known of cognition at depth.

range.nativeRange: Abyssal oceans worldwide.

animals.name: Giant Pacific Octopus
animals.summary: The giant Pacific octopus (Enteroctopus dofleini) is the largest octopus species, with arm spans to 9 m and 50 kg in North Pacific dens. It is listed Least Concern.

sections.heading: Nine-metre arm span
sections.body: Three hearts, blue copper-based blood, and colour-changing skin suit cold Pacific reefs. Dens under boulders hold middens of crab and clam shells.

sections.heading: Crabs, clams, and fish
sections.body: Powerful arms and a hard beak open shellfish and seize fish. Short lifespans end after a single breeding bout — females guard eggs without feeding.

sections.heading: North Pacific rocky coasts
sections.body: Alaska to California and Japan on rocky reefs and kelp forests. Intertidal to 200 m depths.

sections.heading: Fishery and aquarium pressure
sections.body: Least Concern range-wide. Small commercial and sport fisheries and aquarium collection affect local densities; most coast habitat remains extensive.

faqs.question: How big is a giant Pacific octopus?
faqs.answer: Record specimens exceed 9 m arm span and 50 kg, though most adults are smaller.

faqs.question: How long do giant Pacific octopuses live?
faqs.answer: About 3–5 years — they die after reproducing once.

faqs.question: Do giant Pacific octopuses use tools?
faqs.answer: They manipulate objects and open jars in captivity; wild octopuses stack rocks at den entrances.

faqs.question: What colour is giant Pacific octopus blood?
faqs.answer: Blue — copper-based hemocyanin carries oxygen in cold water.

faqs.question: Where can you see giant Pacific octopuses?
faqs.answer: Rocky North Pacific shores and major public aquariums from Seattle to Tokyo.

range.nativeRange: North Pacific from California to Alaska and Japan.

animals.name: Water Bear
animals.summary: The water bear (Milnesium tardigradum) is a microscopic tardigrade famous for surviving vacuum, radiation, and decades of desiccation. Adults reach 1 mm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Eight-legged barrel of resilience
sections.body: Tardigrades walk slowly on four pairs of clawed legs. A stylet mouth pierces plant and animal cells in moss films. Bodies are segmented yet microscopic.

sections.heading: Moss films and lichens
sections.body: They graze on plant cells, bacteria, and rotifers in thin water films on moss, lichen, and soil worldwide — including rooftops and Antarctica.

sections.heading: Every continent including Antarctica
sections.body: Milnesium tardigradum and relatives occur wherever a film of moisture persists. Distribution is essentially global.

sections.heading: Indestructible at micro scale
sections.body: Least Concern with untold billions. Cryptobiosis — tun formation — lets them survive extreme dryness, cold, and radiation experiments in labs.

faqs.question: Can tardigrades survive in space?
faqs.answer: Lab experiments exposed tun-state tardigrades to vacuum and radiation; many revived after rehydration.

faqs.question: How do tardigrades survive drying out?
faqs.answer: They curl into a dry tun, replacing water with protective sugars until moisture returns.

faqs.question: How big is a water bear?
faqs.answer: About 0.3–1 mm — visible only under a low-power microscope.

faqs.question: Where do you find tardigrades?
faqs.answer: In moss, lichen, soil, and roof moss anywhere with occasional moisture.

faqs.question: Are tardigrades endangered?
faqs.answer: No — they are among the most abundant and widespread micro-animals on Earth.

range.nativeRange: Moss and lichen worldwide.

animals.name: Velvet Worm
animals.summary: The velvet worm (Peripatus spp.) is a soft-bodied invertebrate lineage between worms and arthropods that shoots slime to trap prey in tropical leaf litter. Adults reach 10 cm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Slime cannon from a living fossil
sections.body: Velvety skin covers stubby unjointed legs — a body plan unchanged since the Cambrian. Oral papillae squirt rapid-hardening slime that immobilises prey.

sections.heading: Termites, crickets, and spiders
sections.body: Nocturnal hunters spray slime from a range of several centimetres, then bite with jaws. Females retain eggs internally in some species or lay them in moss.

sections.heading: Southern Hemisphere rainforests
sections.body: Tropical forests of South America, Australia, and New Zealand hold most species. Rotting logs and leaf litter provide humidity.

sections.heading: Hidden but secure
sections.body: Least Concern where forest remains. Habitat loss matters locally, but many populations live in extensive undisturbed litter layers.

faqs.question: What do velvet worms shoot?
faqs.answer: Quick-hardening slime from oral papillae that glues prey in place.

faqs.question: Are velvet worms insects?
faqs.answer: No — they are onychophorans, a distinct phylum related to arthropods and annelids.

faqs.question: Why are they called velvet worms?
faqs.answer: Soft, velvety dermal papillae give a plush texture and blue-green sheen.

faqs.question: Where do velvet worms live?
faqs.answer: Moist leaf litter and rotting wood in tropical Southern Hemisphere forests.

faqs.question: How old is the velvet worm lineage?
faqs.answer: Fossils show similar forms over 500 million years — true living fossils.

range.nativeRange: Tropical forests of the Southern Hemisphere.

animals.name: Sea Angel
animals.summary: The sea angel (Clione limacina) is a shell-less pelagic snail that swims with wing-like parapodia and hunts shelled pteropods in Arctic seas. Adults reach 5 cm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Winged snail without a shell
sections.body: Sea angels shed the shell their ancestors carried. Parapodia flap like wings for slow swimming in cold water. Bodies are mostly transparent except an orange gut.

sections.heading: Shell-drilling pteropod hunter
sections.body: Specialised radula teeth hook and extract shelled sea butterflies (Limacina). High predation can structure pteropod populations in Arctic food webs.

sections.heading: Cold Arctic and subarctic seas
sections.body: North Atlantic and Pacific polar waters. Seasonal blooms track their shelled prey in plankton.

sections.heading: Climate sentinel
sections.body: Least Concern currently. Warming and acidification affect pteropod prey; sea angels are studied as indicators of polar pelagic change.

faqs.question: Why is it called a sea angel?
faqs.answer: Wing-like parapodia and graceful swimming in cold clear water suggested angel wings.

faqs.question: Do sea angels have shells?
faqs.answer: Adults are naked — they lost the shell during evolution toward pelagic life.

faqs.question: What do sea angels eat?
faqs.answer: Mainly shelled sea butterflies (Limacina pteropods), extracted with hooked teeth.

faqs.question: Where are sea angels found?
faqs.answer: Cold Arctic and subarctic open waters of the North Atlantic and Pacific.

faqs.question: Are sea angels related to sea slugs?
faqs.answer: Both are gastropods, but sea angels are pelagic pteropods, not benthic nudibranchs.

range.nativeRange: Cold Arctic and subarctic seas.

animals.name: Crown-of-thorns Starfish
animals.summary: The crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster planci) is a venomous coral predator whose outbreaks can devastate Indo-Pacific reefs. Adults reach 80 cm and are listed Least Concern.

sections.heading: Spiny coral predator
sections.body: Up to 21 arms bear venomous thorns. A stomach can be everted to digest coral polyps externally, leaving white scars on living reef.

sections.heading: Coral polyp digester
sections.body: A single adult can consume several square metres of coral yearly. Outbreaks of thousands per reef trigger mass bleaching-like damage.

sections.heading: Indo-Pacific coral reefs
sections.body: From the Red Sea and East Africa to the Pacific islands and Great Barrier Reef. Larvae ride currents for weeks before settling.

sections.heading: Outbreaks, not extinction
sections.body: IUCN lists the species Least Concern. Natural cycles and nutrient runoff drive outbreaks; divers manually remove stars and breeding disruption programs protect tourism reefs.

faqs.question: Are crown-of-thorns starfish venomous?
faqs.answer: Sharp spines deliver painful toxins — gloves are essential when handling them.

faqs.question: Why are outbreaks a problem?
faqs.answer: Thousands of stars can eat live coral faster than reefs recover, causing long-term damage.

faqs.question: What causes crown-of-thorns outbreaks?
faqs.answer: Nutrient runoff boosting plankton food for larvae and removal of natural predators may both play roles.

faqs.question: How do crown-of-thorns eat coral?
faqs.answer: They extrude their stomach onto polyps and digest tissue externally.

faqs.question: Is the crown-of-thorns starfish endangered?
faqs.answer: No — IUCN lists it Least Concern despite its threat to corals during outbreaks.

range.nativeRange: Indo-Pacific coral reefs.

animals.name: Carpenter Bee
animals.summary: The eastern carpenter bee (Xylocopa virginica) drills nest tunnels in soft wood while pollinating spring flowers across eastern North America. Adults reach 2.5 cm and are Least Concern.

sections.heading: Wood-driller pollinator
sections.body: Large bees resemble bumblebees but have shiny hairless abdomens. Females excavate round tunnels in dead wood; males patrol flowers without stinging ability.

sections.heading: Nectar robber and true pollinator
sections.body: Long tongues reach deep flowers; some visits bypass pollen by piercing petals. Nonetheless they pollinate passionflowers, wisteria, and many garden blooms.

sections.heading: Eastern US woodlands and porches
sections.body: Forests, gardens, and structural timbers from Texas to New York. Unpainted softwood fascia and deck rails often host nest galleries.

sections.heading: Pest label, pollinator reality
sections.body: Least Concern and widespread. Structural damage is usually cosmetic; coexistence tips include hardwood trim and bee hotels away from siding.

faqs.question: Do carpenter bees eat wood?
faqs.answer: Females excavate tunnels for nests but do not eat wood — they feed on nectar and pollen.

faqs.question: Can carpenter bees sting?
faqs.answer: Females can sting if handled; males are aggressive but lack stingers.

faqs.question: How do carpenter bees differ from bumblebees?
faqs.answer: Carpenter bees have shiny, mostly hairless abdomens; bumblebees are fuzzy all over.

faqs.question: Why do carpenter bees hover at people?
faqs.answer: Males patrol territories and may fly at intruders without ability to sting.

faqs.question: Are carpenter bees good pollinators?
faqs.answer: Yes — despite occasional nectar robbing, they pollinate many spring and summer flowers.

range.nativeRange: Eastern North America woodlands and gardens.

animals.name: Honey Badger
animals.summary: The honey badger (Mellivora capensis) is a famously fearless mustelid of Africa and Asia, armed with loose, rubbery skin, powerful digging claws, and a remarkable resistance to snake venom. It weighs 9–16 kg (20–35 lb), can run at up to 30 km/h, and lives around 7–8 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Built like a tank
sections.body: The honey badger is a stocky, low-slung member of the weasel family about a metre long including the tail, instantly recognised by the silvery-grey mantle running from its head to the base of its tail. Its skin is up to 6 mm thick and so loose that a bitten animal can twist around inside it and counter-attack with jaws and claws. Powerful foreclaws, strong jaws, and a dogged temperament complete the armoury.

sections.heading: Diet and the taste for honey
sections.body: Honey badgers are opportunistic omnivores recorded eating more than sixty prey species, from dung-beetle larvae to porcupines and pythons. Their name comes from raiding beehives for honey and protein-rich bee brood, shrugging off hundreds of stings thanks to their thick skin. The greater honeyguide bird is famous for leading honey badgers (and people) to wild hives, then feeding on the scraps.

sections.heading: Fearless defence
sections.body: The Guinness Book of Records has called the honey badger the world's most fearless animal, and with reason: individuals have been filmed confronting lions, leopards, and hyenas many times their size. When cornered they snarl, charge, and can release a choking scent from an anal pouch. They also possess a degree of immunity to neurotoxic snake venom, allowing them to survive cobra and puff adder bites that would kill far larger animals.

sections.heading: Behaviour and intelligence
sections.body: Honey badgers are mostly solitary and range over enormous territories — males may cover hundreds of square kilometres. They are considered among the most intelligent mustelids: in captivity they have been filmed stacking and dragging objects to escape enclosures, a rare example of tool use in a carnivore. Much of their activity is nocturnal, especially near human settlement.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The species occupies a huge range across sub-Saharan Africa (avoiding only the densest rainforest and the central Sahara) and east through the Middle East to Iran, Turkmenistan, and India. It thrives in dry savanna, thornscrub, and semi-desert, sheltering in burrows it digs itself or takes over from other animals.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: The honey badger is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN thanks to its wide range and adaptability, but numbers are declining locally. Beekeepers sometimes kill them in defence of hives, and they are caught in traps set for other animals, taken for bushmeat, and used in traditional medicine. Protected areas across Africa and parts of Asia hold healthy populations.

faqs.question: Why is the honey badger so fearless?
faqs.answer: Its defence package — skin up to 6 mm thick that hangs loose on the body, a high pain threshold, powerful jaws and claws, and resistance to snake venom — means most attacks cost a predator far more effort than the meal is worth. Standing its ground is usually the winning strategy.

faqs.question: Are honey badgers immune to snake venom?
faqs.answer: Not fully immune, but highly resistant. Neurotoxins from cobras can temporarily incapacitate a honey badger, which then typically revives within hours and resumes feeding — often on the snake that bit it.

faqs.question: Do honey badgers really eat honey?
faqs.answer: Yes. They raid wild and domestic beehives for honey and especially for the protein-rich larvae, enduring hundreds of stings. The greater honeyguide bird actively leads them to hives and feeds on the leftovers.

faqs.question: Where do honey badgers live?
faqs.answer: Across most of sub-Saharan Africa, plus the Arabian Peninsula, Iran, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent — anywhere dry savanna, scrub, or semi-desert offers food and digging ground.

faqs.question: Can a honey badger kill a lion?
faqs.answer: No — a healthy adult lion can kill a honey badger, and sometimes does. But the badger's ferocity, loose skin, and stamina make the fight so costly that lions and other big predators usually back off.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Omnivore — honey and bee brood, rodents, snakes, scorpions, eggs, roots, and fruit

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Savanna, grassland, and dry scrub across sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: Around 7–8 years in the wild; up to 24 years in captivity

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: 9–16 kg (20–35 lb); males heavier than females

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 30 km/h (19 mph); can dig a burrow and disappear in minutes

range.nativeRange: Savanna and dry scrub across sub-Saharan Africa, plus the Arabian Peninsula, Iran, Central Asia, and India.

animals.name: Arctic Fox
animals.summary: The Arctic fox (Vulpes lagopus) is a small, compact fox of the circumpolar tundra that turns white in winter and brown-grey in summer. Weighing just 2.5–9 kg (6–20 lb), it survives temperatures below −50 °C behind the warmest fur of any mammal, and typically lives 3–6 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Arctic engineering
sections.body: Everything about the Arctic fox minimises heat loss: a rounded body, short muzzle, small ears, and even fur-covered foot pads — unique among canids. Its multi-layered winter coat is the warmest fur of any mammal, so effective that the fox's metabolism does not rise until temperatures approach −50 °C, and it can rest in the open at far lower temperatures.

sections.heading: Two coats a year
sections.body: Most Arctic foxes moult from snow-white winter pelage to a brown-grey summer coat that blends with bare tundra. A second, genetically determined 'blue' morph stays charcoal-grey year-round and is commonest in coastal populations such as those of Iceland and the Aleutian Islands. The seasonal colour swap is triggered by day length.

sections.heading: Diet and scavenging
sections.body: Lemmings and voles are the staple, and fox numbers boom and crash with rodent cycles. Arctic foxes locate prey under snow by sound, then pounce head-first through the crust. They cache surplus food — thousands of seabird eggs in a good season — and trail polar bears across the sea ice to scavenge seal remains.

sections.heading: Wide-ranging travellers
sections.body: Arctic foxes hold the record for long-distance travel in a land carnivore of their size. In one famous tracking study, a young female covered more than 3,500 km from coastal Norway across the sea ice to Canada in 76 days. Most foxes stay closer to home, defending dens that may be used by generation after generation for centuries.

sections.heading: Raising pups in the cold
sections.body: Pairs mate for life and breed in spring, timing the litter to coincide with peak rodent abundance. Litters average six to twelve pups but can exceed twenty in lemming years — among the largest of any wild mammal. Both parents guard the den, which is dug into a frost-free slope or esker with many entrances.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Globally the Arctic fox is listed as Least Concern, with a healthy circumpolar population. The Fennoscandian population is a stark exception: after historical fur trapping it remains critically small — only a few hundred adults across Norway, Sweden, and Finland — and now faces added pressure from red foxes expanding north as the climate warms. Feeding programmes and red-fox control are slowly helping it recover.

faqs.question: Why do Arctic foxes change colour?
faqs.answer: For camouflage. A white winter coat hides them on snow and sea ice, while the brown-grey summer coat matches bare tundra. The change is moult triggered by day length, not by temperature.

faqs.question: How do Arctic foxes survive extreme cold?
faqs.answer: They combine the warmest fur of any mammal with a compact, low-surface-area body, fur-covered paw pads, and counter-current heat exchange in the legs. Their metabolism barely increases until about −50 °C.

faqs.question: What do Arctic foxes eat?
faqs.answer: Mainly lemmings and voles, plus ground-nesting birds, eggs, fish, and carrion. On the coast they scavenge seal carcasses left by polar bears and cache surplus food in the ground for lean times.

faqs.question: Are Arctic foxes endangered?
faqs.answer: Not globally — the IUCN lists the species as Least Concern. However, the isolated population in mainland Norway, Sweden, and Finland is critically endangered and the subject of active recovery programmes.

faqs.question: How far can an Arctic fox travel?
faqs.answer: Remarkably far. One satellite-tracked female travelled over 3,500 km from Norway to Canada in 76 days, one of the fastest long-distance journeys ever recorded for a land mammal of its size.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Lemmings, voles, birds, eggs, fish, carrion, and polar-bear leftovers

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Arctic tundra and coastal sea ice across North America, Greenland, Iceland, and Eurasia

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: 3–6 years in the wild; up to 15 years in captivity

facts.label: Top speed
facts.value: Up to 50 km/h (31 mph) in short bursts

range.nativeRange: Circumpolar Arctic tundra — Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Iceland, Scandinavia, and Russia.

animals.name: Japanese Macaque
animals.summary: The Japanese macaque (Macaca fuscata), or snow monkey, is the world's northernmost wild monkey, famous for bathing in volcanic hot springs in winter. It weighs 8–11 kg (18–24 lb), lives in strict matrilineal troops that can exceed 100 members, and can survive 25–30 years.

sections.heading: The original snow monkey
sections.body: No non-human primate lives further north: Japanese macaques range to the Shimokita Peninsula at 41°N, where winter temperatures drop below −20 °C. Adults have a bare red face, thick brown-grey winter fur, and a short stump of a tail. Males average about 11 kg, females about 8 kg.

sections.heading: Hot-spring culture
sections.body: At Jigokudani Monkey Park in Nagano, macaques have soaked in natural hot springs since the 1960s — a learned behaviour passed down through generations that has become an icon of Japanese wildlife. Bathing is most popular in freezing weather and appears to reduce stress as well as conserve heat.

sections.heading: Famous inventors
sections.body: On the island of Koshima in 1953, researchers watched a young female named Imo begin washing sweet potatoes in the sea — a novel behaviour that spread through her troop and is a classic textbook example of animal culture. The same troop went on to invent wheat-sluicing and other food-handling traditions.

sections.heading: Social structure
sections.body: Troops of 20 to 100 or more are organised around strict female lines: daughters inherit their mother's rank, while males leave at maturity and transfer between troops. Grooming cements alliances, and infants are doted on by the whole group. Macaques communicate with dozens of distinct calls, facial expressions, and body postures.

sections.heading: Diet and habitat
sections.body: Japanese macaques eat a highly seasonal menu — fruit and seeds in autumn, buds and young leaves in spring, bark and winter buds when snow is deep. They live across Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu, from subtropical Yakushima forest to snowy beech and conifer woodland, usually staying within a few kilometres of trees.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: The species is listed as Least Concern and remains widespread, but recovery from historical hunting has brought it into conflict with farmers. Thousands are legally culled each year for raiding fruit orchards and vegetable fields, and hybridisation with introduced rhesus macaques is a local concern in parts of Japan.

faqs.question: Why do snow monkeys bathe in hot springs?
faqs.answer: To keep warm and relax during harsh winters. The habit began at Jigokudani in the 1960s when monkeys copied people using a spa pool, and it has been passed down culturally ever since.

faqs.question: Where do Japanese macaques live?
faqs.answer: Only in Japan — on the islands of Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu, plus smaller islands such as Yakushima. They are the northernmost wild monkeys on Earth.

faqs.question: Do Japanese macaques really have culture?
faqs.answer: Yes — the Koshima troop famously invented sweet-potato washing in 1953, and behaviours such as bathing, wheat-sluicing, and stone play spread socially, which biologists recognise as culture.

faqs.question: How big is a snow monkey troop?
faqs.answer: Typically 20 to 100 animals organised around related females, with a clear dominance hierarchy. Some provisioned troops exceed 150 members.

faqs.question: Are Japanese macaques endangered?
faqs.answer: No — they are listed as Least Concern. The main issues are conflict with agriculture and local hybridisation with introduced rhesus macaques.

facts.label: Habitat

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: 8–11 kg (18–24 lb); males heavier than females

animals.name: Pygmy Hippopotamus
animals.summary: The pygmy hippopotamus (Choeropsis liberiensis) is a small, forest-dwelling cousin of the common hippo found only in West Africa — mostly Liberia. Adults weigh 180–275 kg (400–600 lb) and live around 30–35 years; fewer than about 2,500 mature individuals are thought to remain, making it Endangered.

sections.heading: A pocket-sized hippo
sections.body: Standing 75–100 cm at the shoulder and up to about 1.75 m long, the pygmy hippo is a fraction of its river-hippo cousin — roughly an eighth of the weight. Its skin is smoother, its feet less webbed, and its eyes sit more on the sides of the head, all adaptations to a life spent mostly on land in dense forest.

sections.heading: Life in the forest
sections.body: Unlike the gregarious common hippo, pygmy hippos are solitary or live in pairs and spend the day resting hidden in swamps, rivers, or wallows. At night they forage along a network of well-worn forest trails, staying close to water into which they retreat if threatened.

sections.heading: Diet
sections.body: Pygmy hippos browse rather than graze, feeding on ferns, broad-leaved plants, shoots, and fallen fruit in the forest understorey. Like other hippos they have a multi-chambered stomach that ferments plant material, though they do not ruminate.

sections.heading: Sweating pink
sections.body: Like the common hippo, the pygmy hippo secretes a pinkish fluid often called 'blood sweat' — in reality a natural moisturiser containing hipposudoric acid that acts as both sunscreen and antibiotic, protecting skin in the humid forest.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.body: A single calf of 4.5–6 kg is born after a gestation of about six to seven months. The mother hides her calf in thick vegetation while she forages, returning to suckle it; calves can nurse on land or underwater and stay with their mother for several years.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: The pygmy hippo is listed as Endangered, with an estimated fewer than 2,500 mature individuals scattered across Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Côte d'Ivoire. Deforestation for logging and farms, plus hunting for bushmeat, are the main threats, and civil conflict long hampered surveys. The species breeds well in zoos, which now manage a coordinated captive population.

faqs.question: How big is a pygmy hippo compared to a regular hippo?
faqs.answer: At 180–275 kg it weighs roughly a tenth as much as a common hippopotamus, standing about waist-high to a person — still a solid, barrel-shaped animal, but far better suited to moving through forest.

faqs.question: Where do pygmy hippos live?
faqs.answer: Only in West Africa: chiefly Liberia, with smaller populations in Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Côte d'Ivoire, always in lowland rainforest near rivers and swamps.

faqs.question: Why are pygmy hippos endangered?
faqs.answer: Rainforest loss to logging and agriculture fragments their habitat, and they are hunted for bushmeat. Fewer than about 2,500 mature individuals are thought to survive.

faqs.question: Do pygmy hippos sweat blood?
faqs.answer: No — the pink sheen on their skin is a natural oily secretion containing hipposudoric acid, which moisturises, protects from the sun, and fights infection. It is neither blood nor sweat.

faqs.question: Can pygmy hippos swim?
faqs.answer: Yes, but they are far less aquatic than common hippos. They rest in shallow water and can close their nostrils and ears underwater, yet they feed and travel mostly on land along forest trails.

animals.name: Geoffroy's Spider Monkey
animals.summary: Geoffroy's spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi) is a large, long-limbed monkey of Central American rainforests that swings through the canopy using a prehensile tail as a fifth limb. It weighs 6–9 kg (13–20 lb), lives around 25 years in the wild, and is listed Endangered because of deforestation and hunting.

sections.heading: Built for the canopy
sections.body: Spider monkeys are named for the spindly silhouette made by their long limbs and tail when they hang. Their hands are hook-like with the thumb greatly reduced, an adaptation for swinging, and the prehensile tail — longer than the body, with a naked gripping pad near the tip — can support the animal's full weight, leaving hands free to feed.

sections.heading: Fission–fusion society
sections.body: A community of 20–40 spider monkeys splits each day into small, shifting foraging parties and rejoins later — a 'fission–fusion' pattern that demands sharp social memory. Females leave their birth community at maturity, so the stable core of the group is male; greetings involve embraces, tail-twining, and loud whinnying calls.

sections.heading: Fruit specialists and seed dispersers
sections.body: Ripe fruit can make up 90% of the diet, swallowed with the seeds and deposited across the forest in dung. Because spider monkeys range widely and disperse the seeds of many large-seeded trees, they are considered keystone species for rainforest regeneration.

sections.heading: Arboreal daily life
sections.body: Spider monkeys feed and travel by day and almost never descend to the ground, sleeping high in emergent trees. Mothers carry infants for well over a year — first clinging to the belly, later riding on the back — and give birth only once every two to four years, one reason populations recover slowly.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: Geoffroy's spider monkey lives from the Yucatán Peninsula of southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, in mature evergreen and semi-deciduous forest. Several subspecies are recognised, and it is the only spider monkey found naturally in North America.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Listed as Endangered, Geoffroy's spider monkey has vanished from many areas as rainforest is cleared for ranching and farms, and it is still hunted for bushmeat and the pet trade. All spider monkey species are now threatened, and protecting large, connected blocks of mature forest is the key to their survival.

faqs.question: Why is it called a spider monkey?
faqs.answer: When the monkey hangs by its tail with all four limbs dangling, its long, thin proportions resemble a spider's legs — the likeness that early naturalists used to name it.

faqs.question: Do spider monkeys have thumbs?
faqs.answer: Only a tiny vestigial stub. The thumb is so reduced that the hand works as a hook for swinging; the gripping work is done by the fingers and the prehensile tail.

faqs.question: What do spider monkeys eat?
faqs.answer: Primarily ripe fruit — up to 90% of feeding time — supplemented with young leaves, flowers, seeds, and occasional nuts or insects.

faqs.question: How does the prehensile tail work?
faqs.answer: The tail is muscular and longer than the body, with a bare, fingerprint-like pad on its underside near the tip. It wraps around branches and can hold the monkey's entire weight, effectively acting as a fifth hand.

faqs.question: Why are spider monkeys endangered?
faqs.answer: They need large areas of tall, unbroken rainforest, which is being cleared throughout Central America; they are also hunted for meat and captured for the pet trade. Slow breeding — one infant every two to four years — makes recovery difficult.

animals.name: Common Squirrel Monkey
animals.summary: The common squirrel monkey (Saimiri sciureus) is a tiny Amazonian primate with a white face, black muzzle, and the largest brain relative to body size of any primate. It weighs just 550 g–1.1 kg (1.2–2.4 lb), travels in troops that can exceed 100 monkeys, and lives around 15 years in the wild.

sections.heading: A small monkey with a big brain
sections.body: Squirrel monkeys have the largest brain relative to body mass of any primate — roughly one part brain to seventeen parts body, against about one to thirty-five in humans. The black muzzle set in a white mask, yellow-olive back, and orange limbs make the common squirrel monkey unmistakable; its long tail, longer than its body, aids balance but cannot grasp.

sections.heading: Life in huge troops
sections.body: Troops of 20–75 are typical, but in undisturbed forest several hundred monkeys may travel together — among the largest groups of any primate. Females form the stable core of the troop, while males put on noticeable fat before the breeding season and jostle for rank. Constant soft twittering keeps the moving troop in contact.

sections.heading: Diet and foraging
sections.body: The diet mixes small fruits with insects — crickets, caterpillars, and grasshoppers flushed from the foliage — plus flowers, nectar, and the occasional frog or bat. Squirrel monkeys forage in the middle canopy layers and rarely come to the ground, often associating with capuchins whose feeding stirs up prey.

sections.heading: Communication and intelligence
sections.body: More than two dozen distinct calls have been catalogued, from alarm peeps to contact chucks. Squirrel monkeys also practice 'urine washing', wetting their hands and feet with urine — probably for scent-marking — and they are nimble problem-solvers, long used in learning studies.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.body: Births are tightly synchronised to the rainy season when food peaks. After a gestation of about five months a single infant is born weighing roughly 100 g; it rides on its mother's back and is also carried by other females, a shared-care system known as alloparenting.

sections.heading: Habitat and conservation
sections.body: The common squirrel monkey ranges across the Amazon basin of Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia, and the Guianas, in lowland rainforest and seasonally flooded forest. It is listed as Least Concern and remains common, though the pet trade and forest loss are local pressures; its Central American relative, the black-crowned squirrel monkey, is far more threatened.

faqs.question: Where do squirrel monkeys live?
faqs.answer: Across the Amazon basin of South America — Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia, and the Guianas — in the canopy of lowland rainforest, almost never descending to the ground.

faqs.question: How big is a squirrel monkey?
faqs.answer: Adults have a body of 25–37 cm with a non-prehensile tail of similar length, and weigh only 550 g–1.1 kg — about the size of a grey squirrel, which inspired the name.

faqs.question: Why do squirrel monkeys wash their hands in urine?
faqs.answer: The behaviour, called urine washing, is thought to scent-mark the monkey and the branches it travels over; it may also help with grip or temperature control.

faqs.question: Can squirrel monkeys grab things with their tails?
faqs.answer: No — unlike spider and howler monkeys, the squirrel monkey's tail is not prehensile. It is used purely as a balancing counterweight when leaping through the canopy.

faqs.question: Are squirrel monkeys endangered?
faqs.answer: The common squirrel monkey is listed as Least Concern and is still widespread. Its Central American relative Saimiri oerstedii, however, has a much smaller range and is considered vulnerable to extinction.

animals.name: Red-necked Wallaby
animals.summary: The red-necked wallaby (Notamacropus rufogriseus) is a medium-sized marsupial of eastern Australia and Tasmania, named for the rusty-red fur across its neck and shoulders. Males weigh up to about 26 kg (57 lb), hop at around 40 km/h, and live roughly 9 years in the wild.

sections.heading: Physical description
sections.body: This is one of the largest wallabies: big males can reach 26 kg and about 1.5 m from nose to tail tip. The coat is grizzled grey-fawn with the namesake reddish wash over the nape and shoulders, a pale cheek stripe, and a black nose and paws. Females are roughly two-thirds the male's weight.

sections.heading: Behaviour
sections.body: Red-necked wallabies are mainly solitary grazers, resting in shady forest by day and emerging at dusk to feed in clearings, though they gather loosely where grazing is good. Males establish dominance with upright 'boxing' bouts, balancing on the tail to kick — the classic macropod fighting stance.

sections.heading: Diet
sections.body: They feed mainly on grasses and herbs, cropping them close with sharp incisors, and browse leaves when grass is scarce. Like other kangaroos they ferment plant fibre in a large fore-stomach, which lets them extract moisture efficiently and survive dry spells with little drinking.

sections.heading: Reproduction and the pouch
sections.body: After a gestation of about 30 days, a jellybean-sized joey crawls unaided into the pouch, where it stays for seven to nine months. It continues to suckle as a 'footed joey' for months afterward, and mothers can pause the development of a spare embryo — embryonic diapause — until conditions or pouch space allow.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The species ranges along the Great Dividing Range from Queensland through New South Wales into Victoria, plus Tasmania and the Bass Strait islands, where the local form is known as Bennett's wallaby. Escaped and released animals have established feral populations in New Zealand, Britain, and France.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: The red-necked wallaby is listed as Least Concern and is common across much of its range, sometimes so abundant that it is managed as a pasture pest. Foxes and domestic dogs take young wallabies, and road mortality is significant, but overall numbers are secure.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a wallaby and a kangaroo?
faqs.answer: Mostly size: wallabies are small to medium members of the kangaroo family (generally under about 25 kg), with more compact bodies and slightly different molar teeth suited to browsing as well as grazing.

faqs.question: Where do red-necked wallabies live?
faqs.answer: In the forests and woodlands of eastern Australia from Queensland to Victoria, and across Tasmania. Feral colonies also survive in New Zealand, England, Scotland, and France.

faqs.question: Are there really wild wallabies in Britain?
faqs.answer: Yes — several feral populations descended from zoo escapes and releases. The best-known colony lives on Inchconnachan island in Loch Lomond, Scotland, where they have bred since the 1940s.

faqs.question: How long does a joey stay in the pouch?
faqs.answer: About seven to nine months permanently inside the pouch, after which the young wallaby keeps suckling and sheltering for several more months before becoming independent.

faqs.question: Are red-necked wallabies endangered?
faqs.answer: No — they are listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and are common, even abundant, in many parts of eastern Australia and Tasmania.

animals.name: Alligator Snapping Turtle
animals.summary: The alligator snapping turtle (Macrochelys temminckii) is North America's heaviest freshwater turtle, a prehistoric-looking ambush predator that lures fish within striking range using a worm-like appendage on its tongue. Adults typically weigh 45–80 kg (100–175 lb), grow shells up to 80 cm long, and may live 70 years or more.

sections.heading: A living fossil
sections.body: With a spiked, three-keeled shell, a massive head that will not fit inside it, a hooked beak, and eyes on the sides of the skull, the alligator snapping turtle looks unchanged since the age of dinosaurs. Algae often grows on the shell, completing its camouflage as a mossy log. Big males can exceed 100 kg, though 45–80 kg is typical.

sections.heading: The tongue lure
sections.body: This turtle hunts by deception. It lies motionless on the riverbed with jaws agape and wiggles a pink, worm-shaped appendage on its tongue — the only lingual lure known in any reptile. A fish that swims in to investigate the 'worm' is engulfed by a strike among the fastest movements in the animal kingdom.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The species lives in river systems draining into the Gulf of Mexico: the Mississippi basin and rivers of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia, Alabama, Louisiana, and East Texas, historically north to Kansas, Iowa, and Illinois. It favours deep, slow water with muddy bottoms and plenty of submerged structure.

sections.heading: An aquatic homebody
sections.body: Alligator snappers are almost fully aquatic, able to stay submerged for the better part of an hour, and males may never leave the water. Females come ashore only to nest, sometimes travelling considerable distances to reach a suitable bank. Home ranges can span many kilometres of river.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.body: Females nest in late spring, laying 10–50 eggs in a flask-shaped nest dug above the flood line. Incubation lasts around 100–120 days, and nest temperature determines the sex of the hatchlings. The turtles grow slowly and do not mature until roughly 11–13 years old.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Commercial harvesting for turtle soup in the 1960s and 1970s devastated populations, and the species is now listed as Vulnerable and protected across its range. Dams, channel dredging, and bycatch add further pressure. Genetic work has recently split the complex into additional species — the Suwannee and Apalachicola alligator snapping turtles — and head-start programmes are releasing juveniles in several states.

faqs.question: How strong is an alligator snapping turtle's bite?
faqs.answer: Powerful enough to crush mollusc shells and amputate fingers, although tales of it shearing through broom handles are exaggerated. It is not aggressive but should never be handled — the neck reaches surprisingly far back.

faqs.question: How long do alligator snapping turtles live?
faqs.answer: Captive individuals routinely pass 50 years, and wild lifespans of 70 years or more are considered likely; some authorities suspect they can approach a century.

faqs.question: Where do alligator snapping turtles live?
faqs.answer: In rivers, bayous, and lakes draining to the Gulf of Mexico — the Mississippi basin and waterways of the southeastern United States, from the Florida Panhandle to East Texas.

faqs.question: How does the tongue lure work?
faqs.answer: The turtle rests on the bottom with its mouth open and wriggles a small pink, worm-like projection on its tongue. Fish attracted by the 'worm' swim straight into the open jaws, which snap shut in a split second.

faqs.question: Are alligator snapping turtles endangered?
faqs.answer: They are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN after heavy historical harvesting for soup, and are protected by law throughout their range; captive breeding and release programmes are helping some populations recover.
