animals.name: Indian Rhinoceros
animals.summary: The Indian rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis), or greater one-horned rhino, is an armour-plated giant of Nepal and northeast India with a single black horn. Weighing 1,800–2,700 kg (2–3 tons), it has recovered from fewer than 200 animals a century ago to around 4,000 today, though it remains listed as Vulnerable.

sections.heading: Armour and a single horn
sections.body: The Indian rhino's grey skin hangs in deep folds studded with rivet-like bumps, giving it the look of riveted plate armour. Both sexes carry a single horn of pure keratin — the same material as fingernails — that can reach about 60 cm. Only the African white rhino outweighs it among living rhinos.

sections.heading: Behaviour
sections.body: Indian rhinos are largely solitary, meeting at shared dung heaps that serve as community notice boards. They are semi-aquatic: they wallow for hours in rivers and pools to cool off and protect their skin, feed mostly at dawn and dusk, and despite their bulk can charge at 55 km/h.

sections.heading: Diet
sections.body: Tall grasses are the staple, folded into the mouth with a flexible, almost prehensile upper lip; the rhino also browses leaves and fruit and wades belly-deep to graze aquatic plants. One adult can consume a large share of its body weight in vegetation over a few days of feeding.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The species once ranged across the northern Indian subcontinent from Pakistan to Myanmar; today it survives only in protected pockets of Nepal and India. Kaziranga National Park in Assam holds roughly two-thirds of the world population, with important herds in Chitwan (Nepal), Pobitora, Orang, and Manas.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.body: Females give birth to a single calf after a gestation of about fifteen to sixteen months — one of the longest of any land mammal. The calf, born hornless and weighing around 40–60 kg, stays with its mother for two to four years until she calves again.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Fewer than 200 Indian rhinos survived in the early twentieth century; strict protection, anti-poaching patrols, and translocations have raised the total to around 4,000, one of conservation's great recoveries. The species is nonetheless still Vulnerable: poaching for horn, floodplain habitat loss, and increasingly severe monsoon floods remain serious threats.

faqs.question: How many Indian rhinos are left?
faqs.answer: Around 4,000, the great majority in India's Kaziranga National Park and Nepal's Chitwan. That is a recovery from under 200 a century ago, achieved through armed protection and reintroductions.

faqs.question: Why are Indian rhinos poached?
faqs.answer: For their horn, which is made of keratin — like hair and nails — but commands high prices in illegal wildlife markets for use in traditional medicine, despite having no proven medicinal effect.

faqs.question: Where do Indian rhinos live?
faqs.answer: Only in Nepal and northeast India today: Kaziranga, Pobitora, Orang, and Manas in Assam, plus small populations in West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh, and Chitwan and Bardia in Nepal.

faqs.question: How many horns does an Indian rhino have?
faqs.answer: One — which is why it is also called the greater one-horned rhinoceros. African rhinos and the Sumatran rhino have two.

faqs.question: Is the Indian rhino dangerous?
faqs.answer: It can be. Mothers with calves and surprised adults may charge at up to 55 km/h, and rhinos injure people every year in and around parks. They are best observed at a distance.

animals.name: Sumatran Rhinoceros
animals.summary: The Sumatran rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus sumatrensis) is the smallest and hairiest living rhino, a two-horned rainforest species now reduced to fewer than about 80 animals, nearly all on the island of Sumatra. Weighing 500–960 kg (1,100–2,100 lb), it is the closest living relative of the extinct woolly rhinoceros and is Critically Endangered.

sections.heading: The hairy rhino
sections.body: The Sumatran rhino is a forest rhino in miniature: shoulder height of about a metre to a metre and a half, reddish-brown skin with a fringe of hair on the ears and tail, and two horns, the front one far longer than the rear. Calves are born conspicuously woolly, and adults in damp mountain forest keep a noticeable coat.

sections.heading: A relic of the Ice Age
sections.body: Genetic studies show the Sumatran rhino is the closest living relative of the extinct woolly rhinoceros of Ice Age Eurasia, and its lineage has changed little in millions of years. Within the last two centuries it ranged from India and Bhutan through mainland Southeast Asia to Borneo; now it hangs on in a handful of Sumatran forests.

sections.heading: Solitary forest life
sections.body: Sumatran rhinos live alone in dense forest, feeding before dawn and at dusk and spending midday submerged in mud wallows that cool the skin and deter parasites. They mark trails with dung and bent saplings, climb steep slopes with ease, and are among the most vocal rhinos, producing eerie whistles and song-like calls.

sections.heading: Diet
sections.body: A browser of the understorey, it eats the leaves and shoots of saplings, figs and other fallen fruit, and bark, felling young trees by walking over them. A daily intake of around 50 kg of vegetation sustains a body that, while small for a rhino, still weighs up to nearly a tonne.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.body: Breeding is slow even by rhino standards: a single calf after roughly fifteen to sixteen months of gestation, then several years before the next. Breeding remained elusive in zoos for a century until 2001, when a calf was born at Cincinnati Zoo — knowledge that now underpins the Sumatran Rhino Sanctuary programme in Way Kambas, which has produced several calves.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: With fewer than about 80 individuals scattered in tiny, isolated groups, the Sumatran rhino is Critically Endangered. The greatest danger is no longer only poaching but sheer rarity — groups are so small and dispersed that breeding has nearly stopped in the wild. Indonesia's emergency strategy captures wild rhinos into fenced sanctuaries to form an insurance breeding population alongside habitat protection.

faqs.question: How many Sumatran rhinos are left?
faqs.answer: Fewer than about 80, almost all on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, split between a handful of forest reserves. A tiny remnant may persist in Borneo.

faqs.question: Why is the Sumatran rhino hairy?
faqs.answer: Its reddish hair, thickest on the ears and tail, is a legacy of its ancestry — it is the closest living relative of the Ice Age woolly rhinoceros — suited to cool, damp mountain forest.

faqs.question: Where does the Sumatran rhino live?
faqs.answer: Today almost entirely in Sumatra's remaining rainforests, including Gunung Leuser, Way Kambas, and Bukit Barisan Selatan national parks. It once ranged across Southeast Asia to India and Borneo.

faqs.question: Can Sumatran rhinos be bred in captivity?
faqs.answer: Yes, with great difficulty. The first success came at Cincinnati Zoo in 2001 after years of hormone research, and the Sumatran Rhino Sanctuary in Way Kambas has since produced several calves.

faqs.question: How is it different from other rhinos?
faqs.answer: It is by far the smallest living rhino, the only Asian rhino with two horns, the only hairy one, and a forest browser rather than a grassland grazer.

animals.name: Przewalski's Horse
animals.summary: Przewalski's horse (Equus ferus przewalskii) is the world's last truly wild horse — a stocky, dun-coloured native of the Central Asian steppe that was Extinct in the Wild by the 1960s. Adults weigh 250–360 kg (550–800 lb) and run at up to 55 km/h; today about 2,000 live in reintroduced herds and reserves, and the species is listed as Endangered.

sections.heading: The last wild horse
sections.body: Przewalski's horse — takhi in Mongolian — was never domesticated and differs from domestic horses even in its chromosomes: 66 against the domestic horse's 64. It is compact and big-headed, with a short erect mane that stands up like a mohawk, no forelock, a pale muzzle, and a dun coat marked by a dark dorsal stripe and zebra-like bars on the legs.

sections.heading: Discovery and disappearance
sections.body: The species was described for science in 1881 from reports by the Russian explorer Nikolai Przhevalsky. Within decades, hunting, harsh winters, and competition with livestock pushed it back, and the last confirmed wild sighting came in 1969 in Mongolia. By the 1990s it was formally classed as Extinct in the Wild.

sections.heading: Back from the brink
sections.body: Every Przewalski's horse alive descends from about a dozen animals caught around 1900 and bred in zoos. Coordinated reintroductions began in the 1990s to Mongolia's Hustai National Park and the Gobi, and later to China; the species has since been downlisted from Extinct in the Wild to Critically Endangered and then Endangered — a rare conservation trajectory.

sections.heading: Herd behaviour
sections.body: Wild herds are family groups of one stallion, several mares, and their foals, with surplus males forming bachelor bands. Herds roam widely between water and grazing, paw through snow crust to reach winter grass, and foals stand within an hour of birth — vital on open steppe with wolves about.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The native home is the steppe and semi-desert of Mongolia and adjacent China: open grassland where winter temperatures plunge far below freezing and summer heat exceeds 30 °C. Reintroduced herds now live at Hustai Nuruu, Takhin Tal in the Gobi, and the Kalamaili reserve in Xinjiang, China.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: About 2,000 Przewalski's horses now live in the wild and semi-wild, but the recovery is fragile. Threats include hybridisation with domestic horses, competition with livestock for water and pasture, inbreeding from the tiny founder stock, and catastrophic 'dzud' winters that can kill a large share of a herd in weeks.

faqs.question: Is Przewalski's horse really wild, or just feral?
faqs.answer: It is the one surviving horse population never domesticated — unlike mustangs or brumbies, which descend from escaped domestic horses. It even has a different chromosome count (66 versus 64).

faqs.question: Why does Przewalski's horse have an upright mane?
faqs.answer: The short, erect dark mane with no forelock is a primitive wild-horse trait, matching the dun coat, dorsal stripe, and striped legs seen in ancient cave paintings of horses.

faqs.question: How many Przewalski's horses are left?
faqs.answer: Roughly 2,000 live free-ranging in reintroduced herds in Mongolia and China, with several hundred more in zoos and reserves worldwide — all descended from about a dozen founders.

faqs.question: Can Przewalski's horses breed with domestic horses?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the offspring are fertile despite the different chromosome numbers. Managing that hybridisation is one of the challenges for conservation breeding.

faqs.question: Where can you see Przewalski's horses in the wild?
faqs.answer: Hustai National Park, a short drive from Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, is the most accessible site; reintroduced herds also roam the Gobi's Takhin Tal reserve and Kalamaili in China.

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Semi-desert steppe and grassland of Mongolia and northwest China

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: Around 20 years in the wild; over 30 in captivity

range.nativeRange: Steppe and semi-desert of Mongolia and northwest China, reintroduced to Hustai National Park, the Gobi, and Kalamaili.

animals.name: Goodfellow's Tree-kangaroo
animals.summary: Goodfellow's tree-kangaroo (Dendrolagus goodfellowi) is a striking marsupial of Papua New Guinea's mountain forests — a kangaroo adapted to life in trees, with golden stripes down its back and a long balancing tail. It weighs 6–8.6 kg (13–19 lb), leaps confidently between branches, and is listed Endangered because of hunting and deforestation.

sections.heading: A kangaroo that climbs
sections.body: Tree kangaroos are kangaroos returned to the trees their ancestors left. Goodfellow's has strong forelimbs nearly as long as its hind legs, broad padded feet with curved claws, and a long cylindrical tail used as a counterweight. Its chestnut coat carries two golden stripes down the spine and gold bands on the tail.

sections.heading: Life in the canopy
sections.body: Goodfellow's tree-kangaroo climbs with deliberate, hand-over-hand movements, walks along branches on all fours, and can leap several metres between trees; like other tree kangaroos it can drop from high branches to the ground without injury. It is active in bouts day and night, dozing in forks between feeds.

sections.heading: Diet and digestion
sections.body: The menu is rainforest foliage — leaves of many tree species, plus fruit, flowers, and shoots, including epiphytes such as orchids. A multi-chambered, fermenting fore-stomach, shared with all kangaroos, lets it extract energy from tough leaves that few other canopy mammals can handle.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.body: A single jellybean-sized joey is born after a pregnancy of around six weeks and crawls to the pouch, where it develops for roughly eight months. After emerging, it keeps returning to the pouch to suckle and stays with its mother well into its second year — a slow breeding rate that makes populations vulnerable.

sections.heading: Habitat and range
sections.body: The species lives only in the mountain forests along Papua New Guinea's central cordillera, from roughly 1,000 to 3,000 metres elevation, in dense oak and mossy forest. It is one of about a dozen tree-kangaroo species, nearly all confined to New Guinea.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.body: Goodfellow's tree-kangaroo is listed as Endangered: it is hunted for meat, and its mountain forests are being cleared for gardens and timber. Community-led conservation, such as the tree-kangaroo programmes of the Tenkile Conservation Alliance, works with villages to end hunting, while zoos coordinate breeding as an insurance population.

faqs.question: How do tree kangaroos climb trees?
faqs.answer: With strong, clawed forelimbs and broad gripping soles, moving hind feet independently. The long tail acts purely as a balance — it cannot grip — while the powerful legs allow leaps of several metres between branches.

faqs.question: Why are Goodfellow's tree-kangaroos endangered?
faqs.answer: Hunting for meat has reduced numbers, and forest clearing for subsistence gardens and logging is shrinking and fragmenting their mountain habitat. Slow reproduction makes recovery difficult.

faqs.question: How far can a tree kangaroo jump?
faqs.answer: Between branches they routinely leap several metres, and tree kangaroos as a group are famous for dropping from heights of many metres to the forest floor without injury.

faqs.question: What do Goodfellow's tree-kangaroos eat?
faqs.answer: Mostly leaves from a wide variety of rainforest trees, supplemented with fruit, flowers, and shoots — including epiphytes — all fermented in a kangaroo-style chambered stomach.

faqs.question: Where do Goodfellow's tree-kangaroos live?
faqs.answer: Only in the mountain rainforests of Papua New Guinea's central highlands, at elevations of about 1,000–3,000 metres.

facts.value: An agile climber that leaps metres between branches; slow and awkward on the ground
